context.description: ClickHouse® is a real-time analytics database management system

signals.title: Implement CREATE HANDLER query
signals.text: ## Company or project name ClickHouse ## Use case Creating and managing custom HTTP handlers from SQL without editing configuration files. ## Describe the solution you'd like ### Syntax ``` CREATE [IF NOT EXISTS] HANDLER name [PROTOCOL protocol_name] URL [PREFIX|REGEXP] '/test' [METHODS (GET, POST)] [TYPE query] AS [SELECT|INSERT|...] ... ``` Creates a handler with a specified name. The name is used for managing handlers with SQL queries, diagnostic messages, and ordering handlers. If a protocol name is specified (optional), the handler is active only for the specified protocol, see https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/composable-protocols Otherwise, it is active for all of http/https protocols. URL - mandatory parameter. Can be in the form of URL, URL PREFIX, or URL REGEXP. For exact URLs and prefixes, we should check for ambiguity at creation/alter time and throw an exception if there is ambiguity. For regexp, it's not possible to check for ambiguity. Handlers from the server configuration has the priority above SQL-defined handlers. Then, SQL-defined handlers will be matched in the lexicographical order of their names. There is no other way to specify their priorities in case of ambiguity. The URL is matched without `?` query string and `#` fragment identifier. The list of allowed `METHODS` can be specified. By default, it's only GET. We also support POST, PUT, DELETE, but not arbitrary names. TYPE can be specified, but the only supported type for now is query. It is okay that SQL-defined handlers allow fewer features than configuration-defined. After `AS`, it specifies a SQL query that will be invoked by this handler. The query can be parameterized. The query is parsed for syntactic correctness during handler creation/alter, but not analyzed. For example, the tables referenced by the query can be missed at the time of the handler creation. The FORMAT and similar clauses belong to the query, not the whole CREATE/ALTER statement. The query can be put in parentheses for disambiguation. The handler could support arbitrary queries. The INSERT query should not contain embedded data, it expects that the data will be provided in the HTTP body. ``` DROP [IF EXISTS] HANDLER name ``` Drops the handler with the specified name. ``` ALTER HANDLER name [PROTOCOL protocol_name] URL '/test' [METHODS (GET, POST)] [TYPE query] AS SELECT ... ``` Replaces the handler with the new one. The ALTER query can include only a subset of clauses, e.g., it can be used to only change the URL or the query. ### Storage The handlers are saved in a storage, which can be a local or Keeper storage, similarly to named collections, which is configured in query_rules_storage in the configuration file. ### Access control These queries: CREATE HANDLER, DROP HANDLER, ALTER HANDLER, will require separate grants. Invoking handlers doesn't require any separate grants. But grants are checked as usual during the query invocation. The authentication works in the usual way. For example, a user can provide user/password credentials in the request invoking the handler. There is a popular use-case when handlers are used to encapsulate access to certain queries - when the handler is invokable by one user, but uses a query with tables not accessible directly by this user. For this purpose, you should do it by creating a VIEW with SQL SECURITY DEFINER, and then defining a HANDLER with SELECT from that view. So the handlers are transparent to this logic. Any HTTP URL parameters in the query string, HTTP form variables in POST, and HTTP headers, can be used as usual with handlers - this includes parameters for parameterized queries. Out of scope: defining the default user for the handler. ### Introspection Add new fields to the query_log for the handler name and for the HTTP request URL. Add SQL miscellaneous functions `currentHandler()`, `currentRequestURL()`. These functions can be used to customize the query behavior depending on the invoked handler. ## Describe alternatives you've considered _No response_ ## Additional context Many features will be available automatically. For example, custom HTTP response headers are available through the SETTINGS of the invoked query. URLs with parameters in the paths are supported through the `currentRequestURL()` function. Out of scope: a query to invoke a handlers by its name, so the handlers are accessible in other than http/https protocols.

signals.title: IcebergS3: write_full_path_in_iceberg_metadata writes S3 key path instead of full S3 URI in manifest entries
signals.text: ## Summary When inserting into an IcebergS3 table with `write_full_path_in_iceberg_metadata = 1`, the data file paths written into Avro manifest entries use the S3 key path (e.g., `/my-prefix/my_table/data/data-xxx.parquet`) instead of the full S3 URI (`s3://my-bucket/my-prefix/my_table/data/data-xxx.parquet`). The setting description says "Write full paths (including s3://) into iceberg metadata files" but it only does this for the metadata JSON — not for the manifest entries that reference data files. Per the [Iceberg spec](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/main/format/spec.md), `data_file.file_path` is defined as **"Full URI of a data file with FS scheme"**. A bare `/key` path without scheme is non-compliant. See also [apache/iceberg#13141](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/13141) which confirms only absolute URIs are currently valid. ## ClickHouse Version `25.12.1.1426` (ClickHouse Cloud) ## What happens Manifest entry `data_file.file_path` is written as: ``` /my-prefix/my_table/data/data-xxx.parquet ``` Should be: ``` s3://my-bucket/my-prefix/my_table/data/data-xxx.parquet ``` The metadata JSON (`location`, `manifest-list`, etc.) correctly gets full `s3://` URIs. Only the data file paths inside manifest Avro files are wrong. ## Root Cause In `IcebergMetadata.cpp`, `createInitial()` correctly builds the full URI: ```cpp location_path = configuration_ptr->getTypeName() + "://" + configuration_ptr->getNamespace() + "/" + configuration_ptr->getRawPath().path; ``` But in `IcebergWrites.cpp`, `FileNamesGenerator` is constructed with: ```cpp filename_generator = FileNamesGenerator(persistent_table_components.path_resolver.getTableLocation(), ...); ``` `getTableLocation()` returns the key path without scheme and bucket, so all generated data file paths are missing the `s3://bucket` prefix.

signals.title: Missing sanity check when reading from JSON files
signals.text: ### Company or project name None ### Describe the improvement When reading from a large file in JSONEachRow format, sanity checks are missing. If a file is in fact a single JSON, the parser will keep parsing it until it runs out of memory. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Clickhouse local 26.5.1.882 ### How to reproduce Spin up a machine with sufficiently low memory (8GB) and run: ``` SELECT randomString(7) AS field FROM numbers(1000000000) INTO OUTFILE 'part.json.zstd' TRUNCATE FORMAT JSON SELECT DISTINCT field FROM file('part.json.zstd', 'JSONEachRow') LIMIT 10 ``` **Actual behavior**: The process is killed due to OOM on a 12GB machine. **Expected behavior**: Same as for inserts. ``` CREATE TABLE random_strings ( field String ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO random_strings FROM INFILE 'part.json.zstd' FORMAT JSONEachRow; INSERT INTO random_strings FROM INFILE 'part.json.zstd' FORMAT JSONEachRow Query id: 0b6cf121-c418-46b5-b5ff-af0674242b3d Ok. Received exception: Code: 117. DB::Exception: Size of JSON object at position 104857600 is extremely large. Expected not greater than 10485760 bytes, but current is 104857611 bytes per row. Increase the value setting 'min_chunk_bytes_for_parallel_parsing' or check your data manually, most likely JSON is malformed: (in file/uri /part.json.zstd): While executing ParallelParsingBlockInputFormat: While executing File: data for INSERT was parsed from file. (INCORRECT_DATA) (version 26.5.1.882 (official build)) ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #107669 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1432` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Ensure config under config.d/users.d are read in some deterministic order
signals.text: **Use case** If users are recommended to place custom configuration files under the config.d/ and users.d/ directories, it would be nice to have the ability to have some guarantee for which order those files are parsed in. This would enable one to predictably override settings made in one .xml file under config.d/ by creating an additional one, without editing the original. **Describe the solution you'd like** It probably makes sense to read the configuration files in an alphabetical order or something. Maybe this already takes place under the hood, if so I can't see it documented anywhere. **Describe alternatives you've considered** Can't think of anything good. A secondary conf.d/ directly under .conf.d/? Probably a bad idea.

signals.title: JSONEachRow schema inference fails for valid integer literals above UInt64
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour `JSONEachRow` schema inference fails when an input contains a syntactically valid JSON integer literal larger than `UInt64`. The same value can be parsed successfully when an explicit `Int128`, `UInt128`, `Decimal`, or `String` schema is provided. The failure occurs only when ClickHouse must infer the schema. `input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1` works when ClickHouse has a known `String` destination column: it preserves the unquoted JSON number as its original textual representation. However, it does not prevent the failure during schema inference, where no destination type exists yet. This setting also works as intended with `INSERT`, rather than `DESCRIBE`, since the destination table has a known schema. This prevents applications from discovering the schema of NDJSON containing arbitrary-precision integers before choosing an appropriate target type. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Tested with 26.6.1.1193 ### How to reproduce Schema inference fails: ```sql DESCRIBE TABLE format( 'JSONEachRow', '{"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"}' ); ``` Result: ```text Code: 636. DB::Exception: The table structure cannot be extracted from a JSONEachRow format file. Error: Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected ',' before: '251392,"name":"Matt"}'. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) ``` The setting intended to allow JSON numbers to be read as strings does not change the schema-inference result: ```sql DESCRIBE TABLE format( 'JSONEachRow', '{"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"}' ) SETTINGS input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1; ``` However, parsing succeeds when the structure is known: ```sql DESCRIBE TABLE format( 'JSONEachRow', 'num Int128, name String', '{"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"}' ); ``` It also succeeds for a known `String` target with `input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1` when used during an `INSERT`: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_json_numbers ( num String, name String ) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO test_json_numbers SETTINGS input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1 FORMAT JSONEachRow {"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"} SELECT * FROM test_json_numbers; ``` Result: ```text ┌─num──────────────────────┬─name─┐ │ 2942420318599003496251392 │ Matt │ └──────────────────────────┴──────┘ ``` ### Expected behavior Schema inference should not reject a valid JSON numeric literal solely because it exceeds `UInt64`. Because the same JSON token is accepted for a known `String` destination with `input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1`, schema inference should honor that setting too—for example, infer `String` for this field rather than fail. Alternatively, ClickHouse could infer a wider supported numeric type or document a deliberate inference limit and provide a setting to select a safe fallback type. Example: ``` DESCRIBE TABLE format( 'JSONEachRow', '{"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"}' ) SETTINGS input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1; ``` returns both columns as String ### Error message and/or stacktrace Code: 636. DB::Exception: The table structure cannot be extracted from a JSONEachRow format file. Error: Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected ',' before: '251392,"name":"Matt"}'. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context JSON permits arbitrary-length number literals. Quoting such values is a workaround, but is not always possible for third-party NDJSON sources.
signals.author: dmanchon

signals.title: ORDER BY is not applied globally when reading a Distributed table through a Merge engine: per-shard-sorted streams are concatenated, LIMIT returns wrong rows
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** Reading a `Distributed` table through a `Merge` engine drops the global sort: `SELECT ... ORDER BY x` returns each shard's stream sorted individually and concatenated, not a globally ordered result. With `LIMIT n` this silently returns the wrong rows (the first shard's top-n instead of the global top-n). Querying the same `Distributed` table directly is correct. Aggregations over the `Merge` table (`count`, `max`) are correct — only the sorted path is wrong. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on `26.7.1.408` and near-HEAD master `3090a4fc` (`26.7.1.653`). **How to reproduce** Cluster `two_shards`: two shards on one server with `default_database` `sh0` / `sh1`. ```sql CREATE DATABASE sh0; CREATE DATABASE sh1; CREATE TABLE sh0.t (w Int64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY w; CREATE TABLE sh1.t (w Int64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY w; INSERT INTO sh0.t SELECT number * 3 FROM numbers(100); -- max 297 INSERT INTO sh1.t SELECT number * 3 + 1000 FROM numbers(100); -- max 1297 CREATE TABLE dist_t AS sh0.t ENGINE = Distributed(two_shards, '', t); CREATE TABLE merge_t AS dist_t ENGINE = Merge(currentDatabase(), '^dist_t$'); -- correct: 1297, 1294, 1291 SELECT w FROM dist_t ORDER BY w DESC LIMIT 3 SETTINGS enable_analyzer = 1; -- WRONG: 297, 294, 291 (shard 0's top-3; global maximum 1297 not returned) SELECT w FROM merge_t ORDER BY w DESC LIMIT 3 SETTINGS enable_analyzer = 1; -- also wrong WITHOUT LIMIT: 297, 294, 291, 288, ... (per-shard sorted streams -- concatenated; the result multiset is complete but the order is not global) SELECT w FROM merge_t ORDER BY w DESC SETTINGS enable_analyzer = 1; ``` **Characterization** - `max_threads = 1` (no thread-interleave explanation); deterministic. - Independent of `optimize_read_in_order` and `optimize_skip_unused_shards`. - `count()` / `max()` over `merge_t` are correct (500 rows / global max) — the row set is complete; only the final sort is missing on the `Merge`-over-`Distributed` read path, so any `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` silently returns wrong rows. Found by the optimizer-tester topology differential (`tests/optimizer_tester`, branch `optimizer-tester-framework`) the first run after a `Merge`-over-`Distributed` arm was added; detected by the order-sensitive comparison for total `ORDER BY` queries. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111206
signals.author: zlareb1

signals.title: optimize_aggregation_in_order over a mixed-direction sorting key (a, b DESC) collapses GROUP BY groups — silent wrong result
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** With a mixed-direction sorting key `ORDER BY (a, b DESC)` and `optimize_aggregation_in_order = 1`, a plain `GROUP BY a, b` silently returns one row per `a` instead of one row per distinct `(a, b)` — groups are collapsed and the query succeeds with a wrong result. The same query is correct with the optimization off, and correct on an all-ascending key `ORDER BY (a, b)`. `optimize_read_in_order` over the same table is correct, so this is specific to the aggregation-in-order path. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on masters 26.7.1.1169, 26.7.1.1188 and 26.8.1.102 (`eb577ff401a3`), single part and multi-part alike, with the analyzer on or off. **How to reproduce** ```sql CREATE TABLE md (a UInt32, b UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (a, b DESC); INSERT INTO md SELECT number % 4, number FROM numbers(20); INSERT INTO md SELECT number % 4, number + 7 FROM numbers(20); SELECT count() FROM (SELECT a, b FROM md GROUP BY a, b); -- 40 (correct: 40 distinct (a, b) pairs) SELECT count() FROM (SELECT a, b FROM md GROUP BY a, b) SETTINGS optimize_aggregation_in_order = 1; -- 4 after OPTIMIZE TABLE md FINAL (one row per `a`), 8 on the unmerged two-part layout ``` The surviving rows keep only one `b` per `a`: ```sql SELECT a, b FROM md GROUP BY a, b ORDER BY a, b SETTINGS optimize_aggregation_in_order = 1; -- 0 23 -- 1 24 -- 2 25 -- 3 26 ``` **Expected behavior** `optimize_aggregation_in_order` must either produce the same 40 groups or not apply to a stream whose sort direction does not match the aggregation key order. The `b DESC` key column makes the stream descending in `b` within each `a`, but the in-order aggregation appears to consume it as if it were ascending, so every `(a, b)` group after the first within an `a` run is merged away. Control: with `ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (a, b)` (no `DESC`) the same query returns 40 groups with the optimization on. Found by the optimizer-correctness tester (`opt_toggle`/`truthy`/`forced_plan`/`physical_design` oracles all diverged on the same query over the mixed-direction fixture; reduced by hand — `optimize_aggregation_in_order = 1` is the single culprit setting at otherwise-default settings).
signals.author: zlareb1

signals.title: DataLakeCatalog: DROP then CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS silently ACKs an unusable ghost table (catalog vs object-store existence disagreement)
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong On a `DataLakeCatalog` database (Glue or Iceberg REST catalog), a table's *existence* is decided differently for `CREATE` than for every other operation, and the two systems of record are deliberately left disagreeing by `DROP TABLE`. The result is that `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` **silently returns success for a table that is never registered in the catalog and that no subsequent SQL can query, drop, or create** — a permanent wedge on that table name, on **default settings, with no crash or fault injection**. Two systems of record are consulted: - `CREATE` decides existence by **listing the object store**. `IcebergMetadata::createInitial` lists `metadata/*.metadata.json` under the table location (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/IcebergMetadata.cpp:709-725`). If any `*.metadata.json` is present and `IF NOT EXISTS` was given, it `return`s early (`:719-721`) **without calling `catalog->createTable`** (`:765-770`). Its own comment names the case (`:746-752`): "leftover data after `DROP TABLE` with `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop` off". - Every other operation (`SHOW TABLES`, `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `DROP`) consults the **catalog** (`src/Databases/DataLake/DatabaseDataLake.cpp:488-492`, `:523-524`, `:740`, `:716-726`). `DROP TABLE` removes only the catalog entry and, on default settings, leaves the object-store metadata in place: Glue `DeleteTable` only (`src/Databases/DataLake/GlueCatalog.cpp:655-668`); REST `DELETE ...?purgeRequested=False` (`src/Databases/DataLake/RestCatalog.cpp:1114-1127`); the object-store purge is gated on `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop`, default `false` (`src/Core/Settings.cpp`) — which is the correct, Iceberg-standard behavior. So after a normal `DROP`, the catalog has forgotten the table but `metadata/v1.metadata.json` remains. A later `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` at the same location then finds that leftover `metadata.json`, short-circuits, and never registers the table in the catalog — yet returns success. The table is now a ghost: - it is **absent** from the catalog (`GetTable` / `SHOW TABLES` do not see it); - `SELECT`/`INSERT` fail with `UNKNOWN_TABLE`; - `DROP TABLE` fails with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` "Cannot drop table ... because it does not exist" (`DatabaseDataLake.cpp:721-725`) — there is **no SQL path to clean it up**; - a plain re-`CREATE` (without `IF NOT EXISTS`) throws `TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS` "Iceberg table with path ... already exists" (`IcebergMetadata.cpp:722-724`) — while the catalog simultaneously insists the table does not exist. Only manual object-store surgery (deleting the leftover `metadata/` files) or an external catalog registration can unwedge the name. There is also an **ambiguous-create** variant of the same defect: if the create fails *between* the object-store metadata write (`IcebergMetadata.cpp:746`) and the catalog `createTable` call (`:770`) — e.g. a dropped/timed-out Glue `CreateTable`, or a server crash in that window — the object-store metadata is durable but the catalog was never updated, so the create-commit protocol is **not idempotent**: every retry hits exactly the wedge above and can never repair the catalog. (This variant is source-derived; the deterministic `DROP` → `CREATE IF NOT EXISTS` variant below is empirically confirmed.) ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — empirically reproduced on `master` (26.8.1.119), 3/3 with a positive control, using the AWS Glue catalog backed by a mock (`moto`) + MinIO. The REST-catalog path is source-identical (`RestCatalog::dropTable` uses `purgeRequested=False`, and the same `createInitial` existence-by-listing path is used for all catalog types). ### How to reproduce `DataLakeCatalog` (Glue or REST) is a BETA feature (`allow_database_iceberg` / `allow_database_glue_catalog`, `src/Core/Settings.cpp:7320/7330`). ```sql SET allow_experimental_database_glue_catalog = 1; CREATE DATABASE glue_db ENGINE = DataLakeCatalog('<glue-endpoint>') SETTINGS catalog_type = 'glue', region = 'us-east-1', aws_access_key_id = '...', aws_secret_access_key = '...', storage_endpoint = 'http://<minio>/warehouse'; -- 1. create + register CREATE TABLE glue_db.`ns.t1` (x Int32) ENGINE = IcebergS3('http://<minio>/warehouse/t1/', '<key>', '<secret>'); -- 2. drop: catalog entry removed, warehouse/t1/metadata/v1.metadata.json REMAINS -- (iceberg_delete_data_on_drop is off by default — correct Iceberg behavior) DROP TABLE glue_db.`ns.t1`; -- 3. re-create IF NOT EXISTS: returns OK, but registers NOTHING in the catalog CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS glue_db.`ns.t1` (x Int32) ENGINE = IcebergS3('http://<minio>/warehouse/t1/', '<key>', '<secret>'); -- <-- false ACK -- 4. the table is now a ghost: SELECT count() FROM glue_db.`ns.t1`; -- UNKNOWN_TABLE DROP TABLE glue_db.`ns.t1`; -- BAD_ARGUMENTS "... does not exist" (cannot clean up) CREATE TABLE glue_db.`ns.t1` (x Int32) ENGINE = IcebergS3('http://<minio>/warehouse/t1/', '<key>', '<secret>'); -- TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS ``` Positive control (proves the leftover object-store metadata is the cause): run the identical sequence, but between steps 2 and 3 delete the leftover `warehouse/t1/metadata/*` objects. Step 3 then registers the table normally and `SELECT count()` returns `0` — no wedge. A self-contained rig (MinIO + `moto` Glue mock + ClickHouse) is `tests/clickfawkes/glue_catalog_commit_durability.py recreate_wedge`. ### Expected behavior For a `DataLakeCatalog` database, `CREATE`'s existence check should agree with the system of record used by every other operation — the catalog — rather than the object store. Concretely, one of: - `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` should register the table in the catalog when it is absent there (adopting the leftover metadata), so the acknowledged table is actually usable; or - if the leftover object-store metadata genuinely blocks creation, `CREATE`/`CREATE IF NOT EXISTS` should fail **loudly and consistently with the catalog view** (and there must remain some SQL path to `DROP` the name), rather than silently acknowledging a table that cannot be queried, dropped, or created. Either way, `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` must not return success for a table that is invisible to the catalog and unrecoverable by SQL. ### Error message and/or stacktrace From the wedged (ghost) table, on `master` 26.8.1.119: ``` -- step 3 (CREATE IF NOT EXISTS): returns OK (exit 0), no output -- the false ACK -- step 4: Code: 60. DB::Exception: Unknown table expression identifier 'glue_db.ns.t1' ... (UNKNOWN_TABLE) Code: 60. DB::Exception: Table glue_db.`ns.t1` does not exist. (UNKNOWN_TABLE) -- DROP Code: 57. DB::Exception: Iceberg table with path t1/ already exists. (TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS) -- plain CREATE ``` ### Additional context - Distinct from #108524 / PR #109071: those are the **plain `Iceberg()` table engine** (no catalog) with `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop = 1` (opt-in) failing to delete files, so a re-create fails **loudly** with `TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS`. This report is a **`DataLakeCatalog` database** on **default settings** (delete-flag off, which is the intended Iceberg behavior), where the novel and more severe symptoms are the **silent false ACK** from `IF NOT EXISTS` and the **permanent catalog-vs-object-store desync** with no SQL cleanup path. PR #109071's fix (delete files when the opt-in flag is on) does not touch this: the default path deliberately keeps metadata. - Distinct from #112102 (Glue `updateMetadata` has no CAS) and #112081 (Iceberg `metadata.json` PUT cleanup) — this is the `CREATE`/`DROP` registration protocol, not the write/update commit. - Found by the ClickFawkes durability framework (commit-protocol axis: existence judged against a different system of record than the one used for mutation, so a `DROP` that intentionally desyncs them leaves a create that can never converge).
signals.author: zlareb1

signals.title: A failed BACKUP finalize deletes a backup that already completed, making any incremental chained onto it unrestorable
signals.text:
### Company or project name ClickHouse (ClickFawkes crash-durability testing) ### Describe what's wrong `BackupImpl::finalizeWriting` publishes the backup and only *then* arms the guard that protects it, so an error in the four lines in between deletes a backup that is already complete and externally usable — and takes any incremental chained onto it down with it.
The window (src/Backups/BackupImpl.cpp:1300-1315) ```cpp writeBackupMetadata(); // :1307 `.backup` lands. The backup is complete // and is now a valid `base_backup` target. closeArchive(/*finalize=*/ true); // :1308 setCompressedSize(); // :1309 removeLockFile(); // :1310 a live object-store DELETE LOG_TRACE(log, "Finalized backup {}", backup_name_for_logging); ... writing_finalized = true; // :1314 the guard arms HERE ``` The guard is `setIsCorrupted`, which refuses to mark a finalized backup corrupt and says why in its own log line (`:1339-1343`): ```cpp if (writing_finalized) { LOG_WARNING(log, "An error happened after the backup was completed successfully, the backup must be correct!"); return false; } ``` That is exactly the right intent. It is just armed one step too late to cover the interval in which the backup is already published. `removeLockFile` (`:851-855`) is `checkLockFile(false)` followed by `writer->removeFile(lock_file_name)` — a single object-store DELETE. When it fails: 1. `BackupStarter::onException` (`src/Backups/BackupsWorker.cpp:524`) calls `setIsCorrupted()`, which **succeeds** because `writing_finalized` is still false; 2. `should_remove_files_in_backup` is true — `remove_backup_files_after_failure` defaults to **true** (`BackupsWorker.cpp:340`); 3. `tryRemoveAllFiles` (`BackupImpl.cpp:1363`) builds `files_to_remove` with `".backup"` **first** (`:1385`) plus every data file, and its one bail-out — `if (!checkLockFile(false)) return false;` (`:1395`) — does not fire, because the lock file is still present precisely because deleting it is what failed.
The client is told the `BACKUP` failed, which is why this is easy to miss: it looks like ordinary cleanup of a failed backup. It is not. The backup had already completed, and between `writeBackupMetadata` and the deletion any concurrent `BACKUP ... SETTINGS base_backup = ` succeeds and is acked `BACKUP_CREATED`. An incremental holds none of its base's bytes — only a locator, a UUID and per-file `(base_size, base_checksum)` pairs (`BackupImpl.cpp:485-486`, `:522-530`). Nothing validates the base until a `RESTORE` reaches a file with `base_size != 0` (`BackupImpl.cpp:1037`), by which point the restore has already created databases and tables. So the incremental reports success, is unrestorable from the moment the base is deleted, and only says so partway through a recovery. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce ClickHouse 26.8.1 (`clickhouse-master-now`), single node, MinIO, default settings other than the retry bound noted below. Put a proxy between ClickHouse and the object store that fails `DELETE ///.lock` persistently (a one-shot failure is not enough — the AWS SDK retries it into a success), then: ```sql CREATE TABLE bfs_src (id UInt64, v UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO bfs_src SELECT number, number * 7 FROM numbers(200); -- The `.lock` DELETE for this destination is failed by the proxy. BACKUP TABLE bfs_src TO S3('http://.../bug_bk/', 'minio', 'minioadmin') SETTINGS backup_restore_s3_retry_attempts = 2; -- -> reports failure; `.backup` was written, then deleted along with every data file ``` For the chain, start the base backup, wait until its `.backup` object exists, and only then take the incremental: ```sql BACKUP TABLE bfs_src TO S3('http://.../chain_inc/', 'minio', 'minioadmin') SETTINGS base_backup = S3('http://.../chain_base/', 'minio', 'minioadmin'), backup_restore_s3_retry_attempts = 2; -- -> Backup ... was created successfully RESTORE TABLE bfs_src AS bfs_chain_restored FROM S3('http://.../chain_inc/', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); -- -> Code: 599. DB::Exception: Backup ... not found ``` `backup_restore_s3_retry_attempts` is lowered only to bound the reproduction: it defaults to 1000, so a brief transient blip will be retried away and will not reach this window. The reachable case is an outage that outlasts the retries — expired credentials, a bucket-policy change, or a partition lasting minutes. The retry count changes how long the endpoint has to stay broken, not what happens once the retries are exhausted. Reproduced 3/3 with an automated rig (`tests/clickfawkes`, `--mode backup-finalize-selfdestruct`) that is positive-control gated: | arm | fault | `.backup` published | `.backup` survives | |---|---|---|---| | `control_clean` | none | yes | yes — base + incremental + restore of 200 rows all succeed | | `control_early` | a data-file `PUT` fails, i.e. before `.backup` is written | no | no — cleanup here is correct, and proves the injector really can destroy a backup | | `bug` | the `.lock` `DELETE` fails, i.e. after `.backup` is written | **yes** | **no** | | `chain_victim` | same, with an incremental taken inside the window | yes | no — the incremental is acked `BACKUP_CREATED`, then `RESTORE` fails with `Code: 599` | The `control_early` arm is what makes the `bug` arm meaningful: the same injector, one step earlier in the same sequence, produces the intended behaviour. ### Expected behavior Once `.backup` has been written the backup is complete, and a later error must not delete it — the same rule `setIsCorrupted` already enforces for errors after `writing_finalized`. A failure in `closeArchive`/`setCompressedSize`/`removeLockFile` should leave the backup in place (a leftover `.lock` object is a much smaller problem than a destroyed backup) and, ideally, still report the failure to the client. Setting `writing_finalized = true` immediately after `writeBackupMetadata()`, or having `tryRemoveAllFiles` refuse once `.backup` exists, would both close it. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 599. DB::Exception: Received from 127.0.0.1:19141. DB::Exception: Backup S3('http://127.0.0.1:19113/clickfawkes/chain_inc/', 'minio', '[HIDDEN]') not found ``` raised from the `RESTORE` of an incremental that had reported `BACKUP_CREATED`. ### Additional context Found by ClickFawkes' commit-protocol audit (the `backup_to_s3_finalize` protocol, `ambiguous_cleanup` lens). Distinct from #46211, which is a leaked coordination znode after a failed backup rather than destruction of a completed one.
signals.author: zlareb1

signals.title: BACKUP to S3: concurrent backups to the same destination can both be acked BACKUP_CREATED, one unrestorable (.lock claimed by check-then-create, no conditional write)
signals.text:
### Company or project name ClickHouse QA — durability testing (ClickFawkes crash/commit-protocol campaign) ### Describe what's wrong `BACKUP ... TO S3(...)` protects a destination against concurrent writers with an existence-check-then-create sequence on the `.lock` object, not with a conditional write. When one backup's `.lock` `PUT` is slower than a competing backup's entire runtime, **both backups are acked `BACKUP_CREATED`** against the same destination prefix. Only one `.backup` metadata object survives, so the loser's data objects are physically present but unreferenced, and restoring it fails with `BACKUP_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND`. The user-visible defect is the ack: a `BACKUP` that returns `BACKUP_CREATED` is unrestorable. An operator who backs up on a schedule and checks the query result has no signal that the backup does not exist. Verified empirically, 5/5, with a control (details below). Default configuration — `backups.allow_concurrent_backups` defaults to `true` (`BackupsWorker.cpp:337`).
Code walk (upstream/master @ 1e31a058a12) `BackupImpl::checkBackupDoesntExist` — the claim is a plain existence check: ```cpp /// Check that no other backup (excluding internal backups) is writing to the same destination. if (!params.is_internal_backup) { chassert(!lock_file_name.empty()); if (writer->fileExists(lock_file_name)) throw Exception(ErrorCodes::BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS, "Backup {} is being written already", backup_name_for_logging); } ``` `BackupImpl::createLockFile` — the create is an unconditional overwrite: ```cpp void BackupImpl::createLockFile() { /// Internal backup must not create the lock file (it should be created by the initiator). chassert(!params.is_internal_backup); chassert(uuid); auto out = writer->writeFile(lock_file_name); writeUUIDText(*uuid, *out); out->finalize(); } ``` Between the check and the create there is no atomicity. `checkLockFile` (called at `:257`, `:433`, `:1233`) re-reads the object and compares contents to the backup's own UUID, which closes the *fast* race — the last writer wins and the earlier writer notices at its next check. It does not close the case where the losing racer's `PUT` lands late: by then the other backup has already read back its own UUID, finished, and returned `BACKUP_CREATED`. A conditional write would close it outright, and the mechanism already exists in the codebase but is not wired to the backup writer: - `WriteBufferFromS3.cpp:643-644` sets `SetIfNoneMatch` from `write_settings.object_storage_write_if_none_match`. - `git grep -c -E "if_none_match|SetIfNoneMatch" -- src/Backups/` → **0**. - The only writer of `object_storage_write_if_none_match` anywhere is Iceberg (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/Utils.cpp`); `getWriteSettingsForBackup` (`BackupsWorker.cpp`) never sets it. So the `.lock` `PUT` on the BACKUP path is always unconditional, last-writer-wins.
### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Server 26.8.1.270 (also confirmed on 26.8.1.119), default config plus a `backups` allowed path; MinIO as the S3 endpoint. Two tables so the two backups are distinguishable: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; CREATE TABLE t2 (a UInt64, s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(10000000); INSERT INTO t2 SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(1000); ``` Run two backups to the **same** destination prefix, where the first one's `.lock` `PUT` is stalled longer than the second one's whole runtime. I did this with a byte-transparent TCP relay in front of MinIO that sleeps before forwarding the first `PUT .../.lock` (a raw byte relay, so the SigV4 `Host` header the client signed passes through and MinIO accepts the signature). Backup A goes through the relay, backup B straight at MinIO; both URIs resolve to the same bucket and prefix: ```sql -- A (through the relay on :29923, .lock PUT stalled 3 s) BACKUP TABLE t TO S3('http://127.0.0.1:29923/bkt1/dest', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); -- B (direct to MinIO on :29910, started ~150 ms later) BACKUP TABLE t2 TO S3('http://127.0.0.1:29910/bkt1/dest', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); ``` Both return `BACKUP_CREATED`. Then: ```sql RESTORE TABLE t FROM S3('http://127.0.0.1:29910/bkt1/dest', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); -- RESTORED, 10000000 rows RESTORE TABLE t2 FROM S3('http://127.0.0.1:29910/bkt1/dest', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); -- fails, see below ``` A stall is the mechanism I used to make the window deterministic; in a real deployment the same window opens whenever the `.lock` `PUT` is slow relative to a competing backup — one S3 `SlowDown` retry on that `PUT`, or a small/fast backup racing a slow one. The requirement is only *stall > other backup's runtime + start skew*. **Results, 5/5 with a control.** Both backups acked `BACKUP_CREATED` in all 5 attempts (A `dt ≈ 3.15 s`, B `dt ≈ 0.25 s`), 144 objects under the shared prefix, exactly **one** `.backup` (A's). `RESTORE t` → `RESTORED`, `rows = 10000000`. `RESTORE t2` → `BACKUP_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND`. The negative control is the identical two-endpoint topology and the identical 150 ms stagger with the stall set to **0.0 s**: 5/5 `ONE_CREATED`, with B correctly rejected — `Code: 598 ... A concurrent backup writing to the same destination ... (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS)`. So the topology is not the confound; the stall is causal. Threshold sweep (stall duration → outcome): 0.05 / 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 s → one created; **0.5 / 1.0 / 3.0 s → both created**. ### Expected behavior At most one of two concurrent `BACKUP`s to the same destination is acked `BACKUP_CREATED`; the other fails with `BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS`. A `BACKUP` acked `BACKUP_CREATED` is restorable. ### Error message and/or stacktrace The second backup is acked, and its restore then fails: ``` Code: 605. DB::Exception: Table default.t2 not found in backup. (BACKUP_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND) (version 26.8.1.270 (official build)) ``` The control arm (no stall), where the behaviour is correct: ``` Code: 598. DB::Exception: A concurrent backup writing to the same destination S3(...) detected. (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS) ``` ### Additional context **Suggested fix (not verified — this is a prediction):** claim `.lock` with a conditional write by setting `write_settings.object_storage_write_if_none_match = "*"` for the `createLockFile` write, so the create fails when the object already exists instead of overwriting it. The plumbing is already there (`WriteBufferFromS3.cpp:643-644`, and the Azure buffers have the equivalent), it is simply never set on the backup path. Backends that cannot express a conditional write would need to keep the current best-effort behaviour, which is the `cas_downgrade` shape. Even when the loser *is* correctly rejected, both racers pass the existence check and write data objects into the shared prefix before one is caught at finalize (`system.backups` showed the loser reaching `num_files: 281` before failing). Its `tryRemoveAllFiles` then correctly bails at the `checkLockFile(false)` guard, so it destroys nothing — but it leaves up to ~92 orphan objects in the winner's prefix. That is a leak, not data loss, and is secondary to the ack defect above. **Test coverage gap:** the only test referencing `BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS` is `tests/integration/test_backup_restore_on_cluster/test_disallow_concurrency.py`, which runs with `configs/disallow_concurrency.xml`. The **default-config** same-destination race is untested. **One-step falsification:** run the two backups above with the stall at 0.0 s. If the second is still acked `BACKUP_CREATED`, my control was invalid and the topology (not the stall) is the cause. It was rejected with `Code: 598` in 5/5 control attempts.

signals.title: Row policy on the shard-local table is bypassed with `serialize_query_plan = 1` on a non-local replica
signals.text: 🕵 **Describe the bug** With `serialize_query_plan = 1`, a read shipped to a non-local replica of a `Distributed` table bypasses the row policy defined on the shard-local table: the receiving server deserializes an already-built read plan, so it never applies its own row policies. With `serialize_query_plan = 0` (text shipping) the same query is filtered correctly. This matters because defining the policy on the underlying local table is the documented way to filter reads that go through a `Distributed` table (`docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/row-policy.md`), so the workaround silently returns unfiltered rows in this mode. **How to reproduce** Version: 26.8.1.1 (reproduced on `master`, commit `bde560d7b00`). Server config: a cluster `self` with one replica pointing back at the server itself, and `<process_query_plan_packet>1</process_query_plan_packet>`. ```sql CREATE TABLE rp_leaf (x UInt32, y UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO rp_leaf SELECT number, number FROM numbers(10); CREATE TABLE rp_dist AS rp_leaf ENGINE = Distributed('self', currentDatabase(), rp_leaf); CREATE ROW POLICY rp_l ON rp_leaf FOR SELECT USING y < 5 TO CURRENT_USER; SELECT count() FROM rp_dist SETTINGS prefer_localhost_replica = 0, serialize_query_plan = 0; -- 5, correct SELECT count() FROM rp_dist SETTINGS prefer_localhost_replica = 0, serialize_query_plan = 1; -- 10, policy skipped SELECT count() FROM rp_leaf; -- 5, correct ``` **Expected behavior** Both remote reads return `5`. Either the shipped plan carries the filter, or the receiving server re-applies its local row policies to the deserialized plan, or plan shipping is refused when the shard-local table has a row policy that applies (fail close). **Additional context** Two stateless tests already pin `serialize_query_plan = 0` for exactly this reason: - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04498_row_policy_role_scope_interserver.sh` - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04652_nested_merge_prewhere_type_mismatch.sql` (added by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112326) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112326
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Inconsistent AST formatting: `BACKUP ... SETTINGS <name> = DEFAULT` cannot be parsed back
signals.text: 🕵 **Describe what's wrong** `BACKUP` / `RESTORE` accept `SETTINGS <name> = DEFAULT`, but only when it is the *first* item of the `SETTINGS` list. The formatter then reorders the list so that `<name> = DEFAULT` becomes the *last* item, and the printed query can no longer be parsed back. On a build with the formatting-consistency check enabled (`BuzzHouse`, fuzzers) this raises the logical error `Inconsistent AST formatting`. The reason is that `ParserBackupQuery::parseSettings` uses `ParserSetQuery::parseNameValuePair`, which does not understand `= DEFAULT`. When the *first* item is `<name> = DEFAULT`, the whole `ParserBackupQuery::parseSettings` fails, `pos` is restored, and the trailing `SETTINGS` clause is instead parsed by `ParserQueryWithOutput` via `ParserSetQuery(true)` — which does understand `= DEFAULT` and stores the name in `ASTSetQuery::default_settings`, printed *after* all the regular changes. Re-parsing that output now succeeds for the first setting inside `ParserBackupQuery::parseSettings` and then chokes on `, <name> = DEFAULT`. **How to reproduce** Pure formatter, no table or disk needed (`clickhouse local`): ```sql -- `DEFAULT` last: cannot be parsed at all SELECT formatQuerySingleLine($$BACKUP TABLE t TO Disk('d', 'b') SETTINGS max_final_threads = 14, foo = DEFAULT$$); -- Code: 62. DB::Exception: Syntax error: failed at position 79 (end of query) ... (SYNTAX_ERROR) -- `DEFAULT` first: parses, but is reordered to the end, so the output is not re-parseable SELECT formatQuerySingleLine($$BACKUP TABLE t TO Disk('d', 'b') SETTINGS foo = DEFAULT, max_final_threads = 14$$); -- BACKUP TABLE t TO Disk('d', 'b') SETTINGS max_final_threads = 14, foo = DEFAULT ``` Feeding the second output back in reproduces the first error, which is exactly the `Inconsistent AST formatting` round-trip failure. **Where it was seen in CI** `BuzzHouse (amd_debug)`, STID `1941-1bfa`, on an unrelated pull request: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=96886&sha=357db6092241ff3db624aeb778ec4b830f9b74a6&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_debug%29 The fuzzer-generated query was: ```sql BACKUP FROM SNAPSHOT File('/var/lib/clickhouse/user_files/backup22.zip') TO Disk('local_disk', 'backup91') SETTINGS ..., iceberg_snapshot_id = DEFAULT, iceberg_timestamp_ms = DEFAULT ``` Note that this is not specific to the `iceberg_*` settings — any setting name behaves the same way, and `RESTORE` is affected too. **Expected behavior** Either `ParserBackupQuery::parseSettings` should accept `<name> = DEFAULT` in any position (note that `ASTSetQuery::default_settings` currently holds a single name, so several `= DEFAULT` items in one clause need a decision too), or `BACKUP`/`RESTORE` should reject `= DEFAULT` outright. In both cases the format/parse round-trip must be stable. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110223 (a different manifestation of the same `Inconsistent AST formatting` class)
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'` clamps to the whole second, not to the maximum representable value
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong With `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'`, an out-of-range value is clamped to the whole second and the sub-second component is discarded. The result is therefore below the maximum representable value of the target type, at every scale. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce `253402300800` is `10000-01-01` UTC, out of range at every scale. The check does not assume where the boundary sits — it adds 999999 µs to the saturated value and shows the result is still representable and strictly greater, proving the saturated value was not maximal. Run on `26.2.19.43`, `26.7.1.1315` (latest stable) and master `26.8.1.287`: ```sql SELECT toDateTime64(253402300800, 6) AS saturated, saturated + toIntervalMicrosecond(999999) AS still_representable, still_representable > saturated AS saturation_was_not_maximal SETTINGS date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'; -- 26.7.1.1315 and master 26.8.1.287: -- 9999-12-31 23:59:59.000000 | 9999-12-31 23:59:59.999999 | 1 -- 26.2.19.43 (narrower DateTime64 range, same defect): -- 2299-12-31 23:59:59.000000 | 2299-12-31 23:59:59.999999 | 1 ``` The same shortfall appears at every scale — on `26.7.1.1315` and master `26.8.1.287`: ```sql SELECT toDateTime64(253402300800, 6) SETTINGS date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'; -- 9999-12-31 23:59:59.000000 expected 9999-12-31 23:59:59.999999 SELECT toDateTime64(253402300800, 8) SETTINGS date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'; -- 4892-10-07 21:52:48.00000000 expected 4892-10-07 21:52:48.54775807 SELECT toDateTime64(253402300800, 9) SETTINGS date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'; -- 2262-04-11 23:47:16.000000000 expected 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807 ``` ### Expected behavior `saturate` should clamp to the maximum representable value of the target type, including its sub-second component — the values given in the comments above. ### Error message and/or stacktrace No exception is raised — the returned value is simply below the type maximum. ### Additional context The maxima differ by scale for two different reasons: at scale 6 the bound is the supported date range (`9999-12-31 23:59:59.999999`), while at scales 8 and 9 it is the `Int64` tick range (`9223372036854775807` ticks, i.e. `4892-10-07 21:52:48.54775807` and `2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807`). In all three cases the clamp discards the fractional part rather than clamping to the true maximum tick. Underflow clamps to the true minimum correctly (`toDateTime64(-62167219201, 6)`, checked on `26.2.19.43` and master `26.8.1.287`), so the defect is specific to the **upper** bound. A note for anyone re-testing at scale ≤ 7: #107907 widened `DateTime64` to `[0000-01-01, 9999-12-31]`, so a literal such as `'9999-12-31 22:59:59'` is now *in range* and is returned exactly, and no longer exercises the saturate path. An out-of-range value also cannot be written as a `String` at that scale, because a 5-digit year fails at the parser first (`Code: 41 ... unexpected number of decimal digits: 5`) — hence the numeric literal above. Related: #100471, #101131 (the same setting ignored for numeric sources — a different defect), #111524.
signals.author: samay-sharma

signals.title: Aggregating over `x IN (subquery using shardNum())` from `remote()`/`Distributed` fails: 10 NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK — initiator and shard disagree on the `__set_` id
signals.text: ## Describe the problem When a query over `remote()` or a `Distributed` table (2+ shards) aggregates over an `IN (subquery)` whose subquery uses a shard-dependent function such as `shardNum` or `hostName`, the query fails with exception 10 (`NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`) at pure default settings. The initiator expects a column named with the `__set_` id from its own analysis, while each shard returns a column named with the `__set_` id from its own analysis of the shipped query — the shard folds `shardNum()` to its local constant, so the set hash (and hence the column name) differs — and `RemoteQueryExecutor` fails to match the block by name: ``` Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column sum(in(__table3.number, __set_4038495261199527788_15042459581097328311)) in block. There are only columns: sum(in(__table3.number, __set_16854109006789820482_7702020288925574204)): While executing Remote. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` The semantically equivalent plain-`WHERE` form (`WHERE x IN (...)`) works and returns the expected per-shard-set result, so this is purely a naming/header mismatch on the projection path, not a semantics question about `shardNum` in a distributed subquery. ## How to reproduce Version: `26.8.1.653` (public master build). All settings at defaults; no DDL needed: ```sql SELECT sum(number IN (SELECT number FROM numbers(10) WHERE number = shardNum())) FROM remote('127.0.0.{1,2}', numbers(10)); ``` Observed (deterministic, 20/20 runs): ``` Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column sum(in(__table3.number, __set_4038495261199527788_15042459581097328311)) in block. There are only columns: sum(in(__table3.number, __set_16854109006789820482_7702020288925574204)): While executing Remote. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` Expected: `2` (each of the two shards contributes one matching row; both the pre-analyzer path `enable_analyzer = 0` and the plan-shipping path `serialize_query_plan = 1` return `2`). The equivalent filter form works at defaults and returns the correct result: ```sql SELECT count() FROM remote('127.0.0.{1,2}', numbers(10)) WHERE number IN (SELECT number FROM numbers(10) WHERE number = shardNum()); -- 2 ``` A plain `Distributed` table triggers it identically (no `remote()` needed): ```sql CREATE TABLE t_local (x UInt64) ENGINE=MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO t_local SELECT number FROM numbers(100); -- any 2-shard cluster works the same CREATE TABLE dist_n (x UInt64) ENGINE=Distributed(test_cluster_two_shards, currentDatabase(), t_local); -- any 2-shard cluster SELECT sum(x IN (SELECT number FROM numbers(10) WHERE number = shardNum())) FROM dist_n; -- Code: 10, same two mismatched __set_ ids ``` What is REQUIRED vs incidental: - REQUIRED: default settings only — nothing needs to be changed. - REQUIRED (query shape): 2 or more shards (a single remote shard works); a shard-dependent function inside the `IN` subquery — `shardNum()` and `hostName()` both trigger it, while a constant subquery, `rand()`, and `currentDatabase()` do not; the `IN` must be evaluated in the shard-side projection (an aggregate such as `sum`/`countIf`, or the bare expression in `SELECT`) — the same `IN` in `WHERE` is fine. - Incidental: the aggregate wrapper (`sum`, `countIf`, `ifNull(sum(...))`, `toUInt64(... != 0)` all fail the same way), row counts, whether the initiator's own shard participates (`prefer_localhost_replica = 0` and a pure-remote shard list fail identically). - Not failing on: `enable_analyzer = 0`, or `serialize_query_plan = 1` (plan shipping instead of SQL-text shipping). Note the mismatched `__set_` id in "There are only columns" also changes with which shard the offending block came from, consistent with each shard hashing the subquery after folding `shardNum()` to its own value: `remote('127.0.0.{1,2}')` and `remote('127.0.0.{1..3}')` report `__set_16854...`, `remote('127.0.0.{2,3}')` reports `__set_11166...`, while the expected id `__set_40384...` is always the initiator's. ## Additional context The bare-projection form without aggregation (`SELECT number IN (...) FROM remote(...) LIMIT 1`) fails only sporadically (a race — roughly 4 out of 5 runs with `LIMIT 1`, never without `LIMIT`), while the aggregate form is deterministic, so the aggregate form above is the reliable repro. Nearest prior reports, both closed and mechanically different: `shardNum` folding breaking the outer projection name (no sets involved), and a set-identity mismatch specific to shipped `INTERPOLATE` expression packages: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/80691 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111728

The setting `allow_feature_tier` should be adjusted accordingly. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #113581 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1490` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Inconsistent AST formatting: `view((SELECT ...))` in table-function arguments loses subquery parentheses and cannot be parsed back (STID: 1941-1bfa)
signals.text: 🕵 Found by `AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted, old_compatibility)` on an unrelated PR (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/91993, which only touches hex encoding): [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=91993&sha=eae3a3cbbfb5d81bed061634d53c701167dce04a&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29). The fuzzer produced a query containing `view((SELECT ...))` as an argument of a comparison function nested inside `file(...)` table-function arguments. Formatting the AST drops the parentheses around the `view` subquery argument (`view((SELECT ...))` → `view(SELECT ...)`), and the formatted text cannot be parsed back, so the format-consistency check fails with a logical error (`abortOnFailedAssertion` in the debug build): ``` Logical error: 'Inconsistent AST formatting: the query: DESCRIBE TABLE file(concat(xor(if(indexHint(and(greaterOrEquals(alias5764._time, toLowCardinality(toNullable(1048575)) + number), lessOrEquals(alias5764._time, view((SELECT toUInt16OrDefault(65536, equals(minus(materialize(NULL, arrayElement(b)), greater(lowCardinalityIndices('\\\\', toLowCardinality(NULL)), -1)), toInt8OrZero(2147483646)))))))), a <= toInt256OrDefault(-2147483647), materialize(isNullable(NULL))), and(b >= 257, 1.1754943508222875e-38 > b)), currentDatabase(), toFixedString(toNullable('_04513.orc'), assumeNotNull(256)))) SAMPLE 100 / 5 SETTINGS input_format_orc_use_fast_decoder = 0 cannot parse query back from DESCRIBE TABLE file(concat(xor(if(indexHint(and(greaterOrEquals(alias5764._time, toLowCardinality(toNullable(1048575)) + number), lessOrEquals(alias5764._time, view(SELECT toUInt16OrDefault(65536, equals(minus(materialize(NULL, arrayElement(b)), greater(lowCardinalityIndices('\\\\', toLowCardinality(NULL)), -1)), toInt8OrZero(2147483646))))))), a <= toInt256OrDefault(-2147483647), materialize(isNullable(NULL))), and(b >= 257, 1.1754943508222875e-38 > b)), currentDatabase(), toFixedString(toNullable('_04513.orc'), assumeNotNull(256)))) SAMPLE 100 / 5 SETTINGS input_format_orc_use_fast_decoder = 0'. ``` The two texts differ only in the parentheses around the `view` subquery: the original has `view((SELECT ...))`, the re-formatted text has `view(SELECT ...)`. On a recent master-based **release** build (`clickhouse local`) the asymmetry is observable in the opposite direction — the parenthesized form is the one that does not parse inside table-function arguments: ```sql -- parses fine (special `view` handling in expression context): SELECT lessOrEquals(t, view((SELECT 1))); -- parses fine (unparenthesized subquery): SELECT * FROM file(if(indexHint(lessOrEquals(t, view(SELECT 1))), 'a', 'b')); -- SYNTAX_ERROR (parenthesized subquery inside table-function arguments): SELECT * FROM file(if(indexHint(lessOrEquals(t, view((SELECT 1)))), 'a', 'b')); ``` So whether `view((SELECT ...))` / `view(SELECT ...)` parses depends on context (plain expression vs. table-function argument) and on build/compatibility configuration, while the formatter always emits the unparenthesized form. Either the parser should accept both forms in all contexts where `view` is accepted at all, or the formatter should print the form that is guaranteed to parse back in the surrounding context. Previous distinct manifestations of this dedup bucket (STID: 1941-1bfa) were fixed individually: #109501 (back-quoted numeric type name, fixed by #109720), #106850, #106358, #100131. This `view` parenthesization case is a new one. CIDB shows this check failing on 5 unrelated PRs in the last 30 days (112921, 110886, 113533, 91993, 111061) and never on master — expected, since the AST fuzzer only runs per-PR with random queries. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114658 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1436` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: `BigQueryClient::requestJSON` builds HTTP headers from user-controlled arguments without `HTTPHeaderFilter`, so `billing_project`/`access_token` can inject headers and smuggle a second request
signals.text:
_Found via ClickGap automated review. Please close or comment if this is incorrect or needs adjustment._ ### Describe what's wrong A line break inside the `billing_project` or `access_token` argument of `bigquery(...)` / `ENGINE = BigQuery(...)` is copied verbatim into the outgoing HTTP request, adding attacker-chosen headers and - with a blank line - a complete second HTTP request that the endpoint executes with the same credentials. The identical value is rejected by the `url` table function with `HTTP header "X" has invalid character` (BAD_ARGUMENTS). **Root cause:** src/Storages/BigQuery/BigQueryClient.cpp:218 and :220 add user-controlled header values without routing them through `HTTPHeaderFilter::checkAndNormalizeHeaders`, which src/Common/HTTPHeaderFilter.cpp:24 uses to reject any name or value containing '
' and to enforce the admin `<http_forbid_headers>` list. **Why we believe this is a bug:** `BigQueryConfiguration::fromArguments` (BigQueryConfiguration.cpp:135) accepts `billing_project` and `access_token` as arbitrary strings - `checkIdentifierPart` is applied only to `project`, `dataset` and `table` - then `BigQueryClient::requestJSON` (BigQueryClient.cpp:215-238) puts them into `HTTPHeaderEntries` and passes them to `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP(...).withHeaders(headers)`. `context->getHTTPHeaderFilter().checkAndNormalizeHeaders(...)` is never called on this path, while `Poco::Net::HTTPRequest::set` performs no validation of its own. **Affected locations:** - `src/Storages/BigQuery/BigQueryClient.cpp:218` — Authorization header built from the unvalidated `access_token` - `src/Storages/BigQuery/BigQueryClient.cpp:220` — X-Goog-User-Project header built from the unvalidated `billing_project` - `src/Storages/BigQuery/BigQueryConfiguration.cpp:42` — only project/dataset/table go through `checkIdentifierPart`; billing_project and access_token are unchecked **Impact:** Two concrete consequences. (a) The admin `<http_forbid_headers>` filter, honoured by `StorageURL`, `StorageURLCluster` and the S3/Web object-storage configurations, has no effect on BigQuery requests. (b) Credentials stored in a named collection are meant to be usable without being readable; a user who may only call `bigquery(my_collection, billing_project = '...')` can append `

<any request>` and have ClickHouse issue arbitrary authenticated BigQuery API calls (for example `DELETE .../datasets/x/tables/y`) with the collection's service-account token, against the same host the `remote_host_filter` allowed. ## Assumptions The bot recorded these claims it could not verify directly from source. A maintainer ✅ confirms; ❌ flags a wrong premise (the bot should rework or close the finding). - [ ] **A real BigQuery front end (or any HTTP/1.1 server) processes the smuggled pipelined request** - *Why unverifiable:* the reproduction uses a local raw-socket listener, not googleapis.com - *Falsifiable test:* capture the bytes ClickHouse writes (the test does exactly this) and replay them against an HTTP/1.1 server with keep-alive enabled; the second request line is a syntactically complete request on the same connection ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `aa1a69b2a3c04d`). ### How to reproduce ```sql SET a raw listener and run: SELECT * FROM bigquery('p','d','t', base_url = 'http://127.0.0.1:<port>', access_token = 'tok', billing_project = 'proj
X-Injected: yes'); then inspect the bytes received on <port> - they contain a separate `X-Injected: yes` header line. Contrast with SELECT * FROM url('http://127.0.0.1:<port>/', JSONEachRow, 'a Int64', headers('X' = 'ok
X-Injected: yes')), which fails with BAD_ARGUMENTS before any request is sent. ``` ### Expected behavior ``` CAPTURE_WORKS url: NOT_INJECTED bigquery billing_project: NOT_INJECTED bigquery access_token: NOT_INJECTED ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` CAPTURE_WORKS url: NOT_INJECTED bigquery billing_project: INJECTED bigquery access_token: INJECTED ``` ### Additional context **Open risks:** - The same `HTTPHeaderEntries` path is used for `getTable`, `listTableData` and `insertAll`, so all three request kinds are affected; they share the single call site and need no separate fix. **Suggested fix:** In `BigQueryClient::requestJSON`, pass the assembled `HTTPHeaderEntries` through `context->getHTTPHeaderFilter().checkAndNormalizeHeaders(headers)` before `withHeaders(headers)` - the same call `StorageURL.cpp:1095` makes - or validate `billing_project` and `access_token` in `BigQueryConfiguration::validate` alongside the existing `checkIdentifierPart` checks. **Analysis details:** Confidence HIGH | Severity P1 | Testability: `STATELESS_SQL` Found during automated review of [PR #110166](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110166). --- _ClickGapAI · Confidence: HIGH · Severity: P1 · Finding: `h_pr110166_001`_

signals.title: BACKUP to S3: a crash after the .lock PUT permanently wedges the destination (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS 'is being written already'), no in-server recovery
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong If a `BACKUP ... TO S3(...)` is interrupted (server crash / power loss / OOM kill) after it has created its `.lock` object but before it finalizes, the destination is left **permanently unusable**: every subsequent `BACKUP` to the same destination fails with `Code: 598. DB::Exception: Backup S3('...') is being written already. (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS)`, and nothing in the server ever reclaims the leftover `.lock`. The only recovery is to manually delete the `.lock` object from the bucket. `BackupImpl::createLockFile` (`src/Backups/BackupImpl.cpp`) does an unconditional PUT of `<dest>/.lock` near the start of the backup, before the bulk of the entries and long before `.backup` is finalized. The only places that remove `.lock` are in-process: `removeLockFile` in the normal finalize, and `tryRemoveAllFiles` on an in-process failure. A crash runs neither, and there is no TTL, age, or liveness check on the lock anywhere in `src/Backups/` — so a `.lock` orphaned by a crash survives forever. `BackupImpl::checkBackupDoesntExist` then rejects the next backup to that destination on the mere *existence* of the lock: ```cpp if (writer->fileExists(file_name_to_check_existence)) // ".backup" — absent after a crash, so this passes throw Exception(ErrorCodes::BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS, "Backup {} already exists", ...); if (!params.is_internal_backup) { if (writer->fileExists(lock_file_name)) // ".lock" — the stale one from the crash throw Exception(ErrorCodes::BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS, "Backup {} is being written already", ...); } ``` Because `.backup` was never written, the first guard passes and the second throws on the stale `.lock`. The destination name is bricked until an operator cleans it up out of band. This is distinct from #112407: that issue is about two *concurrent live* backups racing the check-then-create claim. This one is a *single* backup that crashes and never recovers its own destination — a crash-recovery gap, not a concurrency one. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced on `26.8.1.1`; the code path above is present on current `master`. ### How to reproduce `26.8.1.1`, single node, BACKUP to S3/MinIO. Kill the server after the `.lock` PUT reaches the object store and before `.backup` is finalized (e.g. an S3 proxy that forwards the `.lock` PUT and then holds while the server is `SIGKILL`ed): ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, v String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(2000); BACKUP TABLE t TO S3('http://.../bucket/dest/', 'key', 'secret'); -- SIGKILL the server while this is in flight, after <dest>/.lock has been PUT -- (before <dest>/.backup exists). -- restart the server, then retry the same destination: BACKUP TABLE t TO S3('http://.../bucket/dest/', 'key', 'secret'); -- Code: 598. DB::Exception: Backup S3('.../bucket/dest/') is being written already. (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS) -- ... and so is every retry thereafter, until <dest>/.lock is deleted by hand. ``` The bucket after the crash holds `<dest>/.lock` (durable) and no `<dest>/.backup`. Deterministic rig (fault proxy forwards the `.lock` PUT, then `SIGKILL`s the server; a clean BACKUP+RESTORE control and a pre-`.lock` crash control that succeeds on retry, isolating the stale lock as the cause): `5/5` wedge, controls green. ### Expected behavior After a crash mid-backup, the destination remains usable: a subsequent `BACKUP` to the same destination either reclaims/overwrites the stale `.lock` left by the dead writer (there is no `.backup`, so no committed backup is at risk) or reports a clearly recoverable error rather than an indefinite `BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS`. A crashed backup should not permanently claim its destination with no in-server way to recover. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 598. DB::Exception: Backup S3('.../') is being written already. (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS) ``` ### Additional context `backups.allow_concurrent_backups` defaults to `true`, so no non-default setting is involved. Related but distinct: #112407 (concurrent live racers on the same `.lock` claim-check). The lock's UUID-content comparison in `checkLockFile` is a *later* guard used while writing; the initial `checkBackupDoesntExist` gate rejects on existence alone, so a stale lock from any prior (dead) UUID blocks every future backup to that destination.

signals.title: Server crash in `applyRangeFilterFromAST`: `Pipe::getHeader` on an empty per-layer pipe
signals.text: The AST fuzzer running inside stateless/stress tests crashes the server in `applyRangeFilterFromAST` (`src/Processors/QueryPlan/PartsSplitter.cpp`) when the per-layer pipe built by `readByLayers` is empty: `Pipe::getHeader` dereferences the pipe's null `header`. The ASan+UBSan build reports it as undefined behavior, the TSan builds as a segmentation fault: ``` /ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__memory/shared_ptr.h:574:12: runtime error: reference binding to null pointer of type 'element_type' (aka 'const DB::Block') #0 std::shared_ptr<DB::Block const>::operator*() const #1 DB::Pipe::getHeader() const src/QueryPipeline/Pipe.h:45:46 #2 DB::applyRangeFilterFromAST(DB::Pipe&, ...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/PartsSplitter.cpp:1230:34 #3 DB::readByLayers(DB::SplitPartsByRanges, ...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/PartsSplitter.cpp:1263:9 #4 DB::ReadFromMergeTree::readByLayers(...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:1242:18 #5 DB::ReadFromMergeTree::spreadMarkRanges(...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:3654:16 #6 DB::ReadFromMergeTree::initializePipeline(...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4549:16 ... #9 DB::QueryAnalyzer::evaluateScalarSubqueryIfNeeded(...) src/Analyzer/Resolve/evaluateScalarSubqueryIfNeeded.cpp:277:63 #11 DB::QueryAnalyzer::resolveTableFunction(...) src/Analyzer/Resolve/QueryAnalyzer.cpp:4670:13 ... #33 DB::executeASTFuzzerQueries(...) src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp:2375:27 SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior /ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__memory/shared_ptr.h:574:12 ``` `readByLayers` calls `applyRangeFilterFromAST` on every pipe returned by the reading step getter, and a layer can produce an empty `Pipe` (a default-constructed `Pipe` has a null `header`). An empty pipe is legal downstream - `Pipe::unitePipes` starts with `removeEmptyPipes` - so the filter simply has nothing to apply to. Observed in CI on two unrelated pull requests, so it is not caused by either of them: - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=99639&sha=e3675c072cc6c7cb1184a060d9c872ac519c78a2&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29 (`Stress test (amd_asan_ubsan)`, `Stress test (amd_tsan)` and `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, s3 storage, parallel, 3/3)`, 2026-08-03), see https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99639 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103182 (2026-08-05) `applyRangeFilterFromAST` was introduced on `master` on 2026-06-19 by commit `f29978c7cd7e` ("Read per-bucket PK-range layers on the distributed-read worker"). There is no deterministic reproducer: both occurrences come from the AST fuzzer, and the exact fuzzed query is not recoverable from the logs (the server dies before it is logged as finished). <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114177 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1483` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.4.47` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Physical column shadowing `_part`: `SELECT count() ... WHERE isNull(_part > 0)` throws NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** On a table that has a **physical column named `_part`** (shadowing the virtual column), an aggregate query whose `WHERE` wraps that column in `isNull(...)` fails with `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`, at default settings. The same predicate works in a plain `SELECT *`, and the same query works when the column does not shadow a virtual. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on current master, `26.8.1.1061` (official build). 20/20 deterministic. **How to reproduce** ```sql CREATE TABLE t_part_shadow (_part UInt32, x UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t_part_shadow VALUES (1, 100), (2, 200), (3, 300); SELECT count() FROM t_part_shadow WHERE isNull(_part > 0); -- throws ``` ``` Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column _part in block. There are only columns: _partition_id, _part_uuid, _part_data_version, _disk_name. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` No settings required — plain defaults over HTTP and native client, old and new analyzer both throw. **Expected behavior** `0` — `_part` here is the user's `UInt32` column (`_part > 0` is never NULL), which is what `SELECT count() FROM t_part_shadow WHERE isNull(toNullable(_part) > 0)` and `SELECT * FROM t_part_shadow WHERE isNull(_part > 0)` correctly return. **Additional context — scope probed** - `SELECT * ... WHERE isNull(_part > 0)` **works**; `SELECT count()`, `EXPLAIN SELECT count()`, and the `PREWHERE` form all **throw** — the trigger is the read that needs no physical columns, where the filter becomes a candidate for part-level evaluation over virtual columns. - The exception's block dump (`_partition_id, _part_uuid, _part_data_version, _disk_name`) is the virtuals-only filter block: `getHeaderWithVirtualsForFilter` correctly *skips* virtuals shadowed by physical columns (`if (columns.contains(name)) continue;` in `MergeTreeData`), but the predicate analysis still classifies the `isNull(_part > 0)` conjunct as evaluable over virtuals, so `filterPartsByVirtualColumns` evaluates it on a block that (correctly) has no `_part`. - Un-wrapped comparisons on the shadowed column work: `WHERE _part = 2`, `WHERE (_part = 2) AND (_part > 0)` are fine; `isNull(...)` / `IS NULL` composition is what reaches the broken path. `NOT (_part > 0)` and `(_part > 0) = 1` also work. - Shadowing `_partition_id` instead does not trigger it. - The existing test `04201_virtual_column_override_where_filter.sql` pins the simple-predicate forms of this exact shadowing scenario; the `isNull` composition is the gap. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: query_plan_join_swap_table changes the result of ANY INNER JOIN with OR-ed ON conditions (deterministic, max_threads = 1)
signals.text: ### Describe the bug The planner's automatic build-side swap (`query_plan_join_swap_table`, default `auto`) changes the result of an `ANY INNER JOIN` with **OR-ed conditions** in `ON`. On identical single-part tables, single-threaded, the swapped plan deterministically returns **6 rows** and the unswapped plan **3 rows** — the swapped output is a strict superset. `EXPLAIN actions = 1` shows both plans keep `Type: inner | Strictness: any | Algorithm: HashJoin` while the table read order flips, so the `ANY` deduplication is applied to opposite sides. With a single equality condition (no `OR`) both plans agree, so the multi-disjunct key path is the trigger. ### How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE l (a Int32, b Int32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; CREATE TABLE r (a Int32, b Int32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; INSERT INTO l SELECT number % 8, number % 3 FROM numbers(12); INSERT INTO r SELECT number % 5, number % 8 FROM numbers(12); SELECT * FROM l ANY JOIN r ON l.b = r.b OR l.a = r.a ORDER BY ALL SETTINGS max_threads = 1, query_plan_join_swap_table = 'true'; -- 6 rows SELECT * FROM l ANY JOIN r ON l.b = r.b OR l.a = r.a ORDER BY ALL SETTINGS max_threads = 1, query_plan_join_swap_table = 'false'; -- 3 rows ``` Outputs, stable across 20/20 runs per arm (`clickhouse local`, one part per table, `max_threads = 1`): ``` -- swap 'true' (and the default 'auto', which swaps here): 0 0 0 0 0 2 0 2 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 7 3 0 3 3 4 1 4 4 -- swap 'false': 0 0 0 0 0 2 0 2 1 1 1 1 ``` Whatever row choice `ANY` is permitted to make per key, the two plans do not even agree on the **number** of emitted rows, and the divergence is controlled purely by a performance plan setting. Note also that both outputs emit only a small subset of the left keys that have matches (for example `l = (2, 1)` matches `r = (4, 1)` via `b` but is emitted by neither plan), so the intended `ANY` + `OR` semantics may be off in both plans — the deterministic swap-controlled difference is the unambiguous part. ### Affected versions Reproduced on master 26.8.1.1068 and on 26.7. Not bisected. ### Related Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112640 (the `ANY LEFT JOIN` + `OR` face of the swap: racy under `max_threads > 1`; this `INNER` face is deterministic and single-threaded) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111645 Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).
