signals.title: Fix ReadBuffer-canceled abort in GraceHashJoin spilled-block reader
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you do not need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR: ReadBuffer is canceled. Can't read from it.` that could occur in a `grace_hash` join when reading spilled blocks failed mid-read while multiple threads shared the reader. ### Description `GraceHashJoin` shares one `AccumulatedBlockReader` between concurrent `DelayedJoinedBlocksWorkerTransform` threads. If `reader->read` throws while reading a spilled block, `ReadBuffer::next` cancels the underlying buffer and rethrows. Previously the shared reader was not marked finished, so a sibling worker could re-enter `read` on the canceled buffer and throw `LOGICAL_ERROR: ReadBuffer is canceled. Can't read from it.` The query should instead preserve and report the original read exception. The fix marks `AccumulatedBlockReader` finished on every read exception while holding its existing mutex. Subsequent workers return an empty block and cannot re-read the canceled buffer. This covers both the left delayed reader and the right reader that use the same `read` implementation. The new stateless regression deterministically forces a failure only in the shared left delayed reader: it cancels the underlying buffer, throws `FAULT_INJECTED`, verifies the query reports that original exception, and then verifies that the server remains alive. Without the `eof` assignment, a sibling worker re-enters the canceled buffer and triggers the original logical exception.

signals.title: Add `max_rows` setting for databases
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109355 Adds a `max_rows` setting for `Atomic` and `Ordinary` databases: a ceiling on active MergeTree rows counted toward the database limit. It is enforced on `INSERT`, `ATTACH`, and partition-import/move operations. A batch `INSERT` may overshoot, and the next `INSERT` throws `TOO_MANY_ROWS`. The counted total is exposed through the nullable `system.databases.rows` column. It intentionally excludes engines that do not participate in `max_rows` accounting. The setting can be changed at runtime with `ALTER DATABASE ... MODIFY SETTING max_rows = N`; its default value, `0`, is unlimited. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add the `max_rows` setting for `Atomic` and `Ordinary` databases, limiting active MergeTree rows counted across a database. It is enforced on `INSERT`, `ATTACH`, and partition imports, is reconfigurable via `ALTER DATABASE ... MODIFY SETTING`, and is exposed through `system.databases.rows`.

signals.title: Add native Version data type (proof of concept)
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Adds a native `Version` SQL data type for semantic-version-style values (`major.minor.patch.build`), enabling correct numeric ordering instead of lexicographic string comparison. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes: The new `Version` type stores versions of up to 4 components, such as `major.minor.patch.build`. Comparisons between these values correctly evaluate numeric size, meaning `toVersion('1.2') < toVersion('1.10')` is true. `Version` values parse 1-4 dot-separated non-negative integer components, zero-padding missing trailing components (`1.2` is equal to `1.2.0`). ### Description **Summary** Adds a native `Version` SQL data type for semantic-version-style values (`major.minor.patch.build`), so comparisons use correct numeric ordering instead of lexicographic string comparison: ```sql SELECT '1.2' < '1.10'; -- 0 (wrong, string comparison) SELECT toVersion('1.2') < toVersion('1.10'); -- 1 (correct) SELECT toVersion('1.2') = toVersion('1.2.0'); -- 1 (padding equality) ``` Stored as a packed `UInt128` (`(major<<96)|(minor<<64)|(patch<<32)|build`), so `=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `!=` all work natively via plain integer comparison — no custom operator overloads needed. Parsing (`toVersion`/`toVersionOrNull`/`toVersionOrZero`/`toVersionOrDefault`) accepts 1–4 dot-separated non-negative integer components, zero-pads missing trailing components, and rejects more than 4 components or any non-numeric component. Leading zeros parse numerically (`01` → `1`). Pre-release/build-metadata suffixes (`-beta`, `+build1`) are intentionally out of scope for this first pass. **Design decision: numeric-only model, not full semver** Per review discussion (thanks @groeneai), `1.0.0-alpha`-style pre-release ordering was considered and deliberately rejected: the 4 `UInt32` components already fill the `UInt128` with no spare bits, and semver's ordering rule (`0.9.9 < 1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0`) has no integer to sit between two adjacent packed values, so supporting it would require replacing the fixed integer-packing model with a comparison-based one, giving up free integer ordering. `Version` therefore stays a 4-component numeric-only scheme — closer to `ClickHouse`'s own version scheme (`24.3.1.2672`) than to semver — and text with a pre-release/build-metadata suffix is rejected with `CANNOT_PARSE_VERSION` rather than silently truncated. This is now documented directly on the type in `base/base/Version.h`/`DataTypeVersion.h`. **Caveats** This is exploratory. I've verified it manually end-to-end against a real build via `clickhouse local` (parsing, padding-equality, numeric ordering, and both rejection cases all confirmed), but: - It has **not** been run through the full functional/stateless test suite, only the two new test files included here. - The wire-format tag byte choices (`FieldBinaryEncoding.cpp` uses `0x16`, `DataTypesBinaryEncoding.h` uses `0x38`) are new protocol constants — once shipped these are effectively permanent for backward compatibility, so they deserve explicit maintainer review before being treated as final. - No prior design discussion/RFC happened before writing this — I'd like feedback on whether a type like this is wanted at all, and on the packing/validation choices, before investing further in edge cases and full test coverage. **Test plan** - [x] `tests/queries/0_stateless/04614_data_type_version_basic.sql` — parsing/round-trip/padding - [x] `tests/queries/0_stateless/04615_data_type_version_comparison.sql` — ordering + rejection cases - [x] Manual verification via `clickhouse local` against a full local build - [x] Full stateless/functional test suite (not run) - [x] Style/clang-tidy pass 🤖 Generated with heavy AI assistance (agentic exploration + implementation), per [AI_POLICY.md](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/AI_POLICY.md) — disclosing since this was a substantial, multi-file core-engine change built through an unusually AI-heavy process, not just a docs tweak.

signals.title: Fix LOGICAL_ERROR in normal projection optimization with correlated subqueries
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/103695 (same `Invalid number of columns in chunk pushed to OutputPort` error family) ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a `LOGICAL_ERROR` raised when a normal projection was used to read the input of a correlated subquery (decorrelated into a join) and all parts were served from the projection. Depending on the settings it was reported as `Invalid number of columns in chunk pushed to OutputPort` or as `Block structure mismatch in joined block stream`. It is an exception in release builds and aborts the server in debug and sanitizer builds. ### Description Found by the AST fuzzer, reproduces on current master and is unrelated to the pull requests it was seen on: [amd_msan on #100332](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100332&sha=766a499fbbfcfb5b1cbd865a4f435f75c7b5ee28&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_msan%29) (STID 2270-3452), [amd_tsan on #92472](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=92472&sha=0d58afae81ce01111323d3f73a59d6d032d199f7&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29) (STID 0993-3a3c), and `Stress test (arm_debug)` on #108289. Root cause: `optimizeUseNormalProjections` reads the projection over `required_columns = reading->getAllColumnNames()`. Columns of that set which the rebuilt `query.dag` does not consume survive as pass-throughs, because `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` appends every un-consumed input, and they widen the rewritten read's output header. The all-parts-from-projection branch spliced that widened node into the plan without the `blocksHaveEqualStructure` check the Union branch already had, so a downstream step received more columns than its declared header. The default `query_plan_remove_unused_columns = 1` masks both asserts by re-narrowing the stream, so CI hits this only under `compatibility = '25.3'`. Change: hoist the materialize-constants and equal-structure guard so it protects both replacement branches, and on a mismatch skip the projection and keep the regular read. `filterPartsByProjection` mutates the parent analysis result in place, so it now runs only after the check passes and a skipped projection no longer drops parts from the regular read. `has_parent_parts` therefore moves ahead of the filter, computed non-destructively as "does any remaining part belong to `best_candidate->parent_parts`" (equivalent, because the filter keeps exactly those parts). The skipped candidate's stat description is rewritten so `EXPLAIN projections = 1` reports the rejection. Validation: both carriers and both asserts abort before the change and run cleanly after, and projection-on results equal projection-off results. Removing only the hoisted check from the fixed build makes all of them abort again with the original messages. Regression tests for both carriers are in `04410_normal_projection_correlated_subquery_part_offset`. The guard only skips the optimization for queries that were previously failing. <details><summary>Both carriers: error signatures</summary> Carrier 1, virtual columns (`_part_offset` in the projection), output port assert: ``` Invalid number of columns in chunk pushed to OutputPort. Expected 2, found 4 src/Processors/Port.h:425 src/Processors/Transforms/JoiningTransform.cpp:101 DB::JoiningTransform::prepare() ``` Carrier 2, real columns. The inner decorrelation join's right side carries exactly one column by design, so the leaked columns trip its structure check instead of the output port one: ``` Block structure mismatch in joined block stream: different number of columns: __table3.timestamp UInt64 UInt64(size = 0) __table3.timestamp UInt64 UInt64(size = 2), payload String String(size = 2), id UUID Sparse(size = 2, UUID(size = 1), UInt64(size = 0)) src/Core/Block.cpp:863 DB::assertBlocksHaveEqualStructureAllowReplicated src/Interpreters/ConstantJoin.cpp:230 DB::ConstantJoin::addBlockToJoin src/Processors/Transforms/JoiningTransform.cpp:373 DB::FillingRightJoinSideTransform::work() ``` `correlated_subqueries_use_in_memory_buffer = 0` selects the `ConstantJoin` assert; adding `correlated_subqueries_default_join_kind = 'left'` selects the output port one. Runnable reproducers for both are the statements in the new test file. </details>

signals.title: Adaptive Aggregator
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New adaptive algorithm for parallel `GROUP BY` (controlled via setting `enable_adaptive_aggregator`, enabled by default): each thread aggregates into its own hash table until it holds `adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold` keys and then freezes it, so frequent keys keep updating the small cache-resident tables with no coordination, while rare keys are routed by their hash into per-bucket backlogs and aggregated exactly once, inside the bucket-parallel merge. ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1465` (included in `26.8` and later)

signals.title: Preserve unchanged TOAST values in MaterializedPostgreSQL
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83517 Preserve PostgreSQL columns encoded as unchanged TOAST references in `MaterializedPostgreSQL` replication instead of replacing them with default values. The consumer resolves the previous value from an earlier row in the same replication buffer when possible. Otherwise, it reads the current row from the nested `ReplacingMergeTree` by replica identity, batching key lookups to avoid a query per value. The old replica identity tuple is used when an update changes the key. An unchanged TOAST value in a replica identity column is rejected because the replication message does not contain a value that could identify the row. The integration test covers a regular update, multiple updates of the same row in one PostgreSQL transaction, and a replica identity change. The user-facing documentation is updated for both `MaterializedPostgreSQL` engines. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `MaterializedPostgreSQL` now preserves unchanged PostgreSQL `TOAST` values during updates instead of replacing them with default values.

signals.title: Use Gaussian centroids for truncated QBit codes
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109405 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110911 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve reduced-precision `L2DistanceTransposedQuantized`, `cosineDistanceTransposedQuantized`, and `dotProductTransposedQuantized` by reconstructing `p < 8` `QBit(Int8)` codes with Gaussian conditional-mean prefix centroids. Full precision (`p = 8`) remains bit-exact; reduced-precision approximate distances may change, and recall/latency gains are workload-dependent. ### Motivation The existing reduced-precision path selects one middle fine Lloyd-Max reconstruction level for every truncated prefix. That value is not the conditional mean of the complete Gaussian interval represented by the prefix. This change uses the conditional mean `(phi(lo) - phi(hi)) / (Phi(hi) - Phi(lo))` which minimizes scalar MSE for that prefix under the standard-normal source model of the existing Lloyd-Max codec. The 127 positive values are evaluated from the existing `Float32` boundaries at high precision, rounded once to `Float32`, stored as hexadecimal literals, and mirrored exactly for negative prefixes. This keeps the hot distance loop as one LUT lookup and avoids platform-dependent libm work during LUT initialization. ### Validation - A new stateless regression fails on the exact official `26.7.1.1315` binary for all 20 reduced-precision centroid/sign checks and passes its `p = 8` control. The candidate passes all 20 checks and the control. - An independent all-raw probe covers every raw byte and every `p = 1..8`: expected level counts, finiteness, symmetry, prefix-block invariance, index-order monotonicity, independent Gaussian means (maximum 0 ULP), and bit-exact legacy `p = 8` reconstruction. - An engine probe covers all raw bytes and precisions, non-strided and `QBit(Int8, 16, 8)`, `used_dims` 8/16, dot/L2/cosine, and `optimize_qbit_distance_function_reads` 0/1. Partial-read modes match bitwise; bounded SimSIMD tolerances are used for L2/cosine. - Debug `programs/clickhouse` build passes. Updated `04504_transposed_distance_quantized` and new `04628_qbit_lloyd_max_prefix_centroid` match their references with empty stderr in clean `clickhouse local` paths. On 103,000 source-disjoint Nomic embedding vectors (768 dimensions, 200 queries, four randomized-Hadamard seeds), scalar coordinate MSE decreases at every changed precision. The transformed-space retrieval proxy is deliberately reported separately because it is not a production ClickHouse latency benchmark: | `p` | scalar MSE delta | recall@10 delta (pp) | hit@1 delta (pp) | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | -3.83% | 0.000 | 0.000 | | 2 | -3.49% | -0.250 | -0.375 | | 3 | -0.89% | +0.538 | +0.750 | | 4 | -15.17% | +1.738 | +1.625 | | 5 | -17.70% | +1.300 | +1.875 | | 6 | -24.08% | +0.800 | +0.125 | | 7 | -44.32% | +0.588 | +0.250 | | 8 | unchanged | 0.000 | 0.000 | There is no universal retrieval improvement claim: `p = 2` regresses slightly in this proxy. There is also no latency claim until a matched Release-build p50/p95 benchmark is available. The intentional compatibility boundary is numerical output at `p < 8`; function signatures, storage, and `p = 8` results are unchanged. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1507` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.4.48` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Implement PromQL functions clamp(), clamp_min(), clamp_max() and round()
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `clamp`, `clamp_min`, `clamp_max`, and `round`. ### Description Implements four PromQL functions previously reported as not implemented: - `clamp(v, min, max)`, `clamp_min(v, min)`, `clamp_max(v, max)` — new `applyClampFunction` converter mapping to `greatest`/`least` SQL with explicit guards, because vectorized `least`/`greatest` in ClickHouse treat NaN as the largest value and ignore NULLs, which would corrupt NaN sample values and missing points. Prometheus special cases are reproduced exactly: `min > max` returns an empty vector, and a NaN bound propagates NaN. - `round(v[, to_nearest])` — new `applyRoundFunction` converter; replicates Prometheus inverse arithmetic (`floor(v * (1/to_nearest) + 0.5) / (1/to_nearest)`), including ties rounding toward `+Inf` and NaN propagation for `to_nearest = 0` or NaN. Both drop the metric name from results, matching Prometheus. Non-constant scalar bounds (for example, `clamp(v, time()*0-1, 2)`) are supported. No parser changes were needed; arity is enforced by each converter. The embedded support matrices for `prometheusQuery` and `prometheusQueryRange` list the new math functions and retain the implemented range functions `increase`, `changes`, and `resets`. **Semantics verified against Prometheus 3.5.0** for bound combinations `(0, 1)`, `(0, 1e12)`, `(1e12, 0)`, `(1e12, 1e12)`, and fractional `to_nearest`. **Testing**: adds `test_clamp` and `test_round`, plus conversion and aggregation regressions for empty scalar handling and a runtime scalar `quantile` parameter outside `[0, 1]`.
signals.author: valerypetrov

signals.title: Support the NetCDF format
signals.text: Adds support for the [NetCDF](https://www.unidata.ucar.edu/software/netcdf/) format, a self-describing binary format for multidimensional arrays that is the standard way climate, weather, oceanographic and other scientific data is distributed. There is a lot of public data in it (ERA5, CMIP, NOAA, Copernicus), and until now the only way to query it with ClickHouse was to convert it first. Reading is supported for the three "classic" versions of the format: CDF-1, CDF-2 (64-bit offset) and CDF-5 (64-bit data), and writing produces CDF-2 or CDF-5, whichever the data needs. The files are parsed directly, so there is no new dependency. A NetCDF-4 file, which is an HDF5 file with a different data model on top, is recognized and reported with a message that says how to convert it. **Data model.** Every variable of a file becomes a column, and the rows enumerate the Cartesian product of all the dimensions that the variables use; a variable that does not use some of them is repeated along them. The `to_dataframe` method of `xarray` produces a table with the same columns and the same set of rows, though possibly in a different order: `to_dataframe` puts the dimensions in alphabetical order by default, while ClickHouse keeps the order of the dimensions of the variables. So a file with the dimensions `time`, `lat`, `lon` and the variables `time(time)`, `lat(lat)`, `lon(lon)`, `temperature(time, lat, lon)` reads as a table with four columns and `time * lat * lon` rows. The classic format has no string type, so a `char` variable is read as a String whose length is the last dimension of the variable, when that dimension serves only as the length of the strings; a dimension that anything else in the file uses as a real axis stays in the row space, and such a `char` variable is read as one character per row. Only the variables that a query needs are read, the number of rows comes from the header (so `count()` does not read any data), and an input that cannot be seeked is read into memory instead. **Writing.** Every column becomes a variable over a single dimension named `row`, so a file written by ClickHouse is read back with the same column names and the same rows; the types come back as the closest types of the classic format (a `FixedString` as a `String`, an `Enum` or a `LowCardinality` column as the type it wraps, dates and times as plain numbers, a `Nullable` column as its base type unless read with `input_format_netcdf_fill_value_as_null`). The version of the format is chosen automatically: CDF-5 when a column needs a type that only CDF-5 has or takes more than 4 GiB, CDF-2 otherwise. A `Nullable` column is written with the `_FillValue` attribute, and a column with dates or times gets the `units` attribute of the CF conventions, so `xarray` decodes it back into timestamps. **Settings.** `input_format_netcdf_fill_value_as_null` reads the values equal to the `_FillValue` (or `missing_value`) attribute of a variable as NULL, which is how the CF conventions mark missing data such as sea surface temperature over land. `input_format_netcdf_add_dimension_columns` adds a column with the index along every dimension that has no coordinate variable of the same name, for the files that have none. **Testing.** The test files in `tests/queries/0_stateless/data_netcdf` were written by the netCDF C library, not by this code. Beyond the two functional tests, during development the reader was compared value by value against an independent reference implementation for all three format versions, the output was checked by opening it with the netCDF C library for every supported type family, and 321 truncated and bit-flipped files were fed to the reader — all of them either parsed or failed with a clean error, with no crashes. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support the `NetCDF` format for both reading and writing. It is a self-describing binary format for multidimensional arrays, widely used for climate, weather and other scientific data. Reading supports all three classic versions of the format (CDF-1, CDF-2 and CDF-5), and writing produces CDF-2 or CDF-5, whichever the data needs. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Measure the compressed size of aggregate states in `estimateSizeOfCompressedState`
signals.text: `Aggregator::estimateSizeOfCompressedState` estimates how many bytes the aggregate states would take when a replica sends them to the initiator, which is how automatic parallel replicas decides whether distributing a query pays off. It builds a `CompressedWriteBuffer` over a `NullWriteBuffer`, but serializes the sampled states into the `NullWriteBuffer` directly and then reads that buffer's counter: ```cpp NullWriteBuffer wb; CompressedWriteBuffer wbuf(wb); // never written to ... aggregate_functions[j]->serialize(place + offsets_of_aggregate_states[j], wb); ... wbuf.finalize(); res += it ? static_cast<size_t>(table.size() * wb.count() / ((it + period - 1) / period)) : 0; ``` So nothing is ever compressed and, despite the function's name and its own `We only interested in the size of compressed state` comment, it returns the plain serialized size. `recordAggregationStateSizes` then stored that single number as all three of `bytes`, `sample_bytes` and `compressed_bytes`, which pins the compression ratio of the aggregation-state statistics to 1. `recordAggregationStateColumnSizes`, documented as `Mirrors the logic of Aggregator::estimateSizeOfCompressedState` for in-order aggregation, feeds the same `AggregationState` counters via `estimateCompressedColumnSize` and does measure the compressed size - so two producers of one statistic disagreed on what it means. This change serializes the sample through the compressing buffer and returns the sample's uncompressed and compressed sizes alongside the extrapolated total, letting the existing compression-ratio machinery in `RuntimeDataflowStatisticsCacheUpdater` apply the states' real ratio. Taking the ratio from the sample rather than compressing the extrapolated size also keeps the per-compressed-block framing overhead out of the extrapolation, where multiplying it by `table.size() / num_samples` would have inflated it. **Effect on the estimate.** Only queries whose output is dominated by compressible aggregate states move. That is exactly the shape that showed up as a CI failure of `03634_autopr_output_bytes_estimation` on master: `query_28` (`MIN(Referer)` states over a two-level hash table with many groups) estimated 59335657 bytes against a recorded 23722663, a ratio of 2.4996 that left the test's 2.5x bound no margin. Reading the estimates out of the failing job's server log, the ten other queries in that test match their recorded values within 1.00..1.41x, because their output is dominated by aggregation keys or by output columns, both of which were already measured compressed. So the recorded values expect the compressed size and this defect is why that one entry looked wrong. **Two small-sample corrections found while validating this in CI.** The compressed format writes a checksum and a block header in front of every block, so a sample of a few bytes comes out of `CompressedWriteBuffer` larger than it went in and the derived ratio drops below one, *inflating* the estimate. With an early conversion to a two-level hash table (`group_by_two_level_threshold=1`, which the test randomization sets) every one of the 256 buckets holds a handful of states and every per-bucket sample is dominated by that framing, which is what made `04034_autopr_dataflow_cache_reuse_between_different_queries` fail on the first run of this pull request: the two cache-reusing queries lost parallel replicas. When the states are really sent, the framing is amortized over `min_compress_block_size` of data, so such a sample is now reported as incompressible rather than as expanding, keeping the ratio at 1 - exactly what the caller assumed before the ratio was measured at all. The new test `04653_autopr_state_size_estimate_small_buckets` pins `group_by_two_level_threshold` to 1 and fails without that. Reviewing the same statistic end to end also turned up the mirror-image defect on the in-order-aggregation side, reported in review: `recordAggregationStateColumnSizes` totalled `IColumn::byteSize`, which for a `ColumnAggregateFunction` whose states live in a foreign arena (as `AggregatingInOrderTransform` hands them over) counts one pointer per row, so arena-backed states - `min(String)`, `groupArray`, `uniqExact` - were under-counted. That column is now sized from its serialized states too, sampling at most as many of them as the hash-table producer samples per bucket. **Recorded values.** The values in `03634_autopr_output_bytes_estimation` are empirical and need `test.hits`, so they are re-measured from this PR's own CI run rather than guessed - the test reports every query that lands outside the 2.5x band, and I will update whatever it reports. `query_1` and `query_20` are single `count()` states whose estimate becomes the ~29-byte compressed-block framing instead of a 2-3 byte varint; the test's `NOT (res.2 < 100 AND res.3 < 100)` guard already covers those. Verified so far: both changed translation units pass a full `-fsyntax-only` typecheck against master. The estimate itself is validated by CI, since reproducing it needs the stateful dataset. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111981 That PR is the interim, test-only fix for the master CI failure linked below: it re-records `query_28` as the ~58 MB the estimator currently reports. **The two changes touch the same line and are mutually exclusive.** If #111981 merges first, this PR must set `query_28` back to the post-fix measurement (expected to land near the original 23722663); if this PR merges first, #111981 should be closed as unnecessary. https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5baed0f5a10c333cd220b9646d6ef4647425079d&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%20parallel%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the estimation of the size of aggregate states used by automatic parallel replicas: it measured the serialized size of the states instead of their compressed size, overestimating how much data a replica would send for queries that aggregate into large, compressible states.

signals.title: Serialize serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte in the query plan
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112079 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` being dropped from the serialized query plan. With `serialize_query_plan = 1`, a cluster running with the setting disabled could diverge on the in-memory string representation between the initiator and the node executing the deserialized plan, because the setting was read on deserialization but never written on serialization and therefore always resolved to its default on the executing node. ### Description `QueryPlan::serialize` builds a fresh `QueryPlanSerializationSettings` per step and emits only what that step's `serializeSettings` assigned; `readBinary` leaves an absent name at its declared default. Both `AggregatingStep::deserialize` and `MergingAggregatedStep::deserialize` read `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` into `Aggregator::Params`, but neither `serializeSettings` ever wrote it - the only `Params` field those two read without writing. So with `serialize_query_plan = 1` an initiator running the setting at `0` ships a plan the executing node deserializes as `1`. The two then disagree on the aggregation-key byte layout (the flag adds or removes one trailing byte per string in `ColumnString::serializeValueIntoArena`), and since the two-level bucket number hashes those serialized bytes, disagreeing sources can place one logical key in different buckets - the duplicated-group shape documented in `tests/integration/test_string_aggregation_compatibility`. Keeping that layout consistent across a cluster of incompatible versions is the setting's whole purpose. Only an explicit `= 0` diverges, both defaults being `true`, which is why nothing observes it today. **The fix** adds the missing assignment to both `serializeSettings` bodies, for both values and at every serialization version. Restricting it to the non-default value is wrong: a receiver predating the name has no such setting and its GROUP BY key path writes no trailing zero byte at all, so it behaves like `false`, and omitting `true` would silently hand exactly that peer the other layout. Gating on the version fails too: patch releases inside one version disagree on whether they know the name (`v25.8.12.129-lts` does not, `v25.8.13.73-lts` backported it, both at version 0). Writing it always makes such a peer fail closed on the unknown name instead. The new gtest drives `serializeSettings` -> `writeChangedBinary` -> `readBinary` per step, asserting the round-tripped value and that the name reaches the wire, for both values and at version 0 as well as the current one. Reverting either production line fails that step's test. <details><summary>Why a gtest, and a sibling asymmetry deliberately not fixed here</summary> A gtest rather than a functional or integration test, because the divergence is silent: `EXPLAIN` does not surface the flag (`Aggregator::Params::explain` prints only keys and aggregates) and a single-node query never round-trips a plan, so no query output changes deterministically with the fix. The existing `tests/integration/test_string_aggregation_compatibility` does set the setting to `0` against a pinned older node, but never sets `serialize_query_plan`, which is why it misses this. The invariant is: every setting a step's `deserialize` reads must be written by that same step's `serializeSettings`. Because the settings object is per step, a write by one step cannot supply a read by another, so the sweep is per step rather than a global "is this name written anywhere?" check. It finds three asymmetries on master, not two: | step | read but not written by that step | |---|---| | `AggregatingStep` | `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` - fixed here | | `MergingAggregatedStep` | `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` - fixed here | | `ArrayJoinStep` | `enable_lazy_columns_replication` - not in this PR | `ArrayJoinStep::deserialize` reads `enable_lazy_columns_replication`, whose only writer is reached from `JoinStepLogical::serializeSettings` - a different step, hence a different settings object. It is another subsystem, its default direction is the opposite, and its effect is performance rather than correctness, so it needs a different justification, oracle and changelog category. Tracked separately. Also checked: of the steps holding an `Aggregator::Params`, only these two are serializable at all. `CubeStep`, `RollupStep` and `AggregatingProjectionStep` implement neither `serialize` nor `serializeSettings`, so there is no third carrier of this flag. </details> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1435` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend
signals.text: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106136 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes silently missing rows when a query filters on `intDiv(constant, key)` or `divide(constant, key)`. Primary-key and partition analysis reports the wrong direction of monotonicity for a constant divided by a key column, so matching granules are pruned away and the query returns fewer rows with no error. Also fixes `intDiv` with an unsigned constant dividend whose high bit is set, stops claiming monotonicity when a `Decimal` operand makes the division compute in the decimal's native width, and stops key analysis from raising `Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long` for a valid query that divides an `IPv4`/`IPv6` constant by a key column. ### Description `FunctionBinaryArithmetic::getMonotonicityForRange` reports the direction of `c / x` incorrectly in its `const / variable` branch, so `KeyCondition::applyMonotonicFunctionsChainToRange` inverts the transformed range exactly when it must not, the range matches no granule, and matching rows are dropped with no error and exit code 0. Reproduced at completely default settings (no `SETTINGS` clause), 20000-row `Int32`-keyed MergeTree: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t WHERE intDiv(toInt32(-1000000), a) >= 11; -- keyed MergeTree: 0 ENGINE = Memory oracle: 10909 ``` #### Root cause For `f(x) = c / x` on an interval excluding 0, `d/dx (c/x) = -c/x²`, whose sign is `-sign(c)` for every `x != 0` — the `x²` denominator is positive on both sides of 0. So the direction is governed by `sign(c)` alone and is the *same* on the negative and the positive branch; only the values differ. The code instead treated the two arms as needing opposite polarity, which is the intuition that `1/x` "flips" across the branches. It does not: it is monotone on each branch separately, which is exactly why the strict range-sign guards are there. The two arms are now one return with a single `!is_constant_positive`, and the strict guards are kept verbatim. Fixing only that is not sufficient, and on its own would be *worse* than the current code for one shape. Three further defects live in the same branch: * **Unsigned constant dividend.** `intDiv` casts the dividend through `make_signed_t` whenever either operand is a signed integer (`DivisionUtils.h`), so an unsigned constant whose high bit is set divides as negative — `intDiv(toUInt8(200), x)` is `intDiv(toInt8(-56), x)` — while the raw `Field` still compares as positive. The boundary is `2^(8 * width - 1)` of the dividend's own width (verified for 8/16/32/64/128/256-bit dividends; the divisor width is irrelevant). This is reachable with no cast at all, because the literal `200` is `UInt8`. On a *negative* range the un-negated arm is accidentally correct for this shape, so adding the missing `!` alone would turn a correct answer into a wrong one. A new `intDivConstDividendReinterpretsNegative` helper corrects the effective sign; it deliberately does not reuse the existing `intDivConstReinterpretsNegative`, whose width early-out has the opposite polarity here. * **`Decimal` operand.** With a `Decimal` on either operand and no `Float` operand, the division computes in the decimal's native width (`DecimalBinaryOperation` casts both operands to `NativeResultType` and substitutes the integral operation even for `divide`). The divisor is then truncated, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), x)` is periodic in `x` with period `2^32` and not even monotonic. Nothing is claimed for that combination, mirroring the rejection the sibling `variable / constant` branch already performs. A `Decimal`/`Float` pair is exempt: it is converted to `Float64` before the operation, never truncates, and is itself a carrier of the direction defect, so those shapes are fixed rather than rejected. The rejection is deliberately keyed on the operand types and not on the constant's value, so it also covers a *zero* dividend and therefore runs ahead of the `constant == 0` fast path. That ordering is load-bearing: the truncation moves where the quotient is defined, so a range that strictly excludes 0 can still contain a point where the function is undefined, which is exactly what the zero-constant guard assumes away. With `Decimal32` the divisor truncates to `Int32`, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), key)` over an `Int64` key range around `2^32` raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`; letting the zero guard win would claim monotonicity, prune the raising row away, and return a silent answer instead. Pinned by `c5iv`. * **Non-numeric operand (pre-existing exception on a valid query).** `IPv4`/`IPv6` are substituted with `UInt32`/`UInt128`, so their declared width does not describe the arithmetic, and their raw `Field` cannot be compared with a numeric zero. Two existing comparisons against zero therefore raise `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD "Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long"` during key analysis today: one in the single-value fast path (reached when a granule's min equals its max) and one in the zero-constant guard (reached otherwise). Both roles are affected — `intDiv(toIPv4('192.168.0.1'), numeric_key)` and `intDiv(1, ipv4_key)` — and one of them fires even when the key range spans 0. A numeric gate hoisted above the fast path removes both; after it each query returns the correct rows with no pruning. Placing the gate inside the `const / variable` block would cover only the second site, which the new test pins at two granularities. Scope note: "both roles" here means the IP value as the dividend constant and as the key column, both with the constant on the left. The mirror shape, an IP constant as the *divisor* (`intDiv(numeric_key, toIPv4(...))`), still raises the same exception, as do `plus`/`minus`/`multiply` with an `IPv4`/`IPv6` operand. Both are pre-existing (measured byte-identical on `origin/master`) and are tracked separately rather than widened into this PR, since a correct fix for them also has to touch the `multiply` arm and the shared fast path. #### Behaviour changes to be aware of * **Two pre-existing key-analysis exceptions disappear.** As above, a non-numeric operand now reports non-monotonic instead of raising, so the query succeeds unpruned. This is a scope extension beyond "fix the direction", included because those same comparisons against zero are the mechanism being corrected and an exception on a valid query is a bug either way. * **Pruning is lost for `Decimal` shapes with no `Float` operand.** Measured with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`: | shape | before | after | |---|---|---| | `Decimal32(0)` key, `intDiv(toInt32(-1000), a) = -25`, positive range | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 4/4` | | `UInt64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), a) = 250` | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 3/4` | | `Int64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), a) = 5`, range around `2^32` | `Granules: 0/2` | `Granules: 2/2` | The first two queries return the same rows before and after — the index simply stops filtering. The third is the zero-dividend case: it must stop pruning, because the pruned plan silently returned `0` for a query that correctly raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`. This mirrors the decision already shipped for the `variable / constant` branch, where the same truncation applies. `Decimal`/`Float` pairs keep pruning and are additionally fixed. No committed reference in the repository changes. * **Everything else keeps pruning.** Strictly-positive ranges with a signed constant, both-unsigned operands, `Float` divisors, and unsigned key ranges crossing the divisor's own `2^(8W-1)` are all unaffected. That last group is worth naming: the *values* jump across the wrap while the *order* is preserved, which satisfies the non-strict definition of `Monotonicity`, so rejecting them would delete pruning that is correct today. The new test pins them, with plan-level assertions. #### Testing `04651_intdiv_const_variable_monotonicity` compares a keyed MergeTree against an identical `ENGINE = Memory` table on the same data, so each of its 84 count rows prints `1` when index-based pruning agrees with the full-scan ground truth. It covers both range signs for both functions and both constant signs, unsigned dividends at several widths, `Decimal` in either role plus the `Decimal`/`Float` exemption, `Float64`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable` keys, ranges that span zero or have zero as an endpoint, the unsigned wrap shapes, and the `IPv4`/`IPv6` cases at two granularities. Ten further rows assert with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` that the surviving shapes still prune (so the fix cannot silently degrade into "no pruning at all") and that the zero-dividend `Decimal` shape stops pruning — 94 asserted rows in total. On a master-HEAD binary the test fails: 28 rows print `0` and it then aborts with `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD`. On this branch it passes, including 50/50 runs with randomized settings. Each of the four edits was mutation-tested individually — reverting the negation, the sign correction, the `Decimal` rejection, the `Float` exemption, the numeric gate, the gate's hoisted position and its role restriction each make specific named rows fail. `index_granularity` decides whether the range handed to `getMonotonicityForRange` is strictly negative, strictly positive or spans zero, so it is pinned per DDL and the test carries `no-random-merge-tree-settings` with that reason stated inline.

signals.title: Keep an S3Queue file retryable after losing the race for its `processing` node
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `S3Queue`/`AzureQueue` skipping a file forever after losing the race for its `processing` node in Keeper: if the other processor released the file without committing it, the file was not retried by this table until the server restart. ### Description Found during the review of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108977 (the regression test there has to accept losing one file for exactly this reason). When `ObjectStorageQueueIFileMetadata::trySetProcessing` fails because the `processing` node in Keeper already exists, that node belongs to another processor - another server, or another table on the same server. `afterSetProcessing` then updated the local `FileStatus` to `Processing`, and since the non-processable checks in `trySetProcessing` and `prepareSetProcessingRequests` treat `Processing` as terminal, every later attempt short-circuited on that cached state without ever rechecking Keeper. Unlike `Processed` and `Failed`, `Processing` is not backed by a persistent Keeper node: the foreign processor can release the file without committing it - it can die, or fail the file and reset the node. Stale `processing` node cleanup does not evict `local_file_statuses` either; only the processed/failed node cleanup (`ObjectStorageQueueMetadata.cpp`) does. So the file stayed skipped by this table until its file status was evicted from the cache or the server was restarted. The cached `Processing` state is now remembered as a timestamped observation of the foreign `processing` node (`FileStatus::onProcessingByAnotherProcessor`): it is still reported in `system.s3queue`, and it is respected - the file is skipped without touching Keeper - while the observation is fresh (the new table setting `foreign_processing_node_cache_ttl_seconds`, 5 minutes by default; zero means to always check Keeper). After that, the next attempt probes Keeper again and refreshes the observation if the node is still there, so a file released without a commit is retried within the timeout, while a file being processed by another server costs at most one Keeper probe per timeout instead of one per listing pass. As soon as the foreign processor commits the file, the next probe fails on the `processed` (or `failed`) node instead and the state becomes terminal again. `afterSetProcessing` also keeps the cached state untouched when it is already `Processing` and not marked as foreign: in that case the node belongs to a concurrent local processor sharing this `FileStatus` (tables on the same server using the same Keeper path, insert threads), and its owner updates the state on commit. The cached observation participates in the listing pre-filter (`FileIterator::filterProcessableFiles`) as well: a file with a fresh foreign-`Processing` observation is dropped from the batch before the `processed`/`failed` multi-read is built, so the fresh observation avoids Keeper requests on the listing path too. The terminal states which that pre-filter does discover in Keeper are written back into the cached `FileStatus` (unless the state is owned by an active local processor, whose owner updates it on commit), so `system.s3queue_metadata_cache` follows Keeper instead of keeping a stale `Processing` after another processor has committed the file. The write-back replaces the whole cached record, not only the status: the per-attempt data of an abandoned local attempt is cleared, and a file failed by another processor carries the exception and retries from the `failed` node. The write-back is skipped when the cached state already equals the discovered terminal state: such a record describes a finished local attempt (its `rows_processed` and timings must survive relistings). A cached `Failed`, however, also describes retriable local attempts (`retries < loading_retries`), so it is kept only when its retry count matches the `failed` node payload: when another processor exhausts the retries after a retriable local failure, the cached record follows the terminal node instead of keeping the stale local exception. The set-processing probe (`trySetProcessing`/`prepareSetProcessingRequests`) follows the same contract: when it discovers a `processed`/`failed` node (which can appear after the pre-filter ran), it returns the metadata of that node and `afterSetProcessing` refreshes the whole cached record with the same guards, instead of flipping only the status. A skipped file is not simply dropped from the current listing pass: the file iterator keeps it in a recheck list (also filled when `trySetProcessing`/`prepareSetProcessingRequests` observe a foreign `processing` node), and every batch boundary of the pass takes the files whose observation has expired and runs them through the regular filtering. Within a long listing pass the TTL is therefore honored with batch granularity; files whose observation is still fresh when the listing is exhausted are dropped with the iterator, because the observation timestamps live in the shared file status cache and the next pass re-queues them with the original deadlines. The TTL bounds the retry latency even on an otherwise idle queue, where the polling backoff after zero-row cycles can far exceed it: the streaming task schedules its next cycle no later than the earliest pending recheck deadline. That wake-up cap applies only to cycles which actually consume the iterator: a `SYSTEM STOP`/`SYSTEM PAUSE`d table and a table with `s3queue_disable_streaming` never consume it, so a recheck left pending by an earlier active cycle would stay overdue and make the background task reschedule with a zero delay in a tight loop. In `Ordered` mode a foreign-held file also blocks the later files of its ordering domain (the scope of one `processed` pointer: a bucket, and a partition within it when partitioning is used) for the current listing pass. Without this, committing a later file advances the `processed` pointer past the held file, and the next listing pass drops it as already processed - losing it forever if the foreign processor never commits it. The file iterator records foreign-held files per ordering domain and drops the later files of the domain both at the listing pre-filter and before handing a file out (a file returned for retry releases its `processing` node); they are re-listed by the next pass. A held file stops blocking its domain as soon as this server wins its `processing` node or a terminal state for it is discovered in Keeper. With several processing threads sharing one ordering domain (`buckets = 1`), the block alone is not enough: it is recorded only when the set-processing attempt of the held file fails, and a later file handed out to another thread before that could still be committed first. The file iterator therefore registers a file whose set-processing outcome is not yet known at hand-out time (following the hand-out order), and a later file of the domain waits until the outcomes of the smaller files are known before starting its own attempt - so the set-processing attempts of one domain serialize for the duration of one Keeper round trip, and a foreign-held discovery blocks the later files before any of them starts processing. `foreign_processing_node_cache_ttl_seconds` is a per-table setting: `ObjectStorageQueueMetadataFactory` shares a single `ObjectStorageQueueMetadata` between all tables with the same `keeper_path`, so the value is not kept there - it travels from `StorageObjectStorageQueue` through `FileIterator` to `ObjectStorageQueueMetadata::getFileMetadata`, and each table uses (and reports in `system.s3_queue_settings`) the value from its own DDL. The setting can be changed on a live table with `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING`: the storage keeps the value in an atomic member which the file iterators read through a reference, so the new value (for example, zero, to get a stuck file retried immediately) applies to the running streaming task without recreating the table. Tests: `tests/integration/test_storage_s3_queue/test_foreign_processing_node.py` emulates the foreign processor with a real `processing` node in Keeper, checks that the file is not committed while that node exists, removes it, and asserts that the file is then processed - without the fix the count stays one short. A second test in the same file creates two tables sharing one `keeper_path` with different values of the setting and checks both the reported value and the retry window. A third test emulates the foreign processor committing one file and failing another, and asserts that `system.s3queue_metadata_cache` reports `Processed` (respectively `Failed`, with the exception of the processor which failed the file) instead of a stale `Processing`, and that neither file is ingested by this table. A fourth test checks that `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING` shortens the retry window of an already-running table. A fifth test repeats the retry scenario in `ordered` mode, with the foreign processor holding the lexicographically greatest file, asserting that the max processed path does not swallow the skipped file. A sixth test holds the only file of the queue with a two-minute polling backoff configured and asserts that it is retried within the TTL after its holder releases it, not after the backoff. A seventh test parks the `ordered` set-processing attempt at a failpoint between the initial state read and the multi request, fails the file from a fake foreign processor inside that window, and asserts that the cached record carries the exception of the `failed` node instead of an empty one. An eighth test feeds the table a file it cannot parse (a retriable local failure), writes the terminal `failed` node from a fake foreign processor, and asserts that the cached record follows its payload. A ninth test holds a file in the middle of the ordering domain in `ordered` mode and asserts that the later files wait for it: only the files before it are processed until the foreign `processing` node disappears, then the held file and the files after it follow. A tenth test runs two processing threads over one ordering domain, parks the set-processing attempt of the smallest file at a failpoint (the file is held by a fake foreign processor), and asserts that the other thread does not ingest the later files while the outcome of the smallest file is unknown, and that no file is lost after the holder releases it. An eleventh test pauses a table which has a pending foreign-processing recheck and asserts that it keeps its paused backoff instead of rescheduling in a tight loop. `src/Storages/ObjectStorageQueue/tests/gtest_file_status_foreign_processing.cpp` covers the shared `FileStatus` state machine, including the same-server contention case and the reset of the per-attempt data (exception, processed rows, processing end time) of a previous local attempt when the file becomes observed as processed by another processor, and the whole-record refresh on a terminal node discovered by the set-processing probe. The members added by the fix are referenced from `if constexpr (requires ...)` branches, so the gtest also compiles at the merge base (where it fails at runtime), which is what the `Bugfix validation (unit tests)` job checks. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108977

signals.title: Implement PromQL functions sum_over_time(), avg_over_time() and count_over_time()
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `sum_over_time()`, `avg_over_time()` and `count_over_time()`. ### Description Implements three PromQL range-vector functions previously reported as not implemented. `sum_over_time`, `avg_over_time` and `count_over_time` are three different projections of the same `(sum, count)` accumulator, so they share one new header (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSumCountAvg.h`) with a single invertible `Summary{sum, count}` monoid (merge adds both fields, unmerge subtracts them), plugged into the existing generic `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSlidingSum` sliding-window fast path — the same infrastructure already proven by `rate`/`increase`/`delta`. No changes were needed to the generic grid/bucket machinery (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesBase.h`) or to `checkArgumentTypes` (all three take a single range-vector argument, the existing default). Registered `timeSeriesSumToGrid`/`timeSeriesAvgToGrid`/`timeSeriesCountToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the three `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`, matching `rate`/`increase`/`delta`'s convention. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0.** **Testing**: new SQL-level test (`04628_timeseries_sum_avg_count_over_time.sql`) plus cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering all three functions, an empty-window case, a window narrower than the step (grid points with no sample must be absent/NULL, not zero), and a nested `avg_over_time(rate(...)[2m:10s])` case. This flips 19 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.

signals.title: Implement PromQL functions max_over_time() and min_over_time()
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `max_over_time()` and `min_over_time()`. ### Description Implements `max_over_time(v range-vector)` and `min_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. Unlike `sum`/`count`, max/min are not invertible monoids, but they are commutative and associative (merge = `max(a, b)`/`min(a, b)`), so the new header (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesExtremumOverTime.h`, templated on a bool `is_max_`) reuses `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSlidingSum`'s existing non-invertible sliding-window fallback (the same two-stacks/recompute machinery already shipped and tested via `deriv`/`predict_linear`) — no new windowing logic was needed. `Bucket == Summary` directly, following `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesToGridSparse`'s (`last_over_time`'s) simplest-case shape, since max/min don't depend on sample order. The comparison is NaN-aware (`candidate > current || isnan(current)`), matching Prometheus's own "a NaN currently held as the running extremum is unconditionally overwritten by the next sample" semantics. Registered `timeSeriesMaxToGrid`/`timeSeriesMinToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`, matching `rate`/`increase`/`delta`'s convention. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0.** **Testing**: new SQL-level test (`04628_max_min_over_time_timeseries_functions.sql`) including an `AggregatingMergeTree` serialize/deserialize/merge round-trip, plus cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering both functions over a series with decreases (so results differ meaningfully from `last_over_time`), including a more complex nested query. This flips 13 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.

signals.title: Implement PromQL functions stddev_over_time() and stdvar_over_time()
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `stddev_over_time()` and `stdvar_over_time()` (population standard deviation/variance). ### Description Implements `stddev_over_time(v range-vector)` and `stdvar_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. **Key Technical & Numerical Stability Highlights**: 1. **Welford's Algorithm & Chan's Parallel Merge**: Uses a running centered-moment `{count, mean, m2}` accumulator ($M_2 = \sum (x - \bar{x})^2$) in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesVarianceOverTime.h` updated per sample via Welford's formula and merged pairwise via Chan et al.'s parallel merge algorithm. This avoids catastrophic cancellation on large-magnitude counter series (e.g. byte counters $\sim 5 \times 10^8$, where raw $\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2 / N$ loses all precision and produces false zeroes or negative variances). 2. **Prometheus Staleness Handling**: Implements full Prometheus stale-marker (`0x7ff0000000000002`) semantics. Stale markers are flagged at ingestion (`is_stale_marker`), excluded from range-vector aggregations (`WHERE NOT is_stale_marker`) so target disappearance does not pollute range windows with NaNs, while remaining detectable by instant selectors to correctly report series absence. 3. **Non-Invertible Two-Stacks / Recompute Strategy**: Avoids floating-point `unmerge` subtraction on moments to prevent numerical cancellation and drift over long sliding windows. Registered `timeSeriesStddevToGrid`/`timeSeriesStdvarToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`. **Verified numerically against Prometheus 3.5.0**: verified bit-for-bit accuracy against Prometheus 3.5.0 live responses, including cross-architecture (ARM64 vs x86_64) ULP tolerance handling in CI. **Testing**: SQL-level test (`04628_variance_timeseries_functions.sql`) covering empty/single/multi-sample windows and `AggregatingMergeTree` round-trips, plus integration cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` (including stale-marker ingestion and instant/range evaluations). This flips 12 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.

signals.title: Support PromQL timestamp() function on both vector selectors and general expressions
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: `timestamp()` is now implemented for both direct selectors and general expressions, matching Prometheus 3.5.0 semantics. ### Description `timestamp(<expression>)` previously threw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. This PR implements `timestamp()` support for both direct vector selectors and general instant vector expressions (e.g. `timestamp(test)`, `timestamp(test offset 1m)`, `timestamp(test * 1)`, `timestamp(-test)`, `timestamp(timestamp(test))`). Matching Prometheus 3.5.0 semantics: - For direct instant vector selectors (plus optional direct `offset`/`@` modifiers), extracts the raw sample timestamp from storage via `timeSeriesTimestampToGrid`. - For general instant vector expressions (binary math, unary operators, comparisons, nested `timestamp()` calls), evaluates the argument as an instant vector and returns the query step evaluation timestamp ($T_{\text{eval}}$) for each present sample. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0**, including the timestamp-unit conversion (seconds, not milliseconds). **Testing**: Added integration test cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering bare vector selectors, offset/@ modifiers, binary math, unary minus, and nested `timestamp()` calls.

signals.title: Faster Decimal and 64-bit integer to string conversion
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105725 The fractional part of a `Decimal` was written one digit at a time, with a division per digit — up to 76 divisions of a 256-bit integer for a single `Decimal256` value. It is a field of a known width, so it is now emitted in blocks of eight or eighteen digits instead, with one- and two-digit fields written directly. The remaining divisions by 10^18 are done limb by limb, because dividing a `wide::integer` compiles to a long division that walks one bit at a time (513 ns per divmod, against 7 ns limb by limb). All of this is portable. Separately, `itoa` of a 64-bit value uses the AVX-512 IFMA algorithm from Champagne Gareau, J. and Lemire, D., "Converting an Integer to a Decimal String in Under Two Nanoseconds", *Software: Practice and Experience* 56(8), 2026, [doi:10.1002/spe.70079](https://doi.org/10.1002/spe.70079), behind a runtime CPU check. ## Results `clickhouse local`, single thread, best of five runs, AMD Zen 5 (so the AVX-512 path is active), `-march=x86-64-v3` build, against a binary built from the same tree without these changes: | query | before | after | | |---|---|---|---| | `toString` of `Decimal256(76)` | 46868 ms | 244 ms | 192x | | `toString` of `Decimal256(40)` | 35948 ms | 3809 ms | 9.4x | | `toDecimalString(Decimal256(40), 40)` | 35523 ms | 3842 ms | 9.2x | | `toString` of `Decimal128(38)` | 1620 ms | 414 ms | 3.9x | | `toDecimalString(Decimal64(18), 18)` | 341 ms | 210 ms | 1.6x | | `toString` of `Decimal64(18)` | 632 ms | 396 ms | 1.6x | | `toString` of `Decimal64(6)` | 481 ms | 379 ms | 1.3x | | `toString` of `Decimal128(20)` | 312 ms | 247 ms | 1.3x | | `toString` of `Decimal32(9)` | 474 ms | 388 ms | 1.2x | | `toString` of random `UInt64` | 303 ms | 214 ms | 1.4x | | `toString` of random `UInt128` | 445 ms | 379 ms | 1.2x | | `toString` of `UInt64` of mixed lengths | 821 ms | 710 ms | 1.2x | | `toString` of random `UInt256` | 10651 ms | 10515 ms | 1.0x | | `formatRow('TSV', ...)` of `Decimal64(9)` | 447 ms | 395 ms | 1.1x | The `Decimal256` and `UInt256` rows were re-measured after the second commit (best of three); the others are unaffected by it. New perf tests `decimal_to_string.xml` and `uint64_to_string.xml` cover the same ground; the existing `decimal_format.xml` only had a single `Decimal64(6)` query. ### Without AVX-512 IFMA Every aarch64 processor and every x86 processor without IFMA takes the portable path, where the `Decimal` work applies in full but `itoa` of a 64-bit value is unchanged. On aarch64 Neoverse-N1, best of seven runs, against master: | query | speedup | |---|---| | `toString` of `Decimal128(38)` | 4.00x | | `toDecimalString(Decimal64(18), 18)` | 1.92x | | `toString` of `Decimal64(18)` | 1.88x | | `toString` of `Decimal32(9)` | 1.16x | | `toString` of `Decimal64(6)` | 1.15x | | `formatRow('TSV', ...)` of `Decimal64(9)` | 1.12x | | `toString` of `Decimal32(2)` | 1.02x | The third commit exists because the first one made the smallest scales slightly *slower* on this path — `Decimal32(2)` was at 0.95x — which is invisible on a machine with IFMA, since there the widths 1 to 19 never reach the portable code at all. Writing one- and two-digit fields directly, instead of running them through the eight-digit ladder and copying part of the result back out, fixes that and also speeds up what is left over after the eight-digit blocks of the widths 9, 10, 17 and 18. Confirmed on x86-64 as well, by calling `writeFixedDigits` with the AVX-512 implementation turned off (ns per value, Zen 5): width 2 goes from 1.828 to 1.161, width 10 from 3.197 to 2.395, width 18 from 4.519 to 3.716, and the widths 4, 6, 8 and 12 are unchanged. ## A rounding fix `toDecimalString` documents that it rounds the value to the requested number of fractional digits, but it rounded the fractional part *after* the whole part had already been written, so a carry never crossed the decimal point. `toDecimalString(toDecimal64('9.995', 3), 2)` returned `9.00` instead of `10.00`, `toDecimalString(toDecimal32('99.95', 2), 1)` returned `99.0` instead of `100.0`, and `toDecimalString(toDecimal256('-0.5', 2), 0)` returned `-0.` instead of `-1.`. That predates this change; it is fixed here because the rounding now happens on the whole value, before it is split into a whole and a fractional part, and `writeDecimalFractional` no longer rounds at all. It costs one big-integer division instead of two, and it is covered by `04907_to_decimal_string_rounding_carry`. ## What is left What remains for a `Decimal256` is no longer in `itoa`: 93% of the time is now in `DecimalUtils::getWholePart` and `getFractionalPart`, which divide by the scale multiplier through the same slow `wide::integer` path. That is in `Core/DecimalFunctions.h` and used far more widely, so it is left alone here. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Formatting `Decimal` values as text is much faster — up to 190 times for a `Decimal256` with a large scale, and about 1.6 times for a `Decimal64`. On processors with AVX-512 IFMA, converting 64-bit integers to text is about 1.4 times faster. Also fixed the rounding of `toDecimalString`, which dropped a carry out of the fractional part: `toDecimalString(toDecimal64('9.995', 3), 2)` returned `9.00` and now returns `10.00`.

signals.title: Do not deserialize a skip index whose on-disk type is stale
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112213 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106988 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading a stale secondary (skip) index after an `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` type change whose mutation never ran, for example because `KILL MUTATION` removed it: the granules on disk were written with the old type but decoded with the new one, raising `LOGICAL_ERROR`, requesting multi-exabyte allocations, or silently returning a wrong result. Also fixes a wrong result from an index over an expression whose meaning changes while every stored byte stays identical, so no mutation is created at all: a `MODIFY COLUMN` altering only a `DateTime` timezone, or only a custom type name such as `UInt8` to `Bool`. Such an index is now skipped for the affected part. Closes #112213. ### Description `MODIFY COLUMN` updates table metadata at once and schedules a mutation to rewrite the parts. Until it runs, a part's granules hold bytes written with the OLD type while index analysis decodes them with the NEW one. The read gate `canUseIndex` infers that mismatch from a *pending mutation entry* and fails open when there is none. Six measured ways reach the deserializer anyway, including `KILL MUTATION` having removed the entry (the report) and conversions for which no mutation is ever created, being metadata-only for the column but not for the index. The top-k minmax read had no gate at all. **The fix** asks the durable question instead: do the part's bytes match the type about to decode them? It lands in `IMergeTreeIndex::getDeserializedFormat`, which already receives the part, so one predicate covers every read path. Physical discovery splits off into a virtual `getPhysicalFormat`, leaving `getDeserializedFormat` **non-virtual** so no override bypasses it. Each required column's part-side type, taken from the part's own list rather than the type-erasing interned cache, is compared against the metadata type: only representation-preserving differences pass, plus a `getName()` same-meaning check on the equals-equal path. The walk recurses pairwise through `Array`, `Nullable` and `LowCardinality`; adding or dropping a wrapper is refused. A non-trivial expression index is refused on any difference. Over-firing costs pruning, not correctness. Two `MergeTask` text-index sites share the predicate, so a stale text index is rebuilt during a merge instead of hardlinked forward. **Out of scope:** index *identity* staleness (a changed expression, a name reused after a killed `DROP INDEX`), which no type check detects. <details><summary>Measured symptoms on master, and validation</summary> | target type | observed on master | |---|---| | `Nullable(UInt64)` | `LOGICAL_ERROR: Sizes of nested column and null map ... not equal after deserialization` | | `Nullable(UInt64)` release / `UInt64` / absent-column part | `Code: 241`, 4 / 2 / 4 EiB | | `Array(UInt64)` | `Code: 33`, "read just 38 of 18005230136" | | `Int8` to `Enum8` | wrong: prunes a granule the unindexed read rejects (`Code: 691`) | | `DateTime('UTC')` to `DateTime('Asia/Tokyo')`, `INDEX toHour(dt)` | wrong: 0 vs 3 | | `UInt8` to `Bool`, `INDEX toString(v)` | wrong: 0 vs 32 | | `Tuple(x UInt8)` to `Tuple(x Bool)`, `INDEX toString(p.x)` | wrong: 0 vs 32 | `04165_skip_index_stale_type_after_alter.sql`: 29 cases covering the above, whose 21 control fixtures carry 25 `explain ILIKE` granule assertions pinning the over-fire direction (a simple single-column index across the timezone and `Bool` ALTERs, an unchanged subcolumn index, an unchanged `JSON(a DateTime)` column). On the base commit the test **kills the server** with the reported stack (`SerializationNullable.cpp:178` <- `MergeTreeIndexGranuleSet::deserializeBinary` <- `MergeTreeIndexReader::read` <- `filterMarksUsingIndex`); with the fix it passes 50/50. 36 mutations each confirm one line is load-bearing. A 462-test A/B sweep against pure HEAD leaves the failure set unchanged (27 in both arms, all needing infra this sandbox lacks). Perf over 250 parts and 4 indexes is inside noise. No setting or format changes. #110050 overlaps these files and its helper asks the *physical* question, so it should forward to `getPhysicalFormat` on rebase. My #109616 has since merged and independently reached the same physical-vs-usability split, so it needs no forwarding. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108096&sha=25f51f1fddd05350d9c5aa1231aa0e7ee6fc676f&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 </details> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1470` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
