signals.title: Add experimental Wallaby floating-point compression codec
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110613 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the experimental `Wallaby` lossless compression codec for `Float32` and `Float64` columns: it adaptively picks the cheapest of constant, decimal (Frame-of-Reference or zigzag-delta bit-packing, with PFOR-style patching and ULP-adjustment lanes), or XOR encoding per 1024-value block. Gated behind the `allow_experimental_codecs` setting. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation.** This follows the evaluation of the `Chimp` codec proposal (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467) and of the newer floating-point compression literature: `ALP` (SIGMOD 2024), `Elf` (VLDB 2023), `Camel` (SIGMOD 2025), `Kangaroo` (SIGMOD 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3802076, in production in Alibaba Lindorm since 2024), and the independent evaluation "Beyond Compression" (PVLDB 18(11), 2025). No single family dominates: integerization (`ALP`) wins on decimal-mappable data and decompression speed; the XOR family wins on non-decimal and mixed-precision data; run-length collapse wins on repetitive IoT data. `Wallaby` picks per 1024-value block, and its delta-packing of integerized values exploits time-series smoothness that neither `ALP` (plain Frame-of-Reference) nor the XOR codecs use. **Patent note.** The mantissa-erasure preprocessing shared by `Elf`, `Elf+`, `SElf*` and `Kangaroo` (erasing low mantissa bits derived from the decimal-place count and exponent) is covered by patent US 12,289,120 B2 (Chongqing University, granted 2025-04-29), including the decompression side. `Wallaby` deliberately does not implement it. All building blocks used here are prior art or openly licensed: `Gorilla` XOR (2015), windowed references with an explicit index (Chimp128, VLDB 2022), integerization with FOR bit-packing (`ALP`, MIT-licensed reference, already in ClickHouse as the shared `FFOR` helper), and delta/zigzag/run-length encoding. The encoder-side reference search is three O(1) hash probes, not Kangaroo's LZ-history algorithm; the on-disk format is original. **Decimal-scale chooser.** The decimal scale (`alpha`, now signed) is chosen per vector by measurement, not by a fixed rule: candidates are generated from four sources (the scales of 32 sampled values, with the sample grown up to 256 exactly when a stronger pruning bound would pay for itself; the trailing-decimal-zero structure of the quantized reference, which enumerates scales at which subsets of the vector become exact; the minimal scales of exception values, which discovers a high-precision minority the sample missed; and the exact scales behind tolerant votes, for when a voted scale fails on the rest of the vector), each candidate is evaluated against the full vector, and the smallest measured payload wins. Exceptions are bounded only by a size-based budget — a candidate is abandoned exactly when its exceptions alone already make it larger than the best encoding known for this vector, or when the running width of its packed lanes provably cannot come in under it. Pruning uses only provable bounds (counted sampled failures and failure carry-over from wider scales — never width extrapolation, which can prune true winners), so the chooser never skips a scale that could win. The scale that won the previous vector is evaluated first, and homogeneous vectors stay at a single full pass. **Lane capping, ULP-adjustment lanes, signed scales** (added after reading the pcodec, `ALP`, and FastLanes internals). The packed lane width can be capped below the widest value, exiling outliers into the existing exception list — PFOR-style patching, chosen in closed form from a width histogram for Frame-of-Reference and by an exact chain walk for the delta lanes. Values that integerize only up to a small distance are absorbed by a second bit-packed lane set of zigzag ULP adjustments instead of 10-byte raw exceptions (the idea behind pcodec's `FloatMult`): decimals disturbed by lossy arithmetic — a `Float32` round trip, a unit conversion — no longer force the vector to XOR. The scale is signed as in `ALP`'s `(e, f)` factorization: a negative scale divides by a power of ten, so integers ending in decimal zeros (cents, millisecond timestamps holding whole seconds) pack their cofactors, including magnitudes beyond the `Int64` domain. The XOR window search additionally probes the previous value's lookback distance, which interleaved series keep hitting. Per vector, the candidates compete on the cheaper of the exception list and the adjustment lanes, and only the winner takes one capping pass. These mechanisms are what moved sensors `temperature` −7 %, sensors `pressure` −3 %, weather `tempMax` −2.7 %, and the synthetic `smooth gauge` −11 % against the previous revision of the tables below. **Synthetic benchmarks** (this machine, `clickhouse local`, 10M `Float64` values per dataset, `max_threads = 1`, compressed size after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`; insert is the best of 3 runs, `SELECT` is `sum(x)`, mean of 5 runs; `PCO` is the pcodec Rust crate linked as a codec by #110613, compiled into the same binary, at its default level 8; smallest size and fastest insert / select per row in bold — times are in seconds, lower is better; dataset-specific, not a general claim. The `Chimp` numbers in the previous revision of this description were measured against an older encoder revision and are omitted; the qualitative picture for `Chimp` — robust on non-decimal data, slow to decompress — is unchanged): | Dataset | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | FPC | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | sine+2dp noise — size | 33.5 MB | 81.9 MB | 68.7 MB | 22.7 MB | **11.4 MB** | 15.2 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.45 / 0.098 | 0.93 / 0.092 | 0.80 / 0.079 | 0.32 / **0.019** | 1.01 / 0.079 | **0.31** / 0.024 | | random walk 3dp — size | 32.6 MB | 66.0 MB | 64.1 MB | 20.0 MB | 14.6 MB | **13.9 MB** | | — insert / select, s | 0.41 / 0.085 | **0.15** / 0.081 | **0.15** / 0.075 | 0.30 / **0.018** | 0.95 / 0.061 | 0.31 / 0.024 | | prices 2dp (no smoothness) — size | 41.2 MB | 72.5 MB | 74.7 MB | **25.2 MB** | 25.8 MB | 25.2 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.46 / 0.104 | 0.17 / 0.085 | **0.15** / 0.082 | 0.32 / **0.019** | 0.85 / 0.056 | 0.43 / 0.025 | | repeats (runs of 100k) — size | **0.06 MB** | 1.3 MB | 5.0 MB | 0.39 MB | 0.07 MB | 0.13 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.08 / 0.013 | **0.07** / 0.017 | 0.13 / 0.054 | 0.24 / 0.012 | 0.14 / 0.018 | 0.08 / **0.010** | | smooth gauge (full precision) — size | 74.5 MB | 66.6 MB | 54.4 MB | 70.2 MB | **15.5 MB** | 52.0 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.19 / 0.089 | 0.16 / 0.085 | **0.14** / 0.074 | 0.30 / **0.030** | 1.31 / 0.064 | 1.01 / 0.043 | | real doubles (sin×exp) — size | 78.6 MB | 82.5 MB | 73.9 MB | 80.1 MB | **64.1 MB** | 78.2 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.21 / 0.090 | 0.17 / 0.091 | **0.15** / 0.078 | 0.38 / **0.021** | 1.11 / 0.065 | 0.79 / 0.123 | | random bits (incompressible) — size | 80.0 MB | 82.5 MB | 85.0 MB | 80.1 MB | **80.0 MB** | 80.0 MB | | — insert / select, s | **0.12** / 0.023 | 0.23 / 0.091 | 0.15 / 0.081 | 0.27 / **0.022** | 0.79 / **0.022** | 0.50 / **0.022** | **Real datasets** (from the [sample datasets](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/sample-datasets): [ClickBench hits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench), 100M rows — it has no `Float` columns, so representative numeric columns are cast to `Float32`/`Float64`, which is exactly the "floats that are really integers" shape common in practice; [mgbench](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/brown-benchmark) `logs1` machine metrics, 22M rows, `Nullable(Float32)` as in the reference schema; [environmental sensors](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/environmental-sensors) 2019-06 BME280, 31.2M rows, `Float32`; [NOAA weather](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/noaa), 100M rows, tenths stored as `Float32` with 1 decimal). All columns are pre-sorted by the reference schema's `ORDER BY`; compressed size of the column after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`, one binary for all codecs. Best floating-point codec in bold; `ZSTD(3)` shown as the generic-compression baseline: | Column | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | 44.5 MB | 86.1 MB | 88.9 MB | **66.8 MB** | 71.1 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | 32.0 MB | 75.5 MB | 79.0 MB | **53.8 MB** | 58.0 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 73.9 MB | 82.5 MB | **53.7 MB** | 65.5 MB | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 132.3 MB | 59.6 MB | 64.9 MB | **55.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 125.4 MB | 55.7 MB | 82.8 MB | **55.5 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 131.9 MB | 98.1 MB | **79.7 MB** | 95.1 MB | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 102.3 MB | 33.9 MB | **24.5 MB** | 29.3 MB | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | 144.5 MB | 131.9 MB | **33.3 MB** | 72.2 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | 244.4 MB | 215.9 MB | **128.1 MB** | 215.9 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | 37.9 MB | 52.5 MB | 141.7 MB | **43.1 MB** | 46.6 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | 149.7 MB | 152.4 MB | 684.2 MB | **120.3 MB** | 155.2 MB | Compression / decompression time on the same runs, in seconds — lower is better, best per row in bold (insert best-of-3 / `sum(x)` mean-of-5, `max_threads = 1`; the select column includes the scan-and-sum overhead): | Column | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | 0.43 / 0.12 | **0.24** / 0.15 | 0.35 / **0.06** | 0.95 / 0.10 | 2.00 / 0.19 | | mgbench `cpu_user` | 0.39 / 0.10 | **0.22** / 0.14 | 0.33 / **0.05** | 0.79 / 0.10 | 1.66 / 0.16 | | mgbench `mem_free` | 0.37 / 0.13 | **0.24** / 0.15 | 0.26 / **0.05** | 1.05 / 0.10 | 1.46 / 0.16 | | sensors `temperature` | 0.80 / 0.18 | 0.32 / 0.21 | **0.30** / **0.06** | 1.72 / 0.16 | 1.71 / **0.06** | | sensors `humidity` | 0.76 / 0.18 | 0.34 / 0.21 | **0.30** / **0.05** | 1.51 / 0.12 | 1.91 / 0.06 | | sensors `pressure` | 0.42 / 0.15 | 0.33 / 0.21 | **0.31** / **0.06** | 1.65 / 0.11 | 2.49 / 0.07 | | weather `tempMax` | 0.76 / 0.17 | **0.54** / 0.27 | 0.57 / **0.10** | 1.31 / 0.20 | 1.00 / **0.10** | | weather `precipitation` | 1.16 / 0.33 | **0.70** / 0.45 | 1.14 / **0.13** | 3.02 / 0.53 | 2.98 / 0.40 | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 3.31 / 1.09 | **1.02** / 0.57 | 2.59 / **0.16** | 6.59 / 0.47 | 3.19 / 0.18 | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | 0.94 / 0.28 | **0.60** / 0.34 | 0.91 / **0.12** | 2.32 / 0.34 | 1.70 / 0.31 | | hits `UserID` (F64) | 1.57 / 0.42 | **0.85** / 0.45 | 2.16 / **0.24** | 3.42 / 0.44 | 3.33 / 0.50 | **Encoder cost.** Compared with the previous revision of this table, compression is 1.2–2.8x slower while decompression is unchanged or slightly faster (`smooth gauge` decodes 44 % faster now that a decimal mode wins it instead of XOR). Benchmarking the intermediate revision that contains only the provable-bound chooser rework attributes the cost: on the mgbench and sensors `temperature` columns that rework alone accounts for 60–80 % of the slowdown (`load_one` 0.81 → 1.74 s of the final 2.00 s), while on sensors `pressure` and hits `EventTime` the wider candidate space that the new mechanisms open dominates (1.43 → 2.49 s and 2.15 → 3.19 s). The trade was made knowingly: the size wins above come from the same revisions, and the encoder keeps a running lane-width floor that abandons hopeless scans mid-vector and a double-buffered winner so no scale is quantized twice. **Comparison with PCodec.** `PCO` is the strongest competitor overall. On ratio it is the smallest floating-point codec on 9 of the 11 columns, and the standalone `pco` CLI compressing each column as one chunk does better still (e.g. mgbench `load_one` 36.7 MB, weather `precipitation` 32.2 MB): per-64-KiB-block operation costs pcodec 20-45 % of its ratio, since every block re-learns its tANS tables and delta state. On compression speed the two are now roughly at parity — `Wallaby` up to 2x faster on the hits columns and weather `tempMax`, `PCO` up to 2x faster on the mgbench and sensor columns. On decompression `PCO` is 1.5–2.7x slower than `Wallaby` on the columns where a `Wallaby` decimal mode wins (sensors, weather `tempMax`, hits `EventTime`) and *faster* on the XOR-mode columns (mgbench, hits `UserID`) — the serial XOR bitstream is the slowest of `Wallaby`'s decode paths, while pcodec's decode cost is uniform. Against `ALP`, `Wallaby` is smaller on all 11 columns — dramatically so where `ALP`'s Frame-of-Reference degenerates (hits `UserID` 155 MB vs 684 MB, hits `ResolutionWidth` 47 MB vs 142 MB, weather `precipitation` 72 MB vs 132 MB). A correction to earlier revisions of this description: in-engine `PCO` was previously reported as 10-70x slower. That measurement came from a local build affected by a build-system bug that compiles all vendored Rust code with `opt-level = 0` unless `-DSANITIZE=` is passed explicitly (a `contrib/corrosion-cmake` condition mistakes `SANITIZE=OFF` for an enabled sanitizer; CI is unaffected because it always passes the flag). The numbers above are from a corrected build; a separate fix for the build system is being prepared. **Where `Wallaby` is not the winner.** On columns dominated by entropy redundancy rather than numeric structure — the three mgbench columns, weather `precipitation`, hits `ResolutionWidth`/`UserID` — plain `ZSTD` and/or `PCO` produce smaller data. Chaining helps exactly there, because the XOR/EQUAL residues are more entropy-codable than raw floats: | Column | `ZSTD(3)` | `ALP, ZSTD` | `Wallaby, ZSTD` | |---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | **44.5 MB** | 56.0 MB | 49.0 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | **32.0 MB** | 46.1 MB | 35.6 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 54.4 MB | **42.4 MB** | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 58.2 MB | **54.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 55.1 MB | **55.0 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 97.8 MB | **90.1 MB** | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 29.2 MB | **27.6 MB** | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | **54.6 MB** | 65.7 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | **212.8 MB** | 213.0 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | **37.9 MB** | 57.8 MB | 43.2 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | **149.7 MB** | 192.5 MB | 154.5 MB | `CODEC(Wallaby, ZSTD)` is the best of the three on 5 of the 11 columns — on the sensor columns and weather `tempMax` now by a clear margin where the previous revision tied `ALP, ZSTD` — and within 0.1 % on `EventTime`. The interesting exception is `precipitation`, where `ALP, ZSTD` wins because `ALP`'s plain Frame-of-Reference lanes on zero-dominated data are almost pure zero bytes, which `ZSTD` collapses better than `Wallaby`'s already-compact XOR runs. Side observation from benchmarking (independent of this PR): for `Nullable` columns the null-map substream appears to be stored uncompressed (+1 byte per row for every codec, including `LZ4`/`ZSTD`) — visible as a constant +22 MB / +31.2 MB across all codecs on the mgbench / sensors columns. Worth a separate look. Correctness: bit-exact round trip is verified by the encoder for every value with a per-value raw-exception fallback (`NaN` payloads, infinities, denormals, signed zeros, arbitrary bit patterns are all preserved; verified on random bit patterns and on all real datasets by multiset checksums in tests; the sensors dataset contributes 9298 genuine `NaN` values). The decoder validates all lengths and bounds, so corrupt input causes an exception, not undefined behavior; a decompression fuzzer target is included. An adversarial review of the current revision additionally round-tripped ~15M hostile values (per-block scale flips, `NaN` payloads, subnormals, domain edges) bit-exactly on both float widths. Note on the `NativeFormat` spec: the spec enumerates the column codec method bytes accepted on the `decompress=1` input path, so this PR adds the `0xa0` (`Wallaby`) entry with an experimental-status note, matching the existing `SZ3`/`Quantized`/`ZXC` entries. #### CI Settings (Only check the boxes if you know what you are doing): - [ ] Allow: All Required Checks - [ ] Allow: Stateless tests - [ ] Allow: Stateful tests - [ ] Allow: Integration Tests - [ ] Allow: Performance tests - [ ] Allow: All Builds - [ ] Allow: batch 1, 2 for multi-batch jobs - [ ] Allow: batch 3, 4, 5, 6 for multi-batch jobs --- - [ ] Exclude: Style check - [ ] Exclude: Fast test - [ ] Exclude: All with ASAN - [ ] Exclude: All with TSAN, MSAN, UBSAN, Coverage - [ ] Exclude: All with aarch64, release, debug --- - [ ] Do not test - [ ] Woolen Wolfdog - [ ] Upload binaries for special builds - [ ] Disable merge-commit - [ ] Disable CI cache

signals.title: Add a "private preview" feature tier between experimental and beta
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113481 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new `private preview` feature tier between `experimental` and `beta`, so feature tiers are now ordered `experimental < private preview < beta < production`. The server setting `allow_feature_tier` gains a level: `0` allows all tiers, `1` excludes experimental, `2` additionally excludes private preview, and `3` allows production settings only. Configurations that previously pinned `allow_feature_tier = 2` to allow production settings only must now use `3`. Closes #113481. ### Description Adds a fourth maturity tier for features that are on a clear path to general availability but whose applicability is still limited and which are not recommended for production use. Requested in #113481; the numbering below was confirmed by the issue author. `allow_feature_tier` becomes a four-level gate. Only `2` changes meaning: `0` still grants everything, and `1` still grants everything except experimental, because the tier it newly admits contains no setting (this change deliberately moves no existing setting into the new tier). `3` is new and carries today's `2` semantics. The single upgrade-visible change is that a server pinned at `allow_feature_tier = 2` gains beta writability. `Flags::TIER` was two bits with all four encodings taken, so it is widened to three (`0x0c` -> `0x1c`). Every pre-existing encoding decodes identically under the wider mask, and the new tier is appended (`= 16`) rather than inserted, so no existing value of the user-visible `system.settings.tier` enum moves. The tier bits are never serialized: the only flags ever written to the wire are `IMPORTANT` and `CUSTOM`, so no wire format changes and no protocol-version guard is needed. `BaseSettingsHelpers::getTier`'s range check is the tree's only relational comparison on the enum and is re-keyed to the new maximum; every other consumer tests one specific tier, and all of them gain an explicit branch so the tier is neither silently ungated nor silently unreported. Documentation is the `DECLARE` doc string, which the nightly docs job regenerates; no `.mdx` is edited by hand. `allow_feature_tier` is a server setting, so `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` (which tracks user-level `Settings`) does not apply. Related, no overlap in behaviour: #113156 edits the same two functions in `SettingsConstraints.cpp` and `MergeTreeSettings.cpp`, but the two merge cleanly in either order and the merged `sanityCheck` carries both changes, so neither blocks the other. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1490` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Honor an explicit structure argument for data lake table function reads
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113361 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the `structure` argument of the `paimon*` and `iceberg*` table functions being reported by `DESCRIBE` but ignored by `SELECT`, so one expression yielded two schemas and a declared column absent from the lake metadata failed with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` after `DESCRIBE` had listed it. An explicit `structure` is now used for reads, as it already was for `s3` and `file`, so it can select a subset of the columns or override their types; a declared type the data files cannot supply now raises an error instead of silently using the metadata schema. Inserts, the persistent `Paimon*`/`Iceberg*` engines and `deltaLake*` are unchanged. Closes #113361. ### Description `DESC paimonLocal(p, 'Parquet', 'f_int Int64')` reported `Int64` while `SELECT toTypeName(f_int)` on the same expression reported `Nullable(Int32)`. `icebergLocal` diverged too. The table function was already correct: `getActualTableStructure` parses the argument (what `DESC` reads) and `executeImpl` passes the same columns to the storage. The storage then replaced the whole `StorageInMemoryMetadata`, columns included, whenever the per-format schema reload was enabled, unconditional for Paimon and Iceberg. That happens at five sites, one on every query, so fixing the constructor is not enough. A `preserve_structure_for_reads` flag is now computed in both table function `executeImpl` overrides and retained by both storage classes, set only when a structure was supplied, the query is not an `INSERT`, and the format's schema reload is not a user opt-in. All five reload sites go through one helper that still pins `datalake_table_state` unconditionally and, when the flag is set, keeps the declared columns. The snapshot's sorting key is resolved against the metadata schema, and read-in-order consumes it together with the columns, so once the columns are final the key is kept only while every column its expression reads is still present with the same type. A cluster initiator injects its own resolved columns, which are the snapshot's, so a worker keeps the key; a declared type that retypes or omits a key column clears it everywhere. Deliberately unchanged, each measured: the persistent engines, where a DDL column list creates the remote schema; `INSERT INTO TABLE FUNCTION iceberg*(...)`; `DatabaseDataLake` catalog tables; and `deltaLake*`, whose reload is an opt-in. A conflicting structure now fails in the reader; a subset or compatible override works, as for plain `file`. The new stateless test asserts `DESC` and `SELECT` on one expression: green with the change and red without, with ten live lines and twenty-one controls.

signals.title: Do not pin non-serializable placeholder columns into the INTERPOLATE step
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111919 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL ... INTERPOLATE` being rejected with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` when the query also contains an `IN` predicate and runs with `enable_parallel_replicas = 1` (`Serialization is not implemented for data type Set`), or when it selects a lambda expression such as `arrayMap(x -> x || s, ['a'])` (`Cannot insert into Function`, reachable on a single node). ### Description `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL ... INTERPOLATE` made the "Before INTERPOLATE" step declare every column still available in the actions chain as one of its own outputs. Two types in that set have no serialization: the placeholder of an `IN` set (`Set`) and of a lambda (`Function`). Both derive from `IDataTypeDummy`, whose `getSerialization` throws. Pinning such a column as a step output has two user-visible consequences. * Under parallel replicas the placeholder reaches the pipeline output header of a replica producing a mergeable state, and `NativeWriter` cannot send that header: `Code: 48 ... Serialization is not implemented for data type Set`. Deterministic with `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 0` (30 of 30 trials) and intermittent at its default of 1 (8 of 100 trials). * For a lambda no distributed boundary is needed: `FillingTransform` inserts a default into every header column when it synthesizes a filled row, and the placeholder cannot accept one, so a single-node query fails with `Code: 48 ... Cannot insert into Function`. The fix skips those columns when the step's outputs are built. `Set` and `Function` are the complete set of query-plan-reachable types with no serialization: of the three `IDataTypeDummy` subclasses in `src/DataTypes/`, only these two inherit the throwing `doGetSerialization`, while `DataTypeNothing` overrides it and returns a working `SerializationNothing`. That is also why `Nullable(Nothing)` and `Array(Nothing)` travel in headers today and must keep doing so. Every storable column is still pinned as before, so `EXPLAIN PLAN header = 1` is unchanged for any query that works today. This is a residual of the family closed by #111919. That change gated the two sites that *execute* filling, which is correct; the defect is that the step's DAG hoards columns it does not need. None of the 6 stateless tests it shipped uses `IN`. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, one server with a 3-replica `test_cluster_one_shard_three_replicas_localhost`, restarted per arm with `SELECT lower(buildId())` asserted equal to the binary's own build id before every verdict. Both directions, through `tests/clickhouse-test`: the new test fails on unpatched master with `Code: 48 ... data type Set` and passes with the fix. 50 of 50 randomized runs pass with the fix and 50 of 50 fail on unpatched master, so it is not vacuous. The test pins `serialize_query_plan = 0` (as all six tests #111919 shipped do), `enable_analyzer = 1` and `automatic_parallel_replicas_mode = 0`. Each pin was verified load-bearing by removing it and re-running under the CI condition it defends against, reproduced with the real `tests/config/users.d` overlay. Three mutants, each reddening on a distinct error and pinning one rejected alternative: | mutant | error | |---|---| | no filter at all (unpatched master) | `Code: 48` `data type Set` | | filter on `cannotBeStoredInTables()` | `Code: 47` `Unknown column: _CAST`, since it also drops `Nullable(Nothing)` / `Array(Nothing)` | | add the columns as DAG inputs only | `Code: 10` `Not found column __table1.inter2`: an INTERPOLATE expression may reference a column the `SELECT` does not project, and the output pin is what keeps it alive | Name-scoped regression suite (`interpolate` / `with_fill`, 62 runnable tests including the new one, randomization off): 62 verdicts per arm, the fix scoring 61 pass / 1 fail and unpatched master 60 pass / 2 fail. The only-in-fix failure set is empty and the only-in-base one is exactly the new test. The remaining shared failure is `04064_unused_interpolate_columns_without_wrapper`, which carries `no-parallel-replicas` and cannot pass in a parallel-replicas rig (#75186); its three `EXPLAIN PLAN header = 1` outputs were compared directly instead and are byte-identical to its committed reference on both arms. </details>

signals.title: TimeSeries: Pack cold buckets of the `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate states into delta-encoded blobs
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113681 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate functions (PromQL `rate`, `increase`, `delta`, and relatives) now pack finished grid buckets into delta-encoded blobs: a 30-day high-cardinality `rate` query needs 29 GiB of aggregation state instead of 44 GiB and no longer spills to disk, and the states now survive memory-limit exceptions that previously crashed the server under `optimize_aggregation_in_order`. ### Description Builds on #113681 (sorted-append sample container); this PR will rebase after it merges. New commits on top: - Pack cold buckets of the `timeSeries*ToGrid` states into delta-encoded blobs. - Add a regression test for the in-order aggregation segfault under memory pressure. #### Problem The `timeSeries*ToGrid` states buffer every in-window sample as a raw 16-byte `(timestamp, value)` pair until finalization. A 30-day `sum by (ns) (rate(...[5m]))` over 25,600 series peaks at 44 GiB of aggregation state and forces external-aggregation spill on 16-vCPU machines. The old absl hash-map buckets also crashed under memory pressure: a memory-limit exception inside a rehash left a broken map, and the unwind freed garbage pointers. #### Change A bucket now has two lossless representations. It stays a raw sorted vector while the query writes to it. It becomes a packed blob when the write cursor leaves it, when it outgrows a threshold, or on deserialization. The blob delta-encodes timestamps (zigzag-varint delta-of-delta) and tokenizes values; the encoder emits a compact token only if it decodes back to the exact bit pattern. Late samples stay exact: an append past the packed range is O(1), and an interior add unpacks the bucket back to the raw path. The wire format and `FORMAT_VERSION` are unchanged: packed buckets serialize in the old count+pairs layout, so mixed-version peers interoperate. All state containers are now strongly exception-safe; this fixes the crash class above (a segfault during in-order merges under a memory cap). Duplicate timestamps now deduplicate under the IEEE-754 total order; results change only where they previously depended on arrival order (NaN or ±0.0 at a duplicated timestamp). #### Measured effect tsbench corpus: 62.5 B samples, 361 k series. Hardware: 32-core workstation (nikita-office). Cold = first run after server start, median of 3 alternating rounds. The baseline is the benchmark master build, 656 commits older than the branch base — see the attribution note. | query | cold before | cold after | Δ wall | peak memory | external-agg spill | |---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | c01: 30 d `sum by (ns) (rate(cpu[5m]))`, 25.6 k series | 61.1 s | 28.8 s | −52.9% | 44.1 → 29.0 GiB | 16.3 GiB in 3/3 rounds → none | | c03: 30 d fleet p95 (control; does not use the patched state) | 34.2 s | 19.7 s | −42.5% | 6.4 GiB (=) | none | | s09: 6 h memory RSS by ns | 3.5 s | 2.6 s | −26.2% | 0.99 → 0.85 GiB | none | | s11: 24 h CPU by ns | 4.3 s | 4.2 s | −3.5% | 3.3 GiB (=) | none | - Attribution: the c03/s09/s11 deltas are master drift, mostly #113580; those queries do not use the patched container. The peak-memory drop, the spill exit, and the crash fix come from this PR. At 32 threads with no spill, wall time is near neutral. - 16-thread run, 30 GB cap, 15 GB absolute spill trigger (c6a mimic): c01 goes 41.5 → 31.7 s (−23.6%), CPU 624 → 484 s. It still spills there (29 GiB of state > 15 GB trigger); spilled bytes stay equal by design, because spill writes the unchanged wire format. - Isolated container benchmark (5,000 series × 200,000 samples, 32 threads): ~250 samples per bucket cut peak query memory 15.4 → 3.0 GiB (5.2×) at 1.7× better wall time. - Both sides read identical data (c01: 4.424 B rows). c03/s09 results are byte-identical across all rounds; c01/s11 match within 1.0e-15 relative, the same class and magnitude as baseline-vs-baseline controls (pre-existing parallel float-sum nondeterminism). #### Tests New stateless tests: `04816` (all codec token classes, NaN/−0.0 dedup, `AggregatingMergeTree` and `remote()` roundtrips), `04817` (8 M rows aggregate under a 100 MiB memory cap), `04818` (the in-order segfault repro in `clickhouse-local`: the pre-fix binary crashes 6/6 across 180–250 MB caps, the fixed binary passes and its fingerprint equals plain hash aggregation). All 47 timeseries/PromQL stateless tests pass. #### Related - #113681 — sorted-append sample container (base of this PR) - #113580 — `getGroupByID` memoization (in master; the main drift component above) - #113644 — group by raw series id - #113656 — streaming `topk`/`bottomk` Future work: fold each series state into one blob per state. This removes the 12-sample pack threshold that leaves step-60 Grafana shapes raw, estimated ~4× further state reduction on c01. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: Retry the SQLStorm repo clones so one transient timeout cannot abort the check
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `SQLStorm test` failed on step `Clone OLAPBench repo` after a single attempt: ``` fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/SQL-Storm/OLAPBench.git/': Failed to connect to github.com port 443 after 135221 ms: Connection timed out ERROR: command failed after 1/1 attempt(s), exit code: 128 ``` `Shell.check` forwards `retries` to `Shell.run` and both default to `retries=1` (`ci/praktika/utils.py:231`, `:323`), and neither clone in `ci/jobs/sqlstorm_test.py` opted in. Because every later step is gated on `results[-1].is_ok()`, one transient egress timeout to a third-party host aborted a check whose budget is 3 hours. This passes `retries=3` to both `git clone` calls, matching the existing git-clone retry at `ci/jobs/docker_server.py:439-444`. The sibling SQLStorm clone has identical exposure, so both are fixed. Measured, driving the real closures with the upstream command strings and a git shim that reproduces the observed failure (rc=128, and git removes its own partial target, so a retry starts clean): | attempts that fail | before | after | |---|---|---| | 1 (the observed failure) | fails, `1/1` | succeeds on attempt 2 | | 2 | fails, `1/1` | succeeds on attempt 3 | | all | fails, `1/1` | fails, `3/3` | A genuine outage still fails the check, with the full stderr, and each argument is independently load-bearing. Worst case on a permanent outage is about 6.8 min, 3.8% of the 10,800 s job budget; a fast permanent error costs 6.0 s. The `fetch` branches, taken when the repo directory already exists, now carry the same `retries=3` and measure the same way. That branch is unreachable in CI, since every job block scheduling this check runs an unconditional `rm -rf ./ci/tmp` before the run step, but it is reachable on a local rerun, where no workflow step runs and praktika never removes its temp dir. Both `git checkout` calls are local only. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1505` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Support GCS vended credentials in Unity Catalog
signals.text: Unity Catalog on GCS vends an OAuth token in `gcp_oauth_token`, but `UnityCatalog` only parsed AWS temporary credentials for S3-compatible locations. As a result, table metadata could be listed while reads failed because no storage credentials were created. Parse the GCP OAuth token as `GCSCredentials` for both initial credential resolution and refresh. Add focused coverage for GCS parsing and refresh while preserving the existing S3 behavior, and update the user-facing support descriptions. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110149 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support Unity Catalog vended credentials for tables stored in GCS.

signals.title: Check the query cancellation while filling `system.parts` and its siblings
signals.text: The tables based on `StorageSystemPartsBase` (`system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`) build the whole result eagerly in `initializePipeline`, so a cancelled or timed out query kept building rows over every storage and part until the very end. In a stress test with ThreadFuzzer this took minutes and tripped the hung check: a `SELECT` over `system.parts_columns` (with a filter matching every active part on the server) stayed in the process list for 252 seconds with `is_cancelled = 1` and `max_execution_time = 10`. Check the query status per storage and per part, following the pattern of `system.zookeeper` and `system.remote_data_paths`. The check also covers the storage-discovery prepass in `StoragesInfoStream` (the eager enumeration of all databases and tables), the analogous prepass in `StoragesDroppedInfoStream` (so `system.dropped_tables_parts` is interruptible as well), the skip loop in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::next`, and the per-storage part enumeration itself: the `MergeTreeData` helpers (`getDataPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllDataPartsVector`, `getProjectionPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllProjectionPartsVector`) take an optional `need_stop` callback that is checked periodically while the parts snapshot is being built. The two column-oriented tables additionally check the query status inside their column-enumeration loops and their metadata prepass, so a very wide table does not create a long uninterruptible stretch inside a single storage. The return value of `checkTimeLimit` is honored, so with `timeout_overflow_mode = 'break'` the eager build stops at the soft deadline and returns the rows collected so far. The table-lock acquisition in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::tryLockTable` is interruptible as well: instead of a single wait inside `RWLockImpl::getLock` for the whole `lock_acquire_timeout`, the lock is acquired in 100 ms slices with a query-status poll between the attempts (the total timeout and the `DEADLOCK_AVOIDED` semantics are preserved), so a killed or soft-timed-out query does not sit in the lock wait while a concurrent DDL query holds the drop lock. The test `04869_system_parts_lock_wait_cancellation` pins this with a share lock held by a long `SELECT` and a `DROP TABLE` in an `Ordinary` database queued behind it. The test uses the new `slowdown_system_parts_enumeration` failpoint, which only affects the specially named test tables (so concurrently running tests are unaffected). It sleeps 500 ms on every enumerated part, so building the full result for a 20-part table takes at least 10 seconds, and it sleeps 1 second per `COLUMNS_CANCELLATION_CHECK_PERIOD` (128) enumerated columns of a part, so building the full `system.parts_columns` / `system.projection_parts_columns` result over a single part with 1,025 columns (and a projection over all of them) takes at least 8 seconds. The test asserts that queries with a 1 second deadline in the `break` mode finish well under that (the elapsed time is taken from `system.query_log`, because the startup of `clickhouse-client` alone takes seconds in the debug and sanitizer builds), which is only possible by stopping at the per-part and per-column cancellation checkpoints. Timed assertions are needed because a plain row-count assertion cannot distinguish a build with the fix from one without: in the `break` mode the executor drops the eagerly built result after the deadline in both cases. The test also asserts partial row counts under a pre-expired deadline for all five tables, including `system.dropped_tables_parts` over a deterministic dropped-table fixture. The pre-expired-deadline checks also run under the failpoint, so the fewer-rows assertion is deterministic even on a machine fast enough to build the whole result in under a millisecond. For tables with the `_snap` name marker, the failpoint additionally slows down the parts-snapshot walks inside `MergeTreeData` (500 ms per enumerated part) and makes them poll the stop callback on every element, and for tables with the `_meta` name marker it slows down the column-metadata prepass of the column-oriented tables (1 second per 128 enumerated metadata columns), so the timed checks also prove that the snapshot materialization and the prepass are interruptible: all six of these checks fail against a binary with the `need_stop` polls and the prepass checkpoints disabled. Caught by `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113722&sha=ceedb772f6aa36e221d25ce48f9af71f032a7b08&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113722 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Queries over `system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`, and `system.dropped_tables_parts` now react to cancellation and `max_execution_time` while the result is being built.

signals.title: Parquet v3: never schedule a decode into a dropped prewhere output slot
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113841 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a `std::out_of_range` exception (`Logical error: 'std::exception. Code: 1001, type: std::out_of_range'`, which also aborts the server in debug and sanitizer builds) in the Parquet v3 reader when a column needed only for filter evaluation was scheduled for decoding after its output slot had already been dropped. ### Description Related: #113841 `RowSubgroup::output` is sized once per subgroup to `extended_sample_block.columns()`; its tail slots hold columns needed only for PREWHERE and filter evaluation. After the last PREWHERE step `applyPrewhere` pops those tail slots off, and nothing re-grows the vector. `ReadManager` runs the PREWHERE steps as step indices 1..N and the main step **last**, as step 0, selecting columns by `first_step_to_calculate == step_idx`. A primitive column still at `first_step_to_calculate == 0` whose `idx_in_output_block` lands in that tail is therefore decoded after the shrink, and `row_subgroup.output.at(idx_in_output_block)` throws `std::out_of_range`, which fails the query and, in debug and sanitizer builds, aborts the server from the reader's task pool. `Reader::preparePrewhere` now marks such a column with the `SIZE_MAX` sentinel step index that `ReadManager` never matches, the same state the existing injected-`covering.bbox` suppression already produces. A tail-and-unclaimed column has no consumer by construction: the delivered chunk is indexed over `sample_block->columns()`, and every PREWHERE step input gets `steps.size() + 1`. The truncation itself is unchanged. The upper bound against `extended_sample_block.columns()` is load-bearing: `idx_in_output_block` defaults to `UINT64_MAX` and is only `chassert`-checked, so without it an unresolved index would be suppressed silently in release builds. A PREWHERE that reads no file column reaches this from SQL: with `use_hive_partitioning = 1`, a WHERE on a hive partition column stays in the output tail because no PREWHERE step claims it. ```sql SET use_hive_partitioning = 1; SELECT count() FROM file('.../data_hive/partitioning/column0=Elizabeth/sample.parquet') PREWHERE 1 WHERE column0 = 'Elizabeth'; -- throws before this change, returns 101 after ``` All four CI occurrences are the AST fuzzer producing that shape against `03203_hive_style_partitioning`; the recovered query is in the [amd_asan_ubsan master report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=2c4490d11d1e70e9b10986e770308cfb431a63c4&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29). New test `04828_parquet_prewhere_hive_partition_column` covers it; the gtest additionally pins the unresolved-index boundary, which no query can construct. <details><summary>Validation</summary> Both directions, each arm on its own Build-ID-asserted binary. SQL: pre-fix `rc=134` 10/10 runs with `std::out_of_range` in `decodePrimitiveColumn` and the CI stack frame-for-frame; with the fix `rc=0` 10/10 returning `101`, which equals both the no-PREWHERE count and the total row count. Through `clickhouse-test`, the new test fails at the merge base (server dies, exit 134) and passes with the fix; `--test-runs 50` gives 50/50 and `-j 8` leaves no staging dirs. Mutation matrix, each arm its own asserted Build ID: | mutant | result | |---|---| | revert the suppression loop | gtest reddens on the `SIZE_MAX` assertion for the tail column | | drop the tail bound (suppress every step-0 column) | gtest reddens on the in-`sample_block` assertions; `04515` aborts `rc=134`, `04342` dies on `primitive_columns_remaining == 0` | | drop the `first_step_to_calculate == 0` test | gtest reddens on the claimed-PREWHERE-input assertion; `04342` dies the same way | | drop the `extended_sample_block` upper bound | gtest reddens on the unresolved-index case | | delete the pre-existing injected-bbox sentinel | geo pruning tests stay green, so the new loop subsumes it for those cases; the sentinel is kept regardless | Regression: 273 `parquet`/`geo`/`iceberg` stateless tests on both arms, compared as `Reason:`-bucketed sets: 0 verdict changes, 0 reason changes, 0 only-in-fix failures. 200/200 verdict lines pass over 20 randomized runs of the 10 environment-independent geo and prewhere tests. </details>

signals.title: Route old-leader reads through Raft in the Keeper compat snapshot test
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113022 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `test_keeper_snapshot_chunked_transfer/test.py::test_recover_from_snapshot_sent_by_old_leader` can hang for the full 900 s pytest-timeout and take its whole integration shard with it. The stall is not in the code under test. It is on `compat1` / `compat_s3_1`, pinned to the released `25.3` and `25.12` images. Those versions park a read that arrives while a write batch is assembling in `read_request_queue[<last write's session_id>][<that write's xid>]`, which can belong to a different session, and `finishSession` erases that whole session entry without responding. So when a writer session expires, a co-batched read from another session is dropped silently and the client waits on it forever. Master fixed that in 5eb8dd3be12cff3 ("Keeper: fix race between read requests and session close"), which also added `tests/integration/test_keeper_read_during_close`. Neither image has it, so nothing needs fixing in `src/`. In both pinned versions the only `read_request_queue` insertion is guarded by `!quorum_reads`, and the branch above it routes the read through the write path when that setting is on. This PR sets it on those two instances only, making the dropping path unreachable for every read they serve. The followers under test and the quorum fillers keep the default local reads. Bumping the images instead does not work: the earliest release carrying that commit is `26.4`, which is also the earliest release shipping `snapshot_transfer_chunk_size`, so it stops being a leader without chunking and the test's `n_chunks == 1` premise disappears. The test also asserts the effective setting read back from both servers via the 4LW `conf` command, so a later edit that drops the fragment fails there instead of silently restoring the hang. No existing assertion is weakened. Not addressed: `helpers/kazoo_client.py` calls `AsyncResult.get()` with no timeout, so a future lost response would still burn 900 s. That unbounded wait is what lets `test_keeper_read_during_close` detect a stuck reader, and 61 files reach it through `get_fake_zk`. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Config: `quorum_reads` present on exactly `compat1` + `compat_s3_1`, absent on the other four, and the merged effective config (4LW `conf`) still carries `operation_timeout_ms`, `session_timeout_ms`, `snapshot_distance`, `stale_log_gap`, `reserved_log_items` on both, so the fragment adds a setting rather than replacing the generated block. Mechanism, oracle = 4LW `lgif` `last_log_idx` (a quorum read is appended to the Raft log, a local read is not). 40 reads per node: | arm | compat1 (25.3) | compat_s3_1 (25.12) | compat3 (current build) | |---|---|---|---| | with fragment | +40 | +40 | +0 | | fragment set to `false` | +0 | +0 | +0 | A one-write control advances the index by 1 on every node in both arms, so the oracle is not vacuous. (`Processing requests batch` is not usable here: `LOG_TRACE` in 25.3 but `LOG_TEST` in 25.12.) Runs: both parametrizations 20/20 over 10 repeats; `test_keeper_read_during_close`, `test_keeper_snapshot_chunked_transfer/test_concurrent.py` and `test_keeper_snapshot_rotation_race/test.py` all pass unchanged. Cost: `[local_disk]` 38.4 s -> 39.8 s, `[remote_disk]` 32.2 s -> 36.7 s, module 119.9 s -> 126.5 s. </details>

signals.title: Do not derive a DISTINCT limit hint when the LIMIT must read till end
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111326 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results for `SELECT DISTINCT` with a `LIMIT` that has to read its whole input: `LIMIT n WITH TIES` dropped tying rows, `exact_rows_before_limit = 1` reported a truncated `rows_before_limit_at_least`, and `GROUP BY ... WITH TOTALS` computed the totals row from a prefix of the stream. ### Description Related: #111326, which fixed the sibling cases (negative / fractional / bare-offset LIMIT) in these same guards. Here the hint is wrong for an ordinary positive LIMIT too. Three wrong answers on default settings: ```sql -- all 200000 rows tie on k, so all must come back; returns 65409 SELECT count() FROM (SELECT DISTINCT number, 0 AS k FROM numbers(200000) ORDER BY k LIMIT 1 WITH TIES); -- MergeTree t, 200000 rows: totals row is 3125, must be 200000 SELECT DISTINCT c FROM (SELECT n AS k, count() AS c FROM t GROUP BY k WITH TOTALS) LIMIT 1 FORMAT JSONCompact; -- same table: rows_before_limit_at_least is 65536, must be 200000 SELECT DISTINCT n FROM t ORDER BY n LIMIT 3 FORMAT JSONCompact SETTINGS exact_rows_before_limit = 1; ``` `limit_hint` makes the distinct transform call `stopReading()` after `limit + offset` distinct rows, closing its input. All three consumers need rows beyond that: `WITH TIES` needs the unbounded suffix tying with the last row, `exact_rows_before_limit` counts rows passing the Limit/Offset transforms, and `WITH TOTALS` without `ORDER BY` (or below a subquery in `FROM`) aggregates the whole stream. No finite hint is safe for any of them. `WITH TIES` has its own flag on the `LimitStep`, so the guards in both analyzers reject it directly. The other two are exactly the cases in which the `LimitStep` is built with `always_read_till_end`, so the guards reuse that predicate, extracted into one function per analyzer and called both where the `LimitStep` is built and where the hint is decided, so the two cannot drift apart. `limitPushDown.cpp` needs the same check, since it re-introduces the hint through `DistinctStep::updateLimitHint`; it mirrors the `UnionStep` guard just above. This costs nothing: such a LIMIT reads everything anyway, and `rows_read` is identical either way. Otherwise purely restrictive, and no setting or format change. New test `04845_distinct_limit_hint_with_ties` fails on master, passes 100/100 randomized here, and reverting each hunk reddens the matching cases. It also pins the exception: `WITH TOTALS` plus `ORDER BY` on the same query does not read till end, so the hint still applies. One reference line moves: `04539_lazy_final_read_in_order_limit_disabled` asserted lazy FINAL stays disabled for `DISTINCT ... LIMIT n SETTINGS exact_rows_before_limit = 1`, which held only because the hint stopped reading early. That query now reads everything, so lazy FINAL applies, as it already does for the plain `LIMIT` case in the same test. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1496` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Make isProbablePrime observe cancellation and max_execution_time on UInt128/UInt256
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112203 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113886 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `isProbablePrime` on `UInt128`/`UInt256` ignoring `max_execution_time` and `KILL QUERY`. A block of wide values ran to completion inside a single function call with no cancellation point, so a query could run for minutes past its deadline. ### Description Requested in [#112203](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112203). `isProbablePrime` on `UInt128`/`UInt256` evaluated a whole block inside one `executeImpl` call with no cancellation point. The pipeline samples cancellation only between blocks, so neither `max_execution_time` nor `KILL QUERY` could interrupt it, and each wide row costs milliseconds in `boost::multiprecision::miller_rabin_test`. Measured on master, 10000 `UInt256` rows at `rounds = 64` against `max_execution_time = 1`: ``` Code: 159. Timeout exceeded: elapsed 203157.095 ms, maximum: 1000 ms. ``` Observed in CI as `Stress test (amd_msan)` `Hung check failed, possible deadlock found` on an unrelated PR, with one query at `elapsed = 1796 s`, `is_cancelled = 1`, `max_execution_time = 10`: both channels ineffective. The existing `rounds <= 256` cap bounds a *single* call, not the loop over the block. The change adds a checkpoint at the layer owning that loop: - `Primality.h` takes an optional `check_cancellation` callback, invoked once per call just before the Miller-Rabin rounds, i.e. after the three cheap exits. `Common` stays free of `ProcessList`, the same split `Base58.h` uses. Boost is retained. - `isProbablePrime.cpp` builds the callback from the query status and charges a `CancellationBudget` per wide row, bounding a block of only cheap-exit rows (0.04-0.26 us each) without making them pay for a check. Scope is `UInt128`/`UInt256`, as the changelog entry says. The narrow widths are unchanged (1M rows 3766 -> 3632 ms) and keep the between-blocks granularity they share with `isPrime`: 3.5 us per row worst case, so one default block is 232 ms, against 20.4 ms per row and 1333 s per block on the wide path. The regression test was removed in review as it asserted wall-clock deadlines; the evidence of record is the CI report of the hang: [`Stress test (amd_msan)` on #113656](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113656&sha=6eb06bf579ee20a7b121a971148ce563bd29cfb2&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_msan%29). `04201_is_prime`, `04202_is_prime_oracle` and `04203_is_prime_wide` still cover results on every width, but nothing fails if the checkpoint is removed. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1519` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Do not throw when comparing an Enum column with a non-member string literal
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111545 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `UNKNOWN_ELEMENT_OF_ENUM` being thrown when an `Enum` column is compared with a string literal that is not one of its members, even though `validate_enum_literals_in_operators` is disabled by default. Previously the query was rejected if the column was in the primary key or partition key, or merely carried a `minmax`, `set` or `bloom_filter` index, and `!=` was rejected for any `Enum` column. Closes [#111545](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111545). ### Description Closes: #111545 `validate_enum_literals_in_operators` is off by default and documents that non-member enum literals are then not validated, yet comparing an `Enum` column with one threw, and whether it threw depended on physical layout. Two independent causes: 1. **Index analysis.** `KeyCondition::extractAtomFromTree` converts the literal with the throwing `convertFieldToType`, leaving the `isNull()` handling right below it unreachable. Since `minmax` and `set` build a `KeyCondition` over the index expression, that one line served the primary key, the partition key and both indexes. `bloom_filter` repeated the defect at four of its own sites, as did the JSON-subcolumn helper shared by `bloom_filter` and `tokenbf_v1`. The conversions are now wrapped in a catch scoped with `isParseError` (following `ConditionSelectivityEstimator`), so a non-representable literal declines the atom (full scan, never a wrong answer) while fatal errors such as `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` still propagate. 2. **An inverted guard.** In `FunctionsComparison.h`, `!equals && not_equals` selects `notEquals` alone, yet the value it guards, `IsOperation<Op>::not_equals`, was written to serve `notEquals`, so the tolerant branch could only ever return 0. Deleting the guard is the fix: any rewrite that keeps a condition there breaks the four ordered operators, for which both traits are false. Two corrections to the report, both re-measured. `e < '4'` does not throw on a non-key column (the ordered operators all return 0), so there only `!=` was broken; and the column need not be in a key, since a `minmax`, `set` or `bloom_filter` index suffices. `e <=> '4'` and `isDistinctFrom(e, '4')` were affected too. No query that previously succeeded changes its answer, and declining loses no pruning: `LIKE` over an `Enum` key never pruned before, since the converted field is an `Int8` that the `like` atom handler rejects. The tests assert that each index is still used for representable literals, and that the setting still rejects every operator when enabled. <details><summary>Validation</summary> Every carrier measured on a debug build, before and after, each fixture carrying a positive control: | Carrier | Before | After | Control | |---|---|---|---| | primary key `ORDER BY e` | 691 | 0 | `= 'a'` -> 1 | | partition key, `LIKE '%Beta%'` | 691 | 500 | `use_partition_pruning = 0` -> 500 | | `minmax` index, no key | 691 | 0 | `use_skip_indexes = 0` -> 0 | | `set(0)` index, no key | 691 | 0 | `use_skip_indexes = 0` -> 0 | | `bloom_filter` index, no key | 691 | 0 | `use_skip_indexes = 0` -> 0 | | `bloom_filter` over `Array(Enum)`, `has` / `hasAny` / `hasAll` | 691 | 0 | `has(a, 'a')` -> 1 | | `bloom_filter` over `Map(Enum, ...)` keys, `mapContains` | 691 | 0 | `mapContains(m, 'a')` -> 1 | | `JSONAllPaths` `bloom_filter` / `tokenbf_v1` | 691 | 0 | `= 'y'` -> 1, index used | | `!=` on any table | 691 | row count | `NOT (e = 'zzz')` agrees | | `<=>`, `isDistinctFrom` | 691 | 0 / row count | member-literal arms | | `< <= > >=` on a non-key column | 0 | 0 | unchanged | | `IN ('4', 'a')` | 1 | 1 | unchanged (#72686) | Each of the four hunks was reverted independently: every one reddens its own carrier and only its own carrier. The tests assert index *usability* through `force_data_skipping_indices` rather than row counts alone, so neither an over-broad decline nor a missing one can pass silently; four mutations were run and each reddens a new assertion. `Nullable(Enum8)`, `Nullable(Enum16)` and `Enum16` keys covered, including a real `NULL` row (`NULL != '4'` stays `NULL`; `NULL <=> '4'` is 0). `LowCardinality(Enum)` is not covered because `DataTypeEnum` does not override `canBeInsideLowCardinality()`, so the type cannot be constructed. 50 randomized runs of both new tests passed 100/100; `01310_enum_comparison`, `03278_enum_in_unknown_value`, `04049_statistics_enum_invalid_value` and `04539_enum_string_search_dictionary` stay green. </details>

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/metadata
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Adds Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` support for `TimeSeries` tables.** ### Description This adds the Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` endpoint backed by the `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table. ### Why this matters - **Prometheus-compatible tools** use `/api/v1/metadata` to discover **metric types, help text, and units**. - Without this endpoint, clients need separate configuration or lose this metadata when using ClickHouse as a Prometheus-compatible endpoint. - This keeps the `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table as the **source of truth** for that metadata. Supported parameters: - `metric` filters the response to one metric family. - `limit` limits the number of metric families. - `limit_per_metric` limits the metadata objects returned for each family. Other details: - Metadata objects are unique. Entries returned for each family are sorted. - `limit=0` returns no metric families. - Zero and negative `limit_per_metric` values mean no per-family limit. - Positive `limit_per_metric` values bound the number of unique metadata objects returned for each family. The selected subset is not specified. - `FINAL` is used whenever the Metrics target supports it, including wrapped targets. - Metadata parameters stay endpoint-local and are not treated as ClickHouse settings. - The generated query uses the normal query pipeline and is recorded in `query_log`. - Access to the configured `TimeSeries` table and related table functions is checked. - The endpoint works with dedicated handlers and the combined `/api/v1` handler. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - unique metadata across multiple parts. - stable results after `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL`. - JSON escaping for quotes, backslashes, newlines, tabs, and Unicode. - metric filtering and both limit parameters. - invalid limit values. - high-cardinality metadata with per-family limits. - primary-key filtering. - wrapped `FINAL` targets. - aliases and `prefer_column_name_to_alias`. - query logging. - endpoint and table-function access control. - unknown endpoint handling. - GET/HEAD and unsupported-method handling. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Documentation was added to the Prometheus protocols page. It covers the handler configuration and supported parameters.

signals.title: Add a full-featured AI agent to the client (the `?` command)
signals.text: Turns the primitive `??` "generate one SQL query" helper in the client into a full interactive AI agent, available with a single `?` (`??` is kept as an alias). The agent works over a live connection: it is given the context of the recent queries in the session (with results truncated to the first and last lines to save tokens, plus error messages) and can use tools to read the query history from `system.user_query_log`, inspect the schema (`SHOW`/`DESCRIBE`/`SHOW CREATE`), consult the embedded documentation (`system.documentation`, the same source as the `help` command), run read-only queries without confirmation under a sandbox (`readonly = 1`, a 30-second and a 10 GiB limit, no table functions reaching outside of the server's tables; if the session forbids applying these limits, the query fails instead of running without them), and run any other query after asking the user for confirmation. Queries it runs are echoed and executed on the user's connection and displayed exactly as if the user had typed them; it prints its thoughts and tool calls as it works, and the conversation keeps its context across `?` invocations within a session. When no client-side AI provider is configured (neither the `ai` section of the client configuration nor the `OPENAI_API_KEY`/`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variables), the agent falls back to the server-side `aiGenerate` function of the connected server (or of `clickhouse-local`) when it has default credentials configured for it (`ai_function_text_default_credentials`), so it works with no client-side setup when the administrator has already enabled AI functions. Implementation lives in `src/Client/AI/`: the agent loop (`AIAgent`), two model backends (`AIAgentTransport`: native tool-calling via `ai-sdk-cpp`, and a text tool-call protocol on top of `aiGenerate`), the tools (`AIAgentTools`), the read-only statement allowlist (`AIQueryValidation`), and the recent-query context buffer (`QueryContextBuffer`). Unit tests cover the tool-call protocol parsing, the read-only validation, and the context buffer; the end-to-end loop (both backends and the confirmation gate) was validated by driving `clickhouse-local` against a mock OpenAI endpoint. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The embedded AI assistant of `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local` is now a full agent, invoked with a single `?`. It sees the recent queries and their results, explores the schema and the documentation, runs read-only queries on its own (and other queries with confirmation) displayed as if you typed them, and can use the server-side `aiGenerate` function when no client-side AI provider is configured. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Revert "Use libdeflate for gzip/zlib/deflate compression and decompression"
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114045 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108074 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Revert #108074 (use libdeflate for gzip/zlib/deflate): its streaming decompressor suspends only at DEFLATE block boundaries, so decompressing an HTTP request body whose single DEFLATE block spans the whole stream (the shape zlib-ng produces at level 1, which is the default in the official .NET SDK) was `O(n^2)` in the compressed block size and buffered the whole block in memory. A 22 MB gzip body that 26.6 ingested in 0.3 s took 15 s on 26.7. This returns the gzip/zlib/deflate paths to zlib-ng, restoring 26.6 behavior. The `gzip`/`deflate` compression levels `10-12` that 26.7 introduced stay accepted and are clamped to `9`, the maximum level supported by `zlib`, so configurations written against 26.7 keep working. ### Details This is a plain `git revert` of the merge commit of #108074, with the following manual adjustments: - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04230_iceberg_optimize_metadata_not_initialized_104711.sh` and `04240_iceberg_supports_parallel_insert_mv_104891.sh` keep their current (post-#108074) form: they now corrupt Iceberg metadata files directly instead of relying on `output_format_compression_level=11` being rejected, which works regardless of the compression backend. - The relocated doc `docs/reference/statements/select/into-outfile.mdx` documents the compression level range as `1-12` for `gzip`/`deflate` with the clamp, since the old `docs/en` tree no longer exists for the revert to apply to. The text for `http_zlib_compression_level` is changed in the `DECLARE` docstring in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`, because `docs/reference/settings/session-settings/http.mdx` is inside an `AUTOGENERATED` region and hand-editing it fails the `No direct edits to generated or read-only docs` check. **Backward compatibility.** 26.7 shipped `libdeflate` and, with it, `gzip`/`deflate` compression levels `10-12` on every output surface that routes through `CompressionMethod`: `INTO OUTFILE ... LEVEL`, `output_format_compression_level`, `http_zlib_compression_level` and the gRPC `output_compression_level`. A plain revert would narrow the accepted range back to `1-9`, so existing queries and settings profiles would start failing with `Invalid compression level` or `deflateInit2 failed: stream error`. To avoid that, `getCompressionLevelRange` keeps returning `1-12` for `gzip`/`zlib` and `createWriteCompressedWrapper` clamps levels above `9` to zlib's maximum. Levels above `12` are still rejected, as in 26.7. Two tests are restored in a backend-agnostic form instead of being deleted with the feature: - `04842_parquet_gzip_compression_level` round-trips a mixed-compressibility dataset through Parquet with `output_format_parquet_compression_method='gzip'` at levels `1, 3, 6, 9, 12`, keeping non-default-level coverage of `output_format_compression_level` for Parquet. - `04843_outfile_compression_level_range` covers the accepted `INTO OUTFILE ... LEVEL` range for `gzip`/`deflate`, the clamp of `10-12`, and the rejection of `13`. Additionally, gzip-compressed Parquet pages are now decompressed with a one-shot `inflate` loop (`decompressGzip` in `src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Reader.cpp`) instead of the streaming `ZlibInflatingReadBuffer`. The streaming path could not tell a clean end of the gzip stream from a damaged one, because `zlib` validates the trailer (`CRC32` and `ISIZE`) only on the read after the one that filled the output exactly, while the reader stops as soon as it has `uncompressed_page_size` bytes — so a corrupted trailer was accepted silently. The one-shot loop requires `Z_STREAM_END`, while ignoring bytes left in the page after the last member, since `compressed_page_size` is the number of bytes the page owns and a writer may pad it. Two more tests cover this: - `04848_parquet_gzip_corrupted_trailer` corrupts a page's gzip `CRC32` in place and requires the read to be rejected, with and without page checksum verification. - `04892_parquet_gzip_padded_page` pads a gzip dictionary page and requires the file to keep reading back identically. A follow-up PR will re-introduce libdeflate with the streaming decompressor fixed to suspend at symbol granularity (linear time, bounded memory).

signals.title: Fix quadratic gzip/zlib streaming decompression of single-block streams
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114045 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108074 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114054 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/libdeflate/pull/6 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `O(n^2)` decompression of gzip/zlib/deflate streams whose single DEFLATE block spans the whole stream, the shape zlib-ng produces at compression level 1 (the default of the official .NET SDK): a 24 MiB gzip HTTP body that took 11 s to ingest in 26.7 now takes 0.12 s, identical to a multi-block body, with memory bounded by the buffer size instead of the block size. ### Details The root cause: the streaming decompressor added to `contrib/libdeflate` kept its resume checkpoint only at DEFLATE block boundaries. On input exhaustion or output-buffer overflow it rolled back to the start of the current block, so for a stream that is one giant block, every socket refill re-decoded the block from its beginning — quadratic time — and the whole block's output had to be buffered before any byte was exposed — unbounded memory. The work happens in `copyDataImpl` while assembling the query, before the query starts, so it was invisible in `system.processes` and `query_duration_ms`. The fix (https://github.com/ClickHouse/libdeflate/pull/6, now present in `master`'s `contrib/libdeflate`) re-takes the checkpoint at every symbol boundary in the generic decode loop, plus two new decompressor fields (`in_block`, `block_is_final`) that let a resumed call jump straight back into symbol decoding — the litlen/offset decode tables already persist in the decompressor between calls. The fastloop is untouched: suspensions can only trigger from the generic loop, which always runs between the fastloop and input exhaustion. A suspension now loses at most one partially decoded symbol, so decompression is linear-time with bounded memory regardless of block structure. `LibdeflateInflatingReadBuffer` needed no logic changes, only comment updates: its "grow the output buffer" path is now reachable only when a single match (≤ 258 bytes) or stored block (≤ 64 KiB) exceeds the free output region. Verification: - Standalone harness: 5000+ randomized round-trips (zlib streams at all levels with random flush points; crafted static- and dynamic-Huffman single-block streams with matches reaching the full 32 KiB window; input chunking down to 1 byte; random output regions), zlib inflate as decode oracle, one-shot decoder as cross-check, and a progress assertion on every suspension. - End-to-end with the issue's reproducer shape (24 MiB single-block gzip body, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, local release build): **11.25 s before → 0.12 s after**, now identical to a multi-block body of the same content (0.12 s). Verified the vendored zlib-ng really emits this shape: at level 1 it produces 1 block for a 4 MiB input (stock zlib: 80 blocks). - No throughput regression on normal multi-block streams: 685 → 697 MB/s on a 256 MB zlib-level-6 stream. New tests: - `LibdeflateSingleBlock.StreamingConsumesInputWithinBlock` pins the linearity contract (a suspension inside a Huffman block leaves at most a few bytes unconsumed). Against the pre-fix library it fails immediately, with 35 MB left unconsumed on a 32 MiB single-block stream. - `LibdeflateInflateTest.RoundTripFromZlibNgLevelOneLarge` decodes a large stream produced by the vendored zlib-ng at level 1 — the real-encoder shape of the issue. - `LibdeflateInflateTest.SingleDeflateBlockSpanningWholeMember` decodes crafted single-block gzip/zlib members through `LibdeflateInflatingReadBuffer`. - `04836_http_gzip_single_deflate_block` ingests a crafted single-block gzip body over HTTP with chunked transfer encoding, end to end. Because the pre-fix decoder is correct, just quadratic, the assertion is on time: the body is one 36 MB block and the request is capped at 15 s. Ingest time for a single-block body of a given size, release build, `master`'s `contrib/libdeflate` vs this branch's: 10 MB - 1.8 s vs 0.05 s; 20 MB - 6.9 s; 40 MB - 27.3 s vs 0.20 s; 48 MB - 39.1 s vs 0.25 s. So the limit sits 2.6x below the pre-fix time and 60x above the fixed one, and the clean quadratic growth means the pre-fix margin does not depend on the machine speed. The payload is 120 lines of 400 KB so that line parsing and the `MergeTree` write do not dominate. Note: `Bugfix validation (unit tests)` reports `ERROR` (inconclusive, non-blocking) here for a structural reason: the fix itself lives in `contrib/libdeflate`, and the job cannot populate its merge-base "before" worktree at the merge-base submodule revision, so it refuses to build a before-binary that would validate the wrong submodule code. The functional test above is what validates the fix. Note: this PR and the revert #114054 are alternatives on master — if the revert merges first, this branch will be updated to re-apply the integration together with the fix; if this merges first, the revert can be closed (the 26.7 backport of the revert can proceed independently).
