signals.title: Check PREWHERE column support inside lambda bodies
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114206 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a logical error and a `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` error when a `PREWHERE` expression reads a table column inside a lambda body, e.g. `PREWHERE arrayMap(x -> t.c, [1])[1] > 0`. Such a column was never checked against the table expression's supported `PREWHERE` columns, so a `Merge` whose children declare it with different types built the filter against the wrong one rather than refusing it. Also fixes `UNKNOWN_FUNCTION` for a `PREWHERE` expression calling an executable or WebAssembly UDF that does not itself read a `JOIN` column. ### Description `CollectPrewhereTableExpressionVisitor::needChildVisit` skipped `LAMBDA`, so a column read only inside a lambda body never reached `visitImpl`, the one place that picks the table expression `PREWHERE` reads from and enforces `supportedPrewhereColumns`. On master: - A `Merge` whose children declare `x` as `UInt32` and `Nullable(UInt32)` excludes `x` from its contract, but the guard that would refuse it never runs. The filter is built against the root's type while a child reads another, so the lambda's `ColumnFunction` capture fails in the reader: `Cannot capture column N ... incompatible type`, a logical error, so an abort under sanitizers. - With no column visited, `PREWHERE` is pinned to the first table expression, so a lambda over another fails `Code: 10` (#114206). The fix descends into lambda bodies, skipping only the lambda's own parameters by testing for a `LAMBDA_ARGS` column source, as the sibling `CollectSourceColumnsVisitor` already does: a node type, not a function name, so all higher-order functions are covered. Collecting those columns makes two latent omissions live. `ReplaceColumnsVisitor` never entered a lambda either, so the `JOIN` type substitution that `PREWHERE` must roll back survived inside a lambda and aborted at `join_use_nulls = 1`. Rolling it back also re-derives the lambda's parameter types from the array its higher-order function iterates. It also rebuilt every function in the expression, replaced or not, through `FunctionFactory`, which does not own UDFs: hence the `UNKNOWN_FUNCTION`. It is now bounded to replaced subtrees, so a UDF reading a restored `JOIN` column stays refused as on master. Reported by @ nikitamikhaylov on [#113768](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113768#issuecomment-5268962866): one `Server died` in that PR's unrelated Stress test (amd_msan), [report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113768&sha=8f8aef10f381104c26153d7fb829b7e196825b0b&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress+test+%28amd_msan%29). <details><summary>Validation</summary> Reproducer (aborts on master, `ILLEGAL_PREWHERE` with this change): ```sql CREATE TABLE t (x UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); CREATE TABLE t2 (x Nullable(UInt32)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t VALUES (100); INSERT INTO t2 VALUES (300); SET enable_analyzer = 1; SELECT x FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t') AS m PREWHERE (arrayMap(x -> m.x, [1])[1]) > 50; ``` `04879_prewhere_lambda_body_column_check`: 29 arms A/B'd against a base build, 8 refusals and 21 row-returning. Every refusal and every `join_use_nulls` shape is paired with the same query without a lambda, so each expected outcome is justified against master's own answer. | arm | base | with this change | |---|---|---| | diverging child types, lambda reads `m.x` (also `*`, `arrayFilter`) | abort | `ILLEGAL_PREWHERE` | | `ARRAY JOIN`ed alias inside a lambda | `Code: 10` | `ILLEGAL_PREWHERE` | | lambda over the second table of a `JOIN` | `Code: 10` | resolves to that table | | `LEFT JOIN`, right column in `arrayExists`, `join_use_nulls` 0 and 1 (#114206) | abort or `Code: 10` | `1` / `2` | | the same four without a lambda | as after the change | unchanged | | agreeing types; `WHERE`; unrestricted table; shadowed parameter | rows | unchanged | `04889_prewhere_lambda_executable_udf` covers the UDF case in 9 arms, with a built-in control. Five mutation arms, disjoint casualties: reverting `needChildVisit` re-introduces the abort and the `Code: 10`; dropping the `LAMBDA_ARGS` guard breaks `04108`; reverting `ReplaceColumnsVisitor` aborts in `ActionsDAG`; dropping either return-type refresh or the parameter-type re-derivation aborts in planning or in `ColumnFunction::appendArgument`. `04108`, `03036_prewhere_lambda_function`, `00729_prewhere_array_join` and `02955_analyzer_using_functional_args` pass unchanged. Both new tests ran 50x, 0 failures: `04879` under randomized settings, `04889` at `clickhouse-local` defaults. </details>

signals.title: CI: run the full test suite only when review threads are resolved
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114724 While a PR has unresolved review threads, running the full test suite is a waste: the code is expected to change again once the review comments are addressed. This PR implements the gate requested in the issue: - A new `review_threads.py` pre-hook in the `Config Workflow` counts the PR's unresolved review threads (via GraphQL `reviewThreads`) and stores the state in the workflow kv data. While threads are unresolved, `should_skip_job` runs only builds and the preliminary checks (`Style check`, `Fast test`), plus the `Code Review` job — the AI review keeps re-checking pushed code and resolves its own addressed threads, which is what re-triggers the full suite automatically. - The `can_be_merged.py` post-hook re-checks the live thread state at finish time and turns the `Mergeable Check` red while threads are unresolved, or while only the limited pipeline ran (even if the threads were resolved mid-run — the full suite still has not run). The per-run verdict is recorded in a new `Review Threads` commit status, which doubles as immediate feedback on the PR. This also makes the decision on the AI review's comments once they are ready, as suggested in the issue: comments posted during the run are seen by the finish-time check. - A new `Rerun On Review Threads` workflow detects state changes and re-runs the last completed `PR` workflow run for the current head commit whenever the recorded verdict disagrees with the live state (thread resolved/unresolved, new review comments, the override label added/removed). Previously succeeded jobs are restored from the CI cache, so the re-run only executes the previously skipped jobs. Review-thread events on PRs from forks carry a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so they are relayed through a trivial `Review Threads Signal` workflow and handled on its `workflow_run` completion in the trusted default-branch context; `PR` workflow completions are watched too, to catch threads resolved while a run was still in flight. A safety cap (5 attempts per run) prevents any reconciliation bug from re-running one workflow forever. - The gate can be bypassed with the new `ignore-unresolved-threads` label (fetched fresh from the API, so adding the label and re-running works; the label also triggers the re-run automatically). `ci-force-all` still bypasses job filtering, so it runs the full suite, but it does not bypass the merge gate for unresolved threads. - `retry_infra_failures.yml` learned to not treat a `Finish Workflow` failure caused by this merge gate as an infrastructure failure. - Failure direction: if the thread state cannot be fetched at config time, nothing is skipped (fail toward more testing); at finish time the check fails close (the `Mergeable Check` goes red). The `ignore-unresolved-threads` label has been created in the repository. Documentation: a new `Review threads check` section in `docs/resources/develop-contribute/contribute/continuous-integration.mdx`. Tests: `ci/tests/test_review_threads_gate.py` pins the decision functions and their integration into `should_skip_job` (what is skipped, what keeps running, the merge-gate truth table, the commit-status description budget). ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: CI: run only the selected tests in the sanitizer functional tests in PRs
signals.text: The sanitizer flavors of `Stateless tests` ran the whole suite in every pull request: 17 jobs for the ASan/UBSan, TSan and MSan builds. Under the assumption in the issue - that the stress tests with sanitizers are a stronger check than a plain functional run - the ASan/UBSan and TSan jobs now run only the tests selected for the change. The MSan/WasmEdge jobs retain their established full-suite configuration because every existing Wasm UDF functional test is tagged `no-msan`, so the selected-test runner cannot currently exercise that surface. The new `selected tests` option of `ci/jobs/functional_tests.py` runs an ordinary functional test run over the subset that `Targeting` already computes for the targeted check: the tests the pull request changes, the tests that already failed in this pull request, and the tests covering the changed lines according to the coverage database. Unlike the `targeted` check, it does not rerun that selection many times - it is a plain run with a shorter list of tests. The selection is a few hundred tests, so the batches of the converted full-suite jobs collapse into a single job per flavor. What still covers the whole suite in a pull request: the MSan/WasmEdge, debug, and plain binary functional test jobs, plus the stress tests, which run the functional tests under every sanitizer with heavy concurrency and randomized settings. The master workflow is unchanged and keeps running the full suite in every flavor. Also in this change: * When the selection cannot be fetched (the coverage database or the GitHub diff is unavailable), the job fails rather than silently run an unbatched, weaker version of the former sanitizer configuration. Retrying restores the intended selected-test run. * Tests the job flavor would never run (`no-parallel` tests in a `parallel` job and vice versa) are dropped from the selection, and the job is skipped when nothing is left for it. * `clickhouse-test` exits with code 1 when every test it was given is filtered out - e.g. all the selected tests are tagged `no-tsan` in a TSan job. For a run over an explicit list of tests (flaky, targeted, `selected tests`) that is now reported as SKIPPED instead of a failure; for a full-suite run it stays a failure, since there it means a broken filter. Unit tests for the new logic are in `ci/tests/test_selected_tests_run.py`. `.github/workflows/pull_request.yml` was regenerated via `python3 -m ci.praktika yaml`. ### Verification in this pull request's own CI This pull request changes no source file and no test under `tests/queries`, so nothing is relevant to select and the new jobs correctly report SKIPPED. To exercise the path that actually runs a subset, commit 85362432c858e0cd9aadbf57f2895888b9d35863 temporarily touched `00001_select_1.sql` (reverted in the following commit). On that commit, with all builds served from the cache: * `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, parallel, selected tests)` and `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, distributed plan, parallel, selected tests)` ran, and the report shows the three selection passes followed by the single selected test - `00001_select_1 OK 1.01s`. * `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, db disk, distributed plan, sequential, selected tests)` skipped, because the only changed test is parallel-safe and the flavor filter left it nothing to run. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114730&sha=85362432c858e0cd9aadbf57f2895888b9d35863&name_0=PR Possible follow-up, not done here: once the test list is short, the job start dominates the run - in the TSan run above, `Start ClickHouse Server` (which prepares the stateful datasets `test.hits`, `test.visits`, TPC-DS and TPC-H) took 324 seconds out of a 418-second job. Skipping the stateful preparation when no stateful test is selected needs a reliable way to tell, so it is left out of this change. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114725 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ...

signals.title: Adaptive lazy execution of short-circuit function arguments (continues #73776)
signals.text: This continues #73776 by @lgbo-ustc, whose branch was ~17 months behind `master` and could no longer be merged mechanically (27 conflicting files in the hottest central code). The author's commits are preserved; on top of them this reconciles the change with the current `master` and reworks the plumbing. Short-circuit evaluation decides *statically* which arguments of `and`, `or`, `if` and `multiIf` are executed lazily. Lazy execution is not free: the rows which are not needed are filtered out and the result is expanded back to the original size. When the filtered out part is small, or the argument itself is cheap, this overhead is larger than the work it saves. This adds an opt-in adaptive mode: the execution of every function is profiled (elapsed time and processed rows), and every 20000 rows the decision is revisited per action - lazy execution is turned off when the estimated cost of the full execution is lower than the measured cost of the lazy execution, and turned back on when the per-row cost of the action grows significantly. Actions whose function can throw an exception on invalid input values (for example `intDiv(1, 0)`) are never switched to eager execution, so the short-circuit protection is preserved. The mode is disabled by default and enabled with the new experimental setting `enable_adaptive_short_circuit_lazy_execution`. Changes on top of the original branch: * The flag no longer travels through `ExpressionStep`/`FilterStep` constructors, the query plan optimizations, the planner and the step serialization. It lives in `ExpressionActionsSettings` next to `enable_lazy_columns_replication`, which removes ~20 files from the change and all the ripple through `QueryPlan/Optimizations`. * `ExpressionActions::execute` and `executeOnColumns` stay `const`; the free `executeAction` became a member with three virtual hooks (`shouldExecuteLazily`, `executeFunction`, `finalizeBlockExecution`) which `AdaptiveExpressionActions` overrides. * The profile plumbing follows the current `IExecutableFunction` chain, including `executeWithoutReplicatedColumns`, which did not exist when the branch was written. * `is_no_except` is computed only when the setting is enabled, so nothing changes for the default path. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental setting `enable_adaptive_short_circuit_lazy_execution`, which enables dynamic evaluation of whether a short-circuit function's argument should be lazily executed. The execution of the functions is profiled at runtime, and the lazy execution of an argument is disabled when it costs more than executing the argument on all the rows. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/73776

signals.title: Build Debian packages for the release builds only
signals.text: The `Stress test` was the only job installing the Debian packages of the debug, sanitizer and CFI builds, and it can take the plain `clickhouse` binary instead — that binary is built and uploaded for every build type anyway. Every other consumer of the packages (`Install packages`, `Compatibility check`, `Upgrade check`, the server Docker images and the release jobs) runs on a release build. So the release builds keep their packages, and nine of the eleven packaging steps go away, together with the `DESTDIR` install that copies the whole binary, and the upload and download of the resulting packages. The stress test now sets up the paths the packages own from the binary: `install_binary` in `stress_tests.lib` symlinks `/usr/bin/clickhouse*` at it, installs the default `config.xml` and `users.xml`, and unpacks the self-extracting archive up front — decompressing a sanitizer build under `clickhouse start` would eat into its wait for the pid file and race any concurrent `clickhouse local`. `install_packages` stays for the upgrade check, which installs an actual release. Symbolization is unaffected: `clickhouse_split_debug_symbols` leaves `programs/clickhouse` untouched and strips only the copy it installs, so the binary artifact carries its debug info even for a release build. For the sanitizer builds `clickhouse-common-static-dbg` was empty to begin with, since they do not set `SPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1500` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Remove `WINDOW VIEW`
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/61069 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114097 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75191 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/88706 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `WINDOW VIEW` feature is removed, together with the `WATCH` statement and the `windowID` function. It has been non-functional since version 24.12 (inserts into the source table were silently not delivered to window views) and was never supported by the analyzer, which is enabled by default since 24.3. The settings `allow_experimental_window_view`, `window_view_clean_interval`, `window_view_heartbeat_interval`, and `wait_for_window_view_fire_signal_timeout` are kept as obsolete no-ops. The time-window functions `tumble`, `tumbleStart`, `tumbleEnd`, `hop`, `hopStart`, and `hopEnd` are kept. If you still have window views defined, drop them before upgrading: a server that finds a window view in its metadata fails to start (`Cannot parse definition from metadata file ... (SYNTAX_ERROR)`), the same way the removal of the `Lazy` database engine behaves. Similar functionality will be reimplemented on top of streaming queries (issue [#114738](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738)). The removal, in detail: - `src/Storages/WindowView/` (`StorageWindowView`, `WindowViewSource`, `StorageBlocks`), `WatermarkTransform`, the `ParserCreateWindowViewQuery` parser, and the whole `WATCH` statement stack (`ParserWatchQuery`, `ASTWatchQuery`, `InterpreterWatchQuery`, the `IStorage::watch` virtual) — window views were the last implementor of `watch`, and the `WATCH` statement was already documented as deprecated. - The `ASTCreateQuery` watermark/lateness fields and their AST JSON serialization and validation. The `clickhouse_json` boundary fails closed rather than silently reinterpreting legacy payloads: `ASTCreateQuery::readJSON` rejects a set `is_window_view`, watermark strategy or `allowed_lateness` flag and the `watermark_function` / `lateness_function` children (otherwise such a payload deserialized as an ordinary `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` and was executed as an immediate-population table create), while `ASTViewTargets::readJSON` rejects the `Inner` target kind, which nothing produces any more and which formatted back to parser-impossible `INNER ENGINE ...` SQL. Both are covered by `04892_ast_json_removed_window_view_state`; the `PushingToWindowViewSink` and `ViewType::WINDOW` branches in `InsertDependenciesBuilder`; window-view special cases in `InterpreterCreateQuery`, `InterpreterInsertQuery`, `StorageFactory`, `DatabaseOrdinary`, `DatabaseReplicated`, `DDLDependencyVisitor`, `QueryFuzzer`, BuzzHouse, and the ArrowFlight table-type mapping. - The `windowID` function and the `UInt32` single-argument forms of `tumbleStart`/`tumbleEnd`/`hopStart`/`hopEnd` (they only accepted `windowID` output). The rest of the time-window function family stays, since these are ordinary functions usable in a regular `GROUP BY` and are exactly the vocabulary for the streaming-queries replacement. - The keywords `WATCH`, `EVENTS`, `ALLOWED_LATENESS`, and `STRICTLY_ASCENDING` (the `WATERMARK` keyword stays: the streaming-queries `WATERMARK FOR` clause uses it), the error code `QUERY_IS_NOT_SUPPORTED_IN_WINDOW_VIEW`, and the corresponding fuzzer dictionary and ANTLR grammar entries. - Kept for compatibility: `QueryViewsLogElement::ViewType::WINDOW` (so existing `system.query_views_log` tables keep their schema) and `ViewTarget::Inner` (so old DDL log entries still parse), following the same pattern as the `LIVE VIEW` removal. - The `allow_experimental_window_view` constraint in `tests/docker_scripts/stress_tests.lib` is kept (only the constraint, not the profile value, which would mark an obsolete setting as changed and add a `system.warnings` entry): the upgrade check runs the previous release's suite under the previous release's binary, whose window-view tests are not dropped afterwards because `--upgrade-check` implies `--fake-drop`, and the leftover metadata would then stop the new server from starting. - Tests: the four remaining window-view tests are removed. The pure time-window-function coverage of `01049_window_view_window_functions` moved to a new `04891_time_window_functions` test, which also pins the new `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` behavior of `tumbleStart(UInt32)`. - Docs: the `Window View` section of `CREATE VIEW`, the `WATCH` page (with its navigation entries and locale twins) are removed and the old-slug redirects retargeted; the window-view entries are removed from the generated settings/functions reference pages (second commit, hence the `pr-autogenerated-docs` label): the `window-view.mdx` settings page, the four settings' entries in the pages/manifest/navigation/settings explorer, and the `windowID` section of `time-window-functions.mdx`. The unrelated drift accumulated on master since the last nightly regeneration is deliberately not included; the nightly docs-autogen job will pick it up. Why now: the feature has been non-functional since Dec 2024 — commit `ceae84c87a2` removed the explicit view-dependency registration and `DDLDependencyVisitor` never extracted the source table of a `CREATE WINDOW VIEW`, so inserts into the source table were silently not pushed to window views, and direct inserts failed with `std::out_of_range` (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493). Nobody noticed for ~1.5 years. It was never ported to the analyzer (with `enable_analyzer = 1`, the default, existing window views load permanently inert), its tests were removed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/73822 because they were inherently flaky, and it kept costing triage time (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114097 is a recent server SIGSEGV through `getSourceTableSelectQuery`). The full assessment, including the plan for reimplementing this functionality on top of streaming queries (`SELECT ... FROM t STREAM`, `WATERMARK FOR`, emit-on-watermark windowed aggregation), is in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Optimize delayInsertOrThrowIfNeeded overhead
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Optimized the insert backpressure path in `MergeTree` by reducing parts lock contention and short-circuiting the parts count check. ### Optimize 1. `getMaxPartsCountAndSizeForPartitionWithState` now snapshots the parts under the lock and does the aggregation after releasing it, shortening the shared-lock critical section so exclusive-lock writers wait less. 2. The per-partition scan is skipped when the O(1) total active part count is below the delay/throw thresholds, since it cannot change the outcome. This is the common case in healthy tables, so most inserts avoid the scan entirely.

signals.title: Replace the AggregatingInOrderTransform cancellation test with a failpoint integration test
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110104 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107941 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110104 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107941 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `04512_aggregation_in_order_cancellation.sh` guards the per-key-interval cancellation check from #110104, but asserts on aggregation CPU as a multiple of scan CPU after a shell-issued `KILL`. It prints `not cancelled in time` on master again: 6 such failures on 2026-08-13 (2 on master, 4 on unrelated PRs), 5 on `amd_asan_ubsan, distributed plan, parallel`. Eighth rewrite of the assertion. The oracle prices the window between "rows are read" and "the `KILL` flips `is_cancelled`", and two `clickhouse-client` startups sit on that path; `04410_primes_source_cancellation.sh:48-49` records ~8 s for one invocation on a loaded sanitizer build. On all five failures that printed the CPU diagnostics the checkpoint was firing, stopping at 48-75 % of the loop, not 100 %: only the window grew, and the shell cannot close it, since read progress is published only after the source's `work()` returns (`ExecutionThreadContext.cpp:57-75`). So this adopts the mechanism `LimitByTransform` already uses (`e20a67394329867` and follow-ups): a `PAUSEABLE_ONCE` failpoint on interval 6, after the cancellation check and inside the loop, a `LOG_TEST` marker in the existing cancellation branch, and an integration test that pauses there, kills, resumes and asserts the marker appears exactly once. No timing, no threshold, no free constant. Exactly once, not merely present: `is_cancelled` latches, so dropping only the `return` prints the marker once per remaining interval (94 here) while every other assertion still passes. Mid-loop matters for the same reason: a pre-loop pause resumes straight into the first `isCancelled()`, staying green with that check hoisted out of the loop, which is what #110104 fixed. All three mutations (checkpoint deleted, check hoisted, `return` deleted) redden the new test, the failpoint still pausing in each so no arm is vacuous. Removing `SYSTEM ENABLE FAILPOINT` fails loudly; `test_limit_by_transform_kill_query` stays green. Hot-path cost is not measurable, and dropping the 40 M-row fixture removes its `max_estimated_execution_time` exposure. `04409_skip_index_build_cancellation.sh` has a weaker form of the same pattern (bounded `KILL ... SYNC` at `timeout 10`); left unchanged.

signals.title: Speed up window functions by evaluating each `MergeTree` partition independently
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108326 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114645 A window function plan sorts its input partitioned by the window `PARTITION BY` columns: every row is reshuffled across streams by `ScatterByPartitionTransform` (a hash pass over the `PARTITION BY` columns plus a repack of every column of every row through a full cross-stream `Resize`), so that whole window partitions land in single streams before the per-stream sort and `WindowTransform`. If the partition expression of the `MergeTree` table is a deterministic function of the window `PARTITION BY` columns, the reading will now emit each partition through a single port instead: every stream already carries whole window partitions, so the scatter is skipped entirely and the read, sort, and window all stay within per-partition streams. ```sql CREATE TABLE test_16 (a UInt64, b UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() PARTITION BY sipHash64(a) % 16; INSERT INTO test_16 SELECT number % 100000, number FROM numbers_mt(30000000); OPTIMIZE TABLE test_16 FINAL; EXPLAIN PIPELINE SELECT a, sum(b) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM test_16 SETTINGS allow_window_partitions_independently = 1, max_threads = 16; ``` ```response (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 16 (Window) Resize 16 → 16 WindowTransform × 16 (Sorting) MergeSortingTransform × 16 LimitsCheckingTransform × 16 PartialSortingTransform × 16 <- was: fed through Resize 16 → 1 + ScatterByPartitionTransform 1 → 16, reshuffling every row across streams (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 16 (ReadFromMergeTree) MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder) × 16 0 → 1 <- per-partition reading (16 partitions → 16 streams) ``` On `test_str_64 (a UInt64, b UInt64, s String)` with 30M rows, 100k window partitions over 64 balanced table partitions (`PARTITION BY sipHash64(a) % 64`), and a 100-byte random string in `s`, at `max_threads = 16`: | query | off | on | speedup | |--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------|--------|---------| | `SELECT a, s, count(b) OVER (PARTITION BY a) FROM test_str_64` | 1.014s | 0.554s | 1.83× | | `SELECT a, s, sum(b) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM test_str_64` | 1.492s | 0.956s | 1.56× | The scatter repacks every column of every row, so the win grows with the row width. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up window functions on partitioned `MergeTree` tables by reading each partition through its own stream and evaluating the windows per partition, skipping the hash scatter that ordinarily reshuffles every row across threads before the window sort. This applies when the table partition expression is a deterministic function of the window `PARTITION BY` columns and is gated by the same cost heuristic as per-partition `GROUP BY` / `DISTINCT` (enough partitions relative to `max_threads`, no dominant partition). Controlled by the new settings `allow_window_partitions_independently` (enabled by default), `force_window_partitions_independently`, and `max_number_of_partitions_for_independent_window`.

signals.title: Fix TopK filtering dropping NULL and NaN rows from the answer
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113406 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107074 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` silently omitting rows that belong in the answer when TopK filtering is active. A `Float32`/`Float64`/`BFloat16` column holding `NaN` was affected at default settings; nested-`NULL` types such as `Array(Nullable(T))` and `Map(K, Nullable(V))` were affected under `ASC NULLS FIRST` and `DESC NULLS LAST` with `use_top_k_dynamic_filtering_for_variable_length_types` enabled. A sort column containing `JSON`, `Variant` or `Dynamic` at any depth was affected in either direction, and additionally raised a `LOGICAL_ERROR` for `Tuple(Dynamic)` and `Tuple(Variant(...))`. ### Description TopK filtering must order values the way the sorter does. Three mechanisms broke that. `__topKFilter`'s fast path compares through `lessOrEquals`/`greaterOrEquals`. For a composite type those resolve to `GenericComparisonImpl`, which hardcodes the nan/nulls-direction hint to "NULLs and NaNs are greatest", contradicting `ORDER BY` whenever `nulls_direction` is -1. For a float, IEEE comparison leaves `NaN` unordered against everything including itself, so a `NaN` row fails both comparators in every direction. `use_skip_indexes_for_top_k` loses the same rows independently, via `MinMaxGranuleItem::operator<`. Third, a runtime-typed sort column. The threshold reaches `TopKThresholdTracker` as a bare `Field` (`IColumn::get`), which keeps a `Variant`/`Dynamic` payload without its discriminator, while `ColumnVariant::compareAt` ranks by discriminator first. Measured on one constant value per part: `Tuple(Dynamic)` returned `(0)` for `ORDER BY v DESC LIMIT 2` where the answer is `(1000)`, and `Tuple(Variant(UInt64, UInt8))` returned `(3)` for `ASC` where it is `(900)`. Both hold a single runtime type, so mixed alternatives are not required. Floats and nested `NULL`s are routed to the existing general path, which honours `nulls_direction`, and floats are added to the two skip-index gates. Runtime-typed columns instead install no filter, since no comparison here can recover the discriminator. Both predicates recurse over the type rather than listing wrappers, and test the sort column's own type, so sorting on a static subcolumn such as `v.f` of `JSON(f Float64)` keeps the filter. Cost: no pruning for float or runtime-typed sort columns. On a NaN-free `Float64`, 10M rows, `ORDER BY f ASC LIMIT 10` goes from 7 ms to 15 ms and reads 10M rows instead of 81,920; integers are unaffected. The two `TODO`s in the code note what would recover it. The test runs 42 carriers on and off and requires each pair to agree, 12 of them controls. Each guard term is mutation-checked: reverting it reddens only the arm it exists for.

signals.title: Preserve non-clonable sources for deferred set builds
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619#issuecomment-5230196558 The speculative ordered-set build used for index analysis consumed non-clonable source plans before it knew whether the set was complete. If a `ReadFromRemote` pipeline stopped on an unavailable shard before `Set::finishInsert`, the deferred build had no source left and `FunctionIn` received a not-ready set. Preserve non-clonable local sources by skipping the speculative index optimization and letting `DelayedCreatingSetsStep` perform the authoritative build. The regression test uses the deterministic five-part `test_unavailable_shard` reproducer from the linked issue comment and verifies that `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED` propagates normally. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix queries with an `IN` subquery over unavailable remote shards potentially raising the `Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument` logical exception instead of the underlying connection exception.

signals.title: Add byte-weighted bytes_to_do and progress to system.mutations
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114678 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `system.mutations` now exposes byte-weighted mutation progress: `bytes_to_do` (the on-disk size of the data parts that still need to be mutated) and `progress` (an estimated finished fraction from 0 to 1, including the live fraction of the parts currently being rewritten). Part counts are a poor work proxy — parts are unequal in size and a regular merge can retire many pending parts at once — so the byte view is the honest one; the docs gain an "Estimating mutation progress" section with an equivalent parameterized-view recipe for older releases. Implements the conclusion of the research on the issue in two layers: **Columns** (`bytes_to_do` UInt64, `progress` Float64 in `system.mutations`): derived on read like `parts_to_do` — no persisted state, no replication protocol or znode format change. For plain `MergeTree` the sizes ride along the existing per-part scan in `getMutationsStatus`; for replicated tables the queue keeps returning name-only statuses under its state lock and the storage resolves sizes afterwards, so no parts lock is ever taken under the queue mutex (parts gone by then were retired and contribute nothing). The in-flight fraction comes from the merge list (`system.merges` rows with `is_mutation = 1`). Values are estimates by nature: a merge can retire pending parts at any moment, making `progress` jump forward. **Docs**: an "Estimating mutation progress" section on the `system.mutations` page explains why part-count percentages mislead and ships a parameterized-view recipe computing the same number on releases without the columns (the view was validated live against a running mutation, including a merge collapsing 9 pending parts mid-run), plus cross-links from `system.merges`, `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`, and the knowledge base. The stateless test asserts exact values on both engines: with merges stopped (which parks mutation tasks), `bytes_to_do` equals the active parts' total size and `progress` is 0; after completion the entry reports 0 and 1. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: Reuse the previous row's result for equal consecutive rows in Set execution
signals.text: The per-row execution of `x IN <set>` (`Set::executeImplCase`) hashes the full key for every row — SipHash128 for hashed multi-column keys. When the key columns are clustered (e.g. they are a primary-key prefix, so the data arrives sorted), consecutive rows form long runs of equal values, and the previous row's result can be reused after a cheap raw-byte comparison instead of repeating the hash+probe. With this change, when all key columns are non-nullable fixed-width (tuples are flattened element-wise), each row's raw bytes are compared with the previous row's, and on equality the previous result is reused, skipping the hash+probe entirely. Motivation: in SQL transpiled from PromQL selectors over `TimeSeries` tables, the per-row `id IN (tags subquery)` filter computes SipHash128 of a 24-byte `Tuple(UInt64, UUID)` per row into a `HashSet<UInt128>`. On tsbench, a PromQL benchmark over the ClickHouse `TimeSeries` engine (30 days of scrape data at 15s step, scale 1 = 1.06 billion samples / 6112 series, Ryzen 9950X, query result cache disabled, best of 3), this filter took ~17.5% of CPU of a 30-day rate query scanning 69M rows. With this change the hashing disappears from the profile (~3% of cheap byte comparisons remain), and raw-selector benchmark queries improved 1.4–2.3x. The optimization is generic: any `IN` over clustered/sorted key columns benefits; for unclustered data the added cost is a few loads per row. Bitwise comparison is applied only to POD column layouts (fixed-width raw bytes in one contiguous buffer, tuples flattened element-wise), where bitwise equality implies key equality; strings, arrays, `Nullable` and other non-POD layouts keep the existing path. The new performance test `tests/performance/set_in_clustered_keys.xml` covers both the clustered case (runs of equal consecutive keys) and the unclustered regression control (consecutive rows always differ). Note: tsbench scale-64 validation is in progress; numbers will be added before merge. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up execution of `IN` over clustered (e.g. sorted by primary key) columns by reusing the previous row's result for equal consecutive rows. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1512` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Avoid repeated EXPLAIN ANALYZE clock lookups for staged processors
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Performance Improvement** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): - **Avoid repeated wall-clock registry lookups in **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** for multi-stage processors.** ### Why this matters - `StepWallClockRegistry::find()` is keyed by the query-plan step and processor group. - The cache pointer was stored, but the group stayed at its default value of `0`. - For non-default groups, such as aggregation finalization and join build/probe, the old code repeated the lookup for every task. - Normal query execution is unchanged because this registry is only used by **EXPLAIN ANALYZE**. ### Changes - **Store:** the group together with the clock pointer after lookup. - **Keep:** the existing retry behavior when no clock is found. - **Use:** the cached-clock alias consistently in the condition. ### Benchmark This is a focused microbenchmark of the cache lookup section, not end-to-end **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** latency. Setup: Apple arm64, Apple Clang `-O3`, stable group `1`, matching registry entry, 10,000,000 tasks, 9 rounds, median result. | Version | Registry lookups | Median time | Relative | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Before | 10,000,000 | 25.89 ms | 1.00x | | After | 1 | 3.21 ms | 8.07x faster | The lookup count is exact. Wall-clock time is machine-dependent. ### Validation - `git diff --check` - **Validation:** Focused cache lookup microbenchmark - **Validation:** Existing **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** coverage for aggregation and join stages

signals.title: Fix `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup` for single-column complex keys wrapped in `tuple`
signals.text: Since 25.12, the analyzer pass `InverseDictionaryLookupPass` (setting `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup`, enabled by default) rewrites `dictGet(dict, attr, key_expr) <op> const` into a comparison of the key expression against dictionary keys: either constants folded from `dictGetKeys` (`key_expr = const`, `key_expr IN [consts]`, or `0`), or the subquery form `key_expr IN (SELECT <key columns> FROM dictionary(dict) WHERE attr <op> const)`. The key expression is reused verbatim as the left-hand side, while all rewrite shapes produce bare key values on the right-hand side. A complex-key dictionary with a single key column accepts (and much existing SQL uses) the `tuple()`-wrapped call form `dictGet(..., tuple(k))` — for it, the rewrite pits a one-element `Tuple` against a scalar, and a query that works on every release before 25.12 fails with `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT`. Multi-column keys are unaffected: `(k1, k2) IN (SELECT k1, k2 ...)` is the standard SQL form and the types line up. ## How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE dict_source (k UUID, k2 String, attr String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO dict_source VALUES ('11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'a', 'foo'), ('22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222', 'b', 'bar'); CREATE DICTIONARY single_key_dict (k UUID, attr String DEFAULT '') PRIMARY KEY k SOURCE(CLICKHOUSE(TABLE 'dict_source')) LIFETIME(0) LAYOUT(COMPLEX_KEY_HASHED()); CREATE TABLE data (k UUID, k2 String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO data VALUES ('11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'a'), ('33333333-3333-3333-3333-333333333333', 'c'); -- Must return 1, but fails since 25.12: SELECT count() FROM data WHERE dictGet('single_key_dict', 'attr', tuple(k)) = 'foo'; ``` On master the query fails in the constant-fold path: ``` Code: 43. DB::Exception: Illegal types of arguments (`Tuple(UUID)`, `UUID`) of function `equals`. (ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT) ``` On 26.3 (before the `dictGetKeys` constant fold existed) the same query fails in the subquery path with `Illegal type Tuple(UUID) of argument of function toUUID`. The workaround on affected releases is `SETTINGS optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup = 0`, which returns the correct result. The bare-key form `dictGet(..., k)` and multi-column keys work on all versions. ## The fix Normalize the key expression once, before both rewrite paths, when the dictionary key is composite with exactly one key column and the key expression resolves to a one-element tuple: - a syntactic `tuple(k)` call is replaced by its argument; - any other tuple-typed expression (e.g. a column of type `Tuple(UUID)`) is wrapped in `tupleElement(expr, 1)`. The rewrite still fires for these queries — the new test asserts the rewritten plans via `EXPLAIN SYNTAX run_query_tree_passes=1` for all three constant-fold shapes and both subquery shapes. Simple-key dictionaries are deliberately left alone: `dictGet(simple_dict, attr, tuple(id))` is rejected (`Illegal type Tuple(UInt64) of argument of function toUInt64`) even with the optimization disabled, so normalizing there would make otherwise-invalid queries succeed only while the optimization is on. A `Tuple`-typed dictionary key column cannot conflict with the unwrapping because dictionaries reject `Tuple` attribute types (`Unknown type Tuple(UUID) for dictionary attribute`). The new test `04891_optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup_single_key_tuple` covers the failing forms, the bare-key and two-column-key controls, a constant on either side of the comparison, and result equality with the optimization on and off. All existing `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup` tests pass. ## Backport This is a regression in an official stable release (25.12) affecting all later releases, including 26.3 LTS. Please consider labeling for backport to 26.3 (`v26.3-must-backport`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` when `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup` rewrites `dictGet` comparisons for complex-key dictionaries with a single key column and a `tuple()`-wrapped key expression.

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/series
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/series`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus clients** use **`/api/v1/series`** to discover the label sets stored for active series. This endpoint is used by **Prometheus-compatible tools** such as **Grafana** when they need to populate metric and label selectors. ClickHouse **`TimeSeries` tables** can store labels in the main **`tags` Map**, in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, or in a mixture of both layouts. The endpoint needs to expose the **same logical series** regardless of how those labels are stored. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/series` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint is available through both a **dedicated `/api/v1/series` handler** and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**. It supports **GET requests** and **`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` POST requests**. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** selects series by metric name and label matchers. Repeated parameters are combined as a **union** and overlapping results are returned only once through **deduplication**. - **`start` and `end`** select series overlapping the requested **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the number of returned series and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Selector parsing:** parse Prometheus series selectors with equality, inequality, regular-expression, and negative regular-expression matchers. - **Storage compatibility:** support metric names, labels in the **`tags` Map**, dedicated tag columns, and mixed rows that use both storage layouts. - **Label normalization:** normalize missing labels to the **Prometheus empty-value semantics** and include the full logical label set in each response. - **PromQL compatibility:** support quoted label names and anchor regular expressions to the **complete label value**. - **Input validation:** validate selectors and timestamps before executing the query. - **Time ranges:** apply the time-range filter when trusted min/max data is available. When it is not available, keep the request valid and return the **compatible candidate superset** allowed by the Prometheus API. - **Result limits:** support zero and positive limits, exact-limit responses, truncation reporting, and invalid-value errors. - **Access control:** read the underlying series metadata through the **`TimeSeries` table-function path** after checking access to the configured **`TimeSeries` table**. Unknown routes are resolved before authorization, so they keep the normal **404 response**. - **Existing endpoints:** apply the configured **`TimeSeries` table access boundary** consistently to the existing Prometheus query endpoints. - **Query lifecycle:** run the generated query through the **normal query pipeline** and keep **query logging** and **query completion handling** intact. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Matcher operators:** metric-name and label selectors with all matcher operators. - **Repeated selectors:** repeated **`match[]`** parameters, selector unions, and overlapping-result deduplication. - **Storage layouts:** Map labels, dedicated tag columns, missing labels, mixed carriers, conflicting carriers, and **`__name__`**. - **Regex and names:** quoted label names and whole-value regular-expression anchoring. - **Selector validation:** invalid and unbounded selectors, including the valid **`{host!~".*"}`** case. - **Time ranges:** two-sided, one-sided, inclusive, and invalid time ranges. - **Min/max behavior:** requests with and without trusted min/max metadata. - **Limits:** zero, exact, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values. - **HTTP methods:** GET and form POST requests. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants**, access checks for all query endpoint families, and unknown-route handling. - **Observability:** query completion records and the existing query API limit behavior. Also ran **Python syntax checks** and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now covers the Prometheus handler configuration and the **`/api/v1/series` endpoint parameters**. ### Stack This is the **base PR** for the follow-up Prometheus API endpoints: - **#114868** adds **`/api/v1/labels`**. - **#114869** adds **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`**.

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/labels
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/labels`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus-compatible clients** use **`/api/v1/labels`** to discover the label names available in matching series. This is useful for **Grafana dashboards**, variable pickers, and integrations that need to build label selectors without fetching every series first. The endpoint follows the same **logical label model** as the series endpoint. It reads labels stored in the **`tags` Map** and in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/labels` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint returns a **sorted, distinct list of label names**. It includes **`__name__`** when at least one matching series exists and supports both **unfiltered discovery** and filtering by matching series. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** filters the series used to build the label-name list. Repeated selectors are combined as a **union**. - **`start` and `end`** restrict the matching series by their **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the returned label names and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Label discovery:** collect distinct names from the canonical metric name, the **`tags` Map**, and configured dedicated tag columns. - **Selector support:** reuse the Prometheus series-selector and matcher behavior from **`/api/v1/series`**. - **Storage compatibility:** support both normal TimeSeries storage and **`tags_to_columns`** layouts while preserving the logical label set. - **Repeated selectors:** combine repeated **`match[]`** parameters without returning duplicate label names. - **Time ranges:** apply trusted min/max bounds when available and keep ranged requests valid with the **approximate superset** behavior allowed by Prometheus when bounds are unavailable. - **Result limits:** support empty, zero, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values, including the Prometheus truncation warning. - **HTTP handling:** support the dedicated endpoint and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**, with endpoint parameters kept separate from ClickHouse settings. - **Access control:** enforce the configured **`TimeSeries` table authorization boundary** before reading the underlying target tables. - **Query lifecycle:** execute through the **normal query pipeline**, preserve query completion handling, and record the request in **`query_log`**. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Label collection:** distinct names, sorted output, **`__name__`**, Map labels, and dedicated columns. - **Selectors:** metric filters, label filters, repeated **`match[]`** unions, and requests with no matching series. - **Time ranges:** matching and non-matching intervals, including empty optional parameters. - **Limits:** truncation warnings and the **`limit`** parameter behavior. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants** on the configured `TimeSeries` table. - **Observability:** successful requests recorded as **`QueryFinish`** entries. - **Shared behavior:** the related Prometheus query and series API regression coverage. Also ran **Python syntax checks**, **XML parsing**, and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now describes the `/api/v1/labels` handler and its supported parameters. ### Stack This PR is **stacked on #114867** and includes the **`/api/v1/series`** changes. After **#114867** merges, this branch can be rebased onto `master`.

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/label/<name>/values
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus-compatible clients** use **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`** to discover the values available for a label. This is used by **Grafana dashboards**, variable pickers, and integrations that need to populate label-value selectors. Prometheus also supports **escaped UTF-8 label names**. The endpoint must decode those names correctly while preserving malformed or intentionally literal values in a predictable way. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/label/<name>/values` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint returns a **sorted, distinct list of values** for one label. It supports metric names through **`__name__`**, labels from the **`tags` Map**, dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, series selectors, time ranges, and result limits. Supported parameters: - **`<name>`** identifies the label whose values should be returned, including Prometheus **`U__...` escaped names**. - **`match[]`** filters the series contributing values. - **`start` and `end`** restrict the matching series by their **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the returned values and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Value discovery:** return distinct values for ordinary labels and the special **`__name__`** metric-name label. - **Storage compatibility:** read values from the **`tags` Map** and dedicated **`tags_to_columns`** columns using the same logical label semantics as the other metadata endpoints. - **Name decoding:** decode valid Prometheus escaped label names, preserve malformed or overlong escape sequences as literal names, and reject an empty decoded label name. - **Selector support:** filter values by metric and series selectors, including unknown-label and no-match cases. - **Time ranges:** apply trusted min/max bounds when available and keep ranged requests valid with the **approximate superset** behavior allowed by Prometheus when bounds are unavailable. - **Result limits:** support empty, zero, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values, including the Prometheus truncation warning. - **HTTP handling:** add the label-values route to the **combined `/api/v1` handler** and keep endpoint parameters separate from ClickHouse settings. - **Access control:** enforce the configured **`TimeSeries` table authorization boundary** before reading the underlying target tables. - **Query lifecycle:** execute through the **normal query pipeline**, preserve query completion handling, and record the request in **`query_log`**. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Metric names:** values returned through **`__name__`**. - **Label values:** distinct Map values and values from configured dedicated columns. - **Escaped names:** valid UTF-8 decoding, malformed escape sequences, overlong escapes, and empty decoded names. - **Filtering:** selectors, unknown labels, and requests with no matching series. - **Time ranges:** matching and non-matching intervals, including empty optional parameters. - **Limits:** truncation warnings and the maximum valid **UInt64** limit. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants** on the configured `TimeSeries` table. - **HTTP integration:** the main HTTP port, routing, and query completion records. Also ran **Python syntax checks**, **XML parsing**, and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now describes the label-values handler, escaped label names, and its supported parameters. ### Stack This PR is **stacked on #114867** and includes the **`/api/v1/series`** changes. After **#114867** merges, this branch can be rebased onto `master`.

signals.title: Follow-ups for CREATE HANDLER: parse limits of the stored query, docs, refactoring
signals.text: Follow-ups from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106231 (`CREATE HANDLER`). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106231 **Requested in review of #106231:** - The two predicates over `IAST::QueryKind` that describe the `readonly` mode - whether a query of that kind is rejected under it, and whether `readonly = 2` still lets it produce side effects - moved out of `SQLDefinedHandlerFromAST` into `Interpreters/QueryKindUnderReadonly.h`; `queryKindRequiresMutatingMethod` is renamed to `isQueryKindRejectedUnderReadonly` after the property it reports. The handler code keeps the statement-level refinements and the HTTP-method fences. - `currentHandler` and `currentRequestURL` were registered with `IntroducedIn` 26.6 (the development version when they were written); they are released in 26.8. **The one unresolved review finding:** a request could still lower the parse limits of a handler's query. `HTTPHandler::processQuery` relaxed `max_parser_depth` / `max_parser_backtracks` *before* applying the settings the request supplies, and a request names settings freely - so `GET /h?max_parser_depth=1` put the caller's value back and broke a handler the server itself had accepted. The relaxation now happens after the request settings. `max_query_size` had the same hole and did not even need a hostile request: a stored query longer than its default value is creatable and reloadable (both parse without a size limit) but failed on every invocation; it is now raised to fit the query text - not disabled, because `executeQuery` also uses `max_query_size` to decide how much of the request stream to read ahead in search of the query text, where `0` would make it read a single byte. New tests `04897_handler_request_parser_limits` and `04898_handler_large_query_invocation`, both verified to fail without the fix. **Documentation:** the `CREATE HANDLER` page was written into `docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/handler.md` - a path in the legacy Docusaurus tree that `9440ca729a3` had already removed - so the only documentation of `CREATE HANDLER` / `ALTER HANDLER` / `DROP HANDLER` was published nowhere. It moves to `docs/reference/statements/create/handler.mdx`, with the frontmatter and internal links converted to that tree's conventions and the page registered in `docs/reference/navigation.json`. `docs/en/operations/system-tables/handlers.md` was a leftover copy of the generated `docs/reference/system-tables/handlers.mdx` whose hand-written `SHOW HANDLERS` / secret-masking paragraph had been lost; that paragraph is restored and the legacy copy deleted. The statement is now cross-referenced from the HTTP interface page, the `DROP` page and the `ALTER` overview, and the anchored (`RE2::FullMatch`) semantics of `URL REGEXP` are documented. Verified locally: all 30 SQL-defined-handler stateless tests pass against a server built from this branch (the 31st match of the `handler` filter, `03354_tcp_handler_async_insert_bug`, is unrelated and needs a writable `/var/lib/clickhouse/user_files`), and `04844_handler_deep_query_invocation` still passes without the fix, confirming it covered only the session-level limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed HTTP handler invocation so request-level `max_parser_depth`, `max_parser_backtracks`, and `max_query_size` no longer break stored handler queries, and published the `CREATE HANDLER`, `ALTER HANDLER`, and `DROP HANDLER` documentation.

signals.title: Cheaper per-sample add path in timeSeries*ToGrid aggregate functions
signals.text: The `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate functions pay a fixed cost for every incoming sample in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesBase`: computing the grid bucket index and looking the bucket up in a hash map. This PR makes both cheaper: - **Int64 fast path for the bucket-index computation.** `bucketIndexForTimestamp` used Int128 division and modulo per sample to stay overflow-safe for adversarial grid parameters. Now, when all grid parameters are bounded by 2^61 (checked once in the constructor; covers every practical case), the per-sample computation runs in plain Int64 arithmetic, dividing by the fixed `step` through a precomputed `libdivide` reciprocal — the `__udivmodti4` calls disappear from query profiles. The Int128 path is kept as-is for out-of-range parameters and single-point grids (`start == end`). - **Cached last-bucket pointer in the batch add loops.** Samples arrive sorted by timestamp within a series, so consecutive samples usually land in the same bucket; the loops now reuse the last bucket pointer and skip the hash-map lookup for same-bucket runs. Inserting into the map can invalidate the cached pointer, but an insert happens only on a bucket change, which re-acquires the pointer. Measured on tsbench, a PromQL benchmark over the ClickHouse `TimeSeries` engine (30 days of scrape data at 15 s step; scale 1 = 1.06 billion samples / 6112 series, Ryzen 9950X, query result cache disabled, best of 3): on a 30-day PromQL `rate` query scanning 69M samples, the per-sample Int128 division (`__udivmodti4`) was ~2% of CPU and the bucket-index computation ~3% — both disappear from the profile with the Int64 fast path; the whole rate-aggregation add path went from ~12% to ~8% of the query. A new performance test `tests/performance/timeseries_to_grid_scalar_add.xml` targets exactly this path: dense scalar samples (40M rows, 200 series, one sample per 15 s) aggregated with `step` = `window` = 300 s, so every in-range sample contributes to exactly one bucket and ~20 consecutive samples land in the same bucket. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up the `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate functions: per-sample bucket math now avoids Int128 division, and consecutive samples in the same bucket skip the hash-map lookup. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1498` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: TimeSeries: compare consecutive ids via raw columns in getGroupByID
signals.text: The function `timeSeriesIdToGroup` maps time-series ids to per-query group indexes and runs on every scanned row of every transpiled PromQL selector. Its implementation, `ContextTimeSeriesTagsCollector::getGroupByID`, has a fast path for sorted id streams: since samples arrive sorted by id (long runs of equal values), each row is first compared with the previous one, and on equality the previous row's group is reused. That per-row equality check went through a virtual `compareAt` chain (`ColumnTuple` and its two nested columns). This PR makes the fast path compare the raw column data directly for the standard id type `Tuple(UInt64, UUID)`: two integer comparisons per row instead of three virtual calls. Other id types keep the generic `compareAt` path. The standard id type now has a single definition, `standardTimeSeriesIDDataType` in `normalizeTimeSeriesDefinition` (also used where the default id type is resolved); the column check matches against it structurally and asserts the extraction, so a future change of the standard id type cannot silently bypass or desynchronize the fast path. Measured on tsbench, a PromQL benchmark over the ClickHouse `TimeSeries` engine (30 days of scrape data at 15s step; scale 1 = 1.06 billion samples / 6112 series on a Ryzen 9950X, query result cache disabled, best of 3): on a 30-day `rate` query scanning 69M rows, the virtual `compareAt` chain took 10-12% of CPU, reduced to ~4.5% with raw comparisons. The new performance test `tests/performance/timeseries_id_to_group.xml` targets exactly this path: a 40M-row sorted stream of `Tuple(UInt64, UUID)` ids in runs of 20000 equal values flows through `timeSeriesIdToGroup`, with the tags collector populated by `timeSeriesStoreTags` in an `IN` subquery, mirroring the shape of transpiled PromQL selectors. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up PromQL queries over `TimeSeries` tables: comparing consecutive time-series ids in `timeSeriesIdToGroup` now uses raw column data instead of virtual per-row comparisons.

signals.title: Set the current Keeper component in TextIndexCountSource::generate
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113295 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: #113295 `SELECT count() FROM t WHERE hasAllTokens(str, [...])` is rewritten by the trivial-count-from-text-index optimization into a `ReadFromTextIndexCount` step (added in #111494). Its source runs on a pipeline execution thread: `TextIndexCountSource::generate` -> `computeCountForPart` -> `makeTextIndexInputStream` -> `IMergeTreeDataPart::getStreamNameOrHash(..., IDataPartStorage &)`, whose body probes the part storage with `existsFile`. On a disk that keeps part metadata in Keeper that probe is a real Keeper request, and `Coordination::ZooKeeper::pushRequest` throws `LOGICAL_ERROR` when no component is set for the scope. `generate()` is the outermost scope this step owns on that thread, and it set none: the step builds its own `Pipe`, so unlike the ordinary read path it never inherits the guard from `MergeTreeSource::tryGenerate`. This adds the one-line RAII guard at the top of `generate()`. The guard is a nesting-safe thread-local stack and every Keeper-reaching call above is a descendant of that scope, so no deeper placement is needed. Same shape as #113295 for `MergeTreeCodecBlockCountsSource::generate` and the sibling `MergeTreeTextIndexSource::generate`. Of the four callers of `makeTextIndexInputStream`, the other three already have an ancestor guard (`MergeTreeSource::tryGenerate` for both `MergeTreeReaderTextIndex` sites, the mutate/merge task guards for `MergeTextIndexesTask`); this step was the only gap. Category is `CI Fix or Improvement`, as in #113295 and #113386: the metadata-in-Keeper storage type is registered only under `#if CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD`, and `LOGICAL_ERROR` aborts only in debug and sanitizer builds, so this cannot happen in an official stable build. For the same reason no test is added: no public build reaches Keeper through `existsFile`. Validated with the existing `02346_text_index*` suite (plus 50/50 randomized runs of `02346_text_index_optimize_trivial_count`), an `EXPLAIN` assertion that the modified scope is the one the query executes, and a run with `enforce_keeper_component_tracking = 1`. Left alone: the plan-time `getDeserializedFormat` path can also reach `existsFile` for packed skip-index parts and is likewise unguarded, but it predates this step by three weeks and is not this failure's carrier.

signals.title: Fix undefined behavior in DateTime64 reservoir quantiles
signals.text: The reservoir-sampling implementation of `quantile` and `quantiles` interpolates values in `Float64`. `DateTime64` ticks close to the upper `Int64` boundary can round to 2^63 exactly, making the conversion back to the native representation undefined. signals.title: Make a table read by a scalar subquery in a CONSTRAINT a loading dependency
signals.text: Attaching a table analyzes its constraints in `InterpreterCreateQuery::getConstraintsDescription`, and the analysis executes the scalar subqueries of a constraint expression. The tables such a subquery reads were not registered as loading dependencies, because `DDLLoadingDependencyVisitor` only looks at functions, dictionary sources and the storage definition. Nothing prevented dropping such a table, and the server did not start afterwards - attaching the dependent table threw `UNKNOWN_TABLE` and loading the metadata failed: ```sql CREATE TABLE t1 (id UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); CREATE TABLE t2 (conversation UInt64, CONSTRAINT c CHECK (SELECT id FROM t1 LIMIT 15) IN (conversation)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); DROP TABLE t1; -- accepted, and the server cannot start anymore ``` The referential dependency was recorded, since `DDLDependencyVisitor` visits `ASTTableExpression`, so `check_referential_table_dependencies = 1` rejected the `DROP`. But that setting is off by default, and it is the loading graph that the default `check_table_dependencies` check and the `DROP DATABASE` drop order (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97057) use. A constraint declaration is now visited, and the tables of every subquery that the analysis executes are added to the loading dependencies. Subqueries which the analysis does not execute - the right argument of `IN` and the argument of `exists`, see `ExecuteScalarSubqueriesMatcher::visit` - are skipped, because what they read is needed only when the constraint is checked, not to attach the table. That keeps `02916_joinget_dependency`-style patterns working, in particular `02841_not_ready_set_constraints`, which drops the table read by an `x IN (SELECT ...)` constraint on purpose. Seen in CI as a `Cannot start clickhouse-server` stress failure, e.g. https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110231&sha=4de836223549fd5224ca017b8c1a28e344ce38e9&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_msan%29 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114918 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87369 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A table read by a scalar subquery inside a `CONSTRAINT` is now a loading dependency of the table that declares the constraint. Previously such a table could be dropped, after which the server did not start, because attaching the dependent table executes the subquery.

signals.title: Add a style check for the spelling of `ClickHouse`
signals.text: The product name is written `ClickHouse` - one word, with a capital `C` and a capital `H`. Two case variants are accepted, because a mixed case is unusable there: `clickhouse` for identifiers, package, binary and host names, and `CLICKHOUSE` for macros and environment variables. Everything else - `Clickhouse`, `clickHouse`, `click_house`, `CLICK_HOUSE`, `click-house`, `Click House` - is a misspelling, and until now nothing stopped it from being committed. ## The check The new `clickhouse_spelling` check of the style job searches every file tracked by git, and the file names themselves, in code as well as in comments, messages and documentation. A `git grep -P` prefilter finds the candidate lines (a provable superset of what is reported), so the check costs about a second on a warm page cache and a minute on a cold one. Only the space-separated form is anchored at word boundaries, so an unrelated phrase - "click Household" - is not taken for the product name. The other forms are left unanchored on purpose, so that a misspelling inside a longer identifier - `ClickhouseBuffer` - is reported too. Rather than a long list of excused files, the sources of false positives are handled structurally: * `contrib` - third-party sources. * The generated locale directories of the documentation, `docs/<locale>/` and `docs/snippets/<locale>/`, taken from `docs/gt.config.json`. They are a machine translation of the English pages, so a misspelling there is fixed by fixing the English page; the default locale is not excluded, and `docs/en/` stays enforced. * Release notes - a record of what was published, not edited after the fact. Same pattern as the "new analyzer" wording check in `various_checks.sh`, so the landing and status pages that live next to them stay enforced. * `docs/_specs` - API specifications pinned from their generator by `ci/jobs/cloud_api_docs_nightly.py`. * Regions between `AUTOGENERATED_START` and `AUTOGENERATED_END` markers. Their source of truth - a `FunctionDocumentation` string, for instance - is checked instead, which is what a contributor is supposed to edit. * URLs. A link whose path spells the name differently is not a mistake we can fix, and rewriting it would only break the link. `docs/resources/about/adopters.mdx` alone holds eleven of them. What is left goes into `ci/jobs/scripts/check_style/clickhouse_spelling_ignore.txt`, in the spirit of the existing `experimental_settings_ignore.txt`: a path alone exempts a file, a path followed by a literal exempts only the lines containing that literal. It has fifteen entries, each with the reason next to it, and every one of them is text that is not ours to spell: names defined by other projects (the `ClickhouseClientOptions` of our Azure SDK fork, the `clickHouse*` parameters of Google's Dataflow templates, a third-party client library), verbatim quotations (Stack Overflow post titles shown as query output), and the misspellings that tests feed to the server on purpose - `LIKE` / `ILIKE` case variants, `hasPhrase(message, 'Click House')`, `click_house:` as an unknown URI scheme. ## The fixes The check found 191 misspellings, all fixed here. Most are prose and comments. The renamed identifiers are `isClickhouseApp`, `getClickhouseAttemptNumber` / `setClickhouseAttemptNumber`, `getClickhouseTableSchemaById` / `hasClickhouseTableSchemaById`, the `Clickhouse*` classes of `clickhouse-diagnostics`, the `tabClickhouse` / `btnQueryClickhouse` element ids of the `utils` web tools, and `clickHousePartsInserter.js`, which is renamed. No stale reference to an old name survives - one would be a misspelling, and the check reports those. Three of the fixes are visible to tests, and the first two rely on the server being case-insensitive there, which I confirmed against a running server rather than assumed: * the `X-Clickhouse-Format` HTTP header of `02015_async_inserts_1` - Poco header collections compare names case-insensitively; * the `SOURCE(Clickhouse(...))` dictionary source of `03071_fix_short_circuit_logic` - the parser lowercases the source name (`ExpressionElementParsers.cpp`); * a directory named `Clickhouse` in `03600_disk_app_plain_rewritable_disks_list_cmd`, renamed in the command and in the reference. Its position in the listing is unchanged, since `ClickHouse` sorts before `Cloud` either way. The rule is also written down as item 18 of the `Names` section of the style guide, so a contributor can find it before CI tells them. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)
