signals.title: Perf: bulk insert repeated values into nullable columns
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improves repeated value insertion into nullable columns by using the nested column's bulk insertion path. ### What does this PR do? - Uses `insertManyFrom` when the same non-nullable source value is inserted more than once. - Keeps the existing scalar `insertFromNotNullable` path for `length == 1`. - Extends the null map with one zero-filled range instead of pushing `false` one row at a time. - Keeps `length == 0` as a no-op, including when `position` is invalid. - Adds coverage for numeric columns, string columns, repeated single-row insertion, and the zero-length case. - Extends the existing `column_insert_many_from` benchmark with this exact non-nullable-to-nullable path. ### Why? `ColumnNullable::insertManyFromNotNullable` currently does this for every output row: - insert one value into the nested column - append one `false` value to the null map The caller in `MergeJoin::copyRightRange` can insert the same source row many times. The `IColumn::insertManyFrom` contract already represents this operation, and numeric and string columns have bulk implementations for it. For the common `length == 1` case, the existing scalar operation is kept so unique-key joins do not pay bulk setup costs. ### Benchmark The repository benchmark now measures non-nullable source columns inserted into nullable destinations for `Int64`, `String`, and `Decimal128(3)`, with fanouts of **1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256, and 65536**. Focused local measurements with pre-reserved output columns, `clang++ -O3 -march=native`: - Numeric nested columns, batches of 16-256 rows: **1.7x-2.4x faster**. - 16-byte strings, batches of 16-256 rows: **1.6x-1.8x faster**. - Null-map filling alone was up to **8x-20x faster** for 64-256 row batches. - Very small strings and batches can be neutral or slower because the bulk-call setup is not free. The scalar path is retained for `length == 1`. These are method-level numbers. The end-to-end improvement depends on join fanout and the output column types.

signals.title: Fix host path leak in Keeper CLI path resolution
signals.text: Keeper CLI paths are znode names in the coordination service, not host filesystem paths. `KeeperClientBase::getAbsolutePath` used `std::filesystem::weakly_canonical`, which resolves symlinks against the server filesystem. When a path segment is a symlink (for example `/proc/self/cwd`, or a custom symlink such as `/tmp/keeper_leak_symlink_demo -> /root/ClickHouse/build_release/programs`), CLI and HTTP error messages could expose the Keeper process working directory and other host paths that the client never sent. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix host filesystem path leakage in `clickhouse-keeper-client` and the Keeper HTTP CLI when resolving paths through symlinks such as `/proc/self/cwd`.

signals.title: Perf: bulk insert repeated LowCardinality values
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid repeated dictionary work when inserting the same LowCardinality value many times. ## Summary - Add `ColumnLowCardinality::insertManyFrom`. - Read the source dictionary index once. - Translate the value once when dictionaries differ. - Append repeated indexes with `ColumnIndex::insertManyIndexes`. ## Why - The generic `IColumn::insertManyFrom` path calls `insertFrom` once per output row. - For LowCardinality, that repeats the same dictionary lookup and translation. - This keeps the existing result and moves invariant work out of the loop. ## Correctness - `length == 0` remains a no-op. - Shared and separate dictionaries use separate paths. - Tests cover repeated values and index widening from `UInt8` to `UInt16`. - `ColumnIndex::insertManyIndexes` keeps the existing index-widening behavior. ## Benchmark The same binary compares the new bulk path with the old scalar `insertFrom` loop. - `LowCardinality(String)` and `LowCardinality(UInt64)` - Shared and separate dictionaries - Fanouts: `1`, `2`, `4`, `8`, `16`, `64`, `256`, `65536` - Source setup and destination allocation are outside the timed section Run: ```bash ./build/programs/column_insert_many_from \ --benchmark_filter='(BM_insertManyFromLowCardinality|BM_insertFromRepeatedlyLowCardinality)' ``` ## Measured result AArch64 benchmark build, 5-run median CPU time: - Fanout 256: **7.2x–7.9x faster** across `String`/`UInt64` and shared/separate dictionaries. - Fanout 65,536: **324x–634x faster**. - Fanout 1: no meaningful gain, since only one value is inserted.

signals.title: Perf: bulk insert default Map values
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoids unnecessary nested key and value capacity reservation when adding default rows to Map columns. ### What does this PR do? - Adds `ColumnMap::insertManyDefaults`. - Delegates empty-map row insertion to the nested `ColumnArray`. - Pre-reserves only Map offsets for a fresh or larger batch. - Keeps geometric growth for one-row and small repeated calls. - Keeps `length == 0` as a no-op. - Adds coverage for empty maps, existing rows, zero length, and narrow maps. - Adds allocator-boundary cases and retained-allocation counters to the benchmark. ### Why? `IColumn::insertManyDefaults` reserves `size() + length` before inserting each default. For `Map`, that reservation is forwarded to the nested `ColumnArray`, then to the key and value columns. Default Map rows are empty, so reserving key/value capacity is unnecessary. The new path still appends the same repeated offset, but it only reserves the Map offsets for a fresh or larger batch. Small repeated calls stay on the amortized `ColumnArray` growth path. The general `ColumnArray` realloc-chain cleanup is being handled separately in [#113577](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113577). ### Performance For empty Map rows, the important improvement is avoiding child-column allocation: - `Map(UInt8, UInt8)` at 65,536 rows: about **655,742 -> 524,670 bytes** retained. - `Map(UInt64, UInt64)` at 65,536 rows: about **1,573,248 -> 524,672 bytes** retained. - `Map(UInt64, FixedString(256))` at 65,536 rows: about **17,826,183 -> 524,679 bytes** retained. The narrow-map case is also protected around the offset boundary. The 65,520 and 65,521 row cases stay at about 524 KiB after the change instead of growing to the next geometric allocation. ### Benchmark Local Linux arm64 run with LLVM 21 and RelWithDebInfo. Each case used 5 repetitions and a 0.1 second minimum per repetition. Before is the inherited `IColumn::insertManyDefaults` path. After is the `ColumnMap` override. Times are mean per benchmark iteration. Allocation is the retained `allocatedBytes()` counter. | Case | Before time | After time | Speedup | Before bytes | After bytes | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | `Map(UInt8, UInt8)`, 65,520 defaults | 185.4 us | 140.9 us | **1.3x (24.0%)** | 655,582 | 524,542 | | `Map(UInt8, UInt8)`, 65,521 defaults | 179.7 us | 145.7 us | **1.2x (18.9%)** | 655,592 | 524,550 | | `Map(UInt64, UInt64)`, 65,536 defaults | 301.6 us | 141.4 us | **2.1x (53.1%)** | 1,573,248 | 524,672 | | `Map(String, String)`, 65,536 defaults | 259.6 us | 145.8 us | **1.8x (43.8%)** | 1,573,502 | 524,926 | | `Map(UInt64, FixedString(256))`, 65,536 defaults | 220.9 us | 147.7 us | **1.5x (33.2%)** | 17,826,183 | 524,679 | | `Map(UInt64, FixedString(256))`, 4,096 repeated calls | 565.4 us | 12.5 us | **45.1x (97.8%)** | 1,114,503 | 65,799 | For repeated one-row calls, the new path intentionally keeps geometric offset growth. This makes the wide case much faster and avoids repeated exact reallocations. A very narrow map can retain a little more offset capacity in that specific pattern, which is why the benchmark covers both narrow and wide types.

signals.title: Add NEAREST JOIN: match the nearest vector within equality-key groups
signals.text: **TL;DR:** `NEAREST JOIN` picks, for each left row, the closest right row by vector distance among the rows with equal keys - like `ASOF JOIN`, but in vector space. On a real entity-resolution workload (5000 messy uploaded addresses against 11.9 million canonical ones, exact keys plus 768-dimension embeddings): * vector search - either wrong (top-k over the whole table returns false positives from other zip codes) or ~22 hours (one prefiltered search per zip code) * best relational workaround (`LIMIT 1 BY`) - 3.9 s / 660 MiB * `NEAREST JOIN` - **2.8 s / 730 MiB**, 99.76% top-1 accuracy against hand-labeled ground truth And when the equality groups are large (10^9 candidate pairs), the workaround has to materialize the fanout and `NEAREST JOIN` does not: 23 s / 11.3 GiB versus 3.3 s / 155 MiB - **7x faster, 73x less memory**. --- The motivating workload is entity resolution over noisy data. We match customer-uploaded address files (5000 rows, user-entered, messy) against a canonical table of 11.9 million addresses. Zip code and house number must match exactly. Only the fuzzy part - the free-text street line - should be matched by embedding distance (768 dimensions). Every query row carries its own equality prefilter, and the prefilter must apply **before** the neighbor search. We ran this three ways in a cloud data warehouse with a dedicated vector search function before writing this patch: 1. ANN index over the whole table, top-k by cosine distance, check the keys afterwards: 71 seconds, and wrong by construction. The globally nearest embedding is regularly a similar street in a different zip code. Once the true match is not in the top-k, no post-filter can recover it. 2. Prefilter first, one filtered vector search per zip code: correct, but the uploads span 4049 zip codes. The measured rate extrapolates to roughly 22 hours per uploaded file. 3. No vector index at all: equality join on the keys, then keep the closest row per query row with a window function. Exact, and 22 seconds. The lesson: a plain join already beats a vector index at this job. What is missing is a way to say "closest within the group" without materializing every candidate pair. Before - the rewrite everyone writes today. It is exact, and on the workload above the optimizer keeps it competitive (3.9 s, 660 MiB - it can swap the join sides and prefilter by the keys). But its cost is proportional to the candidate pairs it materializes: at 10^9 pairs it needs 23 s and 11.3 GiB. ```sql ```sql SELECT upload.query_id, base.address FROM upload_addresses AS upload INNER JOIN base_addresses AS base ON upload.zip = base.zip AND upload.house_number = base.house_number ORDER BY upload.query_id, cosineDistance(upload.street_embedding, base.street_embedding) LIMIT 1 BY upload.query_id ``` After - one join, same result, and the cost of the fanout is gone: 2.8 s on the workload above, and 3.3 s at 155 MiB on the 10^9-pair one (7x faster, 73x less memory): ```sql SELECT upload.query_id, base.address FROM upload_addresses AS upload NEAREST JOIN base_addresses AS base ON upload.zip = base.zip AND upload.house_number = base.house_number AND cosineDistance(upload.street_embedding, base.street_embedding) ``` The distance function takes the place of `ASOF`'s inequality. The last conjunct of the `ON` section names the vector columns, one from each side, in either order. The join finds the argmin exactly, with a linear scan inside each equality group. Semantics: - Identical results to the `LIMIT 1 BY` rewrite. Checked by `04909_nearest_join_equivalence` and by checksums in every benchmark below. - A distance that is not an ordinary number (for example, the cosine distance to a zero vector) never wins. Among rows at exactly the same minimal distance, one is returned, like `ANY` join for duplicate keys. - `NEAREST LEFT JOIN` keeps unmatched left rows with defaults. - Single-side conditions in the `ON` section filter the candidates before the argmin. Supported: `INNER` (default) and `LEFT` kinds, the `hash` and `parallel_hash` algorithms, `Array(Float32)`/`Array(Float64)` vectors (or types promotable to them), the new analyzer only. Rejected with clear errors: `RIGHT`/`FULL` kinds, `USING`, `grace_hash`/`full_sorting_merge`, missing equality conjunct, zero or multiple distance conjuncts. The join shows up in `EXPLAIN` with `Strictness: nearest` and the distance function. Implementation: buckets store plain row refs (`RowRefList`, as ALL joins do). A probe-time matcher reads candidate vectors in place from the stored blocks, so memory stays proportional to the right table. An earlier draft copied vectors into per-bucket buffers, by analogy with `ASOF`'s sorted arrays; with millions of small equality groups the copies doubled the memory and dominated the build time, so they were removed. Like a plain `INNER JOIN`, an `INNER NEAREST` join may have its inputs swapped by the join order optimizer when the left side is smaller (honoring `query_plan_join_swap_table`). The swapped join builds the small side and streams the large side past it, keeping a per-build-row argmin, and emits the results through the delayed-blocks channel once the probe stream ends. Memory stays proportional to the smaller side, and the result does not depend on the swap (`04911_nearest_join_swapped`). When NDV statistics of the equality keys predict more candidate pairs than streamed rows, the swap is declined: the per-pair argmin updates would outweigh the build savings. `LEFT NEAREST` and distributed plans are never swapped. Measurements (GCE n2d-highmem-32, 32 vCPU / 256 GB, Release build; `NEAREST JOIN` and the rewrite returned identical counts and checksums in every run): 1. The address-matching workload above: 11.9M-row right table in 9.36M equality groups (average 1.3 candidates per group), 768-dimension `Array(Float64)`, 5000 left rows. `NEAREST JOIN` with the automatic swap: **2.8 s at 730 MiB**. Without the swap: 4.7 s at 70 GiB. The rewrite: 3.9 s at 660 MiB. Against hand-labeled ground truth: all 4973 matchable rows matched, 99.76% top-1 accuracy, none of the wrong-zip false positives of the ANN approach. 2. High-fanout: 1M-row right table in 100 equality groups (10000 rows each), 32-dimension `Array(Float32)`, 100k left rows - about 10^9 candidate pairs. `NEAREST JOIN`: **3.3 s at 155 MiB**. The rewrite: 23-29 s at 11.3 GiB, because it materializes and sorts every candidate pair. With `uniq` statistics on the keys, the optimizer detects the fanout and keeps the unswapped plan. There is also `tests/performance/nearest_join.xml` for CI. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `NEAREST JOIN`, which matches every left row with the right row at the minimal vector distance (`L2Distance` or `cosineDistance`) among the right rows sharing the equality keys - the vector-space analogue of `ASOF JOIN`, useful for entity resolution over embeddings. Equivalent to `INNER JOIN` + `ORDER BY` distance + `LIMIT 1 BY`, but without materializing the per-key fanout. Supports `INNER` and `LEFT` kinds with the `hash` and `parallel_hash` algorithms, and participates in join side swapping.

signals.title: Commit the recorded file sizes of a Log family write atomically
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/101796 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an `INSERT` into a `Log`, `TinyLog` or `StripeLog` table that fails while committing the recorded file sizes. Such an insert could keep its rows in the table even though it reported an error, or leave the data files of an array column inconsistent with each other. Reading a `Log` or `TinyLog` table whose array column holds no elements while its offsets claim some now raises an error naming the column instead of reading past the end of the elements. A partially written elements column was already rejected. ### Description **The write commit was not atomic.** `StorageLog::saveFileSizes` recorded each stream's size separately, and each `FileChecker::update` does IO that can throw. A throw partway through left new sizes for some streams and old ones for the rest. The insert had not finished, so the sink destructor calls `FileChecker::repair`, which truncates every file to its recorded size, leaving adjacent streams of one array column at different generations: the outer offsets then described more elements than the inner ones held. A throw inside `save` instead left the files appended but the sizes unchanged, so a failed insert kept its rows. `FileChecker::updateAndSave` now collects the sizes into a candidate map, persists it, and adopts it only on success. `StorageStripeLog` is fixed likewise. The marks file is one of the recorded files, so a rollback truncates it while `num_marks_saved` stayed advanced, leaving in-memory marks that `removeUnsavedMarks` would not trim. The counter is now restored when the size commit fails, on both the insert and restore paths. **Reads no longer trust inconsistent array streams.** `LogSource::readData` already checked the deserialized column's type; it now also checks at every nesting level that the last offset matches the element count, raising `INCORRECT_DATA` naming the column. A short but non-empty elements column was already rejected with `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA`, so the empty case is the one that reached the pipeline and the one this check catches. I found the first defect while investigating a `ColumnArray::indexImpl` assertion failure in `BuzzHouse (amd_tsan)` (STID 2508-2944, [report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101796&sha=628da3c387736525f6398b025afb900437a4f11a&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_tsan%29)), where a sort indexed an array column whose offsets claimed more elements than it held. How that table reached the state is still unknown: the failing run's log shows no truncation by `repair`, so this commit path is not shown to have produced it. That is why the read side is hardened too. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> `tests/queries/0_stateless/04931_log_family_insert_commit_rollback.sh` covers the write half over `Log`, `TinyLog` and `StripeLog` and both failure windows, using two failpoints conditioned so they fire on the commit at the end of the insert and not on the empty baseline commit the sink makes when it starts. Reverting either half of the fix reddens it, with distinct symptoms: reverting the atomic commit aborts on `Invalid number of rows in Chunk`, while reverting only the counter restore leaves the table reporting 180 rows where 140 were written. `tests/integration/test_storage_log_damaged_array/` covers the read half for `Log` and `TinyLog`, over three damage shapes: a missing inner offsets stream, which the top-level check catches; a missing leaf elements stream, which only the recursion into nested levels catches; and a partially written elements stream, which fails earlier with `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA`. Deleting the recursion leaves the first and third passing and reddens the second. It edits the data files directly, so it cannot be a functional test. The new check was run against 1405 existing tests over `log`, `tinylog`, `stripelog`, `nested`, `array`, `object` and `json`; it did not fire once on data written normally. </details>

signals.title: Give Poco::Net::SocketAddress a noexcept move constructor
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110479 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Appending to a system log queue no longer deep-copies the whole queue when it grows. `Poco::Net::SocketAddress` had no move constructor, which made `QueryLogElement` and three other element types not nothrow-move-constructible, so a `std::vector` reallocation copied every element (allocating per address) while the queue mutex was held, blocking every query that writes to `system.query_log`. ### Description Found while investigating a server that accepted and planned queries but executed none for 3.5 minutes on `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, flaky check)`: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110479&sha=038667a9c024695126415fe5f37b76f7a06662fa&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20flaky%20check%29). The sampling profiler shows one thread inside `SystemLogQueue<QueryLogElement>::push` for 177 of 181 seconds, in `vector::__emplace_back_slow_path`, with 31 threads blocked on `std::mutex::lock()` in the same call. `push()` appends under `mutex`, so a `std::vector` reallocation happens in the critical section. libc++ relocates with `std::move_if_noexcept`, which falls back to **copying** every element when the type is not nothrow-move-constructible. `QueryLogElement` was not, for one reason: `Poco::Net::SocketAddress` declared copy operations only, and its copy heap-allocates a new `SocketAddressImpl`. `ClientInfo` holds three of those. The fix belongs in Poco because that is where the cause is: a refcounted-pointer wrapper whose move is nothing but a pointer transfer. The moves of `ClientInfo` and the log elements stay implicit, so their trait is derived. `AutoPtr::swap` is used because `AutoPtr` also declares no move, so assignment would bump the refcount and leave the source non-null. Measured over one reallocation of 8192 elements: 32769 allocations before, 1 after. Four element types were affected (`QueryLog`, `QueryThreadLog`, `SessionLog`, `ZooKeeperLog`); a `static_assert` in `SystemLogQueue` now enumerates every element type at build time (30 here, 32 in a cloud build) and fails on the unpatched tree. A moved-from `SocketAddress` has a null `_pImpl`; all seven accessors already route through `pImpl()`, which throws `NullPointerException`, so that state stays defined. Left out deliberately: the slow `query_log` flush that triggered the reallocation is a separate question, and a move on `Poco::AutoPtr` would be the broader fix. This is one mechanism proven on one artifact, not a claim about every `Server died` report. No SQL test, because a C++ relocation trait is not observable from SQL.

signals.title: Clean reusable continue-all-prs worktrees
signals.text: Clean reusable worker worktrees before every PR assignment, discarding tracked, untracked, and ignored changes while retaining root-level `build*` directories for incremental rebuilds. When free disk space falls below 100 GiB, remove the oldest managed `tmp` and `build*` directories first, followed by stale managed worktrees if necessary. Cleanup is restricted to registered worktrees under the configured worker base, protects active worker roots, and stops a worker after a cleanup failure. Root-owned files left by containerized integration tests are removed by retrying the same path-scoped cleanup through non-interactive `sudo`; if cleanup still fails, the orchestrator exits instead of repeating the failure in later rounds. A live run reclaimed 47 GiB (95 GiB to 142 GiB free) while preserving all four reusable worker roots. It also verified immediate Ctrl+C termination during cleanup. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog.

signals.title: Read all summed columns for SELECT FINAL from SummingMergeTree
signals.text: `SELECT ... FINAL` from a `SummingMergeTree` table returned wrong results when the query read only a subset of the columns of the summation. A merge removes a row when the values in **all** of the columns of the summation are zero after summing. The FINAL read applied the same rule, but only over the columns the query happened to read. Two ways to misbehave follow from that: - A query reading a subset of the summed columns removed every group whose visible columns summed to zero, even though an unread summed column made the row survive a real merge — rows silently disappeared. The most common victim is bare `count()`, which reads a single smallest column (plus the internally added sorting key): on a table `(c0 Int8, c1 Int32, c3 UInt64) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree ORDER BY c3` with two overlapping parts where `c0` sums to zero for some keys, `SELECT count() FROM t FINAL` returned 10 instead of 15, and `SELECT c0, c3 FROM t FINAL` lost the same 5 rows. - A query reading none of the summed columns (e.g. only the sorting key) never removed anything, keeping rows that a real merge deletes. The fix always includes all columns that a merge would aggregate into the FINAL read set (and into the set protected from plan-level column pruning), so the removal decision is taken over the same set of columns as in a real merge. This makes `SELECT ... FINAL` agree with `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` followed by a plain `SELECT`. Note that queries over `SummingMergeTree FINAL` that previously read a subset of the summed columns now read all of them, which is the price of the correct result. Found by the nightly SQLancer `FinalMerge` oracle (`SELECT count() FROM t0 FINAL` returned 9947 before `OPTIMIZE TABLE t0 FINAL` and 9999 after it on the same data): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5c9f28ed5a2c585ad46bf74d6600cdcf3aa07a9e&name_0=NightlySQLancer&name_1=SQLancer%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29&name_1=SQLancer ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results of `SELECT ... FINAL` from `SummingMergeTree` when the query reads only a subset of the columns of the summation: the decision to remove a row whose sums are all zero is now taken over all columns of the summation, as in a real merge, instead of only the columns the query reads. Previously, rows could silently disappear from the result (for example, `SELECT count() FROM table FINAL`). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Fix an adaptive aggregator abort on lazily replicated columns
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111459 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `Aggregator::sealPendingChunks` coalesces several staged mini-chunks into one, concatenating each aggregate argument column across the minis. It clones the destination from the first source and then calls `prepareForSquashing` and `insertRangeFrom`, both of which `assert_cast` every source to the destination's class. That assumes all minis share one physical representation per position. They do not. Lazy column replication is decided per block: a join materializes a block whose replication does not grow the output and leaves the others wrapped in `ColumnReplicated` (`HashJoinResult.cpp`), so one stream legitimately mixes wrapped and dense blocks for the same column. `recursiveRemoveSparse` in the staging path deliberately preserves the wrapper, so the mix reaches the seal and the cast aborts: ``` Logical error: 'Bad cast from type DB::ColumnReplicated to DB::ColumnVector<unsigned long>' Received signal Aborted (6) ``` Two sites abort, both reproduced locally: `insertRangeFrom` for the numeric vectors, which do not override `prepareForSquashing` (the signature above), and `prepareForSquashing` itself for String, Nullable, Array, Map, Tuple, Variant, Dynamic and Object. The fix normalizes the whole `sources` vector, including the front, before the destination is cloned, so one gate covers both sites and destination and sources stay drawn from the same normalized set. The `structureEquals` gate keeps the homogeneous case allocation-free, so lazy replication keeps its benefit where it is uniform, and mirrors what `Squashing.cpp` already does for the identical hazard. Reachable from ordinary SQL: a `JOIN` feeding a `GROUP BY` with `enable_adaptive_aggregator = 1` and `enable_lazy_columns_replication = 1`, both defaults. In a release build `assert_cast` degrades to `static_cast`, so the same input reads a `ColumnReplicated` through a `ColumnVector` layout and copies from a bogus data pointer instead of failing loudly. `AdaptiveAggregation.cpp` was added by #111459 and is on no release branch, so no backport applies. Found by CI in `Stress test (arm_msan)` on an unrelated pull request: [report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110838&sha=db62fd0ad673a4eaf5411e8b75df5b1750bdcb93&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_msan%29), [fatal.log](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/PRs/110838/db62fd0ad673a4eaf5411e8b75df5b1750bdcb93/stress_test_arm_msan/fatal.log).

signals.title: Fix out-of-bounds read in pointInPolygon on an unbounded bounding box
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/11375 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/11375 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an out-of-bounds read in `pointInPolygon` with a constant polygon whose bounding box is unbounded, for example when a coordinate reaches `+-DBL_MAX`. Such a polygon is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`, and a polygon with an empty ring is treated as having no interior. Previously the query could return a wrong result, or abort the server in builds with hardening or sanitizers enabled. ### Description `SELECT pointInPolygon((1e308, 1.), [(-1.7976931348623157e308, 0.), (1.7976931348623157e308, 0.), (0., 2.)])` reads a `cells` element out of range, on default settings and with no elevated privileges. With libc++ hardening or a sanitizer it aborts (`vector[] index out of bounds`); otherwise it switches on a garbage cell type. Found by the targeted AST fuzzer: [report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112930&sha=27e32067e2142071df32a1cd106e533e54ae645e&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29) (the carrier PR is unrelated to this code). **Root cause.** `calcGridAttributes` validated the derived scales for finiteness but tested the bounding-box span only for `== 0`. `1 / +-inf` is `+-0.0`, which is finite, so an infinite span passed validation; `contains` then computed `inf * 0.0 = NaN`, which compared false against both range guards, `static_cast<int>(NaN)` gave `INT_MIN`, and the cell index overflowed. **Change.** Classify the span where it is computed: non-positive means no interior (`has_empty_bound`), non-finite is rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. Six lines in the only writer of the grid scales, so every reader is covered at once. `<= 0` rather than `!(span > 0)` keeps a NaN span throwing, as it does today. **Scope.** Only the preprocessed grid used for constant polygons is changed. A non-constant polygon column takes the on-the-fly ray-casting path, which builds no grid and cannot reach this out-of-bounds read; it does lose precision on an unbounded span (`inf/inf` in the edge formula), a separate pre-existing issue deliberately left alone here. **Validation.** Measured against pristine HEAD. Three carriers stop aborting: the wide polygon above, an empty ring, and an empty ring inside a multipolygon (which tripped a boost R-tree assertion). A fourth, an unbounded span on the y axis, silently returned **wrong** answers (`1` where an affine analogue proves `0`). Wide but finite polygons (`1e200`) keep their results. 3 existing tests extended, each verified to fail before the change; the `polygon` suite is green. <details> <summary>Behavior matrix (pristine HEAD vs this PR)</summary> `01940_point_in_polygon_ubsan` changes expectation from `0` to `BAD_ARGUMENTS`: its polygon has an `inf` vertex, so the span is now rejected before `contains` runs, where its `0` came from the query point guard. That guard stays covered by `00500_point_in_polygon_nan`. | statement | settings | HEAD | this PR | |---|---|---|---| | `(1e308,1.)` vs `[(-M,0.),(M,0.),(0.,2.)]` | default | abort | `BAD_ARGUMENTS` | | same, multipolygon / with a hole | default | abort | `BAD_ARGUMENTS` | | empty ring, large point | `validate_polygons=0` | abort | `0` | | `[[[]]]` multipolygon | `validate_polygons=0` | boost assertion | `0` | | y-unbounded `[(0.,-M),(1.,M),(2.,0.)]`, `(1.,-1e308)` | `validate_polygons=0` | **`1` (wrong)** | `BAD_ARGUMENTS` | | NaN span `[(inf,0.),(inf,0.1),(inf,0.2)]` | `validate_polygons=0` | `BAD_ARGUMENTS` | `BAD_ARGUMENTS` | | `1e200` span, `(0.,1.)` / `(1e199,0.5)` | default | `1` / `1` | `1` / `1` | | zero span, point polygon | `validate_polygons=0` | `0` | `0` | | issue #11375 NaN-point repro | default | `0` | `0` | `M = 1.7976931348623157e308`. </details>

signals.title: Add stateless and fuzzer jobs to the WeeklyCFI workflow
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100419 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112152 The `amd_cfi` build is the only test build with ThinLTO enabled — the same compile profile as official release builds — so besides CFI violations the WeeklyCFI workflow also catches ThinLTO-only behavior differences that no other CI job can see. The latest example is the `__functional` frame-name suppression surfaced by `test_crash_log` in the weekly runs of 2026-07-20 through 2026-08-10 and fixed in #112152. This PR broadens the workflow's coverage: - **Stateless tests** (parallel + sequential lanes, mirroring `amd_debug`). `clickhouse-test` now detects the CFI build from `-fsanitize=cfi` in the `CXX_FLAGS` row of `system.build_options`, so tests that cannot pass in this build profile can carry a `no-cfi` tag (the same generic `no-<flag>` skip mechanism the sanitizer builds use). CFI is deliberately not treated as a sanitizer: it has near-zero runtime overhead, so tests tagged `no-sanitizers` still run under CFI. - **AST fuzzer and BuzzHouse**: fuzzers assert only on crashes, never on exact query output, so the build profile cannot produce false positives there, and fuzzing reaches virtual-call combinations the curated suites never exercise. The fuzzer job configs are shared out into `_common_ast_fuzzer_job_config` / `_common_buzz_fuzzer_job_config`; master and PR workflows are unchanged. Not added, and why: unit tests (`ENABLE_CFI` is incompatible with `ENABLE_TESTS` — ThinLTO is disabled when building tests), performance comparison (it compares against the non-CFI master-head binary, so results are uninterpretable), upgrade/compatibility checks (version and data compatibility are orthogonal to CFI instrumentation), Keeper Jepsen (requires the standalone `clickhouse-keeper` build, which the CFI build omits). **Note for review:** the last commit temporarily switches the workflow to a `pull_request` trigger so this PR's CI exercises the full `amd_cfi` build + new test jobs (same validation approach as #100419). It will be reverted to the schedule-only trigger before merge. Any stateless tests that turn out unable to pass under ThinLTO will get `no-cfi` tags in follow-up commits. Workflow: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/workflows/weekly_cfi.yml ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: Do not treat an unaccounted skip-index file as a materialized index
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109595 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104431 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a query failure on a part that carries both a `skp_idx.packed` archive and a leftover standalone skip-index file with no `checksums.txt` entry. The leftover file was counted as a materialized index, so a valid query was rejected with a `file_size` filesystem error. ### Description Reported on https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104431#issuecomment-5306256247, on the corrupted-part shape of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109595 `indexFileExistsInChecksums` says whether a skip-index substream is materialized in a part. When the part carried `skp_idx.packed` it fell through to `storage->existsFile`, which tries the archive and then does a raw disk stat, and that one answer served two callers needing different ones. A read-time probe must not accept a file that neither `checksums.txt` nor the archive accounts for: it is an orphan, its index already dead, and counting it as materialized fails a valid query with `Code: 1001 ... in file_size: No such file or directory`. Mutation cleanup does need the wider answer, to strip the orphan from inherited checksums and keep it out of the hardlink loop; narrowing it there leaks the stale file forward and `CHECK TABLE` fails with `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART`. Each caller now asks by mode. One behaviour delta: read-time no longer calls generic part storage. The union answer is unchanged on every part, so nothing new reaches cleanup or `system.data_skipping_indices`. On a Keeper-backed metadata disk that stat reached Keeper with no component set, so the server threw `Current component is empty, please set it for your scope using Coordination::setCurrentComponent`. That is the private-sync failure in `Stress test (amd_tsan, SharedCatalog, meta in keeper)`, whose frames end in `DataPartStorageOnDiskFull::existsFileImpl`: the generic fallback, not the archive probe. I worked from those frames and cannot read the private logs. Asking the archive directly needs no new guard, since its loader already sets a component. This covers every unguarded probe of the class, not just the frame above: the rest of `getDeserializedFormat` is in-memory type comparison. Reachable on defaults: `packed_skip_index_max_bytes` is on and text indices are never packed. Building the shape needs a write into a part directory, so the test is `tests/integration/test_packed_skip_index_orphan`; each case fails on exactly the binary it targets.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Spill the adaptive aggregator's learning-phase tables under memory pressure
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114987 --> Closes: #114987 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Requested by @ nihalzp in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114987#issuecomment-5307798148. **The problem.** `Aggregator::executeOnBlock` ends in a baseline tail that converts the table to two-level, checks limits and spills past `max_bytes_before_external_group_by`. The adaptive block returns before that tail. Its thaw arm stands down first and its frozen arm runs a drain valve, but the learning arm returned with no memory response at all. A producer leaves learning only by freezing at `adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold` keys or by giving up after 16x that many rows, so with the threshold raised neither bound fires inside one query and the table grows in RAM with no byte bound. **The change.** A learning table has no frozen twin to pair with and nothing staged, so under pressure it can stand down for good and spill through the branch that already exists below. Gating it on the pressure trigger matters: the tail can convert the table to two-level, after which `isConvertibleToTwoLevel()` is false and the producer could never freeze again, so an unconditional fall-through would disable the feature rather than fix it. **Reachability is narrower than the report implies.** At the default `adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold = 16384` the spill still works, so this needs a raised threshold, not stock settings. The reporter agreed on the issue. **Validation.** On the report's query with the threshold raised, `ExternalAggregationWritePart` goes from 0 to 46, matching the feature-off arm, and under `max_memory_usage = 700000000` the query changes from `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` to completing. Each new defect cell fails on the unfixed binary, the freeze counters are byte-identical on the fast path, and the two files passed 100 randomized runs. Left alone deliberately: the stand-down reuses `Reason::TooFewDistinctKeys` rather than adding a `MemoryPressure` enumerator, since that field has no readers today; and a frozen local table stays unbounded in bytes for growing states such as `groupArray`, which the issue raises separately.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Offer the `/`-commands of the client, and name them when misspelled
signals.text: Typing `/` at the beginning of the input now shows the client's own commands (`/clear`, `/help`, `/man`) as as-you-type hints, and typing more of a name narrows the list down. `Tab` completes the command being typed, which is also how they are completed when the instant hints are disabled (`--hints 0`, `--highlight 0`, `--disable_suggestion`). Until now these commands could only be found in the documentation; now the prompt itself lists them. A mistake in the name of a command is reported as such, with the commands it may have meant, instead of being parsed as SQL and reported as a syntax error at the `/`: ``` :) /hepl Exception on client: Code: 36. DB::Exception: Unknown command `/hepl`. Maybe you meant: ['/help']. Type `/` at the beginning of the line to see all the commands. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` An argument given to a command that takes none (`/clear now`) is reported the same way. Batch `clickhouse-client` still parses such input as the SQL it is, exactly like it already does for `help` and `clear`; `clickhouse-local` reports it like the interactive client. The commands come from a single list, `clientSlashCommands`, shared by the hints, the completion and the diagnostics. An offered command replaces the whole typed prefix including the `/`, which `replxx` counts as a word break character and would otherwise leave in place. The offer is off for `keeper-client` and `clickhouse-disks`: they reuse the same line reader, and a leading `/` is the beginning of a path there. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114043 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `/`-commands of the client (`/help`, `/man`, `/clear`) are now offered by the line editor: typing `/` at the beginning of the input lists them as hints, and `Tab` completes the command being typed. A mistake in the name of a command is reported with the similar commands suggested, instead of being parsed as SQL.

signals.title: Fix the lost wakeup that hangs the BackgroundSchedulePool schedule tests
signals.text: Fix the lost wakeup that hangs the BackgroundSchedulePool schedule tests <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `TEST(BackgroundSchedulePool, Schedule)` can block forever. The unit tests run sequentially in a single binary, so one hang consumes the job's whole 90 minute budget and the binary is killed before it writes `gtest.json`: the job reported 2 rows instead of the usual ~20,285, losing every other gtest's result. `ScheduleAfter` has the same defect. Root cause: the task callback called `condvar.notify_one()` without holding the mutex the waiter uses, and the waiter's `condvar.wait` was unbounded. If the last iteration increments the counter and notifies after the waiter evaluated its predicate but before it blocked, the notification is dropped. That iteration is also the one that stops re-scheduling, so the pool goes idle and nothing can notify again; the wait is permanent rather than slow. The fix takes the mutex around the increment and the notify, closing that window, and bounds the wait at 60 seconds. `pool->join()` now runs before the assertions, because the pool's destructor requires `join()` and a fatal assertion before it would abort the binary on the timeout path. The bound waits on the wait's status, not on the predicate: the predicate overload of `wait_for` re-evaluates the predicate after the deadline and returns its value, so a dropped notification, which leaves the counter complete, would report success and keep the test green on the very regression the bound exists to catch. Validated by injecting a delay inside the waiter's predicate to force the losing interleaving: before the change the test hangs with a backtrace matching the reported one, after it the probe passes, and against that state the predicate overload passes in 301 ms while the status loop fails at the deadline. 50 repetitions of both arms pass in Debug and under TSan. Found on a private-repo `Unit tests (tsan)` run, so there is no public CI report to link.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Bucket `timeSeries*ToGrid` samples in runs
signals.text: Based on #114889 — the new changes are the last four commits. The add path of `timeSeries*ToGrid` paid the bucket-index math and a hash-map lookup per sample. Samples arrive sorted by timestamp within a series and a bucket covers many scrape intervals, so the batch add path now works in runs: `classifySampleFast` returns the `(lo, hi]` timestamp range sharing the sample's fate (the bucket's time range, or a range of rejected timestamps — e.g. the whole gap between buckets when `window < step`), a vectorizable scan finds the run of consecutive in-range samples, and the run is appended to the bucket in bulk. One classification, one lookup, one append per run; two comparisons and a store per sample; unsorted input degenerates to the old per-sample cost. `addBatch` is also overridden to split batches into runs of the same aggregation state, hoisting the per-row `typeid_cast`s. The kernel is additionally compiled for x86-64-v4 with runtime dispatch; end-to-end neutral on the AVX2 baseline (the loops are bandwidth-bound), kept as future-proofing. Bit-identical to master on a differential test over all 12 functions: all window/step shapes, `DateTime`/`DateTime64`, `Float32/64`, NaN, duplicate/unsorted timestamps, `Nullable`, `-If`, arrays, two-level/external aggregation, `-State`/`-Merge`, extreme parameters (which keep the `Int128` path). On top of #114889 (100M rows, 1000 series, 16 threads, min of 7): rate 1.18x, rate with `window < step` 1.29x, instant rate 1.24x, deriv 1.24x, changes 1.15x; unsorted and finalize-heavy unchanged. Single-threaded (add path isolated): 1.26-2.09x. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Process samples of the `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate functions in runs of consecutive samples falling into one grid bucket, speeding up the sample-ingestion stage of `timeSeriesRateToGrid` and related functions by 1.2-2x on sorted time series data.
signals.author: nikitamikhaylov

signals.title: Enable CORS in clickhouse-local by default
signals.text: `clickhouse-local` can serve HTTP after `SYSTEM START LISTEN HTTP`, but it normally runs without a config file, so it had no `http_options_response` section and answered the CORS preflight with a bare `204` carrying no `Access-Control-*` headers. A browser therefore refuses every cross-origin request to it - including the Web UI opened from a `file://` URL, whose origin is `null`. Now `clickhouse-local` sets the same default `http_options_response` headers that the `clickhouse-server` configuration ships (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and friends). A configuration file with its own `http_options_response` section still replaces them entirely, and the headers are sent only for requests that carry an `Origin`, exactly as in `clickhouse-server`. Note the implication, which is now documented next to the existing security warning for the listeners: while an HTTP listener is open, any web page you visit can query the local instance over the loopback address and read the results. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `clickhouse-local` now answers CORS preflight requests with the same permissive headers as `clickhouse-server`, so the HTTP interface opened by `SYSTEM START LISTEN HTTP` can be used from a browser out of the box, including the Web UI opened from a `file://` URL.
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Perf: Reuse consecutive HashJoin probe results for fixed-width keys
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reduce HashJoin probe overhead by reusing lookup results for repeated fixed-width join keys. ### What does this PR do? - Adds a **probe-only** consecutive-key cache for fixed-width HashJoin getters. - Reuses the previous **mapped pointer and hash-table offset** when the next probe key has the same raw bytes. - Keeps build-side insertion on the existing path. - Preserves duplicate right-side row handling through RowRef and RowRefList. - Covers **key32/key64**, packed keys32/64/128/256, and the corresponding two-level variants. - Leaves key8/key16, strings, nullable keys, range joins, and the build path unchanged. - Adds ALL INNER, RIGHT, and FULL correctness coverage. - Covers duplicate and unmatched rows. - Adds packed **keys256** correctness coverage with repeated probe keys. - Adds a run-length sweep, large build-map coverage, and packed keys128/keys256 benchmark cases. ### Why? - **Current path:** calculates the probe key and probes the hash table for every left-side row. - **Typical input:** primary-key ordered or clustered data often has long runs of the same join key. - **Repeated work:** the old path repeats the same key calculation and hash-table lookup for every row in a run. - **New path:** the first row does the normal lookup; later equal-key rows reuse its result. - **Unclustered input:** different keys still use the normal lookup path. - **Safety:** the generic consecutive-key cache is not used because HashJoin needs the real hash-table offset. - **Mapped values:** the cache stores the pointer from the real hash-table cell instead of copying RowRefList. - **Join behavior:** matched rows, duplicate right-side rows, and RIGHT/FULL join flags stay unchanged. ### Performance - **Clustered input:** avoids repeated key calculation and hash-table lookup for equal-key runs. - **Interleaved input:** adds only the key-equality check before the normal lookup. - **Expected benefit:** grows with the number of repeated rows per key. - **Regression control:** run length 1 and interleaved cases measure the no-hit cost. ### Benchmark - **Fixture:** `hashjoin_consecutive_keys`. - **Probe input:** 20M rows per measured query. - **Run lengths:** 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, and 10,000 rows per key. - **Small build map:** 2,000 keys. - **Large build map:** 2,000,000 keys. - **Packed keys:** clustered and interleaved cases for keys128 and keys256. - **Join settings:** hash algorithm with table swapping disabled.
signals.author: fallintoplace

signals.title: convertColumnToType: column-native wide-int / Decimal / Date-DateTime conversions (close B3, part 1)
signals.text: Grows the column-native fast paths in `convertColumnToType` so that more conversions no longer reconstruct a `Field` and delegate to `convertFieldToType` internally. This is one step of closing bridge **B3** in the `DB::Field`-removal effort (making `convertColumnToType` `Field`-free internally, so its callers - and eventually the whole `Field` API - can be removed). This PR adds faithful column-native paths for: - **wide integers** (`Int128`/`Int256`/`UInt128`/`UInt256`) - `convertFieldToType` dispatches them through the same `accurate::convertNumeric` template as native numbers, so the existing `castColumnAccurateOrNull` fast path serves them too; - **`Decimal` targets** (integer/wide/float/Decimal sources, default and `strict`) - reusing the exact primitives `convertFieldToType`'s Decimal helpers call (`canStoreWhole`/`getScaleMultiplier`, `convertToDecimal`, `convertDecimals`, and `accurateEquals` for the strict exactness check); - **numeric → `Date`/`Date32`/`DateTime`** - mirroring each target's quirk (range-checked `UInt16`; `Int32` day number in the extended window; raw truncation for `DateTime`); - **cross-calendar `Date`/`Date32` ↔ `DateTime`** - the timezone-aware `toDayNum`/`fromDayNum` branches. **Behaviour is unchanged**: every conversion above produced identical results through the `Field` fallback before; this only removes the per-value `Field` materialization for them. Note that `castColumn` is deliberately *not* used - it shares the low-level primitives but wraps them with different overflow/clamping semantics (`DECIMAL_OVERFLOW`, saturation to `MAX_DATETIME_TIMESTAMP`), so the shared primitives are called directly to match `convertFieldToType` bit for bit. Equivalence is pinned throughout by the differential unit test `gtest_convert_column_to_type` (`convertColumnToType` must equal `convertFieldToType`), extended here with wide-integer, Decimal, and date-family cases (widen/narrow/overflow/sign, extended-window bounds, raw truncation, cross-calendar round-trips). The remaining `convertFieldToType` surface (`DateTime64`/`Time`/`Time64`, composites, `String`, `IPv4`/`IPv6`/`UUID`, …) stays on the `Field` fallback and will be closed in follow-up PRs. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Internal refactoring (no user-visible change): `convertColumnToType` now performs wide-integer, `Decimal`, and `Date`/`DateTime` constant conversions column-natively instead of materializing a `Field`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
signals.author: yakov-olkhovskiy

signals.title: Perf: Coalesce contiguous unmatched ranges in MergeJoin
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/12118 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid materializing a temporary filtered column for dense unmatched ranges in partial_merge RIGHT and FULL JOINs. ### What does this PR do? - Counts unmatched runs before choosing the append path. - Appends dense unmatched ranges directly with insertRangeFrom. - Uses the existing filtered-column path when unmatched rows are too fragmented. - Keeps the existing whole-block path when no right rows were matched. - Adds RIGHT and FULL correctness coverage with nullable and string right columns. - Adds dense and interleaved RIGHT cases to the partial_merge_join performance fixture. ### Why? - The old path calls filter for every right column. - Direct range insertion avoids temporary filtered columns for dense runs. - One insertRangeFrom per range is not good for fragmented masks. - The fallback keeps fragmented cases on the existing path. - The result and row order stay unchanged. ### Performance - Dense unmatched runs use bulk range insertion. - Fragmented masks use the filtered-column path. - The fixture covers sparse, dense, and interleaved RIGHT and FULL JOIN shapes. ### Benchmark - Status: Fixture updated; results pending. - Fixture: partial_merge_join. - Cases: ALL RIGHT JOIN, ALL FULL JOIN, and interleaved ALL RIGHT JOIN. - Data: 10,000 sparse left keys and 1,000,000 dense right keys, plus multiples-of-2 and multiples-of-3 tables. - Output: count and sum(b.k) keep the right-side output in the query.
signals.author: fallintoplace

signals.title: Do not abort server startup when a database's named collection is missing
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110529 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the server refusing to start when a database created with `S3`, `Remote`, `RemoteSecure`, `MySQL` or `PostgreSQL` referenced a named collection that no longer exists. Such a database is now skipped with a logged error and the server starts; recreating the collection and restarting brings the database back. ### Description A database whose engine arguments name a missing named collection stops the whole server from starting: `Caught exception while loading metadata: Code: 669 ... There is no named collection 'nc_cfg': while loading database 'db_cfg'`, then `shutting down`. Retiring a `config.d/*.xml` collection and restarting reaches this. Recovery meant moving `metadata/<db>.sql` aside by hand, since the collection cannot be recreated with the server down. A **table** in the same state does not: the server boots and only that table's load job fails, so an admin recovers with a plain `CREATE NAMED COLLECTION`. That asymmetry is the bug. `loadDatabase` runs with `create = true`, so `setForceAttach` is never called and databases derive `ATTACH` rather than the `FORCE_ATTACH` that gives tables their tolerance. The two startup loops in `loadMetadata` now skip such a database instead of aborting, under four conditions that must all hold: the process is `clickhouse-server`, the error is exactly `NAMED_COLLECTION_DOESNT_EXIST`, the database is not the configured default, and its engine is in an audited list of engines owning no local table metadata (`S3`, `Remote`, `RemoteSecure`, `MySQL`, `PostgreSQL`). Everything else is unchanged: other error codes still stop startup, `Replicated` and `MaterializedPostgreSQL` still do because they own local tables, `clickhouse-local` still fails, and `ATTACH DATABASE` still fails loudly. The metadata file is untouched, so recreating the collection and restarting restores the database. The *default* database is excluded because `assertDatabaseExists(default_database)` runs right after. Validated both directions on identical on-disk state: the pre-fix binary exits 157, the fixed one starts and logs the skip. `test_named_collections` passes 29/29 with 13 new cases, plus a `clickhouse-local` stateless test. Each of the four conditions has its own test that fails on a build with that one condition removed, so none is vacuous. The related PR fixes this class for URL **tables**, not databases.

signals.title: Tag functional tests averaging over 60s under MSan with `no-msan`
signals.text: MSan stateless jobs are the slowest functional-test jobs in CI and sit right at the edge of the 9000 s job timeout. In a recent run the private `Stateless tests (amd_msan, distributed cache, meta in keeper, s3 storage, sequential, 2/2)` job spent 8324 s of its 9000 s budget on tests and was then killed during teardown, even though all 526 tests had passed. MSan is ~5.8× slower than release on the same tests, and the cost is concentrated in a long tail: under MSan, 8 tests take over 180 s each, and the 30 slowest account for ~48% of a sequential shard's runtime. This tags every functional test whose mean duration under MSan exceeds 60 s with `no-msan`. ### How the set was chosen From `play.clickhouse.com`, over the public MSan stateless checks (`Stateless tests (amd_msan, WasmEdge, parallel, N/M)` and `Stateless tests (amd_msan, WasmEdge, sequential, N/2)`, excluding the flaky-check and selected-tests flavors): ```sql SELECT test_name, count() AS runs, avg(test_duration_ms)/1000 AS avg_s FROM checks WHERE check_name LIKE 'Stateless tests (amd_msan, WasmEdge, %' AND check_name NOT LIKE '%flaky%' AND check_name NOT LIKE '%selected%' AND test_status = 'OK' AND check_start_time >= now() - INTERVAL 30 DAY GROUP BY test_name HAVING runs >= 20 AND avg_s > 60 ORDER BY avg_s DESC ``` 351 tests matched. 30 of them no longer exist in `master` (reverted, split into smaller tests, or removed), leaving 321. One of those, `04062_text_index_json_all_values_ghdata`, already carried `no-msan`, so 320 files change here. Only `OK` runs are counted, so timeouts and failures do not inflate the averages. ### Effect | Flavor | MSan test time per commit | Removed | Share | |---|---|---|---| | parallel | 129025 s | 24766 s | 19.2% | | sequential | 11236 s | 4108 s | 36.6% | ### 25 slowest of the tagged tests | Test | Mean under MSan | Runs | |---|---|---| | `03988_cached_read_big_at` | 384.6 s | 9014 | | `03008_deduplication_insert_several_blocks_replicated` | 337.2 s | 9116 | | `03008_deduplication_several_mv_into_one_table_nonreplicated` | 308.8 s | 9118 | | `03008_deduplication_insert_several_blocks_nonreplicated` | 282.6 s | 9118 | | `04039_merge_tree_snapshot_teardown_race` | 275.2 s | 9347 | | `01195_formats_diagnostic_info` | 234.6 s | 9278 | | `02475_bson_each_row_format` | 206.1 s | 9264 | | `00626_replace_partition_from_table_zookeeper` | 202.5 s | 9323 | | `01019_alter_materialized_view_atomic` | 192.5 s | 9340 | | `04062_text_index_json_all_values_ghdata` | 190.4 s | 1806 | | `01721_join_implicit_cast_long` | 182.8 s | 9339 | | `00746_sql_fuzzy` | 180.5 s | 9340 | | `03755_large_primary_key_explain` | 180.2 s | 9337 | | `02943_variant_type_with_different_local_and_global_order` | 180.2 s | 9284 | | `02448_clone_replica_lost_part` | 177.4 s | 9263 | | `02372_analyzer_join` | 176.3 s | 9345 | | `04327_cluster_functions_huge_num_streams_no_crash` | 171.8 s | 9261 | | `01721_join_implicit_cast_long_oldanalyzer` | 168.9 s | 9346 | | `01079_bad_alters_zookeeper_long` | 166.8 s | 9322 | | `01747_system_session_log_long` | 165.9 s | 9014 | | `03208_array_of_json_read_subcolumns_1` | 165 s | 9339 | | `00429_long_http_bufferization` | 160.9 s | 9277 | | `04411_deep_nested_field_to_type` | 156.8 s | 9262 | | `01383_log_broken_table` | 156.4 s | 9340 | | `03326_protobuf_schemas_race` | 155.1 s | 9279 | (321 tests in total; the full list is the diff.) ### Trade-off A large share of these are the ZooKeeper, replication, mutation and race tests — precisely where MSan is most likely to find real uninitialized-memory bugs. They continue to run under ASan, UBSan and TSan, but this is a genuine reduction in MSan coverage rather than a pure win. An alternative that keeps the coverage is duration-aware sharding of the sequential jobs: the split is currently `crc32(test filename) % total_batches`, which gave one recent shard 8248 s against its sibling's 5514 s (1.50×), so balancing alone would have reclaimed ~23 min on the shard that timed out. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ...

signals.title: Perf: Coalesce contiguous runs in ColumnFixedString filtering
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Bulk copy contiguous selected runs while filtering FixedString columns. ### What does this PR do? - Adds **contiguous-run copying** to the mixed-mask path in `ColumnFixedString::filter`. - Keeps the existing fast path for fully selected 64-row blocks. - Uses one resize and one bulk copy for each selected run in the out-of-place path. - Uses one `memmove` for each selected run in the in-place path. - Keeps isolated rows on the existing small-copy path. - Adds correctness coverage for clustered, dense-hole, empty, full, and boundary masks. - Adds out-of-place and in-place benchmark cases. ### Why? - **Current path:** copies every selected fixed string separately for a mixed 64-row mask. - **Dense masks:** one missing row can turn a large contiguous range into dozens of small copies. - **New path:** finds adjacent selected rows and copies each range at once. - **Fragmented masks:** keep the existing small-copy behavior. - **Result:** selected values and row order stay unchanged. ### How is it faster? - **Dense 64-row mask:** 63 selected rows with one hole become two contiguous ranges. - **Out-of-place path:** 63 row-sized resizes and small copies become two resizes and two bulk copies. - **In-place path:** 63 row-sized `memmove` calls become two range `memmove` calls. - **Longer runs:** amortize loop and copy overhead over more FixedString bytes. - **Random and alternating masks:** isolated rows stay on the existing path, so the optimization is focused on masks with useful runs. ### Performance - **Clustered masks:** fewer copy calls and fewer result-size updates. - **Dense masks with one hole:** large ranges are copied around the hole instead of row by row. - **Random and alternating masks:** provide regression-control cases with few useful runs. ### Benchmark - **Fixture:** `benchmark_column_fixed_string_filter`. - **Patterns:** clustered, random, alternating, and dense-with-hole. - **Paths:** out-of-place and in-place filtering. - **Column:** `FixedString(16)`. - **Rows:** 1,048,576. - **Status:** Fixture added; results pending.

signals.title: Perf: Bulk copy selected runs in ColumnVector filtering
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Coalesce contiguous selected rows in the generic ColumnVector filter fallback. ### What does this PR do? - Adds **contiguous-run copying** to the generic mixed-mask fallback. - Keeps isolated rows on `insertSingle`. - Leaves the existing prefix, suffix, and AVX-512 paths unchanged. - Covers both out-of-place and in-place filtering through the shared inserter. - Adds correctness coverage for clustered, dense-hole, empty, full, and boundary masks. - Adds a benchmark for clustered, random, alternating, and dense-with-hole masks. ### Why? - **Current path:** copies every selected value separately for a mixed 64-row mask. - **Dense masks:** adjacent selected rows still take the per-value path. - **New path:** finds adjacent selected rows and copies each range at once. - **Fragmented masks:** keep the existing `insertSingle` behavior. - **Result:** selected values and row order stay unchanged. ### How is it faster? - **Dense 64-row mask:** 63 selected values with one hole become two contiguous ranges. - **Out-of-place path:** 63 `insertSingle` calls become two `insertRange` calls. - **In-place path:** 63 single-value moves become two range `memmove` calls. - **Longer runs:** reduce per-value inserter and loop overhead while copying more data per call. - **Single rows:** the adjacent-bit check keeps isolated selections on the existing cheap path. ### Performance - **Clustered masks:** fewer inserter calls for each selected run. - **Dense masks with one hole:** large ranges are copied around the hole instead of value by value. - **Random and alternating masks:** provide regression-control cases with few useful runs. ### Benchmark - **Fixture:** `benchmark_column_filter`. - **Patterns:** clustered, random, alternating, and dense-with-hole. - **Column:** generic `ColumnUInt128` path. - **Rows:** 1,048,576. - **Status:** Fixture added; results pending.

signals.title: Record an index's absent columns when materializing it on a wide part
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114990 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112484 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes an unreleased regression from #112484 (`master` only): `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE INDEX` produced an index that never prunes when the indexed column had been added by a metadata-only `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` and the part is wide. No stable release carries #112484, so no changelog entry and no backport are owed. ### Description Reported by @ clickgapai. #112484 merged on 2026-08-15 and is an ancestor of no release branch, so only `master` is affected. **What breaks.** `ADD COLUMN c ... DEFAULT ...` on a wide part is metadata-only, so the part holds no bytes for `c`. A following `MATERIALIZE INDEX idx` writes the index files but does not add `c` to the part's column list, and since #112484 the reader refuses an index whose columns the part does not describe. The index occupies disk and never prunes: `Granules: 16/16` on the reporter's fixture versus `1/16` before, results correct both ways. **Root cause.** `splitAndModifyMutationCommands` has two branches. The compact one turns an index's required-but-absent columns into `READ_COLUMN` commands; the wide one had no such step, so `c` never enters `updated_header` and `getColumnsForNewDataPart` erases it. The missing type is the defect, so the fix belongs on the write side. **The change.** On a wide part, `MATERIALIZE INDEX` now also reads the index's absent columns, so the part records them at the type the granules were built from. The column list belongs to the part, so it records the column only when every other index holding files there either does not read it or has its granules rebuilt by this same mutation: a carried-over granule keeps its build-time type, so recording the column now would hand the reader a matching type for a stale granule. What the mutation rebuilds is decided from its own commands, and an undecidable index counts as carried over, keeping the pre-fix behaviour. Compact parts and the reader are untouched, so every #112484 refusal holds. **Cost.** The mutation now writes column data: +247 bytes before, +806,931 after on a 200k-row wide fixture; the next merge writes it anyway. No format, serialization or default change, so no `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` entry. <details> <summary>Validation, rejected alternative, known-unfixed shape</summary> **Rejected alternative:** recording build-time types in a new per-part file - a format change needing ~9 seams, a protocol bump and upgrade/downgrade paths. **Known-unfixed:** on a part with orphan index files (#109595) `hasSecondaryIndex` is true, so the read is suppressed and the index stays inert - the status quo, never wrong results. | arm | absent arm | control arm | |---|---|---| | pristine master | `16/16` (inert) | 1/16 | | this PR | `1/16` | 1/16 | Counts identical with and without `use_skip_indexes` in every cell; the control prunes on both. Four mutation arms cover the restriction, each red on the build missing its guard: without it, a hardlinked granule's column is rewritten at the new type and the next read attempts a 4 EiB allocation; keyed to the index named in the command rather than the column, a second index over that column has its stale granules re-enabled and the next read aborts; without the rebuilt-sibling exemption, a batched update that does rebuild the sibling still suppresses it, leaving the new index inert - covered both for a sibling reached by a named column and for one reached via a TTL target. Tests: `04869_skip_index_stale_type_absent_column` gains cases 26 (the regression), 26b (subcolumn index, absent parent recorded), 27, 28 (two indices, one absent column), 29 and 30 (rebuilt sibling). Cases 11/22/23/24 moved from `ADD COLUMN` to a column TTL expiry, since the fix makes the old route no longer leave a column absent; each gained an `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` refusal assertion, and every such assertion now pins the granule count rather than matching a substring. `04246_materialize_index_force_recalc` (the #104872 compact tripwire), `04165`, `04870` and `04871` pass unchanged; 250/250 across a 50-run randomized loop. Unrelated columns stay hardlinked (by inode), so the mutation does not escalate to a full part rewrite. </details>

signals.title: Fix out of range exception on a zero event number in sequenceMatch patterns
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an `out_of_range` exception raised as an internal `Code: 1001` error when a `sequenceMatch`, `sequenceCount` or `sequenceMatchEvents` pattern contains the event number `0`, for example `sequenceMatch('(?0)')`. Such a pattern is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. ### Description Event numbers in the pattern language are 1-based, but the bound check validated only the upper bound, so a pattern such as `(?0)` passed it. The subsequent conversion to a 0-based condition index underflowed `UInt64` to `SIZE_MAX`, and `std::bitset<32>::set()` rejected that with `std::out_of_range`. Because the exception is thrown from the aggregate function constructor during query analysis, it surfaced as an internal `Code: 1001` logical error, and aborted the server in debug and sanitizer builds. Two more inputs reached the same state: an event number overflowing `UInt64` such as `(?18446744073709551616)`, and a sign with no digits, `(?+)`. In both cases `tryReadIntText` fails after consuming at least one byte, and its pointer overload discards the boolean result while reporting a non-zero consumed length, so the existing "Could not parse number" check does not fire and the output parameter keeps its initialiser `0`. The fix adds the missing lower bound to the same check, which validates the parsed value and therefore covers all three inputs at once. The error code and message are unchanged. `sequenceMatch`, `sequenceCount` and `sequenceMatchEvents` share this parser and were all affected; all three are covered by the new assertions in `00222_sequence_aggregate_function_family`, which abort on an unfixed binary. Found by `AST fuzzer (amd_tsan)`, `std::out_of_range, e.what() = bitset set argument out of range` (STID 2508-34fb): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115019&sha=7be817c59e288cab7aa329a76ed1ba65b9d555e9&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29. Also seen on `Stress test (arm_tsan)`. Both carrier pull requests are bystanders; the defect reproduces on pristine master. No related open issue found. Two malformed patterns remain accepted or imprecisely reported and are not addressed here: `(?t>+)` is accepted as `(?t>0)` (unchanged by this fix), and an overflowing event number is reported as event number `0`.

signals.title: Add a test for case-insensitive column name matching from #92851
signals.text: Issue [#92851](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92851) asked for input formats that carry column names to match them case-insensitively when there is no ambiguity. That works now, through `input_format_column_name_matching_mode` (default `auto`), but the reproducer from the issue was not covered by a test. The existing tests (`04027_json_input_format`, `04209_column_name_matching_mode_default`, and the `CSV`/`JSONColumns`/`BSON`/`RowBinaryWithNames` ones) exercise the mechanism only in the direction "lowercase table columns, uppercase input fields". The issue shows the opposite: a table with the columns `Hello` and `World`, fed by `JSONEachRow` data that spells the field names in lowercase, which used to silently insert empty strings. The new test runs exactly that scenario with default settings. It is a real regression guard: with `input_format_column_name_matching_mode = 'match_case'` (or `compatibility = '26.4'`) it produces the empty strings from the issue instead of the values. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92851 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required)
