signal.title: CI: run the full test suite only when review threads are resolved
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114724 While a PR has unresolved review threads, running the full test suite is a waste: the code is expected to change again once the review comments are addressed. This PR implements the gate requested in the issue: - A new `review_threads.py` pre-hook in the `Config Workflow` counts the PR's unresolved review threads (via GraphQL `reviewThreads`) and stores the state in the workflow kv data. While threads are unresolved, `should_skip_job` runs only builds and the preliminary checks (`Style check`, `Fast test`), plus the `Code Review` job — the AI review keeps re-checking pushed code and resolves its own addressed threads, which is what re-triggers the full suite automatically. - The `can_be_merged.py` post-hook re-checks the live thread state at finish time and turns the `Mergeable Check` red while threads are unresolved, or while only the limited pipeline ran (even if the threads were resolved mid-run — the full suite still has not run). The per-run verdict is recorded in a new `Review Threads` commit status, which doubles as immediate feedback on the PR. This also makes the decision on the AI review's comments once they are ready, as suggested in the issue: comments posted during the run are seen by the finish-time check. - A new `Rerun On Review Threads` workflow detects state changes and re-runs the last completed `PR` workflow run for the current head commit whenever the recorded verdict disagrees with the live state (thread resolved/unresolved, new review comments, the override label added/removed). Previously succeeded jobs are restored from the CI cache, so the re-run only executes the previously skipped jobs. Review-thread events on PRs from forks carry a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so they are relayed through a trivial `Review Threads Signal` workflow and handled on its `workflow_run` completion in the trusted default-branch context; `PR` workflow completions are watched too, to catch threads resolved while a run was still in flight. A safety cap (5 attempts per run) prevents any reconciliation bug from re-running one workflow forever. - The gate can be bypassed with the new `ignore-unresolved-threads` label (fetched fresh from the API, so adding the label and re-running works; the label also triggers the re-run automatically). `ci-force-all` still bypasses job filtering, so it runs the full suite, but it does not bypass the merge gate for unresolved threads. - `retry_infra_failures.yml` learned to not treat a `Finish Workflow` failure caused by this merge gate as an infrastructure failure. - Failure direction: if the thread state cannot be fetched at config time, nothing is skipped (fail toward more testing); at finish time the check fails close (the `Mergeable Check` goes red). The `ignore-unresolved-threads` label has been created in the repository. Documentation: a new `Review threads check` section in `docs/resources/develop-contribute/contribute/continuous-integration.mdx`. Tests: `ci/tests/test_review_threads_gate.py` pins the decision functions and their integration into `should_skip_job` (what is skipped, what keeps running, the merge-gate truth table, the commit-status description budget). ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signal.title: Bucket `timeSeries*ToGrid` samples in runs
signal.text: Based on #114889 — the new changes are the last four commits. The add path of `timeSeries*ToGrid` paid the bucket-index math and a hash-map lookup per sample. Samples arrive sorted by timestamp within a series and a bucket covers many scrape intervals, so the batch add path now works in runs: `classifySampleFast` returns the `(lo, hi]` timestamp range sharing the sample's fate (the bucket's time range, or a range of rejected timestamps — e.g. the whole gap between buckets when `window < step`), a vectorizable scan finds the run of consecutive in-range samples, and the run is appended to the bucket in bulk. One classification, one lookup, one append per run; two comparisons and a store per sample; unsorted input degenerates to the old per-sample cost. `addBatch` is also overridden to split batches into runs of the same aggregation state, hoisting the per-row `typeid_cast`s. The kernel is additionally compiled for x86-64-v4 with runtime dispatch; end-to-end neutral on the AVX2 baseline (the loops are bandwidth-bound), kept as future-proofing. Bit-identical to master on a differential test over all 12 functions: all window/step shapes, `DateTime`/`DateTime64`, `Float32/64`, NaN, duplicate/unsorted timestamps, `Nullable`, `-If`, arrays, two-level/external aggregation, `-State`/`-Merge`, extreme parameters (which keep the `Int128` path). On top of #114889 (100M rows, 1000 series, 16 threads, min of 7): rate 1.18x, rate with `window < step` 1.29x, instant rate 1.24x, deriv 1.24x, changes 1.15x; unsorted and finalize-heavy unchanged. Single-threaded (add path isolated): 1.26-2.09x. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Process samples of the `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate functions in runs of consecutive samples falling into one grid bucket, speeding up the sample-ingestion stage of `timeSeriesRateToGrid` and related functions by 1.2-2x on sorted time series data.

signal.title: Fix MATERIALIZED columns frozen at their INSERT-time value after ALTER UPDATE
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/100613 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/50237 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99281 ## Problem A `MATERIALIZED` column computed from another `MATERIALIZED` column is never recalculated by `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`. It keeps the value `INSERT` computed, forever, no matter how many mutations run. ```sql CREATE TABLE t (x Int32, m1 Int32 MATERIALIZED x + 1, m2 Int32 MATERIALIZED m1 + 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t (x) VALUES (10); -- m1 = 11, m2 = 12 ALTER TABLE t UPDATE x = 20 WHERE 1; ALTER TABLE t UPDATE x = 30 WHERE 1; SELECT x, m1, m2 FROM t; -- 30 31 12 <- m2 frozen at its INSERT-time value -- expected: 30 31 32 ``` Concretely, on `master`: - `m2` and everything downstream of it are stale for the lifetime of the table. - A projection over a recalculated `MATERIALIZED` column keeps answering from pre-mutation data: `SELECT sum(m1)` returns `500500` through the projection versus `1000500500` without it. - A `minmax` skip index over such a column prunes every granule, so a filter that matches all rows returns `0`. - With `apply_mutations_on_fly = 1` and the mutation still pending, the same query returns different values depending on its select list: `SELECT m2` gives `12` while `SELECT x, m1, m2` gives `22`. - Also with a pending mutation, reading a `MATERIALIZED` column whose expression mentions an `EPHEMERAL` column fails outright with `Code: 47 ... Missing columns: 'e' while processing: 'x + e' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER)`. ## Root cause `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` collected the `MATERIALIZED` columns to recalculate from **direct** dependencies only. It analysed each `MATERIALIZED` default expression and recorded an edge `dependency -> materialized column`, but only when `updated_columns` already contained the dependency: ```cpp for (const auto & dependency : required_columns) if (updated_columns.contains(dependency)) column_to_affected_materialized[dependency].push_back(column.name); ``` For `m2 MATERIALIZED m1 + 1` the dependency is `m1`, which the user did not update, so `m2` never entered `affected_materialized`, and the guard added by #99281 skipped it: ```cpp if (column.default_desc.kind == ColumnDefaultKind::Materialized && affected_materialized.contains(column.name) && column.default_desc.expression) ``` Before #99281 every `MATERIALIZED` column was recalculated in a single stage, so `m2` *was* rewritten — but from the pre-stage `m1`, i.e. always one mutation behind. That second half is #50237. Both halves come from the same place: the affected set is not transitive, and even a transitively dependent column was evaluated in the same stage as the column it reads. The remaining symptoms are the same "direct dependencies only" assumption in the neighbouring consumers. The skip-index, projection and dependency-analysis predicates only looked at `updated_columns`, `changed_columns` and `patch_updated_columns`, none of which ever names a recalculated `MATERIALIZED` column. `AlterConversions::addColumnsRequiredForMaterialized`, which decides what an on-fly mutation must read, walked one level and then required the dependency to be an updated column, so a read set of `{m2}` stayed `{m2}`, `filterMutationCommands` dropped the `UPDATE x` command because nothing overlapped, and the stale value was returned. That same function analysed default expressions against `getAllPhysical`, which excludes `EPHEMERAL` columns, hence the `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. ## Solution In `src/Interpreters/MutationsInterpreter.cpp`: 1. Record **every** edge of the `MATERIALIZED` dependency graph, including `MATERIALIZED -> MATERIALIZED` edges. 2. `getAffectedMaterializedByLevel` walks that graph from the columns a command updates and groups the reachable columns by **longest-path** dependency level. 3. Emit one mutation stage per level. Stage *N* reads the output of stage *N-1*, so an expression sees the recalculated value of the column it depends on instead of the stale on-disk one — this is what closes #50237, not merely refreshing the value. 4. `validateUpdateColumns` receives the same transitive closure, so an `UPDATE` reaching a `MATERIALIZED` **key** column through another `MATERIALIZED` column is rejected with `CANNOT_UPDATE_COLUMN`, as the direct case already was. Without this, step 3 would rewrite a sorting-key column and break the part's sort order. 5. Feed the recalculated columns into the skip-index, projection and dependency analysis. In `src/Storages/MergeTree/AlterConversions.cpp`: 6. `addColumnsRequiredForMaterialized` follows the chain, pulling in an intermediate `MATERIALIZED` column when an updated column is reachable through it. 7. `EPHEMERAL` columns enter its analysis set, as `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` already does, and a `MATERIALIZED` column reading one is excluded from the walk because it cannot be recalculated anyway. The pre-existing `EPHEMERAL` exclusion that #99281 added is preserved: such a column is skipped before its incoming edges are recorded, so the walk never reaches it. The exclusion removes that column from the graph, not the subgraph behind it — a column that also reads an updated column directly (`mc MATERIALIZED x + e`, `mc2 MATERIALIZED mc + x`) is still recalculated, from the stored `mc`, which is well defined because its own expression reads only stored columns. ### Why items 5-7 are fixed here All three are pre-existing defects rather than regressions of this change, so it is worth being precise about why each one is in scope. In every case leaving it out would make items 1-3 produce a table that contradicts *itself*, which is harder to diagnose than the uniformly stale table they replace. **Item 5 — stale projections and skip indices.** On `master` the recalculated column and any projection over it are both stale, so they agree. Items 1-3 make the column correct on disk while the projection still answers from pre-mutation data, so `sum(m2)` returns one value through the projection and another without it (measured: `501500` vs `1000501500`; a `minmax` index over such a column prunes every granule and a matching filter counts `0`). Reproducible on `master` for a *directly* recalculated column as well, so this is not new — but shipping items 1-3 without it would trade an obvious wrong answer for a self-inconsistent one. Note it only surfaces when the mutation rewrites *some* columns of the part; `MutateAllPartColumns` rebuilds everything and hides it, which is why the regression test keeps an untouched column `y`. **Item 6 — on-fly mutations missed transitive dependencies.** This inconsistency *is* introduced by items 1-3. On `master`, `SELECT m2` and `SELECT x, m1, m2` both return the stale `12`, which at least agrees. After items 1-3 the second returns `22` while the first still returns `12` — the same table at the same instant answers differently depending on the select list. **Item 7 — reading a `MATERIALIZED` column that uses an `EPHEMERAL` one failed outright.** `addColumnsRequiredForMaterialized` resolved default expressions with `metadata_snapshot->getColumns().getAllPhysical()`, and an `EPHEMERAL` column is not physical — it exists only during `INSERT`. So `TreeRewriter` could not resolve the identifier: ``` Code: 47. DB::Exception: Missing columns: 'e' while processing: 'x + e', required columns: 'x' 'e', available columns: 'me2' 'me' 'y' 'x'. (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` Purely pre-existing — reproducible with only `AlterConversions.cpp` reverted to `master`, where `SELECT me` throws for `me MATERIALIZED x + e` while a mutation is pending. It is in scope because item 6 *widens* it: `master` only ever analysed the requested column's own expression, so `SELECT me2` for `me2 MATERIALIZED me + 100` was fine, while the transitive walk descends into `me` and analyses `x + e`, making a query that used to work start throwing. The fix mirrors what `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` already does — add `EPHEMERAL` columns to the analysis set so the expression resolves — and then stops the walk at any `MATERIALIZED` column that reads one, since `MutationsInterpreter` will not recalculate it and an `EPHEMERAL` column can never be read from disk. After the fix `SELECT me2`, `SELECT me` and `SELECT x, me, me2` all succeed and correctly leave `me` and `me2` at their `INSERT`-time values (`2 8 108`). ### Tests `tests/queries/0_stateless/04869_transitive_materialized_column_update.sql` covers nine cases, one per clause of the fix: chain, diamond (longest-path placement), `EPHEMERAL` must-not-recalculate, `EPHEMERAL` with converging paths, `MATERIALIZED` key column, projection (direct and transitive), skip index, on-fly chain, on-fly `EPHEMERAL`. Each assertion was verified to be load-bearing by reverting only its own clause: the chain freezes at `12 13`, the diamond gives `5 6 60 26` when a re-reached column is placed at its first level instead of its deepest, the projections return `500500` / `501500`, the skip index returns `0`, and the on-fly reads return `12` / `13` or throw. `04044_mutation_ephemeral_materialized`, the test #99281 added, still passes. The projection and skip-index cases keep an untouched column `y`, because a mutation that rewrites every column goes through `MutateAllPartColumns`, which rebuilds everything and hides the bug. ### Notes for reviewers - **Behaviour change:** `UPDATE` of a column that transitively feeds a `MATERIALIZED` key column now throws `CANNOT_UPDATE_COLUMN` where it previously succeeded and left the key stale. The direct equivalent already throws on `master`, so this makes the two consistent. - Tables with `MATERIALIZED -> MATERIALIZED` chains now get one mutation stage per dependency level; everything else keeps the single stage that existed before. - More projections and skip indices are rebuilt than before. That is the point of item 5, but it does make such mutations more expensive. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `MATERIALIZED` columns computed from another `MATERIALIZED` column keeping their `INSERT`-time value forever after `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`. Projections and skip indices over a recalculated `MATERIALIZED` column were also left stale, returning wrong results.

signal.title: Fix out of range exception on a zero event number in sequenceMatch patterns
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an `out_of_range` exception raised as an internal `Code: 1001` error when a `sequenceMatch`, `sequenceCount` or `sequenceMatchEvents` pattern contains the event number `0`, for example `sequenceMatch('(?0)')`. Such a pattern is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. ### Description Event numbers in the pattern language are 1-based, but the bound check validated only the upper bound, so a pattern such as `(?0)` passed it. The subsequent conversion to a 0-based condition index underflowed `UInt64` to `SIZE_MAX`, and `std::bitset<32>::set()` rejected that with `std::out_of_range`. Because the exception is thrown from the aggregate function constructor during query analysis, it surfaced as an internal `Code: 1001` logical error, and aborted the server in debug and sanitizer builds. Two more inputs reached the same state: an event number overflowing `UInt64` such as `(?18446744073709551616)`, and a sign with no digits, `(?+)`. In both cases `tryReadIntText` fails after consuming at least one byte, and its pointer overload discards the boolean result while reporting a non-zero consumed length, so the existing "Could not parse number" check does not fire and the output parameter keeps its initialiser `0`. The fix adds the missing lower bound to the same check, which validates the parsed value and therefore covers all three inputs at once. The error code and message are unchanged. `sequenceMatch`, `sequenceCount` and `sequenceMatchEvents` share this parser and were all affected; all three are covered by the new assertions in `00222_sequence_aggregate_function_family`, which abort on an unfixed binary. Found by `AST fuzzer (amd_tsan)`, `std::out_of_range, e.what() = bitset set argument out of range` (STID 2508-34fb): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115019&sha=7be817c59e288cab7aa329a76ed1ba65b9d555e9&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29. Also seen on `Stress test (arm_tsan)`. Both carrier pull requests are bystanders; the defect reproduces on pristine master. No related open issue found. Two malformed patterns remain accepted or imprecisely reported and are not addressed here: `(?t>+)` is accepted as `(?t>0)` (unchanged by this fix), and an overflowing event number is reported as event number `0`.

signal.title: Record an index's absent columns when materializing it on a wide part
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114990 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112484 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes an unreleased regression from #112484 (`master` only): `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE INDEX` produced an index that never prunes when the indexed column had been added by a metadata-only `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` and the part is wide. No stable release carries #112484, so no changelog entry and no backport are owed. ### Description Reported by @ clickgapai. #112484 merged on 2026-08-15 and is an ancestor of no release branch, so only `master` is affected. **What breaks.** `ADD COLUMN c ... DEFAULT ...` on a wide part is metadata-only, so the part holds no bytes for `c`. A following `MATERIALIZE INDEX idx` writes the index files but does not add `c` to the part's column list, and since #112484 the reader refuses an index whose columns the part does not describe. The index occupies disk and never prunes: `Granules: 16/16` on the reporter's fixture versus `1/16` before, results correct both ways. **Root cause.** `splitAndModifyMutationCommands` has two branches. The compact one turns an index's required-but-absent columns into `READ_COLUMN` commands; the wide one had no such step, so `c` never enters `updated_header` and `getColumnsForNewDataPart` erases it. The missing type is the defect, so the fix belongs on the write side. **The change.** On a wide part, `MATERIALIZE INDEX` now also reads the index's absent columns, so the part records them at the type the granules were built from. The column list belongs to the part, so it records the column only when every other index holding files there either does not read it or has its granules rebuilt by this same mutation: a carried-over granule keeps its build-time type, so recording the column now would hand the reader a matching type for a stale granule. What the mutation rebuilds is decided from its own commands, and an undecidable index counts as carried over, keeping the pre-fix behaviour. Compact parts and the reader are untouched, so every #112484 refusal holds. **Cost.** The mutation now writes column data: +247 bytes before, +806,931 after on a 200k-row wide fixture; the next merge writes it anyway. No format, serialization or default change, so no `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` entry. <details> <summary>Validation, rejected alternative, known-unfixed shape</summary> **Rejected alternative:** recording build-time types in a new per-part file - a format change needing ~9 seams, a protocol bump and upgrade/downgrade paths. **Known-unfixed:** on a part with orphan index files (#109595) `hasSecondaryIndex` is true, so the read is suppressed and the index stays inert - the status quo, never wrong results. | arm | absent arm | control arm | |---|---|---| | pristine master | `16/16` (inert) | 1/16 | | this PR | `1/16` | 1/16 | Counts identical with and without `use_skip_indexes` in every cell; the control prunes on both. Four mutation arms cover the restriction, each red on the build missing its guard: without it, a hardlinked granule's column is rewritten at the new type and the next read attempts a 4 EiB allocation; keyed to the index named in the command rather than the column, a second index over that column has its stale granules re-enabled and the next read aborts; without the rebuilt-sibling exemption, a batched update that does rebuild the sibling still suppresses it, leaving the new index inert - covered both for a sibling reached by a named column and for one reached via a TTL target. Tests: `04869_skip_index_stale_type_absent_column` gains cases 26 (the regression), 26b (subcolumn index, absent parent recorded), 27, 28 (two indices, one absent column), 29 and 30 (rebuilt sibling). Cases 11/22/23/24 moved from `ADD COLUMN` to a column TTL expiry, since the fix makes the old route no longer leave a column absent; each gained an `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` refusal assertion, and every such assertion now pins the granule count rather than matching a substring. `04246_materialize_index_force_recalc` (the #104872 compact tripwire), `04165`, `04870` and `04871` pass unchanged; 250/250 across a 50-run randomized loop. Unrelated columns stay hardlinked (by inode), so the mutation does not escalate to a full part rewrite. </details>

signal.title: Fix data race on DataTypeAggregateFunction version during Native serialization
signal.text: Related: found by the `arm_tsan` and `azure, amd_tsan` Stress tests (STID 3977-4818, ThreadSanitizer data race). No existing issue. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/94859 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog. ### Description A single `DataTypeAggregateFunction` instance is shared across query result blocks: it lives once in the table's column description and is aliased by shallow column copies. `NativeWriter`/`NativeReader` called `setVersionToAggregateFunctions`, which walked to the leaf type and wrote its `mutable version` field in place. Two concurrent `Native` serializations of the same aggregate-function-typed column then raced on that field, and the version written for one old connection stayed on the shared type, so every later query read the states at that version - for `sumMap` over `Decimal32` that returns wrong values. Reports: * https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109496&sha=62eeb400eafe86cedff9b5a4e9a36aa722633cda&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 * https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=b59441bd06c2fcb6b103a30874528cc398afc723&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_tsan%29 **That fix has since landed on `master`** through #94859 and #112052: `setVersionToAggregateFunctions` now replaces every versioned nested type instead of mutating it, and `replaceNestedSimpleTypes` carries the custom names (`Nested`, `SimpleAggregateFunction`) over the rebuild. This branch is therefore resolved in favour of that implementation, and what it added on top of it - an `IDataType::transformChildren` override per container type, and the `unique_ptr` to `shared_ptr` switch of `DataTypeCustomNamePtr` - is dropped as duplicate machinery. What remains here is what `master` does not have, and it keeps this PR's intent - the race cannot come back, because the version can no longer be assigned in place at all: * `DataTypeAggregateFunction::setVersion` and `updateVersionFromRevision` are removed, and `version` is no longer `mutable`. Both mutators were left without callers by the rewrite on `master`; the version is now set only at construction (parsed from AST, decoded from the binary type encoding, or chosen by `setVersionToAggregateFunctions`, which builds a new type). * Unit and functional coverage of the behaviour, which `master` has only indirectly. ### Testing * `gtest_aggregate_function_version_race` (14 tests) pins the type-level behaviour: the shared type object is not mutated; a wrapper is rebuilt only when a leaf was actually replaced; the `Point`, `Nested` and `SimpleAggregateFunction` custom names survive, including a `Tuple`-backed `SimpleAggregateFunction`; a `Variant` keeps its discriminator order and throws when two alternatives would collapse; a `JSON` typed path keeps the version spelled in its own type name; and an 8-thread x 2000-iteration stress over one shared type object is race-free. * `04612_aggregate_function_version_custom_type_names` round-trips `Nested`, `SimpleAggregateFunction` and a wrapper-named type through `Native` (which assigns the version in the writer and again in the reader) and through `DETACH`/`ATTACH`, and checks that a deeply nested `Nested` stays linear in the nesting depth. * `04613_aggregate_function_version_not_sticky` asks for a `Native` response at a revision below the one that introduced versioning and then checks the column again, so a version pinned for that one response would be visible both in the values read back (`sumMap` over `Decimal32`) and in `system.columns`. The revision is pinned explicitly and the type name the response carries is asserted, so the test cannot pass without that path having run.

signal.title: Check the query cancellation while filling `system.parts` and its siblings
signal.text: The tables based on `StorageSystemPartsBase` (`system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`) build the whole result eagerly in `initializePipeline`, so a cancelled or timed out query kept building rows over every storage and part until the very end. In a stress test with ThreadFuzzer this took minutes and tripped the hung check: a `SELECT` over `system.parts_columns` (with a filter matching every active part on the server) stayed in the process list for 252 seconds with `is_cancelled = 1` and `max_execution_time = 10`. Check the query status per storage and per part, following the pattern of `system.zookeeper` and `system.remote_data_paths`. The check also covers the storage-discovery prepass in `StoragesInfoStream` (the eager enumeration of all databases and tables), the analogous prepass in `StoragesDroppedInfoStream` (so `system.dropped_tables_parts` is interruptible as well), the skip loop in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::next`, and the per-storage part enumeration itself: the `MergeTreeData` helpers (`getDataPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllDataPartsVector`, `getProjectionPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllProjectionPartsVector`) take an optional `need_stop` callback that is checked periodically while the parts snapshot is being built. The two column-oriented tables additionally check the query status inside their column-enumeration loops and their metadata prepass, so a very wide table does not create a long uninterruptible stretch inside a single storage. The return value of `checkTimeLimit` is honored, so with `timeout_overflow_mode = 'break'` the eager build stops at the soft deadline and returns the rows collected so far. The table-lock acquisition in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::tryLockTable` is interruptible as well: instead of a single wait inside `RWLockImpl::getLock` for the whole `lock_acquire_timeout`, the lock is acquired in 100 ms slices with a query-status poll between the attempts (the total timeout and the `DEADLOCK_AVOIDED` semantics are preserved), so a killed or soft-timed-out query does not sit in the lock wait while a concurrent DDL query holds the drop lock. The test `04869_system_parts_lock_wait_cancellation` pins this with a share lock held by a long `SELECT` and a `DROP TABLE` in an `Ordinary` database queued behind it. The test uses the new `slowdown_system_parts_enumeration` failpoint, which only affects the specially named test tables (so concurrently running tests are unaffected). It sleeps 500 ms on every enumerated part, so building the full result for a 20-part table takes at least 10 seconds, and it sleeps 1 second per `COLUMNS_CANCELLATION_CHECK_PERIOD` (128) enumerated columns of a part, so building the full `system.parts_columns` / `system.projection_parts_columns` result over a single part with 1,025 columns (and a projection over all of them) takes at least 8 seconds. The test asserts that queries with a 1 second deadline in the `break` mode finish well under that (the elapsed time is taken from `system.query_log`, because the startup of `clickhouse-client` alone takes seconds in the debug and sanitizer builds), which is only possible by stopping at the per-part and per-column cancellation checkpoints. Timed assertions are needed because a plain row-count assertion cannot distinguish a build with the fix from one without: in the `break` mode the executor drops the eagerly built result after the deadline in both cases. The test also asserts partial row counts under a pre-expired deadline for all five tables, including `system.dropped_tables_parts` over a deterministic dropped-table fixture. The pre-expired-deadline checks also run under the failpoint, so the fewer-rows assertion is deterministic even on a machine fast enough to build the whole result in under a millisecond. For tables with the `_snap` name marker, the failpoint additionally slows down the parts-snapshot walks inside `MergeTreeData` (500 ms per enumerated part) and makes them poll the stop callback on every element, and for tables with the `_meta` name marker it slows down the column-metadata prepass of the column-oriented tables (1 second per 128 enumerated metadata columns), so the timed checks also prove that the snapshot materialization and the prepass are interruptible: all six of these checks fail against a binary with the `need_stop` polls and the prepass checkpoints disabled. Caught by `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113722&sha=ceedb772f6aa36e221d25ce48f9af71f032a7b08&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113722 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Queries over `system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`, and `system.dropped_tables_parts` now react to cancellation and `max_execution_time` while the result is being built.

signal.title: Perf: Coalesce contiguous unmatched ranges in MergeJoin
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/12118 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid materializing a temporary filtered column for dense unmatched ranges in partial_merge RIGHT and FULL JOINs. ### What does this PR do? - Counts unmatched runs before choosing the append path. - Appends dense unmatched ranges directly with insertRangeFrom. - Uses the existing filtered-column path when unmatched rows are too fragmented. - Keeps the existing whole-block path when no right rows were matched. - Adds RIGHT and FULL correctness coverage with nullable and string right columns. - Adds dense and interleaved RIGHT cases to the partial_merge_join performance fixture. ### Why? - The old path calls filter for every right column. - Direct range insertion avoids temporary filtered columns for dense runs. - One insertRangeFrom per range is not good for fragmented masks. - The fallback keeps fragmented cases on the existing path. - The result and row order stay unchanged. ### Performance - Dense unmatched runs use bulk range insertion. - Fragmented masks use the filtered-column path. - The fixture covers sparse, dense, and interleaved RIGHT and FULL JOIN shapes. ### Benchmark - Status: Fixture updated; results pending. - Fixture: partial_merge_join. - Cases: ALL RIGHT JOIN, ALL FULL JOIN, and interleaved ALL RIGHT JOIN. - Data: 10,000 sparse left keys and 1,000,000 dense right keys, plus multiples-of-2 and multiples-of-3 tables. - Output: count and sum(b.k) keep the right-side output in the query.

signal.title: Offer the `/`-commands of the client, and name them when misspelled
signal.text: Typing `/` at the beginning of the input now shows the client's own commands (`/clear`, `/help`, `/man`) as as-you-type hints, and typing more of a name narrows the list down. `Tab` completes the command being typed, which is also how they are completed when the instant hints are disabled (`--hints 0`, `--highlight 0`, `--disable_suggestion`). Until now these commands could only be found in the documentation; now the prompt itself lists them. A mistake in the name of a command is reported as such, with the commands it may have meant, instead of being parsed as SQL and reported as a syntax error at the `/`: ``` :) /hepl Exception on client: Code: 36. DB::Exception: Unknown command `/hepl`. Maybe you meant: ['/help']. Type `/` at the beginning of the line to see all the commands. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` An argument given to a command that takes none (`/clear now`) is reported the same way. Batch `clickhouse-client` still parses such input as the SQL it is, exactly like it already does for `help` and `clear`; `clickhouse-local` reports it like the interactive client. The commands come from a single list, `clientSlashCommands`, shared by the hints, the completion and the diagnostics. An offered command replaces the whole typed prefix including the `/`, which `replxx` counts as a word break character and would otherwise leave in place. The offer is off for `keeper-client` and `clickhouse-disks`: they reuse the same line reader, and a leading `/` is the beginning of a path there. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114043 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `/`-commands of the client (`/help`, `/man`, `/clear`) are now offered by the line editor: typing `/` at the beginning of the input lists them as hints, and `Tab` completes the command being typed. A mistake in the name of a command is reported with the similar commands suggested, instead of being parsed as SQL.

signal.title: Import/export AST as JSON
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Use case Aid various dev tools. Help analyze query logs. ### Describe the solution you'd like Implement a mode for the EXPLAIN AST statement that will output JSON. The JSON should have the following structure. ``` { "type": "Expression", // a string representing the type of AST node, "child_type": "where", // optional string representing the association of the child to the parent, "begin": 123, // optional offset in bytes in the original query to the beginning of the node, could be preserved or lost during various AST transformations "end": 456, // optional offset in bytes in the original query to the end of the node, could be preserved or lost during various AST transformations // node-specific fields, e.g., "alias", "limit_offset", etc. "children": // an array of objects of the same structure [ { ... }, ... ] } ``` Implement a set of SQL functions for transforming between SQL and JSON: ``` parseQueryToJSON(str) -- returns a String with JSON formatQueryFromJSON(str) -- takes JSON and formats it back to SQL formatQueryFromJSON(str, original_query) -- takes JSON and formats it back to SQL, with best effort to preserve comments, space, and indentation from the original query. ``` Implement a `dialect` (which is a setting for switching dialects) named `clickhouse_json`, which can be used to pass JSON AST directly as a query. ### Describe alternatives you've considered This is an alternative to a more high-level approach: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75033 ### Additional context The problem is that we can't guarantee compatibility of the AST.

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions clamp(), clamp_min(), clamp_max() and round()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `clamp`, `clamp_min`, `clamp_max`, and `round`. ### Description Implements four PromQL functions previously reported as not implemented: - `clamp(v, min, max)`, `clamp_min(v, min)`, `clamp_max(v, max)` — new `applyClampFunction` converter mapping to `greatest`/`least` SQL with explicit guards, because vectorized `least`/`greatest` in ClickHouse treat NaN as the largest value and ignore NULLs, which would corrupt NaN sample values and missing points. Prometheus special cases are reproduced exactly: `min > max` returns an empty vector, and a NaN bound propagates NaN. - `round(v[, to_nearest])` — new `applyRoundFunction` converter; replicates Prometheus inverse arithmetic (`floor(v * (1/to_nearest) + 0.5) / (1/to_nearest)`), including ties rounding toward `+Inf` and NaN propagation for `to_nearest = 0` or NaN. Both drop the metric name from results, matching Prometheus. Non-constant scalar bounds (for example, `clamp(v, time()*0-1, 2)`) are supported. No parser changes were needed; arity is enforced by each converter. The embedded support matrices for `prometheusQuery` and `prometheusQueryRange` list the new math functions and retain the implemented range functions `increase`, `changes`, and `resets`. **Semantics verified against Prometheus 3.5.0** for bound combinations `(0, 1)`, `(0, 1e12)`, `(1e12, 0)`, `(1e12, 1e12)`, and fractional `to_nearest`. **Testing**: adds `test_clamp` and `test_round`, plus conversion and aggregation regressions for empty scalar handling and a runtime scalar `quantile` parameter outside `[0, 1]`.

signal.title: For input formats with column names, search columns case-insensitively if there is no ambiguity
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Use case We already have the settings, `input_format_arrow_case_insensitive_column_matching`, `input_format_parquet_case_insensitive_column_matching`, `input_format_orc_case_insensitive_column_matching`. I don't like them. The proper solution was proposed in the comment here: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/61750#issuecomment-2019201049 ### Describe the solution you'd like Add a setting, `input_format_with_names_case_insensitive_column_matching`. It will control the behavior of all formats containing column names, including binary (e.g., `RowBinaryWithNames`) and text formats, including those containing names in each record (e.g., `JSONEachRow`) and in the header (e.g., `CSVWithNames`), as well as column-oriented formats (e.g., `Native`, `Parquet`). The setting effectively overrides existing ones, `*_case_insensitive_column_matching`. The modes should be: `match_case`, `ignore_case`, and `auto`. The `auto` mode will search for a matching column case-insensitively, if the direct match isn't found. In contrast, the `case-insensitive` mode should throw an exception if the data contains ambiguous names. We will use the `auto` mode by default. ### Describe alternatives you've considered _No response_ ### Additional context A good chance to undo the damage of a previously wrong implementation. ``` milovidov@milovidov-pc:~/work/ClickHouse/tests$ ch ClickHouse local version 26.1.1.1. :) CREATE TABLE test (Hello String, World String) CREATE TABLE test ( `Hello` String, `World` String ) Query id: 10d3efb3-285f-464b-80b7-5a586321469e Ok. 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 0.018 sec. :) INSERT INTO test FORMAT JSONEachRow {"hello": "hi!", "world": "universe"} INSERT INTO test FORMAT JSONEachRow Query id: 7641c158-5908-4e7a-a023-56640f790c27 Ok. 1 row in set. Elapsed: 0.005 sec. :) SELECT * FROM test SELECT * FROM test Query id: 5c405c62-97fa-48e2-9ca5-af7a6f2f19fb ┌─Hello─┬─World─┐ 1. │ │ │ └───────┴───────┘ 1 row in set. Elapsed: 0.002 sec. ```

signal.title: Fix signed integer overflow reading Iceberg decimal bounds
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114929 Decoding a `Decimal` column bound from an Iceberg manifest ran in `int64_t` regardless of how wide the bound was, in `deserializeFieldFromBinaryRepr` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/ManifestFileIterator.cpp`). Three steps overflow: * the big-endian accumulation `unscaled_value = (unscaled_value << 8) | byte`, once the bound is more than eight bytes wide; * the sign extension `sign_extension <<= (str.size() * 8)`, which shifts by 64 or more for a bound of eight bytes or more; * the scaler loop `scaler *= 10`, which computes `10^scale` and leaves `int64_t` at scale 19. A `Decimal(38, 30)` column reaches all three: its bounds are 14 bytes wide. Bounds are parsed for every column of a manifest entry, so any query with a filter is enough and the filter does not have to touch the decimal column. A build with the undefined behaviour sanitizer aborts, as reported in the issue. Only `Decimal32` and `Decimal64` bounds are ever turned into a `Field` (everything else already returned `std::nullopt` a few lines below), and both fit into `Int64`. So the fix decodes exactly those and rejects anything wider before the arithmetic, which keeps the observable behaviour: a bound that used to be computed and then discarded is now not computed at all. Two smaller defects in the same expression are fixed along the way: * the sign extension is skipped when the value already fills all 64 bits. Previously it shifted an `int64_t` by 64, which is undefined; on the usual targets the shift count is taken modulo 64, so `-1` was left unchanged and OR-ing it in turned every eight-byte negative bound into `-1`. That is a wrong bound, not just undefined behaviour, and a wrong bound prunes files that do contain matching rows. * the widening `unscaled_value += scaler` and the narrowing to `Int32` are range checked. The bound comes from the manifest and is not validated against the declared precision, so a malformed manifest could otherwise wrap it into a bogus bound. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04907_iceberg_decimal_bounds_overflow.sh` reads a `Decimal(38, 30)` Iceberg table with a filter. The table is the one attached to the issue, produced by Spark, repacked without the Spark checksum files and embedded as base64: ClickHouse cannot write a decimal column to Iceberg (`Unsupported type for iceberg Decimal(38, 30)`), so the test cannot build it itself. Because the overflowed bound was discarded anyway, the query results are the same before and after this change; the test fails before the fix only under the undefined behaviour sanitizer, and pins the results everywhere else. I verified the reproducer and the resulting query output against the official master build `26.8.1.1463`; I have not built this branch locally, so the compile and the sanitizer runs are left to CI. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading Iceberg tables whose manifests carry `Decimal` column bounds that do not fit into 64 bits, such as those of a `Decimal(38, 30)` column. Such a bound is now ignored instead of being decoded into a meaningless value, and a negative bound stored in eight bytes is no longer read as `-1`, which could skip files that do contain matching rows.

signal.title: Fix a Keeper server never joining the cluster when background snapshot IO is enabled
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/NuRaft/pull/123 ## Problem With `nuraft_use_bg_thread_for_snapshot_io` enabled, a Keeper server added to the cluster never joins. The leader's catch-up loop waits indefinitely for a response that cannot arrive, so the configuration change is never committed. The setting is off by default, which is why this has gone unnoticed. ## Root cause `sync_log_to_new_srv` builds one of two requests for the joining server — a snapshot request when the peer is below the retained log, or a log-pack `sync_log_request` otherwise — and then dispatches on the snapshot IO mode: ```cpp if (!params->use_bg_thread_for_snapshot_io_) { srv_to_join_->send_req(srv_to_join_, req, ex_resp_handler_); } else { snapshot_io_mgr::instance().invoke(); } ``` Only the *snapshot* branch hands its work to the IO thread. Nothing ever enqueues a log pack with `snapshot_io_mgr` — `create_sync_snapshot_req` is its only producer — so with background snapshot IO on, invoking the thread does not send the log-pack request. It is dropped. Observed on the unfixed build as the new server absent from the cluster configuration and stuck at log index 1 while the leader was at 12. ## Solution Dispatch on what was actually built rather than on the IO mode. The snapshot branch leaves the request null exactly when it has queued the work with the IO thread; in every other case — including the log-pack branch in *both* IO modes — there is a request and it must be sent. Covered by `log_sync_with_async_snapshot_io_test` in NuRaft's `learner_new_joiner_test`, verified to fail against the exact pre-patch code while the four existing tests in that binary keep passing. NuRaft pull request #123 is merged, and the submodule now points at NuRaft's merge commit `2fcee8a` rather than the branch, so the Keeper integration tests, `nightly_keeper` and Jepsen exercise the merged code here. Relative to `master`'s previous pin `dd3d098`, the only NuRaft change this brings in is that fix. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a Keeper server never joining the cluster when `nuraft_use_bg_thread_for_snapshot_io` is enabled: the log batch sent to a joining server was silently dropped, so the membership change never completed.

signal.title: Implement CREATE HANDLER query
signal.text: ## Company or project name ClickHouse ## Use case Creating and managing custom HTTP handlers from SQL without editing configuration files. ## Describe the solution you'd like ### Syntax ``` CREATE [IF NOT EXISTS] HANDLER name [PROTOCOL protocol_name] URL [PREFIX|REGEXP] '/test' [METHODS (GET, POST)] [TYPE query] AS [SELECT|INSERT|...] ... ``` Creates a handler with a specified name. The name is used for managing handlers with SQL queries, diagnostic messages, and ordering handlers. If a protocol name is specified (optional), the handler is active only for the specified protocol, see https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/composable-protocols Otherwise, it is active for all of http/https protocols. URL - mandatory parameter. Can be in the form of URL, URL PREFIX, or URL REGEXP. For exact URLs and prefixes, we should check for ambiguity at creation/alter time and throw an exception if there is ambiguity. For regexp, it's not possible to check for ambiguity. Handlers from the server configuration has the priority above SQL-defined handlers. Then, SQL-defined handlers will be matched in the lexicographical order of their names. There is no other way to specify their priorities in case of ambiguity. The URL is matched without `?` query string and `#` fragment identifier. The list of allowed `METHODS` can be specified. By default, it's only GET. We also support POST, PUT, DELETE, but not arbitrary names. TYPE can be specified, but the only supported type for now is query. It is okay that SQL-defined handlers allow fewer features than configuration-defined. After `AS`, it specifies a SQL query that will be invoked by this handler. The query can be parameterized. The query is parsed for syntactic correctness during handler creation/alter, but not analyzed. For example, the tables referenced by the query can be missed at the time of the handler creation. The FORMAT and similar clauses belong to the query, not the whole CREATE/ALTER statement. The query can be put in parentheses for disambiguation. The handler could support arbitrary queries. The INSERT query should not contain embedded data, it expects that the data will be provided in the HTTP body. ``` DROP [IF EXISTS] HANDLER name ``` Drops the handler with the specified name. ``` ALTER HANDLER name [PROTOCOL protocol_name] URL '/test' [METHODS (GET, POST)] [TYPE query] AS SELECT ... ``` Replaces the handler with the new one. The ALTER query can include only a subset of clauses, e.g., it can be used to only change the URL or the query. ### Storage The handlers are saved in a storage, which can be a local or Keeper storage, similarly to named collections, which is configured in query_rules_storage in the configuration file. ### Access control These queries: CREATE HANDLER, DROP HANDLER, ALTER HANDLER, will require separate grants. Invoking handlers doesn't require any separate grants. But grants are checked as usual during the query invocation. The authentication works in the usual way. For example, a user can provide user/password credentials in the request invoking the handler. There is a popular use-case when handlers are used to encapsulate access to certain queries - when the handler is invokable by one user, but uses a query with tables not accessible directly by this user. For this purpose, you should do it by creating a VIEW with SQL SECURITY DEFINER, and then defining a HANDLER with SELECT from that view. So the handlers are transparent to this logic. Any HTTP URL parameters in the query string, HTTP form variables in POST, and HTTP headers, can be used as usual with handlers - this includes parameters for parameterized queries. Out of scope: defining the default user for the handler. ### Introspection Add new fields to the query_log for the handler name and for the HTTP request URL. Add SQL miscellaneous functions `currentHandler()`, `currentRequestURL()`. These functions can be used to customize the query behavior depending on the invoked handler. ## Describe alternatives you've considered _No response_ ## Additional context Many features will be available automatically. For example, custom HTTP response headers are available through the SETTINGS of the invoked query. URLs with parameters in the paths are supported through the `currentRequestURL()` function. Out of scope: a query to invoke a handlers by its name, so the handlers are accessible in other than http/https protocols.

signal.title: Add server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread`
signal.text: Each thread accumulates up to `max_untracked_memory` (4 MiB by default) of allocations before reporting them to the server-wide `MemoryTracker`. With many threads, this unreported memory can sum to a large amount, causing the server's tracked memory usage to under-count actual consumption and leading to OOM. This PR introduces a server-level setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) and speculatively charges this amount to the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. The global tracked memory becomes a tighter upper bound on actual consumption when `max_untracked_memory` for those workers does not exceed this setting; operators that permit a larger per-query value must raise the server setting accordingly. The reservation is charged on the server-wide (total) tracker only — deliberately not through the query's tracker chain. Query-level accounting feeds heuristics that compare memory deltas against byte thresholds (conversion of aggregation hash tables to two-level via `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes`, spill-to-disk decisions), and phantom reservations of `num_threads * 4 MiB` trip those thresholds immediately: an earlier revision of this PR that charged the query tracker showed consistent slowdowns of GROUP BY queries in performance tests for exactly this reason. The reservation itself does not alter query-level or user-level accounting (`max_memory_usage`, `memory_usage` in `system.processes`); however, every pipeline worker flushes its pending real allocation reports before releasing its outermost reservation, so those counters and memory-based heuristics can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. The speculative reservation uses the throwing path of the memory tracker, so when it would exceed the server memory limit the corresponding job is treated as failed with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — the same behavior as if the job itself had exceeded the limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) which speculatively reserves this amount on the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. When it is at least the workers' `max_untracked_memory`, it makes server-wide tracked memory a tighter upper bound on actual consumption and reduces the risk of OOM with many concurrent pipeline workers. The reservation does not alter query-level or user-level accounting, but workers flush pending real allocation reports before releasing their outermost reservation, so those counters can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - signal.title: Codex tries to learn from its mistakes
signal.text: The unattended PR continuation workflow made two kinds of unsafe decisions. It incorrectly closed PR #114849 after confusing commit visibility with containment by the current `master`, and it force-pushed PR #111032 from a malformed single-parent commit that changed 673 files and deleted 26,457 lines. Require an explicit base-branch ancestry check and a separate current-state check so reverted changes are not considered integrated. Before committing or pushing, the workflow must inspect the staged and complete PR diffs, preserve the existing remote head as an ancestor, and stop on unexplained scope changes. A `pre-push` hook now enforces fast-forward-only updates and rejects branch deletion even if an agent attempts a force-push. An audit of recent automation activity found eight account-level force-pushes since 2026-08-13. PR #111032 was the only malformed large-diff outlier; the other seven replacement heads changed 2–8 files. The audit also found a smaller scope failure in PR #104495, where conflict resolution accidentally staged three unrelated untracked test files. The new explicit-path staging rule and staged-diff inspection cover that failure mode. The safety hook was tested in a throwaway repository: normal fast-forward updates were accepted, while non-fast-forward updates, branch deletion, and the exact PR #111032 rewrite were rejected. Shell syntax and ShellCheck validation also pass. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114849 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111032 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104495 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog.

signal.title: Add stateless and fuzzer jobs to the WeeklyCFI workflow
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100419 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112152 The `amd_cfi` build is the only test build with ThinLTO enabled — the same compile profile as official release builds — so besides CFI violations the WeeklyCFI workflow also catches ThinLTO-only behavior differences that no other CI job can see. The latest example is the `__functional` frame-name suppression surfaced by `test_crash_log` in the weekly runs of 2026-07-20 through 2026-08-10 and fixed in #112152. This PR broadens the workflow's coverage: - **Stateless tests** (parallel + sequential lanes, mirroring `amd_debug`). `clickhouse-test` now detects the CFI build from `-fsanitize=cfi` in the `CXX_FLAGS` row of `system.build_options`, so tests that cannot pass in this build profile can carry a `no-cfi` tag (the same generic `no-<flag>` skip mechanism the sanitizer builds use). CFI is deliberately not treated as a sanitizer: it has near-zero runtime overhead, so tests tagged `no-sanitizers` still run under CFI. - **AST fuzzer and BuzzHouse**: fuzzers assert only on crashes, never on exact query output, so the build profile cannot produce false positives there, and fuzzing reaches virtual-call combinations the curated suites never exercise. The fuzzer job configs are shared out into `_common_ast_fuzzer_job_config` / `_common_buzz_fuzzer_job_config`; master and PR workflows are unchanged. Not added, and why: unit tests (`ENABLE_CFI` is incompatible with `ENABLE_TESTS` — ThinLTO is disabled when building tests), performance comparison (it compares against the non-CFI master-head binary, so results are uninterpretable), upgrade/compatibility checks (version and data compatibility are orthogonal to CFI instrumentation), Keeper Jepsen (requires the standalone `clickhouse-keeper` build, which the CFI build omits). **Note for review:** the last commit temporarily switches the workflow to a `pull_request` trigger so this PR's CI exercises the full `amd_cfi` build + new test jobs (same validation approach as #100419). It will be reverted to the schedule-only trigger before merge. Any stateless tests that turn out unable to pass under ThinLTO will get `no-cfi` tags in follow-up commits. Workflow: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/workflows/weekly_cfi.yml ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/labels
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/labels`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus-compatible clients** use **`/api/v1/labels`** to discover the label names available in matching series. This is useful for **Grafana dashboards**, variable pickers, and integrations that need to build label selectors without fetching every series first. The endpoint follows the same **logical label model** as the series endpoint. It reads labels stored in the **`tags` Map** and in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/labels` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint returns a **sorted, distinct list of label names**. It includes **`__name__`** when at least one matching series exists and supports both **unfiltered discovery** and filtering by matching series. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** filters the series used to build the label-name list. Repeated selectors are combined as a **union**. - **`start` and `end`** restrict the matching series by their **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the returned label names and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Label discovery:** collect distinct names from the canonical metric name, the **`tags` Map**, and configured dedicated tag columns. - **Selector support:** reuse the Prometheus series-selector and matcher behavior from **`/api/v1/series`**. - **Storage compatibility:** support both normal TimeSeries storage and **`tags_to_columns`** layouts while preserving the logical label set. - **Repeated selectors:** combine repeated **`match[]`** parameters without returning duplicate label names. - **Time ranges:** apply trusted min/max bounds when available and keep ranged requests valid with the **approximate superset** behavior allowed by Prometheus when bounds are unavailable. - **Result limits:** support empty, zero, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values, including the Prometheus truncation warning. - **HTTP handling:** support the dedicated endpoint and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**, with endpoint parameters kept separate from ClickHouse settings. - **Access control:** enforce the configured **`TimeSeries` table authorization boundary** before reading the underlying target tables. - **Query lifecycle:** execute through the **normal query pipeline**, preserve query completion handling, and record the request in **`query_log`**. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Label collection:** distinct names, sorted output, **`__name__`**, Map labels, and dedicated columns. - **Selectors:** metric filters, label filters, repeated **`match[]`** unions, and requests with no matching series. - **Time ranges:** matching and non-matching intervals, including empty optional parameters. - **Limits:** truncation warnings and the **`limit`** parameter behavior. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants** on the configured `TimeSeries` table. - **Observability:** successful requests recorded as **`QueryFinish`** entries. - **Shared behavior:** the related Prometheus query and series API regression coverage. Also ran **Python syntax checks**, **XML parsing**, and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now describes the `/api/v1/labels` handler and its supported parameters. ### Stack This PR is **stacked on #114867** and includes the **`/api/v1/series`** changes. After **#114867** merges, this branch can be rebased onto `master`.

signal.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/series
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/series`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus clients** use **`/api/v1/series`** to discover the label sets stored for active series. This endpoint is used by **Prometheus-compatible tools** such as **Grafana** when they need to populate metric and label selectors. ClickHouse **`TimeSeries` tables** can store labels in the main **`tags` Map**, in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, or in a mixture of both layouts. The endpoint needs to expose the **same logical series** regardless of how those labels are stored. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/series` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint is available through both a **dedicated `/api/v1/series` handler** and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**. It supports **GET requests** and **`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` POST requests**. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** selects series by metric name and label matchers. Repeated parameters are combined as a **union** and overlapping results are returned only once through **deduplication**. - **`start` and `end`** select series overlapping the requested **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the number of returned series and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Selector parsing:** parse Prometheus series selectors with equality, inequality, regular-expression, and negative regular-expression matchers. - **Storage compatibility:** support metric names, labels in the **`tags` Map**, dedicated tag columns, and mixed rows that use both storage layouts. - **Label normalization:** normalize missing labels to the **Prometheus empty-value semantics** and include the full logical label set in each response. - **PromQL compatibility:** support quoted label names and anchor regular expressions to the **complete label value**. - **Input validation:** validate selectors and timestamps before executing the query. - **Time ranges:** apply the time-range filter when trusted min/max data is available. When it is not available, keep the request valid and return the **compatible candidate superset** allowed by the Prometheus API. - **Result limits:** support zero and positive limits, exact-limit responses, truncation reporting, and invalid-value errors. - **Access control:** read the underlying series metadata through the **`TimeSeries` table-function path** after checking access to the configured **`TimeSeries` table**. Unknown routes are resolved before authorization, so they keep the normal **404 response**. - **Existing endpoints:** apply the configured **`TimeSeries` table access boundary** consistently to the existing Prometheus query endpoints. - **Query lifecycle:** run the generated query through the **normal query pipeline** and keep **query logging** and **query completion handling** intact. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Matcher operators:** metric-name and label selectors with all matcher operators. - **Repeated selectors:** repeated **`match[]`** parameters, selector unions, and overlapping-result deduplication. - **Storage layouts:** Map labels, dedicated tag columns, missing labels, mixed carriers, conflicting carriers, and **`__name__`**. - **Regex and names:** quoted label names and whole-value regular-expression anchoring. - **Selector validation:** invalid and unbounded selectors, including the valid **`{host!~".*"}`** case. - **Time ranges:** two-sided, one-sided, inclusive, and invalid time ranges. - **Min/max behavior:** requests with and without trusted min/max metadata. - **Limits:** zero, exact, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values. - **HTTP methods:** GET and form POST requests. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants**, access checks for all query endpoint families, and unknown-route handling. - **Observability:** query completion records and the existing query API limit behavior. Also ran **Python syntax checks** and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now covers the Prometheus handler configuration and the **`/api/v1/series` endpoint parameters**. ### Stack This is the **base PR** for the follow-up Prometheus API endpoints: - **#114868** adds **`/api/v1/labels`**. - **#114869** adds **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`**.

signal.title: Fail Iceberg writes when the parent snapshot is missing from `snapshots`
signal.text: Follow-up to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107473 (review escalation: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107473#discussion_r3535058378). If Iceberg metadata carries a live `current-snapshot-id` whose entry cannot be resolved in `snapshots` (the array is missing, empty, or the matching entry was pruned — malformed external metadata or an over-aggressive catalog), `MetadataGenerator::getParentSnapshot` returned `nullptr` and the write still committed: the summary totals restarted from zero and the manifest-list copy loop found no parent, so the new snapshot silently orphaned all previously visible data. `generateNextMetadata` now throws `ICEBERG_SPECIFICATION_VIOLATION` on an unresolvable live parent, matching the read path's handling of a missing snapshot set. Compaction opts out via the new `tolerate_missing_parent_snapshot` parameter: it replays a filtered history onto rebuilt metadata (non-append records are skipped), so a record's parent may be legitimately absent there. Covered by `gtest_iceberg_metadata_generator` (suite extended to 9 cases: positive parent-chain append, empty-array, and pruned-entry rejections). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107473 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Iceberg writes now fail with an `ICEBERG_SPECIFICATION_VIOLATION` error instead of silently orphaning previously committed data when the metadata's current snapshot cannot be found in its `snapshots` list. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Add native Version data type (proof of concept)
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Adds a native `Version` SQL data type for semantic-version-style values (`major.minor.patch.build`), enabling correct numeric ordering instead of lexicographic string comparison. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes: The new `Version` type stores versions of up to 4 components, such as `major.minor.patch.build`. Comparisons between these values correctly evaluate numeric size, meaning `toVersion('1.2') < toVersion('1.10')` is true. `Version` values parse 1-4 dot-separated non-negative integer components, zero-padding missing trailing components (`1.2` is equal to `1.2.0`). ### Description **Summary** Adds a native `Version` SQL data type for semantic-version-style values (`major.minor.patch.build`), so comparisons use correct numeric ordering instead of lexicographic string comparison: ```sql SELECT '1.2' < '1.10'; -- 0 (wrong, string comparison) SELECT toVersion('1.2') < toVersion('1.10'); -- 1 (correct) SELECT toVersion('1.2') = toVersion('1.2.0'); -- 1 (padding equality) ``` Stored as a packed `UInt128` (`(major<<96)|(minor<<64)|(patch<<32)|build`), so `=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `!=` all work natively via plain integer comparison — no custom operator overloads needed. Parsing (`toVersion`/`toVersionOrNull`/`toVersionOrZero`/`toVersionOrDefault`) accepts 1–4 dot-separated non-negative integer components, zero-pads missing trailing components, and rejects more than 4 components or any non-numeric component. Leading zeros parse numerically (`01` → `1`). Pre-release/build-metadata suffixes (`-beta`, `+build1`) are intentionally out of scope for this first pass. **Design decision: numeric-only model, not full semver** Per review discussion (thanks @groeneai), `1.0.0-alpha`-style pre-release ordering was considered and deliberately rejected: the 4 `UInt32` components already fill the `UInt128` with no spare bits, and semver's ordering rule (`0.9.9 < 1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0`) has no integer to sit between two adjacent packed values, so supporting it would require replacing the fixed integer-packing model with a comparison-based one, giving up free integer ordering. `Version` therefore stays a 4-component numeric-only scheme — closer to `ClickHouse`'s own version scheme (`24.3.1.2672`) than to semver — and text with a pre-release/build-metadata suffix is rejected with `CANNOT_PARSE_VERSION` rather than silently truncated. This is now documented directly on the type in `base/base/Version.h`/`DataTypeVersion.h`. **Caveats** This is exploratory. I've verified it manually end-to-end against a real build via `clickhouse local` (parsing, padding-equality, numeric ordering, and both rejection cases all confirmed), but: - It has **not** been run through the full functional/stateless test suite, only the two new test files included here. - The wire-format tag byte choices (`FieldBinaryEncoding.cpp` uses `0x16`, `DataTypesBinaryEncoding.h` uses `0x38`) are new protocol constants — once shipped these are effectively permanent for backward compatibility, so they deserve explicit maintainer review before being treated as final. - No prior design discussion/RFC happened before writing this — I'd like feedback on whether a type like this is wanted at all, and on the packing/validation choices, before investing further in edge cases and full test coverage. **Test plan** - [x] `tests/queries/0_stateless/04614_data_type_version_basic.sql` — parsing/round-trip/padding - [x] `tests/queries/0_stateless/04615_data_type_version_comparison.sql` — ordering + rejection cases - [x] Manual verification via `clickhouse local` against a full local build - [x] Full stateless/functional test suite (not run) - [x] Style/clang-tidy pass 🤖 Generated with heavy AI assistance (agentic exploration + implementation), per [AI_POLICY.md](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/AI_POLICY.md) — disclosing since this was a substantial, multi-file core-engine change built through an unusually AI-heavy process, not just a docs tweak.
signal.author: valerypetrov

signal.title: Mask credentials of the Azure data lake table engines
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114939 `IcebergAzure`, `DeltaLakeAzure` and `PaimonAzure` appear in neither branch of the table engine dispatch in `FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder::findTableEngineSecretArguments` (`src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.cpp`): the S3 branch lists the S3 family lake engines (`DeltaLake`, `DeltaLakeS3`, `Hudi`, `Iceberg`, `IcebergS3`, `Paimon`, `PaimonS3`, `S3Queue`) and the Azure branch lists `AzureBlobStorage` and `AzureQueue`. With no branch matching, none of the three engines has any argument marked secret, so the storage account key stays verbatim in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, in `system.tables.engine_full` and in the logged query text, at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0` and without the `displaySecretsInShowAndSelect` privilege. Both spellings leak: the `AccountKey=` inside a connection string and the positional `account_key` of the five argument form. The three engines take the same leading arguments as `AzureBlobStorage`, and `findAzureBlobStorageTableEngineSecretArguments` already handles both spellings, so this routes them to it. The Azure *table functions* (`icebergAzure`, `deltaLakeAzure`, `paimonAzure` and their `*Cluster` variants) were already dispatched there, which is why a `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT * FROM icebergAzure(...)` masked while the engine did not. As the issue notes, this is not a regression: `git log -S "IcebergAzure"` over the secret finder's history is empty, so the engines were never masked. `findBackupNameSecretArguments`, the other dispatch in the same file, is left alone: it resolves a `BACKUP ... TO` destination, and the lake engines are not backup destinations. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04908_azure_lake_engines_secret_mask.sh` covers all three engines and both argument spellings against an unreachable endpoint, so no Azure endpoint or emulator is needed: * `DeltaLakeAzure` defers reading the table when the columns are given, so its `CREATE` succeeds and `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and `system.tables.engine_full` are asserted directly. * `IcebergAzure` and `PaimonAzure` read their metadata while the table is created, so theirs fail against that endpoint. The masking happens when the query is formatted for the log, before the failure, so for those two the assertion is that the logged query text carries no key. Against the official master build `26.8.1.1463` the test prints the raw account key in all four `SHOW CREATE` and `engine_full` rows and reports 4 logged queries containing it; the committed reference is the masked output with 0. I have not built this branch locally, so the compile and the test run are left to CI. The Azure part of `tests/integration/test_mask_sensitive_info/test.py` is untouched: it runs against Azurite, and these three engines need a real table to exist there, which the unreachable-endpoint approach above avoids. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `IcebergAzure`, `DeltaLakeAzure` and `PaimonAzure` table engines now hide the Azure storage account key in `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and in `system.tables.engine_full`, as the `AzureBlobStorage` engine already did. Previously any user allowed to run `SHOW CREATE TABLE` or read `system.tables` could see the key of such a table.
