signal.title: Serialize serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte in the query plan
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112079 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` being dropped from the serialized query plan. With `serialize_query_plan = 1`, a cluster running with the setting disabled could diverge on the in-memory string representation between the initiator and the node executing the deserialized plan, because the setting was read on deserialization but never written on serialization and therefore always resolved to its default on the executing node. ### Description `QueryPlan::serialize` builds a fresh `QueryPlanSerializationSettings` per step and emits only what that step's `serializeSettings` assigned; `readBinary` leaves an absent name at its declared default. Both `AggregatingStep::deserialize` and `MergingAggregatedStep::deserialize` read `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` into `Aggregator::Params`, but neither `serializeSettings` ever wrote it - the only `Params` field those two read without writing. So with `serialize_query_plan = 1` an initiator running the setting at `0` ships a plan the executing node deserializes as `1`. The two then disagree on the aggregation-key byte layout (the flag adds or removes one trailing byte per string in `ColumnString::serializeValueIntoArena`), and since the two-level bucket number hashes those serialized bytes, disagreeing sources can place one logical key in different buckets - the duplicated-group shape documented in `tests/integration/test_string_aggregation_compatibility`. Keeping that layout consistent across a cluster of incompatible versions is the setting's whole purpose. Only an explicit `= 0` diverges, both defaults being `true`, which is why nothing observes it today. **The fix** adds the missing assignment to both `serializeSettings` bodies, for both values and at every serialization version. Restricting it to the non-default value is wrong: a receiver predating the name has no such setting and its GROUP BY key path writes no trailing zero byte at all, so it behaves like `false`, and omitting `true` would silently hand exactly that peer the other layout. Gating on the version fails too: patch releases inside one version disagree on whether they know the name (`v25.8.12.129-lts` does not, `v25.8.13.73-lts` backported it, both at version 0). Writing it always makes such a peer fail closed on the unknown name instead. The new gtest drives `serializeSettings` -> `writeChangedBinary` -> `readBinary` per step, asserting the round-tripped value and that the name reaches the wire, for both values and at version 0 as well as the current one. Reverting either production line fails that step's test. <details><summary>Why a gtest, and a sibling asymmetry deliberately not fixed here</summary> A gtest rather than a functional or integration test, because the divergence is silent: `EXPLAIN` does not surface the flag (`Aggregator::Params::explain` prints only keys and aggregates) and a single-node query never round-trips a plan, so no query output changes deterministically with the fix. The existing `tests/integration/test_string_aggregation_compatibility` does set the setting to `0` against a pinned older node, but never sets `serialize_query_plan`, which is why it misses this. The invariant is: every setting a step's `deserialize` reads must be written by that same step's `serializeSettings`. Because the settings object is per step, a write by one step cannot supply a read by another, so the sweep is per step rather than a global "is this name written anywhere?" check. It finds three asymmetries on master, not two: | step | read but not written by that step | |---|---| | `AggregatingStep` | `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` - fixed here | | `MergingAggregatedStep` | `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` - fixed here | | `ArrayJoinStep` | `enable_lazy_columns_replication` - not in this PR | `ArrayJoinStep::deserialize` reads `enable_lazy_columns_replication`, whose only writer is reached from `JoinStepLogical::serializeSettings` - a different step, hence a different settings object. It is another subsystem, its default direction is the opposite, and its effect is performance rather than correctness, so it needs a different justification, oracle and changelog category. Tracked separately. Also checked: of the steps holding an `Aggregator::Params`, only these two are serializable at all. `CubeStep`, `RollupStep` and `AggregatingProjectionStep` implement neither `serialize` nor `serializeSettings`, so there is no third carrier of this flag. </details> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1435` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix race between mutation registration and KILL TRANSACTION leaving an orphaned mutation
signal.text: ## Problem `KILL TRANSACTION` racing with `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`/`DELETE` executed inside a transaction can leave an orphaned mutation entry: registered in the table's mutation map, but its transaction is rolled back and gone, and its CSN will never be assigned. The consequences (reproduced deterministically with the failpoint added in this PR): - Debug/sanitizer builds: the server **aborts** — the `ALTER`'s `waitForMutation` hits `chassert(txn || mutation_entry.tid.isNonTransactional() || from_another_mutation)` in `getIncompleteMutationsStatusUnlocked`, and the background `selectPartsToMutate` independently raises a logical error `Cannot find transaction ... that has started mutation ... and mutation CSN is still unknown`. - Release builds: the `ALTER` hangs, the background job throws the logical error on every scheduling round, and the orphaned entry is never removed (`clearOldMutations` handles only finished mutations), blocking all subsequent mutations of the affected parts until a server restart. ## Root cause `prepareMutationEntry` calls `txn->addMutation` **before** `startMutation` registers the entry in `current_mutations_by_version`. A rollback in that window snapshots the transaction's mutation list (which already contains the new mutation) and calls `killMutation`, which finds nothing to remove because the entry is not registered yet. The registration then completes, creating the orphan. The window has existed since the ordering was introduced; it is merely a few instructions wide, which is why it is hit rarely in practice. ## Solution After `addPreparedMutationEntry`, re-check the transaction state **under the same critical section** as the registration. If the transaction was rolled back in the window, unregister the entry immediately, remove the mutation file (logged), and fail the query with `INVALID_TRANSACTION` — the same error the client would get if the `KILL` had landed a moment earlier. Both interleavings are covered: a rollback that starts after the critical section finds the registered entry and removes it via `killMutation` as usual; a rollback that started before is detected by the re-check (its CSN change precedes its `killMutation` call, so it is visible). Holding the lock across registration and re-check also keeps the transient state invisible to `selectPartsToMutate`, which reads the map under the same mutex. The metadata-`ALTER` path in `StorageMergeTree::alter` also registers a prepared mutation entry with a wider gap, but killing a rename mutation on rollback there would be incorrect (the durable metadata commit cannot be rolled back, and removing the rename mutation while keeping the new metadata reopens the #80648 data-loss scenario); metadata alters inside transactions have separate unresolved semantics and are out of scope here. A `PAUSEABLE` failpoint `mt_pause_before_register_mutation` and a stateless test reproduce the race deterministically: without the fix, the test aborts a debug server; with the fix, the `ALTER` fails with `INVALID_TRANSACTION`, no mutation entry or file is left behind, and subsequent mutations proceed. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110202 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83252 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a race between `KILL TRANSACTION` and `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE/DELETE` executed inside a transaction: a rollback landing between the mutation's registration in the transaction and its registration in the table left an orphaned mutation entry, which raised a logical error (`Cannot find transaction ... that has started mutation ...`) in background jobs and blocked all subsequent mutations of the affected parts until server restart. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Do not abort server startup when a database's named collection is missing
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110529 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the server refusing to start when a database created with `S3`, `Remote`, `RemoteSecure`, `MySQL` or `PostgreSQL` referenced a named collection that no longer exists. Such a database is now skipped with a logged error and the server starts; recreating the collection and restarting brings the database back. ### Description A database whose engine arguments name a missing named collection stops the whole server from starting: `Caught exception while loading metadata: Code: 669 ... There is no named collection 'nc_cfg': while loading database 'db_cfg'`, then `shutting down`. Retiring a `config.d/*.xml` collection and restarting reaches this. Recovery meant moving `metadata/<db>.sql` aside by hand, since the collection cannot be recreated with the server down. A **table** in the same state does not: the server boots and only that table's load job fails, so an admin recovers with a plain `CREATE NAMED COLLECTION`. That asymmetry is the bug. `loadDatabase` runs with `create = true`, so `setForceAttach` is never called and databases derive `ATTACH` rather than the `FORCE_ATTACH` that gives tables their tolerance. The two startup loops in `loadMetadata` now skip such a database instead of aborting, under four conditions that must all hold: the process is `clickhouse-server`, the error is exactly `NAMED_COLLECTION_DOESNT_EXIST`, the database is not the configured default, and its engine is in an audited list of engines owning no local table metadata (`S3`, `Remote`, `RemoteSecure`, `MySQL`, `PostgreSQL`). Everything else is unchanged: other error codes still stop startup, `Replicated` and `MaterializedPostgreSQL` still do because they own local tables, `clickhouse-local` still fails, and `ATTACH DATABASE` still fails loudly. The metadata file is untouched, so recreating the collection and restarting restores the database. The *default* database is excluded because `assertDatabaseExists(default_database)` runs right after. Validated both directions on identical on-disk state: the pre-fix binary exits 157, the fixed one starts and logs the skip. `test_named_collections` passes 29/29 with 13 new cases, plus a `clickhouse-local` stateless test. Each of the four conditions has its own test that fails on a build with that one condition removed, so none is vacuous. The related PR fixes this class for URL **tables**, not databases.

signal.title: Idempotency key for DDL operations
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Use case Retries after network connection errors are really complex in distributed systems. There are many operations that are quite risky to be retried such as `EXCHANGE TABLE` and we do not have easy way to check that previous operation succeeded or not for example, when disconnect was result of completely disappearing node and we have query log local to this node. ### Describe the solution you'd like - Add optional query setting `idempotency_key` that can be passed from a client with a query similar to `insert_deduplication_token`. - When it is passed operations that change state(or go through keeper) will commit the `idempotency_key` to a special node in keeper. - idempotency_key work the same way as insert_deduplication_token - it will be cleaned up with the similar window logic. - Client libraries can set this key automatically and retry on network error preserving `idempotency_key`. It will make most retries completely safe. - Server will check if key exists before running query and also include it during operation commit to keeper. This way you can also cancel one of 2 parallel EXCHANGE TABELS so only one will succeed. ### Describe alternatives you've considered Other option is to pass some key similar to query_if from a client and on error check that this query was not running before. Saving this information somehow to keeper with operations that change metadata in keeper will allow to later check if we had one already finished. But we do not have guarantee that there is none inflight with unreachable node, that is still connected to keeper. So it will add more complexity if we can not store a tombstone saying this operation should not succeed after you checked. ### Additional context Language clients suffer a lot of disconnects as sometimes there is a race for connections to be not closed for up to 5 minutes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92046 They can't easily detect if this case was there i.e. no bytes were sent from client and just ordinary disconnect when network is bad.

signal.title: Never cancel a query before its `max_execution_time` has elapsed
signal.text: `CancellationChecker::appendTask` derived a query's cancellation deadline from the current time truncated to whole milliseconds, and then aligned it up to the 100 ms grid the worker batches deadlines on. The alignment normally hides the truncation, but when the deadline already sits on the grid - one query in a hundred - it adds no padding, and the deadline lands up to 1 ms before `now + max_execution_time`. The query is then cancelled ahead of its own timeout and fails with a self-contradictory message: ``` Code: 159. DB::Exception: Timeout exceeded: elapsed 999.672 ms, maximum: 1000 ms. (TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED) ``` The current time is now rounded up to a whole millisecond instead, which is the direction the code around it already promises: *"Tasks may be cancelled slightly later than their exact timeout, but never before"*. Only the `throw` overflow mode was affected: in `break` mode the checker re-reads the elapsed time before acting on the deadline, so an early wake-up does nothing. This is what makes `02122_join_group_by_timeout` flaky - it asserts that a `max_execution_time = 1` cancellation takes at least 1000 ms, and `query_duration_ms` is measured from a stopwatch that starts before the deadline is computed. The failure shows up as `query_duration 1` becoming `query_duration 0`, always on one of the two `throw`-mode queries and never on the `break`-mode ones. In the server logs of both `Fast test` runs below, the query was cancelled early - at 999.672 ms and at 999.630 ms of its 1000 ms timeout. The deadline computation moved into `CancellationChecker::taskDeadlineMs` so that the invariant can be tested directly: the new unit test checks every sub-millisecond phase of `now` against every phase of the grid, for a range of timeouts, and fails with the old truncation. CI reports of the flaky test: - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=gh-readonly-queue/master/pr-113021-93e2851fddb5add7bad5b28bcef780be2f6ff7bb&sha=bef88e3d96ecb0f57a0f8d81f6b7ee2117db19fd&name_0=MergeQueueCI&name_1=Fast%20test - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=gh-readonly-queue/master/pr-110451-2f02abe52a79c02fb554728f14d8fa847dcbc1e6&sha=2eba84a8a12a21c36516158d4fbe9530d3f0af8c&name_0=MergeQueueCI&name_1=Fast%20test The truncation is as old as the checker itself. Before deadlines were aligned to a grid in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/95563 the deadline was plainly `floor(now) + timeout`, i.e. early for every query rather than for one in a hundred; and the assertion that catches it was only sharpened from `round(query_duration_ms / 1000) BETWEEN 1 AND 60` to `query_duration_ms BETWEEN 1000 AND 60000` in daf1b4980b1, which is why the flake is recent. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A query could be cancelled up to 1 ms before its `max_execution_time` had passed, failing with a self-contradictory `Timeout exceeded: elapsed 999.672 ms, maximum: 1000 ms`.

signal.title: Push join key filters into MergeTree index during recursive CTE evaluation
signal.text: When a recursive CTE joins against a `MergeTree` table, each recursion step previously scanned the entire table, because the join condition (e.g. `ON e.from_id = t.current_id`) was not pushed into `MergeTree`'s key condition. This change analyzes the recursive query's join tree to find equi-join conditions between the CTE working table and real tables. Before each step it reads the join-key values from the working table and injects them as an `IN (...)` predicate directly into the `WHERE` clause of each recursive `QueryNode` that joins against the CTE (the original `WHERE`/`HAVING`/`QUALIFY` clauses are snapshotted at construction and restored after each step, so nothing accumulates across steps). The planner then lowers this predicate into `ReadFromMergeTree`'s key condition. The injected set is bounded by the new setting `recursive_cte_max_in_filter_cardinality`, and injection fails closed to a plain scan whenever it could otherwise change results — when the generated set would exceed `max_rows_in_set`/`max_bytes_in_set`, cannot be materialized under `max_memory_usage`, or the `IN` predicate cannot be resolved for the join-key type. Parallel replicas are disabled for the recursive step queries to avoid stale cached `GLOBAL JOIN` tables returning incorrect results; the forcing mode `allow_experimental_parallel_reading_from_replicas = 2` raises `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` for the recursive part rather than silently downgrading. For a table with ~1M rows and 10 recursion steps, `read_rows` drops from ~10M to ~120. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75026 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `WITH RECURSIVE` queries that use `ON` or comma equi-joins against `MergeTree` tables can now use the primary key index, reducing the number of rows read per recursion step. The optimization is controlled by the new setting `recursive_cte_max_in_filter_cardinality`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) No separate documentation page is needed — this is a transparent performance improvement. The only user-visible addition is the setting `recursive_cte_max_in_filter_cardinality`, which is documented at the source level in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches recursive CTE execution and query settings, and dynamically injects `additional_table_filters`, which could affect correctness/performance for some JOIN patterns despite being scoped to recursive steps. > > **Overview** > Improves recursive CTE performance by detecting equi-join conditions between the CTE working table and real tables, then **pushing join-key values into `additional_table_filters`** (built as `IN (...)` predicates) on each recursive step so MergeTree reads can use the primary-key index; user-provided `additional_table_filters` are merged rather than overwritten. > > Also **disables parallel replicas** for recursive CTE step queries to avoid incorrect results from reused cached GLOBAL JOIN tables, and adds a stateless test (`03924_recursive_cte_join_index`) asserting both correct output and low `read_rows` for explicit `INNER JOIN` and comma-join forms. > > <sup>Written by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/dashboard?tab=bugbot) for commit 37f26180bfa2189247b6862712551c7ecc41ed18. This will update automatically on new commits. Configure [here](https://cursor.com/dashboard?tab=bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/label/<name>/values
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus-compatible clients** use **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`** to discover the values available for a label. This is used by **Grafana dashboards**, variable pickers, and integrations that need to populate label-value selectors. Prometheus also supports **escaped UTF-8 label names**. The endpoint must decode those names correctly while preserving malformed or intentionally literal values in a predictable way. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/label/<name>/values` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint returns a **sorted, distinct list of values** for one label. It supports metric names through **`__name__`**, labels from the **`tags` Map**, dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, series selectors, time ranges, and result limits. Supported parameters: - **`<name>`** identifies the label whose values should be returned, including Prometheus **`U__...` escaped names**. - **`match[]`** filters the series contributing values. - **`start` and `end`** restrict the matching series by their **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the returned values and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Value discovery:** return distinct values for ordinary labels and the special **`__name__`** metric-name label. - **Storage compatibility:** read values from the **`tags` Map** and dedicated **`tags_to_columns`** columns using the same logical label semantics as the other metadata endpoints. - **Name decoding:** decode valid Prometheus escaped label names, preserve malformed or overlong escape sequences as literal names, and reject an empty decoded label name. - **Selector support:** filter values by metric and series selectors, including unknown-label and no-match cases. - **Time ranges:** apply trusted min/max bounds when available and keep ranged requests valid with the **approximate superset** behavior allowed by Prometheus when bounds are unavailable. - **Result limits:** support empty, zero, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values, including the Prometheus truncation warning. - **HTTP handling:** add the label-values route to the **combined `/api/v1` handler** and keep endpoint parameters separate from ClickHouse settings. - **Access control:** enforce the configured **`TimeSeries` table authorization boundary** before reading the underlying target tables. - **Query lifecycle:** execute through the **normal query pipeline**, preserve query completion handling, and record the request in **`query_log`**. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Metric names:** values returned through **`__name__`**. - **Label values:** distinct Map values and values from configured dedicated columns. - **Escaped names:** valid UTF-8 decoding, malformed escape sequences, overlong escapes, and empty decoded names. - **Filtering:** selectors, unknown labels, and requests with no matching series. - **Time ranges:** matching and non-matching intervals, including empty optional parameters. - **Limits:** truncation warnings and the maximum valid **UInt64** limit. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants** on the configured `TimeSeries` table. - **HTTP integration:** the main HTTP port, routing, and query completion records. Also ran **Python syntax checks**, **XML parsing**, and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now describes the label-values handler, escaped label names, and its supported parameters. ### Stack This PR is **stacked on #114867** and includes the **`/api/v1/series`** changes. After **#114867** merges, this branch can be rebased onto `master`.

signal.title: Perf: Bulk copy selected runs in ColumnVector filtering
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Coalesce contiguous selected rows in the generic ColumnVector filter fallback. ### What does this PR do? - Adds **contiguous-run copying** to the generic mixed-mask fallback. - Keeps isolated rows on `insertSingle`. - Leaves the existing prefix, suffix, and AVX-512 paths unchanged. - Covers both out-of-place and in-place filtering through the shared inserter. - Adds correctness coverage for clustered, dense-hole, empty, full, and boundary masks. - Adds a benchmark for clustered, random, alternating, and dense-with-hole masks. ### Why? - **Current path:** copies every selected value separately for a mixed 64-row mask. - **Dense masks:** adjacent selected rows still take the per-value path. - **New path:** finds adjacent selected rows and copies each range at once. - **Fragmented masks:** keep the existing `insertSingle` behavior. - **Result:** selected values and row order stay unchanged. ### How is it faster? - **Dense 64-row mask:** 63 selected values with one hole become two contiguous ranges. - **Out-of-place path:** 63 `insertSingle` calls become two `insertRange` calls. - **In-place path:** 63 single-value moves become two range `memmove` calls. - **Longer runs:** reduce per-value inserter and loop overhead while copying more data per call. - **Single rows:** the adjacent-bit check keeps isolated selections on the existing cheap path. ### Performance - **Clustered masks:** fewer inserter calls for each selected run. - **Dense masks with one hole:** large ranges are copied around the hole instead of value by value. - **Random and alternating masks:** provide regression-control cases with few useful runs. ### Benchmark - **Fixture:** `benchmark_column_filter`. - **Patterns:** clustered, random, alternating, and dense-with-hole. - **Column:** generic `ColumnUInt128` path. - **Rows:** 1,048,576. - **Status:** Fixture added; results pending.

signal.title: Schedule text-index virtual columns first in the PREWHERE cost model
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110695 The `cost_with_selectivity` score from #110695 orders PREWHERE conditions by bytes-per-rejected-row, but conditions with `columns_size == 0` fall back to a score of `estimated_row_count` — a plain row count. The two units are not comparable. `__text_index_*` virtual columns are not physical columns, so they always score through the fallback (millions) and lose to any byte-based score of a physical predicate (hundreds). The expensive raw predicate then runs first, on all rows, reading the whole `text` column; the near-free index check runs last, where it filters nothing. Our internal full-text-search benchmark (59M rows of StackOverflow data, multi-KB `text` column with a `text` index) caught this the day after #110695 merged, on 14 query shapes: an equality residual (`hasToken(...) AND text = concat(...)`) went from 89 ms to 3.45 s on every execution (~39x), `match` residuals slowed 2–2.4x, `multiMatchAny`/`multiSearchAny` by 30–40%. The fix is deliberately narrow. Conditions that read only text-index virtual columns get cost 0: their posting lists are read for granule pruning anyway, so their marginal evaluation cost is a bitmap lookup per row, with no column I/O. Every other zero-size case (compact parts, table virtual columns like `_part`, columns not yet materialized after `ALTER`, subcolumns without size info) keeps the existing pessimistic selectivity fallback, because their evaluation cost is unknown and they must not be scheduled first. Standalone reproduction (wide part required — on compact parts all sizes are 0, every condition ties, and the bug hides): ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, v UInt64, text String, INDEX idx_text text TYPE text(tokenizer = 'splitByNonAlpha')) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, min_rows_for_wide_part = 0; -- insert rows where the token filter is index-answerable and the residual is per-row -- then run with send_logs_level='test': SELECT count() FROM t WHERE hasToken(text, 'alpha') AND text = concat('x', toString(id)); ``` The `Condition ... moved to PREWHERE` log lines print in scheduling order. Before this fix: `equals(text, ...)` (columns_size 293748504, score ≈ 877) is scheduled before `__text_index_*` (columns_size 0, score = 165000). After: the virtual column comes first. Note `EXPLAIN` cannot show this — the printed argument order of the `AND` is the reverse of the evaluation order — hence the new test asserts on `read_bytes` instead: with the correct order the equality never reads `text`, because the token conditions reject every row first. After the fix, the internal benchmark returned to its pre-#110695 numbers (0 regressions), and one query improved 11.6x beyond its old baseline (a per-row `LIKE concat(...)` residual that had been misordered by an earlier heuristic as well). cc @avogar ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: Perf: Coalesce contiguous runs in ColumnFixedString filtering
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Bulk copy contiguous selected runs while filtering FixedString columns. ### What does this PR do? - Adds **contiguous-run copying** to the mixed-mask path in `ColumnFixedString::filter`. - Keeps the existing fast path for fully selected 64-row blocks. - Uses one resize and one bulk copy for each selected run in the out-of-place path. - Uses one `memmove` for each selected run in the in-place path. - Keeps isolated rows on the existing small-copy path. - Adds correctness coverage for clustered, dense-hole, empty, full, and boundary masks. - Adds out-of-place and in-place benchmark cases. ### Why? - **Current path:** copies every selected fixed string separately for a mixed 64-row mask. - **Dense masks:** one missing row can turn a large contiguous range into dozens of small copies. - **New path:** finds adjacent selected rows and copies each range at once. - **Fragmented masks:** keep the existing small-copy behavior. - **Result:** selected values and row order stay unchanged. ### How is it faster? - **Dense 64-row mask:** 63 selected rows with one hole become two contiguous ranges. - **Out-of-place path:** 63 row-sized resizes and small copies become two resizes and two bulk copies. - **In-place path:** 63 row-sized `memmove` calls become two range `memmove` calls. - **Longer runs:** amortize loop and copy overhead over more FixedString bytes. - **Random and alternating masks:** isolated rows stay on the existing path, so the optimization is focused on masks with useful runs. ### Performance - **Clustered masks:** fewer copy calls and fewer result-size updates. - **Dense masks with one hole:** large ranges are copied around the hole instead of row by row. - **Random and alternating masks:** provide regression-control cases with few useful runs. ### Benchmark - **Fixture:** `benchmark_column_fixed_string_filter`. - **Patterns:** clustered, random, alternating, and dense-with-hole. - **Paths:** out-of-place and in-place filtering. - **Column:** `FixedString(16)`. - **Rows:** 1,048,576. - **Status:** Fixture added; results pending.

signal.title: Fix `rows_before_limit_at_least` under parallel replicas local plan (#113279)
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113279 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `rows_before_limit_at_least` returning 0 when querying with LIMIT under parallel replicas local plan (`parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1`). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is not required for this bug fix --- ### Detailed Description #### Problem With parallel replicas enabled (`parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1`), queries with a `LIMIT` incorrectly returned `rows_before_limit_at_least = 0` even when `exact_rows_before_limit = 1`. #### Root Cause In `createLocalPlanForParallelReplicas` (`src/Processors/QueryPlan/ParallelReplicasLocalPlan.cpp`), `select_query_options.is_local_shard_plan` was previously only initialized to true when `processed_stage == QueryProcessingStage::WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`. For queries planned at `QueryProcessingStage::WithMergeableState`, `is_local_shard_plan` evaluated to false. Consequently, `addPreliminaryLimitStep` in `src/Planner/Planner.cpp` did not invoke `limit->markAsShardLimit()`, causing `initRowsBeforeLimit` in `src/QueryPipeline/QueryPipeline.cpp` to treat the preliminary limit as a top-level query accounting boundary and terminate processor traversal without attaching the rows-before-limit counter to the local input stream. #### Solution Set `select_query_options.is_local_shard_plan` to true for both `QueryProcessingStage::WithMergeableState` and `QueryProcessingStage::WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`. This marks the preliminary limit on the local replica branch as a shard limit, enabling `initRowsBeforeLimit` to traverse through it and attach the statistics counter to the local input stream matching remote replica behavior. #### Test Plan - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/02590_parallel_replicas_local_plan_rows_before_limit.sh` and reference test asserting correct `rows_before_limit_at_least` row count under `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1`.

signal.title: Mask the Azure shared access signature carried in a url argument
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114946 A storage account url is a documented, working way to authenticate: when the url contains a `?`, `processURL` (`src/Disks/DiskObjectStorage/ObjectStorages/AzureBlobStorage/AzureBlobStorageCommon.cpp`) takes everything after it as `sas_auth`, and `tests/integration/test_storage_azure_blob_storage/test.py::test_sas_token` exercises exactly that form. `maskAzureConnectionString` (`src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.cpp`) skips any argument starting with `http`, so the token stayed verbatim in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, in `system.tables.engine_full` and in `system.query_log.query` at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0`. The same credential spelled as a connection string (`...;SharedAccessSignature=...`) was hidden, and the positional `account_key` was hidden, so the url spelling was the one gap. A shared access signature is a bearer credential: whoever holds it gets the access it was issued for until it expires. This masks the `sig` parameter, the HMAC over the signed fields and the only part of the token that cannot be guessed. The remaining parameters (`sv`, `sp`, `se`, `sr`, ...) grant nothing without it and stay visible, which keeps the url diagnosable, the same way `maskPresignedURLParameters` keeps a presigned S3 url readable. The new `maskAzureSASSignature` sits next to it in `src/Common/maskURIPassword.h` and is written the same way. The url argument is replaced in place (`result.replaced_arguments`) rather than hidden whole, and the function keeps returning `false`, so a positional `account_key` in the same call is still masked by the caller. That is the mechanism the S3 url masking already uses, and it composes with the other masking. All the call sites of `maskAzureConnectionString` are covered by the one change: the `AzureBlobStorage` and `AzureQueue` engines, and the `azureBlobStorage` table function with its `*Cluster` and named collection forms. If masking the whole query string is preferred over masking only `sig`, that is a one line change here; I went with the narrower one because the other parameters are not secret and are useful in a log. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04909_azure_sas_url_secret_mask.sql` covers the engine through `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and `system.tables.engine_full`, and the table function and its cluster variant through `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE run_passes = 0`, which leaves them unresolved so nothing is read. A url with no signature in it is asserted to be left alone. The `CREATE` needs no reachable endpoint: with a shared access signature the engine skips the container probe. Against the official master build `26.8.1.1463` every one of those surfaces prints the signature verbatim; the committed reference is the same output with `sig=[HIDDEN]`. I also compiled `maskAzureSASSignature` standalone and checked it over multiple occurrences, a fragment, an empty value, a missing `=`, and the near-miss names `signature`, `xsig` and `SIG`. I have not built this branch, so the compile and the test run are left to CI. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): When an Azure shared access signature is passed inside the url of the `AzureBlobStorage` engine or the `azureBlobStorage` table function, its `sig` value is now hidden in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, `system.tables.engine_full` and `system.query_log`. Previously the whole token was stored and displayed in plain text, even though the equivalent connection string spelling was already hidden. The rest of the signature stays visible so the url is still readable in a log.

signal.title: Fix ReadBuffer-canceled abort in GraceHashJoin spilled-block reader
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you do not need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR: ReadBuffer is canceled. Can't read from it.` that could occur in a `grace_hash` join when reading spilled blocks failed mid-read while multiple threads shared the reader. ### Description `GraceHashJoin` shares one `AccumulatedBlockReader` between concurrent `DelayedJoinedBlocksWorkerTransform` threads. If `reader->read` throws while reading a spilled block, `ReadBuffer::next` cancels the underlying buffer and rethrows. Previously the shared reader was not marked finished, so a sibling worker could re-enter `read` on the canceled buffer and throw `LOGICAL_ERROR: ReadBuffer is canceled. Can't read from it.` The query should instead preserve and report the original read exception. The fix marks `AccumulatedBlockReader` finished on every read exception while holding its existing mutex. Subsequent workers return an empty block and cannot re-read the canceled buffer. This covers both the left delayed reader and the right reader that use the same `read` implementation. The new stateless regression deterministically forces a failure only in the shared left delayed reader: it cancels the underlying buffer, throws `FAULT_INJECTED`, verifies the query reports that original exception, and then verifies that the server remains alive. Without the `eof` assignment, a sibling worker re-enters the canceled buffer and triggers the original logical exception.

signal.title: Add experimental PCO compression codec (linking the pcodec Rust crate)
signal.text: Adds an experimental `PCO` compression codec that links the [pcodec](https://github.com/pcodec/pcodec) (`pco`) Rust crate — the reference implementation — rather than reimplementing it. `pco` is a lossless codec specialized for sequences of fixed-width numbers; on numeric columns with smooth, multimodal, or high-entropy distributions (measurements, timings, counters, identifiers) it often beats `Gorilla`/`FPC`/`ZSTD`/`ALP` on ratio. This is the Rust-library counterpart to the native C++ port explored in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106222. Instead of maintaining a C++ reimplementation, it links the upstream crate. ### Runtime CPU dispatch `pco` has no explicit SIMD: it relies on the compiler autovectorizing its per-batch loops, which only happens when the crate is compiled with the relevant instruction sets enabled (its `build.rs` warns to build with `-C target-feature=+avx2,+bmi1,+bmi2`). That does not work for ClickHouse, which compiles all Rust once at a fixed baseline micro-architecture level for a binary that must run on a range of CPUs. So `pco` is taken from a ClickHouse fork patched to add runtime CPU-feature dispatch of its hot loops — the same mechanism ClickHouse's C++ uses via `TargetSpecific.h`. The vectorizable loop bodies (decode `read_offsets`; encode `write_short_uints`/`write_uints`/`set_offsets`) are compiled at the crate baseline and again for `x86-64-v3` (AVX2 + BMI1/2 + FMA) and `x86-64-v4` (AVX-512), and the widest variant the running CPU supports is selected once and cached. On aarch64 the baseline already includes NEON, so the baseline body is used directly. Verified at baseline `-C target-cpu=x86-64`: the `read_offsets` v3 trampoline emits AVX2 (`ymm`) and v4 emits AVX-512 (`zmm`). The patch is merged into `ClickHouse/pcodec` (a fork of pcodec/pcodec in the ClickHouse organization) via its own PR: https://github.com/ClickHouse/pcodec/pull/1. The crate is added as the `contrib/pcodec` submodule and linked through a thin FFI wrapper crate (`rust/workspace/pco`). Its one not-yet-vendored dependency, `rand_xoshiro`, was added to `contrib/rust_vendor` in https://github.com/ClickHouse/rust_vendor/pull/72. ### Codec Supported types are all fixed-width numerics of 1/2/4/8 bytes via their underlying integer/float representation: `Int8`..`Int64`, `UInt8`..`UInt64`, `Float32`/`Float64`, and the types backed by them (`Date`, `DateTime`, `Decimal32`/`Decimal64`, `IPv4`, `Enum`, ...). The on-disk block stores a 2-byte header (element width + partial-tail byte count) followed by a raw partial-value tail (as in `Gorilla`/`FPC`) and the payload. The payload is a standalone `.pco` stream, wire-compatible with the reference pcodec implementation; when compression would not shrink a block the raw bytes are stored instead (a per-block "stored" flag), so the output never expands by more than the 2-byte header and `getMaxCompressedDataSize` is tight. The codec is gated behind `allow_experimental_codecs`. Because it needs the column type, it can only be specified per column: it is rejected in `TTL ... RECOMPRESS` and in the untyped compression settings that resolve codecs without a type. `CompressionCodecMultiple` propagates the experimental / column-type-requiring properties so a chain such as `CODEC(Delta, PCO)` is still gated, and a codec-only `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN x CODEC(PCO)` validates against the existing column type. Tests: `04512_pco_codec` round-trips every supported numeric and backed type (per-element verification, edge cases, codec chaining, compression-ratio check) and `04513_pco_codec_gating` covers the experimental gate, the `TTL RECOMPRESS` rejection, and the codec-only `ALTER`. The FFI wrapper has its own Rust unit tests (round-trip of all types, the no-expansion fallback, and fail-closed handling of malformed/mismatched streams). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new experimental compression codec `PCO`, which links the [pcodec](https://github.com/pcodec/pcodec) library (patched for runtime CPU dispatch), specialized for fixed-width numeric columns. It is wire-format compatible with pcodec `.pco` streams and is enabled with `allow_experimental_codecs`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes: - [x] Documentation is written (the `PCO` codec is documented in `docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/table.md`, and the compression-frame method byte in `docs/en/interfaces/specs/NativeFormat.md`).

signal.title: Support per-authentication-method GRANTS clause in CREATE USER and ALTER USER
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109117 Implements per-authentication-method grant limits, the first part of the linked issue: ```sql ALTER USER vasya ADD IDENTIFIED WITH password BY 'WYmdFyas8PftrHbHQQo8' VALID UNTIL '2026-12-31' GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table) ``` When a user logs in with such a method, the access rights of the session are the intersection of the user's access rights (including granted roles) with the listed elements. The clause never adds rights: a listed privilege that is not granted to the user stays unavailable. This provides a way to create tokens for applications: an additional credential with an expiration date and a limited set of grants, which is tied to the user — it is displayed in `query_log` and `processlist` as the user, stops working if the user is deleted, and is narrowed when the user loses grants. Details: - The clause is parsed after the per-method `VALID UNTIL`, works with `CREATE USER`, `ALTER USER [ADD] IDENTIFIED`, and `NOT IDENTIFIED`, is shown by `SHOW CREATE USER`, and persists through the SQL serialization of access entities (and therefore backups). Elements without a database name are bound to the current database when the query is interpreted. - The intersection erases all grant options (the clause cannot express them), so such sessions cannot `GRANT` anything. Role administration is denied entirely (fail-close), including per-role admin option. `EXECUTE AS`, `ALTER USER`, `CREATE USER` and similar escapes require the corresponding rights to be listed explicitly and granted to the user. - Reattaching to a named session (`session_id`) with a different credential re-applies the limit of the credential used by the new connection, so a limited credential cannot pick up the full rights of a session created by an unrestricted one. - The limit is captured at login: `ALTER USER` affects new sessions, not established ones (same as `VALID UNTIL`). - A new `auth_grants` column in `system.users` exposes the limit of each authentication method. - `ContextData`'s copy constructor now preserves `external_roles` and the new field: previously a recalculation of access rights on a copied context silently dropped external roles; for the new field that would mean silently widening the rights. - `EXECUTE AS <user> <statement>` now keeps the current database of the caller's session. `Context::setUser` sets the current database from the target user's `DEFAULT DATABASE`, so the wrapped statement used to be re-scoped and an unqualified table name resolved in a different database; the session form (`EXECUTE AS <user>` without a statement) already preserved it. Test `04907_execute_as_preserves_current_database` covers both forms. Known limitations (consistent with `VALID UNTIL` and external roles): the limit is not propagated to other nodes of a cluster in distributed queries or `ON CLUSTER` DDL (the query is checked on the initiator), and the clause is not available in `users.xml`. The `CREATE TOKEN` syntactic sugar and the separate grant for self-service `ADD IDENTIFIED` mentioned in the issue are left for a follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Authentication methods in `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER ... ADD IDENTIFIED` support a `GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table, ...)` clause which limits the access rights of sessions authenticated with that method to the intersection with the listed grants. This allows using additional credentials as tokens for applications: `ALTER USER vasya ADD IDENTIFIED WITH password BY '...' VALID UNTIL '2026-12-31' GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table)`. Closes [#109117](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109117). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Convert the JOIN keys to the type of the values that they have in common
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/21794 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/21794 There is no type that is able to hold all the values of both `UInt64` and `Int64`, so a JOIN on such keys was rejected: ``` SELECT * FROM (SELECT number FROM numbers(10)) AS a INNER JOIN (SELECT number FROM numbers(10)) AS b ON a.number = b.number - 1 Code: 386. DB::Exception: There is no supertype for types UInt64, Int64 ... ``` But a JOIN does not need the least supertype. It is enough to convert both keys to the type of the values that they have in common - the most subtype, which is `UInt64` for this pair, holding the values from `0` to `9223372036854775807`. A value outside of this range is not equal to any value from the other side, so `accurateCastOrNull` converts it to NULL, and it does not match anything. This is applied to the equality conditions in the `ON` section, and to the `USING` section of an `INNER JOIN` or a `SEMI JOIN`, where the result contains only the matched values. It is not applied to: - the kinds of JOIN with `USING` that can emit unmatched rows (`LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL`, `ANTI`), where the key is also a column of the result and can hold the unmatched values; - null-safe comparisons (`IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`), where NULL matches NULL, so the values converted to NULL would match each other; - the ASOF inequality (the last column in the `USING` list), which needs the order of the values, not only their equality; - a `Join` table engine whose stored key is not itself the common type, because its hash table is prebuilt over the original key values and cannot be converted - the opposite direction, where only the probe key has to be converted, is supported. A runtime filter is not built for such a JOIN, because a `NOT IN` filter over a set with NULLs would drop the rows that have to be preserved. Only the queries that were failing before are affected - the type inference is unchanged whenever the least supertype exists. It is implemented in the analyzer, which is enabled by default; with `enable_analyzer = 0` the old `TableJoin::inferJoinKeyCommonType` path still rejects such a JOIN, exactly as before. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow a JOIN on keys that have no common supertype, such as `UInt64` and `Int64`. Previously such a query was rejected with `There is no supertype for types UInt64, Int64`. Now the keys are converted to the type of the values that they have in common, and a value outside of this range does not match anything. This requires the analyzer (`enable_analyzer = 1`, the default).

signal.title: Add PCAP input format for reading packet captures
signal.text: # Add PCAP input format for reading packet captures ## (Human) Introduction As someone who works with ClickHouse but also occasionally opens a pcap in Wireshark, I've always had a wish to be able to do some quick stats on a pcap using ClickHouse SQL. Especially for large files, I always thought it would also be nice to be able to persist them in a MergeTree, so they don't have to be re-scanned every time. So this is my first draft at making this a reality: adding PCAP as an (experimental) input format which can be read by Clickhouse directly (and consequently be ingested, as well). It currently only parses very basic stuff (mostly L2-L4), but this could be extended in the future (imagine having all Wireshark dissectors 😍 ) I realize this may be considered "unfinished" (in the sense: lacking features), but I wanted to open a PR and get feedback on the idea early on, to see if it was worth pursuing. Full transparency: this is basically 100% vibe-coded -- ideas and some design decisions are mine, but I didn't really write any code. Thanks Claude. In that spirit, here's the Claude-generated description including some notes that may be relevant to reviewers: ## AI-generated Overview Adds a `PCAP` input format that reads packet capture files (classic `pcap` and `pcapng`) and produces one row per packet with decoded L2–L4 fields — timestamp, lengths, link type, the ordered protocol chain, Ethernet/IPv4/IPv6/TCP/UDP header fields, the L4 payload, and the raw frame. Modelled structurally on the `DWARF` format. Parsing uses `libtins` for dissection and `libpcap` for reading the capture container, added as contrib submodules behind a new `USE_PCAP` flag (`libpcap` built offline-only with pre-generated BPF grammar/scanner; WPA2/ACK-tracking disabled to avoid OpenSSL and Boost.ICL). Includes documentation and a stateless test with small Wireshark sample captures. > Transparency note: this PR was vibe-coded with Claude (Anthropic `claude-opus-4-8`) in an agentic workflow, with human review and direction. The AI co-authorship is recorded via `Co-authored-by` trailers on the commits. ### Notes for reviewers - **New contrib submodules:** `libtins` (v4.5) and `libpcap` (1.10.5), gated behind `ENABLE_PCAP`/`USE_PCAP` (on by default with `ENABLE_LIBRARIES`). They use the upstream repositories directly (not ClickHouse forks). - **libpcap build:** built offline-only using the `null` capture backend (no live capture / remote / optional backends). Its BPF grammar/scanner are pre-generated with bison/flex and checked in under `contrib/libpcap-cmake/generated/` so the build needs no flex/bison. A hand-written `config.h` targets Linux/glibc. - **libtins build:** hand-written `config.h`; WPA2 decryption and ACK tracking are disabled to avoid pulling in OpenSSL and Boost.ICL for now. Deeper protocol dissection can be layered on later. - **Disabled-build safety:** the format is wrapped in `#if USE_PCAP` with empty registration stubs, so linking succeeds when the feature is off (e.g. fasttest builds with `ENABLE_LIBRARIES=0`). The stateless test is tagged `no-fasttest` for the same reason. - **Test fixtures license:** the capture files under `tests/queries/0_stateless/data_pcap/` are sample captures from the Wireshark test suite (GPL-2.0); provenance is recorded in that directory's `README.md`. Happy to swap them for self-authored synthetic captures if the GPL-2.0 provenance is a concern. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New input format `PCAP` for reading network packet captures (`pcap` and `pcapng`), producing one row per packet with decoded Ethernet/IP/TCP/UDP fields, the protocol chain, payload, and raw frame.

signal.title: Reimplement the KQL (Kusto) dialect on a lexer, an AST and AST translation
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/61742 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reimplemented the experimental KQL (Kusto) dialect. It now has its own lexer and parser and builds an AST directly, instead of translating a token stream into SQL text and reparsing it. This fixes an expression-injection hole in the string operators (`contains`, `has`, ...), several results that silently disagreed with Kusto (`7 / 2`, `substring` with a negative start, `bin`), and 28 functions that were registered but did nothing. The supported subset is smaller and documented; anything outside it is now rejected by name instead of being mistranslated. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes `docs/guides/clickhouse/kusto-query-language.mdx` --- ## Why The dialect was contributed in 2022 and abandoned by its authors; the rewrite they promised in #62668 was closed unmerged. Since then it has been emergency-disabled once (#59305) and gated behind `allow_experimental_kusto_dialect` (#74224), and #61742 ("Remove KQL support if this code will not be fixed") has stayed open. The implementation translated a KQL token stream directly into ClickHouse SQL **text** and reparsed it — 298 `fmt::format` sites, 41 places that re-lexed generated text, and no AST anywhere in the function layer. Everything below follows from that: | | before | after | |---|---|---| | `T \| where s contains "x') OR 1 = 1 OR ilike(s, 'y"` | injected the expression | needle is an `ASTLiteral`; no injection is representable | | `'50x' contains '50%'` | `true` — needle was pasted into a LIKE pattern | `false` | | `substring('abcdefg', -3, 2)` | `'ab'` | `'ef'` | | `7 / 2` | `3.5` | `3` | | `format_timespan(col, 'hh:mm')` | `stoi: no conversion` — `std::stoi` on generated SQL | rejected by name | | `series_fir(...)` | `Function series_fir does not exist` (one of 28 stubs) | rejected by name | | `search 'x'` | `Unknown table expression identifier 'search'` | `'search' is not a supported KQL operator` | | `let` bindings | `static thread_local`, leaked between queries | scoped to one parse | ## What is here Two commits: the removal, then the reimplementation. ``` src/Parsers/Kusto/ KQLLexer KQL's own tokens: !in, =~, .., timespans (2.5h), verbatim @'...', datetime(...). A bad literal is an Error token carrying a reason, so nothing downstream asks isValidKQLPos() — the core of #61742. KQLAST the tabular level only. Scalar expressions are ClickHouse AST directly; a parallel expression hierarchy would add only conversions. KQLParser recursive descent. `let` bindings are an ordinary member. KQLTranslator each operator fills a still-empty clause of the select being built, or wraps what exists so far in a subquery and starts a new one. KQLFunctions name -> builder returning an ASTPtr. src/Functions/Kusto/ kqlDivide `7 / 2` is 3 in KQL and 3.5 in SQL — the choice depends on operand kqlBin types, so it is made by an IFunctionOverloadResolver during analysis rather than guessed from how the argument was spelled. ``` KQL now has its own entry point (`parseKQLQuery`) and never touches the SQL tokenizer. Because `ClientBase` already catches, the parser can simply throw — so there is no `tryParseKQLQuery`, and no `catch` anywhere in the new code. **`src/Parsers/Kusto` no longer needs its carve-out from check 19** ("do not catch exceptions in src/Parsers"), and this PR deletes it. `src/Parsers/Kusto` goes from 13017 lines to 3967, plus 337 lines of runtime functions. ## Scope Deliberately smaller than before, and written down in the guide. A construct is either translated with the semantics Kusto documents, or rejected by name. Rejected in this PR: `search`, `parse`, `mv-apply`, `lookup`, `evaluate`, `invoke`, `facet`, `top-nested`, `make-series` and friends; the `series_*`, `bag_*`/`pack_*` and `ipv4_*` families; `parse_url`, `parse_csv`, `parse_json`, `toscalar`, `format_timespan`; and `dynamic` **objects** (arrays map onto ClickHouse `Array`). Three known divergences are documented rather than papered over: subtracting two datetimes yields seconds instead of a timespan, `project-rename` moves the renamed column to the end, and `union` needs compatible schemas. ## Testing `04670`–`04673` cover the pipeline, the string operators (including the injection cases), the scalar semantics that used to be wrong, and 47 constructs that must be rejected. A 2500-query random fuzz found no crashes or logical errors. The 302 conformance cases that were deleted with the old implementation are being reintroduced separately, on top of this branch.

signal.title: [WIP] Byte stream split Codec
signal.text: ### Changelog category Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry Added experimental ByteStreamSplit codec for fixed-width columns. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation:** : Floating-point and integer columns often have bytes at the same positional offset that are nearly identical across rows (e.g. the exponent byte of Float32 values in a narrow range). Grouping those bytes together can sometimes increases the compressibility of the data for general-purpose compressors. In tests on public GeoIP IPv6 datasets, this approach improved compression ratios by 2.43x over standard Zstd and 3.85x over LZ4. Similar gains were observed in UUIDv7 data, where BSS-LZ4 outperformed standard LZ4 by 1.94x. I also reproduced the https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PARQUET-1716, and it saw similar gains in scientific floating point datasets. Because the ipv6 was my target use case, I added specialization for w=16 bytes so the performance is acceptable. **Enabling:**: The codec is gated behind the experimental codecs setting: ```sql SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; ``` **Parameters:**: ByteStreamSplit accepts one optional integer argument — the element byte width. When omitted, the width is inferred from the column data type. - No argument (default) — element width inferred from column type (e.g. 4 for Float32, 8 for Float64, 16 for UUID/IPv6) - Explicit integer (e.g. ByteStreamSplit(4)) — override the element width; useful with FixedString Supported types: Any fixed-size type with element width ≥ 2: Float32, Float64, Int16/32/64/128, UInt16/32/64/128, Date, DateTime, DateTime64, IPv4, IPv6, UUID, FixedString(N) for N ≥ 2 and N<=255 (for now) Need to see if FixedString(N) is worth it. **Example use:** ```sql SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; CREATE TABLE example ( val_f32 Float32 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit, LZ4), val_f64 Float64 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit, ZSTD(1)), val_u128 UInt128 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit(16), LZ4), val_fs FixedString(8) CODEC(ByteStreamSplit(8)) ) ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY val_f32; ``` ### Implementation - Registered under method byte 0x9d. - Maximum element width: 255 bytes. ### Testing - Tested using my Harness in the misc_script_folder and using in real dataset, need to run the clickhouse static test. - Benchmark Compression: [Google Sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1h-Rcg6oXKD6pdf_GzaEe0YUvP41-K32B0idnsNAy-GU/edit?gid=0#gid=0) - Benchmark Speed: #### Specs - CPU: Intel i7-12500H (Alder Lake) - Data: 256–500 MiB, multiple rounds with inner iterations - Compiler: Clang -O2 #### Results Median (GB/s) | W | Ours Encode | Ours Decode | Arrow Encode | Arrow Decode | Speedup Encode | Speedup Decode | |-----|------------|------------|--------------|--------------|----------------|----------------| | 1(memcopy) | **19.4** | **19.9** | **19.4** | **19.9** | **1.0×** | **1.0×** | | 2 | 10.5 | 10.8 | 9.7 | 10.7 | 1.08× | 1.01× | | 4 | 10.4 | 10.8 | 10.0 | 10.9 | 1.04× | 0.99× | | 8 | 9.1 | 10.3 | 10.5 | 10.9 | 0.87× | 0.94× | | 16 | 7.4 | 10.2 | 4.6 | 4.7 | 1.61× | 2.17× | | 20 | 5.1 | 5.5 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 1.13× | 1.20× | | 32 | 4.9 | 5.4 | 3.7 | 4.1 | 1.32× | 1.32× | | 64 | 4.5 | 5.2 | 2.5 | 2.6 | 1.80× | 2.00× | | 128 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 2.4 | 2.4 | 1.88× | 1.92× | ***Arrow supports W > 255; ours would need VLA or dynamic allocation.***

signal.title: Deduplicate the final DISTINCT in parallel
signal.text: The final `DISTINCT` merged all of its input streams into one and deduplicated them on a single thread, so `SELECT DISTINCT` did not scale with `max_threads` while the equivalent `GROUP BY` did - aggregation parallelizes its merge over two-level hash tables, `DISTINCT` had nothing of the sort. This repartitions the input streams by the hash of the `DISTINCT` columns instead of merging them: equal values then land in the same stream, so every stream can be deduplicated on its own, and what is left to merge is already deduplicated. The repartitioning uses `scatterByPartition`, which `SortingStep` and `ShuffleSendStep` already use. Whether the order of the step's output is free to change is only known where the sorting properties are, so the decision is taken in `applyOrder`. The new setting `allow_parallel_distinct`, enabled by default, controls it. It is not applied when: - the input is already globally sorted, because then `DISTINCT` keeps the order of its input and the repartitioning would break it; - there is a `LIMIT`, because the transform stops early anyway and the single stream keeps `LIMIT` returning the first values of the input rather than an arbitrary subset; - the streams are already disjoint - `allow_distinct_partitions_independently` covers that case and skips the merge entirely. `max_rows_in_distinct` and `max_bytes_in_distinct` keep their global meaning: the streams hold disjoint parts of one `DISTINCT` set, so the transforms add up the sizes of their sets in a shared counter and check the limits against the total. Enforcing them in the single final transform instead would have disabled the optimization for everyone who sets them - including all of CI, where the test profile sets both to `10G`. Every input chunk is split across all partitions, so the number of partitions is capped rather than following `max_threads`. On `SELECT DISTINCT number FROM numbers_mt(4e7)` the total CPU time the scatter adds grows by 8% at 4 partitions, 20% at 16 and 96% at 96; without the cap that turned into a wall-clock regression at high `max_threads`. Wall clock, minimum of 3 runs, aarch64: | workload | `max_threads` | before | after | speedup | |---|---|---|---|---| | 20M distinct `UInt64`, `MergeTree` | 4 | 0.442 s | 0.205 s | 2.16x | | | 16 | 0.458 s | 0.148 s | 3.09x | | | 96 | 0.502 s | 0.165 s | 3.04x | | 40M distinct `UInt64`, `numbers_mt` | 4 | 0.965 s | 0.545 s | 1.77x | | | 16 | 0.929 s | 0.360 s | 2.58x | | | 96 | 0.886 s | 0.299 s | 2.96x | | 8M distinct `String`, `numbers_mt` | 4 | 0.515 s | 0.288 s | 1.79x | | | 16 | 0.517 s | 0.093 s | 5.56x | | | 96 | 0.518 s | 0.083 s | 6.24x | The measurements were taken on a busy machine, hence the minimum of several runs; the existing `distinct_in_order`, `distinct_high_cardinality` and `sorted_distinct` performance tests cover these shapes, so the performance comparison job is the authoritative check. `DISTINCT` without `ORDER BY` has no defined row order, and the repartitioning changes the order it happens to produce. Two existing tests relied on it: `04109_sort_propagation_apply_order` asserts that per-stream sortedness reaches `DISTINCT`, so it pins the setting off, and `00585_union_all_subquery_aggregation_column_removal` gets the explicit `ORDER BY` it was missing. Other tests that depend on the incidental order of a `DISTINCT` may surface in CI and should be fixed the same way. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114532 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/48988 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Evaluate the final `DISTINCT` on several threads by repartitioning its input by the hash of the `DISTINCT` columns, instead of merging everything into a single stream and deduplicating it on one thread. Up to 6x faster on high-cardinality `DISTINCT`. Controlled by the new setting `allow_parallel_distinct`, enabled by default. Note that this changes the order in which a `DISTINCT` without `ORDER BY` returns rows, which was never defined. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Iceberg writer declares `timestamp` (without zone) in metadata but writes Parquet with `isAdjustedToUTC=true` — CH-written tables with DateTime are unreadable by pyiceberg
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** When ClickHouse writes an Iceberg table containing a `DateTime` or `DateTime64` column, the table metadata and the data files contradict each other: - the Iceberg schema declares the column as `timestamp` — which the [spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#primitive-types) defines as *microsecond precision **without** timezone*, and whose required [Parquet mapping](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#parquet) is `timestamp(isAdjustedToUTC=false, unit=MICROS)`; - the Parquet data files are written with `isAdjustedToUTC=true` (`timestamp[us, tz=UTC]`). Spec-following readers refuse the combination. pyiceberg 0.10.0 fails the scan of every ClickHouse-written Iceberg table that contains a timestamp column: ``` ValueError: Unsupported schema projection from timestamp[us, tz=UTC] to timestamp[us] ``` Either consistent choice would fix interoperability: declare `timestamptz` in the Iceberg schema (arguably the right mapping for `DateTime`, which is epoch-based instant semantics), or write the Parquet files with `isAdjustedToUTC=false`. ClickHouse's own reader accepts its own output, so the bug is invisible in ClickHouse-only round-trips. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1375, on every write. Same behavior for `DateTime` and `DateTime64(6)`. **How to reproduce** ```bash clickhouse local --path . --query " CREATE TABLE t (k Int64, ts DateTime) ENGINE = IcebergLocal('\$PWD/ice/', 'Parquet') SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + number * 3600 FROM numbers(50) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; " grep -ho '"type" : "timestamp[^"]*"' ice/metadata/*.json | sort -u python3 - <<'PY' import glob import pyarrow.parquet as pq from pyiceberg.table import StaticTable print(pq.read_schema(sorted(glob.glob('ice/data/**/*.parquet', recursive=True))[0]).field('ts').type) t = StaticTable.from_metadata(sorted(glob.glob('ice/metadata/*.metadata.json'))[-1]) t.scan().to_arrow() PY ``` **Expected behavior** Metadata and data files agree — either `timestamptz` + `isAdjustedToUTC=true`, or `timestamp` + `isAdjustedToUTC=false` — and external readers can scan the table. **Actual behavior** ``` "type" : "timestamp" timestamp[us, tz=UTC] ValueError: Unsupported schema projection from timestamp[us, tz=UTC] to timestamp[us] ``` Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114848 (the same writer also serializes day/hour partition transform names non-canonically; both were found probing writer output against external readers). Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signal.title: Anchor the Build profile diff master baseline windows on the run's own event
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `Build profile diff` fails closed with `No master baseline with build profile data found - cannot compare` when CI is re-run days after it was triggered, even though the baseline rows are present. Failing run: [PR #113672 @ `494760825`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113672&sha=494760825526a945d48dd1b90c9965dfd8721df9&name_0=PR&name_1=Build%20profile%20diff). `find_baseline` intersects two sets measured from different origins: the candidates are the frozen first-parent chain of the head's master parent (`master_track_commits_sha`, chain relative), while the row filter was `date >= today() - BASE_DAYS` (wall-clock relative). A re-run replays the frozen event payload, so the chain stays anchored on the old merge base while `today()` moves on, and once the gap exceeds `BASE_DAYS` the intersection is empty by construction. On the run above, `created_at` is `2026-08-06T13:03:49Z` against a `run_started_at` of `2026-08-16T01:28:41Z`: ten days, seven-day window. Eight more sites share the mismatch, so fixing only `find_baseline` relocates the error. Every master-side window now derives from `info.event_time`, frozen with the event, as a closed interval `[anchor - N, min(anchor + 4 days, today)]`. The first-parent walk takes the same anchor and stops a whole upload day further back, so the chain it returns is a superset of what those windows can match. Closed rather than half-open because `date` leads the primary key of the profile tables: the width is then fixed however old the event is, so the window slides rather than grows. The upper bound allows for profiles uploaded after their commit, measured at 4 hours p99 and 85 hours max over 673 master `arm_release` builds. Pull request side windows keep `today() - PR_DAYS`: those rows are uploaded by the run itself. An anchor at today emits the same windows as before, a local run keeps the wall-clock ones, and both fail-closes stand. Driving the job with that run's real values reproduces the error on the current module and resolves the baseline here.

signal.title: Parallelize aggregation-in-order via key-hash reshuffle (aggregation_in_order_shuffle)
signal.text: ## Description `optimize_aggregation_in_order` is not enabled by default because it is often slower than the default hash aggregation. The reason is structural: for a multi-stream read the whole aggregation is funneled through a single `FinishAggregatingInOrderTransform`, so it runs on ~2–6 cores regardless of `max_threads` and is 8–16× slower than the default parallel hash path for high-cardinality `GROUP BY` (it does *less* total CPU work, but cannot parallelize it). This PR adds an experimental setting **`aggregation_in_order_shuffle`** (default `0`) that removes that funnel by repartitioning, reusing the shuffle primitive introduced for the sharded aggregator (`BufferedShardByHashTransform`): ``` read N sorted streams -> scatter each stream by hash(GROUP BY keys) into num_shards (BufferedShardByHashTransform) -> per shard: MergingSortedTransform(N -> 1) -- groups are disjoint by key -> per shard: streaming AggregatingInOrderTransform + FinalizeAggregatedTransform ``` Each shard aggregates a disjoint set of keys, so there is no cross-shard coordination and no single-threaded merge, while each shard still streams out completed key groups (bounded, O(1) memory). It is only used when the `GROUP BY` order is not relied upon downstream (`!memoryBoundMergingWillBeUsed()`, no bucket-order requirement, no `LIMIT` push-down), and the output is therefore not ordered by the keys. ### Making the shuffle deadlock-free and bounded-memory The M per-shard merges share the N scatters, so a naive scatter deadlocks: a slow/exhausted lane blocks the shared scatter from feeding the others, and a per-shard *sorted* merge is a selective consumer. Two fixes in `BufferedShardByHashTransform` (unbounded mode, used only by this path): - **Demand-driven scheduling**: push to every ready lane first, and pull a new input chunk only to feed an output that is ready *and* starving (empty queue). The shared scatter never stalls on a slow lane (its data is just buffered), so there is no cross-lane cycle, and read-ahead — hence memory — is bounded by how far the fastest consumer runs ahead of the slowest. - **Per-output drain on EOF**: when the input is exhausted, finish each output whose queue is already empty, so a sorted merge gets EOF on exhausted inputs instead of waiting forever (this hung deterministically for non-overlapping parts). Verified: 0 deadlocks over 120+ runs across all cardinalities, overlapping and non-overlapping parts, and `max_threads` 8..128; results are byte-identical to the default for order-independent aggregates. ### Results (200M rows, 50M keys, 96 threads; median of 5) | GROUP BY | default | in-order (funnel) | **shuffle** | |---|---|---|---| | `sum`, 50M groups | 870 ms / 23 GB / 42 cores | 5779 ms / 0.8 GB / 4 cores | **1341 ms / 0.83 GB / 20 cores** | | `uniqExact`, 50M groups | 12040 ms / 56 GB | 5744 ms / 1.5 GB | **1049 ms / 2.0 GB / 22 cores** | For high-cardinality `GROUP BY` the shuffle is **4–11× faster than the current aggregation-in-order at the same O(1) memory**, and for `uniqExact` it is faster than the default while using ~28× less memory. ### Known limitation (why it stays off by default) It scatters raw rows, so it regresses for low/medium cardinality (where in-order is already fast and the shuffle gives no benefit, and long key-runs make the scatter buffer more). Gating it to high cardinality (e.g. from the primary-key granule estimate) is a natural follow-up. `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` is also fixed to render the scatter/merge stage of the in-order pipeline (it was previously omitted). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental setting `aggregation_in_order_shuffle` that parallelizes `optimize_aggregation_in_order` by repartitioning the sorted input by the hash of the `GROUP BY` keys into independent shards, removing the single-threaded merge bottleneck while keeping the bounded memory of aggregation-in-order. For high-cardinality `GROUP BY` it is several times faster than the ordinary aggregation-in-order. Disabled by default. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (the new setting is documented in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`).
