signal.title: DataLakeCatalog: DROP then CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS silently ACKs an unusable ghost table (catalog vs object-store existence disagreement)
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong On a `DataLakeCatalog` database (Glue or Iceberg REST catalog), a table's *existence* is decided differently for `CREATE` than for every other operation, and the two systems of record are deliberately left disagreeing by `DROP TABLE`. The result is that `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` **silently returns success for a table that is never registered in the catalog and that no subsequent SQL can query, drop, or create** — a permanent wedge on that table name, on **default settings, with no crash or fault injection**. Two systems of record are consulted: - `CREATE` decides existence by **listing the object store**. `IcebergMetadata::createInitial` lists `metadata/*.metadata.json` under the table location (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/IcebergMetadata.cpp:709-725`). If any `*.metadata.json` is present and `IF NOT EXISTS` was given, it `return`s early (`:719-721`) **without calling `catalog->createTable`** (`:765-770`). Its own comment names the case (`:746-752`): "leftover data after `DROP TABLE` with `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop` off". - Every other operation (`SHOW TABLES`, `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `DROP`) consults the **catalog** (`src/Databases/DataLake/DatabaseDataLake.cpp:488-492`, `:523-524`, `:740`, `:716-726`). `DROP TABLE` removes only the catalog entry and, on default settings, leaves the object-store metadata in place: Glue `DeleteTable` only (`src/Databases/DataLake/GlueCatalog.cpp:655-668`); REST `DELETE ...?purgeRequested=False` (`src/Databases/DataLake/RestCatalog.cpp:1114-1127`); the object-store purge is gated on `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop`, default `false` (`src/Core/Settings.cpp`) — which is the correct, Iceberg-standard behavior. So after a normal `DROP`, the catalog has forgotten the table but `metadata/v1.metadata.json` remains. A later `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` at the same location then finds that leftover `metadata.json`, short-circuits, and never registers the table in the catalog — yet returns success. The table is now a ghost: - it is **absent** from the catalog (`GetTable` / `SHOW TABLES` do not see it); - `SELECT`/`INSERT` fail with `UNKNOWN_TABLE`; - `DROP TABLE` fails with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` "Cannot drop table ... because it does not exist" (`DatabaseDataLake.cpp:721-725`) — there is **no SQL path to clean it up**; - a plain re-`CREATE` (without `IF NOT EXISTS`) throws `TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS` "Iceberg table with path ... already exists" (`IcebergMetadata.cpp:722-724`) — while the catalog simultaneously insists the table does not exist. Only manual object-store surgery (deleting the leftover `metadata/` files) or an external catalog registration can unwedge the name. There is also an **ambiguous-create** variant of the same defect: if the create fails *between* the object-store metadata write (`IcebergMetadata.cpp:746`) and the catalog `createTable` call (`:770`) — e.g. a dropped/timed-out Glue `CreateTable`, or a server crash in that window — the object-store metadata is durable but the catalog was never updated, so the create-commit protocol is **not idempotent**: every retry hits exactly the wedge above and can never repair the catalog. (This variant is source-derived; the deterministic `DROP` → `CREATE IF NOT EXISTS` variant below is empirically confirmed.) ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — empirically reproduced on `master` (26.8.1.119), 3/3 with a positive control, using the AWS Glue catalog backed by a mock (`moto`) + MinIO. The REST-catalog path is source-identical (`RestCatalog::dropTable` uses `purgeRequested=False`, and the same `createInitial` existence-by-listing path is used for all catalog types). ### How to reproduce `DataLakeCatalog` (Glue or REST) is a BETA feature (`allow_database_iceberg` / `allow_database_glue_catalog`, `src/Core/Settings.cpp:7320/7330`). ```sql SET allow_experimental_database_glue_catalog = 1; CREATE DATABASE glue_db ENGINE = DataLakeCatalog('<glue-endpoint>') SETTINGS catalog_type = 'glue', region = 'us-east-1', aws_access_key_id = '...', aws_secret_access_key = '...', storage_endpoint = 'http://<minio>/warehouse'; -- 1. create + register CREATE TABLE glue_db.`ns.t1` (x Int32) ENGINE = IcebergS3('http://<minio>/warehouse/t1/', '<key>', '<secret>'); -- 2. drop: catalog entry removed, warehouse/t1/metadata/v1.metadata.json REMAINS -- (iceberg_delete_data_on_drop is off by default — correct Iceberg behavior) DROP TABLE glue_db.`ns.t1`; -- 3. re-create IF NOT EXISTS: returns OK, but registers NOTHING in the catalog CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS glue_db.`ns.t1` (x Int32) ENGINE = IcebergS3('http://<minio>/warehouse/t1/', '<key>', '<secret>'); -- <-- false ACK -- 4. the table is now a ghost: SELECT count() FROM glue_db.`ns.t1`; -- UNKNOWN_TABLE DROP TABLE glue_db.`ns.t1`; -- BAD_ARGUMENTS "... does not exist" (cannot clean up) CREATE TABLE glue_db.`ns.t1` (x Int32) ENGINE = IcebergS3('http://<minio>/warehouse/t1/', '<key>', '<secret>'); -- TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS ``` Positive control (proves the leftover object-store metadata is the cause): run the identical sequence, but between steps 2 and 3 delete the leftover `warehouse/t1/metadata/*` objects. Step 3 then registers the table normally and `SELECT count()` returns `0` — no wedge. A self-contained rig (MinIO + `moto` Glue mock + ClickHouse) is `tests/clickfawkes/glue_catalog_commit_durability.py recreate_wedge`. ### Expected behavior For a `DataLakeCatalog` database, `CREATE`'s existence check should agree with the system of record used by every other operation — the catalog — rather than the object store. Concretely, one of: - `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` should register the table in the catalog when it is absent there (adopting the leftover metadata), so the acknowledged table is actually usable; or - if the leftover object-store metadata genuinely blocks creation, `CREATE`/`CREATE IF NOT EXISTS` should fail **loudly and consistently with the catalog view** (and there must remain some SQL path to `DROP` the name), rather than silently acknowledging a table that cannot be queried, dropped, or created. Either way, `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` must not return success for a table that is invisible to the catalog and unrecoverable by SQL. ### Error message and/or stacktrace From the wedged (ghost) table, on `master` 26.8.1.119: ``` -- step 3 (CREATE IF NOT EXISTS): returns OK (exit 0), no output -- the false ACK -- step 4: Code: 60. DB::Exception: Unknown table expression identifier 'glue_db.ns.t1' ... (UNKNOWN_TABLE) Code: 60. DB::Exception: Table glue_db.`ns.t1` does not exist. (UNKNOWN_TABLE) -- DROP Code: 57. DB::Exception: Iceberg table with path t1/ already exists. (TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS) -- plain CREATE ``` ### Additional context - Distinct from #108524 / PR #109071: those are the **plain `Iceberg()` table engine** (no catalog) with `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop = 1` (opt-in) failing to delete files, so a re-create fails **loudly** with `TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS`. This report is a **`DataLakeCatalog` database** on **default settings** (delete-flag off, which is the intended Iceberg behavior), where the novel and more severe symptoms are the **silent false ACK** from `IF NOT EXISTS` and the **permanent catalog-vs-object-store desync** with no SQL cleanup path. PR #109071's fix (delete files when the opt-in flag is on) does not touch this: the default path deliberately keeps metadata. - Distinct from #112102 (Glue `updateMetadata` has no CAS) and #112081 (Iceberg `metadata.json` PUT cleanup) — this is the `CREATE`/`DROP` registration protocol, not the write/update commit. - Found by the ClickFawkes durability framework (commit-protocol axis: existence judged against a different system of record than the one used for mutation, so a `DROP` that intentionally desyncs them leaves a create that can never converge).

signal.title: Fix JSON/XML format statistics race condition with parallel replicas
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `rows_read` and `rows_before_limit_at_least` reported as 0 or stale in JSON/XML format output when a query with `LIMIT` reads from remote connections (parallel replicas or the `remote` table function). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) No documentation changes needed — this is a bug fix with no user-facing API changes. --- ## Summary - When parallel replicas are used with `LIMIT`, `rows_read` in JSON/XML output is reported as 0 - Root cause: race condition where `finalizeImpl` writes statistics BEFORE `PipelineExecutor::finalizeExecution` collects remaining progress from connection draining - Fix: two-phase output format finalization — statistics are written AFTER all progress has been collected - The same drain also delivers late `ProfileInfo` packets that update the `rows_before_limit_at_least` / `rows_before_aggregation` counters, so the deferral covers the whole trailer, and the native-protocol `ProfileInfo` sent to the client is refreshed from the post-drain counters ## Approach Split the output format's finalization so statistics are written AFTER `finalizeExecution` collects all remaining progress: - **Phase 1** (during pipeline, in `finalizeImpl`): Write everything EXCEPT the trailer after the `rows` field (`rows_before_limit_at_least`, `rows_before_aggregation`, the `"statistics"` section) and closing delimiter - **Phase 2** (after `finalizeExecution`): Re-read the rows-before-* counters, write the trailer and close the document via a finalize callback ### Key changes: - `IOutputFormat`: Added `hasDeferredStatistics`, `writeDeferredStatisticsAndFinalize`, `completeDeferredStatistics` mechanism; `snapshotRowsBeforeCounters` re-reads the shared counters before the deferred trailer is written - `PipelineExecutor`: Added `setFinalizeCallback` called at end of `finalizeExecution` after progress collection - `CompletedPipelineExecutor`: Sets the finalize callback to invoke `completeDeferredStatistics` - `JSONRowOutputFormat`, `XMLRowOutputFormat`, `JSONColumnsWithMetadataBlockOutputFormat`: Override deferred statistics methods; the whole trailer (`rows_before_limit_at_least`, `rows_before_aggregation`, `statistics`) is deferred to phase 2 (`JSONUtils::writeRowsBeforeAndStatistics` factors out the shared writer) - `ParallelFormattingOutputFormat`: Propagates deferred statistics through the parallel formatting pipeline - `LazyOutputFormat` / `PullingOutputFormat`: `getProfileInfo` re-snapshots the rows-before-* counters, so the `ProfileInfo` packet sent to native-protocol clients (TCP `clickhouse-client`, gRPC, `LocalConnection`) carries the post-drain values — by the time it is sent, the executor thread has been joined and the counters are final - New failpoint `tcp_handler_sleep_before_secondary_query_trailing_packets` delays a secondary query's trailing `Totals` / `Extremes` / `ProfileInfo` / `Progress` / `EndOfStream`, making the race deterministic for tests Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85785 ## Test plan - [x] Build succeeds (Release) - [x] Test `00365_statistics_in_formats` passes - [x] JSON format tests pass (`00159_parallel_formatting_json_and_friends_1/2`, `00378_json_quote_64bit_integers`, `00685_output_format_json_escape_forward_slashes`, `01447_json_strings`, `01449_json_compact_strings`, `01486_json_array_output`, `02554_format_json_columns_for_empty`) - [x] XML format tests pass (`00307_format_xml`, `02122_parallel_formatting_XML`) - [x] `03918_statistics_in_formats_parallel_replicas` — forward guard: parallel-replicas `rows_read` matches the single-node value - [x] New deterministic reproducer `04603_rows_before_limit_parallel_replicas_late_packets` — fails without the fix (failpoint forces the trailing packets into the drain window); checks `rows_read` under parallel replicas and `rows_read` + `rows_before_limit_at_least` through the `remote` table function, over HTTP (server-side formatting) and native TCP (client-side formatting), across `JSON`, `JSONColumnsWithMetadata`, and `XML` - [ ] CI: Run with parallel replicas to verify `rows_read` is no longer 0 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches query pipeline execution, cancellation, and output formatting/finalization paths; while scoped to statistics/progress reporting, it changes timing and thread-synchronization and could affect query completion/cancellation behavior under parallel replicas. > > **Overview** > Fixes a race where JSON/XML output could report `rows_read=0` with parallel replicas + `LIMIT` by ensuring final `Progress` packets (drained after cancellation/early completion) are incorporated before statistics are emitted. > > This introduces **two-phase output finalization**: `IOutputFormat` can defer writing statistics/closing delimiters (`hasDeferredStatistics`/`writeDeferredStatisticsAndFinalize`), and `PipelineExecutor` now supports a `setFinalizeCallback` invoked at the end of `finalizeExecution()` after collecting remaining progress; `CompletedPipelineExecutor` wires this to `IOutputFormat::completeDeferredStatistics()`. > > Cancellation/draining logic is tightened to preserve trailing progress and avoid blocking hard cancels: `PipelineExecutor` triggers a `PartialResult` cancel on normal completion, `ISource::cancel` skips `onCancel` for `PartialResult` but allows later escalation, `RemoteSource` adds explicit cancel-reason upgrades and aborts drain via `RemoteQueryExecutor::abortDrain`, and `RemoteQueryExecutor::finish()` drains until all replica connections complete while swallowing expected cancel exceptions. Adds a stateless regression test `03918_statistics_in_formats_parallel_replicas` to assert `rows_read > 0` across JSON/XML formats over TCP/HTTP. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 5818266286a7645dcf1b57212bf9b3214cfd2ec8. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: Print invisible characters as escape sequences in Vertical format
signal.text: ### What this PR does Non-printable characters (NUL, SOH, etc.) were silently swallowed in `Vertical` output format. Since `Vertical` is a "pretty" format, C0 control characters (`0x00`..`0x1F`) and `DEL` (`0x7F`) are now displayed as Unicode "Control Pictures" (`U+2400`..`U+2421`, e.g. `␀`, `␉`, `␊`, `␡`), which unlike C-style escape sequences cannot be confused with the literal characters they represent. The new setting `output_format_vertical_display_control_characters` (enabled by default) restores raw-byte output when disabled. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85179 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Display non-printable control characters as Unicode "Control Pictures" in `Vertical` format by default; the new setting `output_format_vertical_display_control_characters` can be disabled to restore raw-byte output. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written

Related: #112931, already merged, which carries the fix. #112931 stopped `ReadFromMerge` from narrowing the per-shard-sorted streams of a `Distributed` child. Its tests (`04666`, `04813`) assert the resulting row order. The same concatenation also produced a wrong result *multiset* under `DISTINCT` - `DistinctSortedStreamTransform` removes only adjacent duplicates, so the second shard's sorted run survived and every value came back twice - and an order assertion cannot express that. @ zlareb1 reported this manifestation on #111211. The aggregating queries cover the stage above `WithMergeableState`, where the sort is merge-only because the shards already aggregated and sorted. `04813` asserts a pipeline shape for that stage, not a result. Both directions, default settings apart from `max_threads`, on the pre-fix release binary `26.7.4.27` (its `should_not_narrow` lacks the guard) and on master `068ec6d2ae62` (which has it): | Queries | pre-fix | master | |---|---|---| | `DISTINCT` / `DISTINCT ON` over the `Merge` table | 42 | 21 | | `GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 3` over the `Merge` table | 9 8 7 | 9 9 8 | | the same `DISTINCT` straight through the `Distributed` table (control) | 21 | 21 | 50 of 50 runs pass under `clickhouse-test` with setting randomization on, and corrupting any asserted line to its pre-fix value fails the test. `optimize_distinct_in_order = 1` and `max_threads = 1` are pinned because the runner randomizes them and either one hides the bug. The row count comes from a subquery carrying the `LIMIT`: a bare `SELECT count()` lets the optimizer drop the `ORDER BY` and returns 21 even before the fix. signal.title: Revert "Revert "NATS: add inline credentials setting""
signal.text: Reverts https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178, restoring the `nats_credentials` setting of the `NATS` table engine (originally added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733), and fixes the reason of the original revert: the possibility of referencing arbitrary server paths through `nats_credential_file`. `nats_credential_file` is a path on the server filesystem: the server opens it with its own privileges, and during authentication the credentials are sent to `nats_url`, which comes from the same query. So a path taken from SQL lets anyone who can define a `NATS` source probe the local filesystem (the error text distinguishes a missing file, a permission error, and a file without a seed), and exfiltrate files the server can read to a NATS server they control (the part of the file before the seed line is sent verbatim in the `CONNECT` frame's `jwt` field). See the analysis in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733#discussion_r3750203599. This hole predates #110733 (`nats_credential_file` exists since 24.2), but with the inline `nats_credentials` setting restored, the path form is no longer needed in SQL at all. The restriction, modelled on `StorageMySQL::getSSLParams` (`e700bbec4c84c585`): `nats_credential_file` is accepted only from a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. Every SQL spelling — the `SETTINGS` clause, an engine-argument override `NATS(collection, nats_credential_file = ...)`, or a named collection created by `CREATE NAMED COLLECTION` — throws `BAD_ARGUMENTS` with a message directing to `nats_credentials`. It is rejected on provenance, whether the query assigned the key at all, rather than on the resulting value, so an override with the empty string cannot silently drop the credentials the operator configured. Loading from previously-validated metadata (server startup, force-restore, and short-syntax `ATTACH`) is exempt via `isLoadingFromExistingMetadata`, so existing tables keep working after an upgrade; a user-issued full `ATTACH TABLE` query is still checked. `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING` is not a bypass: the `NATS` engine does not support settings alter. Replacing a configured path with inline `nats_credentials` from the query remains allowed — the path itself is not used then — as long as the named collection permits it. Because the contents are the only spelling a query has, `nats_credentials` inherits the override permission of the path key it replaces, the same way `ssl_ca_pem` does for `ssl_ca` in `findOverrideForbiddingKey`: credentials the operator pinned with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">` cannot be replaced through the contents form either, in either spelling, while the contents form stays usable when `allow_named_collection_override_by_default` is disabled (it is not a new key, it replaces one the collection defines). The `SETTINGS` clause is applied on top of the collection values without passing through the named-collection override check, so `resolveCredentialSource` enforces the same permission for both spellings. An empty `nats_credentials` is refused as well: it can only drop the credentials a collection carries, in either form, never replace them with other ones. Tests: a new stateless test `04891_nats_credential_file_path_restriction` covers all rejected SQL spellings and the accepted configuration-file sources, using `NATS` named collections added to the stateless-test server configuration (`tests/config/config.d/named_collection.xml`, with `nats_url = '127.0.0.1:1'`, so passing the validation surfaces as `CANNOT_CONNECT_NATS`) — one with a plain `nats_credential_file`, one where it is locked with `overridable="false"`, and one without credentials at all; `04665_nats_credentials_named_collection` is updated — the `nats_credential_file` query-override direction is now rejected. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85213 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `NATS` table engine accepts credentials inline in the new `nats_credentials` setting (the same payload as a `.creds` file), and no longer accepts `nats_credential_file` from SQL: the path is a reference to a file on the server filesystem, which the server opens with its own privileges, so it can only be specified in a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. A query may replace such a configured path with inline `nats_credentials`, unless the operator pinned it with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">`. Tables created before this restriction keep working after an upgrade.

signal.title: Recover a dead py4j gateway in ResilientSparkSession
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112175 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112175 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Requested on #112175 as a separate PR. Every test in a spark-dependent integration module can error at fixture setup with `Py4JError: SparkConf does not exist in the JVM`, losing the module's coverage and failing the job. Seen on `Integration tests (amd_asan_ubsan, db disk, old analyzer, 5/6)`, 6 of 805 ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112175&sha=5af55d5ac9dbe8d076e99c2022053c89a17accd9&name_0=BackportPR&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%2C%20db%20disk%2C%20old%20analyzer%2C%205%2F6%29)). CIDB, 21 days: 11 rows, that shard only, none on master. **Root cause.** The message is not a missing class: py4j's `GatewayClient.send_command` swallows a `Py4JNetworkError` and returns `proto.ERROR`, which `JVMView.__getattr__` re-labels (`java_gateway.py:1722-1725`): the gateway socket is dead. pyspark caches that socket in class state and relaunches the JVM only `if not SparkContext._gateway` (3.5.5 `context.py:435-437`). Neither `stop()` clears it, so once the JVM dies no relaunch happens in that process, and xdist reuses it across modules. The wrapper could not recover either: `_is_alive` guards an already-built wrapper, but the failure is in `__init__`. **Change.** Probe the cached gateway before building a session and discard it only when it stops answering. The probe is conditional: the JVM survives `stop()` (the failing job's log shows it answering 10 minutes later), so an unconditional reset would orphan a live JVM per module. `_restart()` shares the path, so restarting on a live gateway still reuses the JVM. It recovers from the death, not prevents it; the trigger is not recoverable from the artifacts. Also drops a dead `builder._options` line. **Validation.** Reproduced in the runner image on the CI-pinned pyspark, with the message and frame above. The new test fails on pristine master at its recovery arm and passes with the fix, 10/10 stable; mutants confirm the arms are live. It reports the relabel as `SparkSession$`, not `SparkConf`: `getOrCreate` asks for that name first while `_instantiatedSession` is set (`session.py:502`). Out of scope: `test_sts.py:42` and `test_storage_delta_shuffles/test.py:121` bypass the wrapper, and `retry_ok` is consumed only under LLVM coverage. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.841` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.4.45`, `26.6.3.45` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Prometheus HTTP handler endpoints do not increment rows/bytes metrics during inserts or selects, and do not send queries to system.query_log.
signal.text: ### Company or project name N/A ### Describe what's wrong Prometheus HTTP handler endpoints do not create (or do not reliably create) entries in `system.query_log` with the expected row/byte metrics: - **Remote write** (`/write`): Requests that insert time series data do not produce a `QueryFinish` row with `written_rows` or `written_bytes`. - **Remote read** (`/read`): Requests that read time series do not produce a `QueryFinish` row with `read_rows` or `read_bytes`. - **Query API** (`/api/v1/query`): Requests do not reliably appear in `system.query_log` with `read_rows > 0` and `read_bytes > 0` in a way that integration tests can assert (count-based). So either they are not logged, or the logged entries do not have read metrics set as expected. - **Query range API** (`/api/v1/query_range`): Same as Query API — integration tests that expect one additional `QueryFinish` row with `read_rows > 0` and `read_bytes > 0` after a request fail. Additionally, passing `query_id` as a URL parameter to the Query API is rejected (setting is not supported), which makes it harder to correlate specific requests with log entries even when logging exists. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce 1. Configure Prometheus HTTP handlers (remote write, remote read, Query API, query_range) and enable the query log. 2. Create a TimeSeries table and send a remote write with at least one time series. 3. Run: `SYSTEM FLUSH LOGS query_log; SELECT count() FROM system.query_log WHERE type = 'QueryFinish' AND written_rows > 0;` The count does not increase for the remote write. 4. Send a remote read request (e.g. protobuf ReadRequest to the read endpoint). Check the same style of count for `read_rows > 0`, it does not increase for the remote read. 5. Call the Query API, e.g. `GET /api/v1/query?query=up&time=<timestamp>`. After` SYSTEM FLUSH LOGS query_log`, the count of rows with `type = 'QueryFinish' AND read_rows > 0 AND read_bytes > 0` does not increase by one as expected. 6. Call the query_range API, e.g. `GET /api/v1/query_range?query=up&start=...&end=...&step=15`. Same count check fails. Integration tests in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/compare/master...JTCunning:ClickHouse:test/prometheus-query-log-integration-test reproduce these failures (remote write, remote read, Query API, query_range). ### Expected behavior - Remote write: Each successful remote write should produce a QueryFinish entry in system.query_log with written_rows and written_bytes set from the inserted data. - Remote read: Each remote read should produce a QueryFinish entry with read_rows and read_bytes set from the data read. - Query API and query_range API: Each request should produce a QueryFinish entry with read_rows and read_bytes set so that observability and auditing tools can see Prometheus API traffic in the query log. ### Error message and/or stacktrace N/A ### Additional context - A fix can add explicit query_log entries for remote write and remote read (with written/read row and byte counts) and ensure Query API and query_range API requests are logged with read metrics (whether via the existing executeQuery path or by adding handler-level logging). - Supporting query_id as a URL parameter for the Query API would allow correlating requests with log entries by query_id. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #112825 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1514` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Add a failpoint inside the Paimon incremental-read at-most-once window
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/102343 Paimon incremental reads have documented at-most-once semantics: the Keeper watermark advances at file-collection time, before the collected batch is delivered, so a crash inside that window loses the batch. This window has been untestable — nothing can deterministically crash a server between two statements inside one query's execution. This adds a pauseable failpoint, `paimon_incremental_read_pause_after_watermark_commit`, exactly between the watermark commit and delivery. Integration tests can enable it, observe the committed watermark in Keeper while the read is paused, restart the server, and assert the batch is lost — pinning the at-most-once contract deterministically. The test flips the day delivery becomes at-least-once. The failpoint is inert unless enabled via `SYSTEM ENABLE FAILPOINT`, like every other failpoint. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1511` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Assign merges for all partitions at once for OPTIMIZE FINAL
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/46770 For a non-replicated `MergeTree` table, `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` without an explicit partition used to process partitions one by one: it selected and ran the merge for one partition, waited for it to finish, and only then moved on to the next one. On a table with many partitions this serialized all the work and only ever showed a single merge in `system.merges`. Now the per-partition merges are assigned and executed in parallel, so all partitions are merged at once. The degree of parallelism is bounded by the configured `background_pool_size` and reserves only currently available merge-executor capacity. This mirrors how `StorageReplicatedMergeTree::optimize` already assigns a merge per partition and then waits for all of them. Notes: - Tables inside an explicit transaction keep the sequential path, because parallel merges would otherwise share a single transaction object that is not made for concurrent use. - The wait for already-running merges inside `selectPartsToMerge` (the `OPTIMIZE FINAL` path) is now scoped to the current partition: merges in other partitions cannot prevent selecting all the parts of this one, and waiting for them would needlessly serialize the parallel assignment. Verified on a local build: on a table with 8 partitions, `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` now runs 8 merges concurrently (observed via `system.merges`) instead of one at a time, and every partition is still correctly merged into a single part (checked for `MergeTree`, `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL DEDUPLICATE`, and `ReplacingMergeTree`, plus the `optimize_skip_merged_partitions` / `optimize_throw_if_noop` no-op paths and two concurrent `OPTIMIZE FINAL` queries). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on a non-replicated `MergeTree` table now assigns and runs the merges for all partitions at once instead of processing them one partition at a time.

signal.title: Improve the performance of `MODIFY TTL`
signal.text: `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` currently rewrites every part of the table, which on a large table means reading and writing all of its data just to change when rows expire. Very often the new TTL is the old one shifted in time - the retention period is extended or shortened, e.g. `create_time + INTERVAL 300 DAY` becomes `create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY`. In that case every row's expiry time moves by the same constant number of seconds, so the parts do not have to be rewritten at all: it is enough to shift the expiry timestamps ClickHouse already stores per part. This pull request adds that fast path, and the result for the user is that such a `MODIFY TTL` completes almost instantly instead of taking minutes or hours: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_fast_ttl (`id` UInt32, `name` String, `create_time` DateTime) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id TTL create_time + toIntervalDay(300); INSERT INTO test_fast_ttl SELECT number, 'AAA', date_sub(day, 100, now()) from numbers(100000000); -- Before ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 25.564 sec. -- After ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 0.046 sec. ``` There is nothing to enable and no new syntax: the optimization is applied automatically inside the `MATERIALIZE TTL` mutation that `MODIFY TTL` already produces, and a plain `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from it as well. The observable result is exactly the same as before - the same rows expire and the parts end up with the same TTL bounds - only the work is avoided. Per part, the mutation now does one of the following: - the part is fully expired under the new TTL - it is replaced with an empty part; - no row of the part is expired yet - the part is cloned (its data files hardlinked) and only its stored TTL bounds are shifted; - otherwise - the part is rewritten exactly as before. The fast path is only taken when it is provably equivalent to the rewrite. It requires that the unconditional rows TTL (`TTL <expr>`) is the only TTL of the table, and that the old and the new TTL are the same date/time column shifted by constant fixed-length intervals, so that `new_ttl(row) - old_ttl(row)` is one constant for every row. Calendar `MONTH`/`YEAR` intervals, `DAY`/`WEEK` intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, and row-dependent expressions are all rejected. The proof is redone for each part against the TTL expression (and time zone) that the part's stored timestamps were actually computed under, so a part that lags the table metadata, or was written by an older server, falls back to the regular rewrite rather than being shifted unsoundly. The same applies to the boundary cases of the stored timestamps themselves: a part containing a row whose TTL timestamp is exactly `1970-01-01 00:00:00` UTC (which ClickHouse treats as "no TTL"), a shift that would move some timestamp onto that value, and a part whose stored TTL is already fully expired (which the regular rewrite drops wholesale, even when the new TTL is longer) all take the regular rewrite. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` no longer rewrites the table's data when the new TTL is the old one shifted by a constant amount of time (the same date/time column plus fixed-length intervals), which is the common case of extending or shortening the retention period. Fully expired parts are replaced with empty ones and the rest are cloned with only their stored TTL metadata shifted, which makes such an `ALTER` nearly instant. Cases where the shift is not provably constant - calendar month/year intervals, day/week intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, or row-dependent TTL expressions - fall back to the regular rewrite. `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from the same optimization. <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. signal.title: Add UUID2 data type with correct sorting
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110066 Introduces `UUID2`, a variant of the `UUID` data type with correct (lexicographic) sorting. ## Motivation For historical reasons, the `UUID` data type sorts by the *second half* of the value. This is unexpected and, in particular, hurts the performance of primary indexes built on `UUIDv7` columns, whose most significant bits are a timestamp: with sorting by the second half, primary-key analysis cannot prune granules by the timestamp. ## What this does `UUID2` stores the 128-bit value as a plain big-endian integer of the 16 canonical bytes, so that natural integer comparison of the underlying value matches the textual (lexicographic) order and the canonical byte order used by most other systems. It reuses the `UUID` column and `Field` representation (like `DateTime` reuses `UInt32`), so sorting is correct with no extra comparison code, and its binary/interchange serialization is the canonical big-endian byte order. - `UUID1` is an alias of the current `UUID` type. - A new setting `uuid_type_version` (default `1`) controls whether the bare name `UUID` resolves to `UUID` (`1`) or `UUID2` (`2`) at `CREATE`/`ALTER` time. The resolved concrete type is materialized into the stored table definition (including nested types such as `Array(UUID)`), so reads never depend on the session setting and existing tables are never rewritten. The default will be flipped to `2` in a later, separate change. - Conversions to/from `String`, `UInt128`, `FixedString(16)` and `UUID`, plus `toUUID2` / `toUUID2OrZero` / `toUUID2OrNull`. - Parity across functions (`hex`/`bin`, `reinterpretAs*`, `UUIDv7ToDateTime`, `UUIDToNum`, `empty`/`notEmpty`, `min`/`max`, hashing, `uniq`), formats (`RowBinary`, `Native`, `JSON`, `CSV`, `TSV`, `Arrow`, `Parquet`, `Avro`, `BSON`, `MsgPack`, `Protobuf`, `CapnProto`, `JSONExtract`) and storage (`generateRandom`, `bloom_filter` skip index). The `UUID` type is unchanged (verified: still sorts by second half, identical conversions, default `uuid_type_version = 1`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new data type `UUID2`, a variant of `UUID` that sorts by its textual (lexicographic) representation instead of by the second half of the value. The setting `uuid_type_version` (default `1`) selects whether the type name `UUID` resolves to `UUID` or `UUID2`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: EXPLAIN SYNTAX: return a single record (default on)
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/80410 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107925 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` now returns the reformatted query as a single `String` record (with embedded newlines) instead of one record per line, so its output is a recoverable single row that is directly usable (for example, `SELECT count() FROM (EXPLAIN SYNTAX ...)` returns `1`). This is controlled by the new `single_record` option, which defaults to `1`; set `single_record = 0` to restore the historical one-record-per-line output. Other `EXPLAIN` kinds (`PLAN`/`PIPELINE`/`AST`) keep their per-line tree output. ### Description Per the discussion on #80410, `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` is a reformatted, copy-pasteable query, so returning the whole query as a single record is far more usable than splitting it across N rows. This is done in two commits: 1. Add a `single_record` option to `EXPLAIN SYNTAX`, off by default (no behavior change). The single-record code path already existed (used by `EXPLAIN PLAN` JSON output); this wires it to the new option for the `SYNTAX` kind and renames the internal `single_line` flag to `single_record`. 2. Flip the default to `single_record = 1`. This is backward-incompatible: existing `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` consumers now see one row instead of N. The `oneline` option still controls physical-line rendering (default `0`, i.e. embedded newlines). The affected stateless `.reference` files (including `.oldanalyzer.reference` variants) were regenerated for the new default. The `optimize_syntax_fuse_functions` docstring example was switched from `FORMAT TSV` to `FORMAT TSVRaw` so its multi-line output stays literal now that the single record carries the embedded newlines. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Add `/dialect`, `/lang`, `/language` client commands
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added client-side commands `/dialect`, `/lang`, `/language` to `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local` — an equivalent of `SET dialect = '...'` that is handled before parsing, so it also works when the current dialect cannot express a `SET` query (for example, to leave `kusto` or `promql`). While a non-default dialect is active, it is displayed in the prompt after the server display name, e.g. `clickhouse-cloud (polyglot) :)`. The command without an argument prints the current dialect. A plain `SET dialect = '...'` also updates the prompt, since the prompt now renders the dialect from the client-side session settings on every line. Implementation notes: - The prompt is now rendered by `getPrompt` on every line from a template that keeps the `{display_name}` placeholder: the current dialect is appended to the display name in parentheses (with a separating space if the display name is non-empty), and the `:) ` smiley is appended at the end, preserving the previous behavior for the default dialect. - The command works in `clickhouse-client`, `clickhouse-local`, and the embedded client (SSH/web terminal). - Documentation: a new "Switching the SQL dialect" section in the client page. - Test: `04892_client_dialect_command.expect`, verified locally for the prompt display, alias forms, plain `SET dialect` transitions in both directions, and the escape from a non-default dialect back to `clickhouse`.

signal.title: Columns Cache
signal.text: Implement the deserialized columns cache that keeps columns in memory. In comparison to the uncompressed cache, this saves time on deserialization and copying. Closes #82335. The cache identifies entries by table UUID, so it is only active for tables in databases that assign UUIDs (`Atomic` and `Replicated`); tables in `Ordinary` databases are silently excluded. The feature is gated behind the `EXPERIMENTAL` settings `use_columns_cache`, `enable_reads_from_columns_cache`, and `enable_writes_to_columns_cache`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Implement an experimental columns cache that keeps deserialized columns in memory for `MergeTree` tables. In comparison to the uncompressed cache, this saves time on deserialization and copying. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Declarative function signatures, continuation of #3775
signal.text: This is an experimental continuation of [#3775 (2018)](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/3775) by @alexey-milovidov, which proposed a declarative way to describe function signatures so that argument validation and return-type inference can be driven by a small DSL instead of hand-written `getReturnTypeImpl` logic per function. ### What's in this branch A `getSignatureString()` method on `IFunction` and `IFunctionOverloadResolver`. When a function exposes a non-empty signature, the base `getReturnTypeImpl(ColumnsWithTypeAndName)` parses and applies it via a small grammar of type **matchers** (`UInt`, `Number`, `Array(T)`, `MaybeNullable(T)`, `Function((args), R)`, `T : Any` capture, …) and type **functions** (`leastSupertype`, `nativeNumber`, `aggregateFunctionReturnType(AggregateFunction(name, …))`, `subcolumnTypeOf`, `typeFromString`, `DateTime64(scale, tz)`, …). The DSL supports variadic positions (`…`), ellipsis grouping for repeated argument units (`T1, V1, …` repeats the pair), `OR` between alternatives, optional positions `[T]`, const-value capture (`const name String`), lambdas, etc. The grammar / parser / type matchers / type functions live under `src/DataTypes/FunctionSignature.h`, `FunctionSignature.cpp`, `TypeMatchers.cpp`, `TypeFunctions.cpp`. ### Coverage ~191 commits on top of master, each is a small per-family round titled `Function signatures: round N — …`. Current state on this branch: ``` SELECT count(*) AS total, countIf(signature != '') AS with_sig, round(countIf(signature != '') * 100.0 / count(*), 1) AS pct FROM system.functions WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND alias_to = '' AND origin = 'System'; 1416 1395 98.5 ``` (With \`allow_experimental_nlp_functions = 1\`; the few remaining unset ones are setting / config-gated functions like \`aiClassify\`, \`region*\`, \`synonyms\`, whose \`create\` throws unless the relevant config block / setting is present, so \`system.functions.tryGet\` returns null even though the signature is in source. With the right config + setting they all surface — verified in tmp/ test config.) Roughly: - **Authoritative** (DSL drives type-check and return type, the legacy `getReturnTypeImpl` is either gone or bypassed): higher-order array functions (`arrayMap`, `arrayFilter`, `arrayFirst*`, …), `toIntervalX`, comparison, `multiSearch*` / `multiMatch*`, vector L-norms / distances / dot product, `UUIDv7ToDateTime`, `arrayReduce` / `arrayReduceInRanges`, `reverse`, `mapKeys` / `mapValues`, `getSubcolumn`, the `least` / `greatest` resolver, paired-variadic `timeSeriesTagsToGroup` / `timeSeriesStoreTags`, … - **Documentation-only** (signature surfaced via `system.functions` but the legacy `getReturnTypeImpl` still runs because the result type uses promotion / widening / setting-dependent dispatch the current DSL can't express): arithmetic (`plus`, `minus`, `multiply`, `divide`, modulo / intDiv family), array widening (`arraySum` / `arrayCumSum*` / `arrayDifference`), `mapContains*Like`, `dateTrunc`, `toStartOfWeek`, `parseDateTime*`, `transform`, `range`, `toX` conversions, etc. There is a `signature_documentation` opt-in alongside `signature` in the binary-arithmetic, unary-arithmetic, FunctionArrayMapped, and FunctionMapToArrayAdapter families specifically so a function can advertise a signature without the DSL accidentally hijacking the legacy widening logic. ### Status Draft / experimental. - This is an experiment — I'm not asking for it to be merged. There's significant disruption (191 commits touching every function family), and the gain is mostly documentation: today only ~30% of the converted functions are actually DSL-authoritative; the rest are decorative. The arithmetic promotion matrix and the per-Op widening rules in particular would need a richer type-function vocabulary (or new matchers) before they can be expressed declaratively. - The branch has been kept rebased on master throughout and builds cleanly. I've run the stateless test suite on each round. The pre-existing-on-master test failures I hit are listed in commit messages of the rounds where I encountered them (none introduced by this work). - The original PR has been open since 2018 — this branch is intended as a concrete data point on \"what fraction of ClickHouse functions can be reasonably described by a declarative signature, and what would the DSL need to grow to cover the rest.\" That's the question I'd love feedback on. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Correlated scalar subquery: max() over a non-empty group returns NULL for a subset of rows under a small max_block_size (nondeterministic wrong result)
signal.text: ### Summary A correlated scalar subquery whose aggregate is `max` (and, we expect, any aggregate) returns `NULL` for a subset of the outer rows of a **non-empty** correlation group, when the query runs with a `max_block_size` below the default. `max` over a non-empty set can never be `NULL`, so the result is silently wrong. It is also **nondeterministic**: the number of wrongly-`NULL` rows changes from run to run (observed `0`, `16384`, `54464`) at fixed settings, which points to a race in the correlated-subquery decorrelation join rather than a plan-level mistake. At the default `max_block_size` the same query is correct. This is distinct from the empty-group family (#111615 / #111832 — those return `NULL` instead of `0`/`[]` for a genuinely *empty* group): here the group is provably non-empty (it has 120000 rows and its true `max(k)` is `339999`), and the trigger is the physical `max_block_size`, not the group being empty. It is also distinct from #112576 (a `NULL` *correlation value*): the correlation column `s` is never `NULL` here. Correlated subqueries require the new analyzer (`enable_analyzer = 1`, the default) and `allow_experimental_correlated_subqueries = 1` (also the default on this build). ### ClickHouse version Reproduced on `master` (`26.8.1.1485` and `26.8.1.1448`, both from the CI build cache). ### How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE t (g UInt32, k UInt64, s LowCardinality(String)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (g, k); INSERT INTO t SELECT intHash32(number) % 30000, number, 'g' || toString(number % 200) FROM numbers(220000); INSERT INTO t SELECT number % 512, 220000 + number, 'hot' FROM numbers(120000); INSERT INTO t SELECT 3000000000 + number, 340000 + number, 'x' || toString(number) FROM numbers(60000); -- The 'hot' group is non-empty; its true max(k) is 339999, so no output row may carry a NULL max: SELECT max(k) FROM t WHERE s = 'hot'; -- 339999 -- The offending query: the same correlated max subquery in the SELECT and in the WHERE. -- The WHERE predicate `mk >= o.k` is always true (mk is the group's max), so every one of the -- 400000 rows must be returned, each with a non-NULL mk. SELECT o.s, (SELECT max(i.k) FROM t AS i WHERE i.s = o.s) AS mk FROM t AS o WHERE (SELECT max(i.k) FROM t AS i WHERE i.s = o.s) >= o.k SETTINGS max_threads = 1, max_block_size = 100; ``` **Expected:** 400000 rows, and no row has `mk = NULL` (every group is non-empty). **Actual:** the output still has 400000 rows, but 16384 of the `('hot', …)` rows carry `mk = \N` (NULL). Counting them: ``` $ clickhouse-client --query "$Q" --max_threads=1 --max_block_size=100 | grep -Pc '^hot\t\\N$' 16384 ``` Run it again (dropping the mark cache in between is not required) and the count changes — we observed `0`, `16384` and `54464` `NULL`-max `hot` rows across runs at the identical settings, with `max_threads = 8` making the nondeterminism more pronounced. At the default `max_block_size` (`65409`) the query is stable and correct (`0` NULL rows); the wrong result appears once `max_block_size` drops below roughly `32768`. ### Reproducibility Deterministically wrong in 19 of 20 consecutive runs on a freshly started, otherwise-idle server (one run happened to return the correct `0`, which is the nondeterminism itself). The output is complete every time (all 400000 rows), so this is not truncation. Wrapping the query in an outer `SELECT count() FROM (…)` re-plans it and hides the bug, and restricting the outer query to `WHERE o.s = 'hot'` also hides it — the divergence only surfaces in the bare multi-group query with the correlated subquery in both the `SELECT` and the `WHERE`. ### Related - Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111615 - Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112576 - Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111440 Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework.

signal.title: DataLakeCatalog: aws_external_id setting leaks in plaintext in SHOW CREATE DATABASE / system.databases.engine_full (masked everywhere else)
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** A `DataLakeCatalog` database masks every credential-bearing setting in `SHOW CREATE DATABASE` and `system.databases.engine_full` **except `aws_external_id`**, which is shown in plaintext — at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0` and without the `displaySecretsInShowAndSelect` privilege. Any user who can run `SHOW CREATE DATABASE` or read `system.databases` sees it. `aws_external_id` is the external ID passed to AWS STS `AssumeRole`, matching the `sts:ExternalId` condition on the role's trust policy (its own setting description in `src/Databases/DataLake/DatabaseDataLakeSettings.cpp` notes it is for roles owned by a third party, such as ClickHouse Cloud). ClickHouse already treats this value as a secret in the *inline* `s3()` / `extra_credentials` form: `external_id` is a member of `s3_secret_keys` in `src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.h`, whose own comment calls it "the shared secret of the assume-role triple". So the identical value is masked in one surface and leaked in another. The cause is that the `SETTINGS_TO_HIDE` masking map in `src/Databases/DataLake/DataLakeConstants.h` lists `catalog_credential`, `auth_header`, `aws_access_key_id`, `aws_secret_access_key`, the `storage_*` variants, `onelake_*`, `google_adc_client_secret` / `google_adc_refresh_token`, and `dlf_*`, but has no entry for `aws_external_id`. (`aws_role_session_name` is likewise absent from the map, but that is an operator-chosen session label rather than a secret; the concern here is `aws_external_id`.) **How to reproduce** Any ClickHouse build with the Glue `DataLakeCatalog` backend. The Glue catalog is constructed lazily, so no live endpoint is needed to observe the masking: ```sql SET allow_database_glue_catalog = 1; CREATE DATABASE ge ENGINE = DataLakeCatalog('https://glue.us-east-1.amazonaws.com') SETTINGS catalog_type = 'glue', region = 'us-east-1', aws_access_key_id = 'AKIAEXAMPLE', aws_secret_access_key = 'SECRET', aws_role_arn = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/r', aws_external_id = 'my-external-id-value'; SELECT engine_full FROM system.databases WHERE name = 'ge'; ``` Output (note `aws_secret_access_key` is `[HIDDEN]` but `aws_external_id` is verbatim): ``` DataLakeCatalog('https://glue.us-east-1.amazonaws.com') SETTINGS catalog_type = 'glue', region = 'us-east-1', aws_access_key_id = '[HIDDEN]', aws_secret_access_key = '[HIDDEN]', aws_role_arn = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/r', aws_external_id = 'my-external-id-value' ``` `SHOW CREATE DATABASE ge` shows the same unmasked value. **Expected behavior** `aws_external_id` should be masked as `'[HIDDEN]'` in `SHOW CREATE DATABASE`, `system.databases.engine_full`, and any other formatted-with-secrets-hidden surface, consistent with how the inline `external_id` argument is masked via `s3_secret_keys` and with the other credential settings in `SETTINGS_TO_HIDE`. **Which ClickHouse server versions are incompatible** Reproduced on master (26.8). By code inspection the gap exists on every version whose `SETTINGS_TO_HIDE` map omits `aws_external_id`.

signal.title: Concurrent `ALTER NAMED COLLECTION` on a Keeper-backed store silently loses one update: both ALTERs report success, one change vanishes
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong With `named_collections_storage.type = zookeeper` (or `keeper`), named-collection metadata is a single SQL blob per collection stored in one Keeper znode. `ALTER NAMED COLLECTION` is a read-modify-write of that blob with **no optimistic-concurrency (version) check**, so two concurrent ALTERs issued on different replicas both return success while only one survives in the durable Keeper state. The other change is silently discarded — no error, no warning, no log line. `NamedCollectionsMetadataStorage::update` reads the current CREATE query (`readCreateQuery`), applies the ALTER delta in memory, and writes the whole blob back with `replace = true` (`src/Common/NamedCollections/NamedCollectionsMetadataStorage.cpp:578-586`). `ZooKeeperStorage::write` (`:308-315`) calls `zkutil::ZooKeeper::createOrUpdate`, which is `trySet(path, data, /* version */ -1)` (`src/Common/ZooKeeper/ZooKeeper.cpp:906-914`) — version `-1` means "any version", i.e. no CAS. The per-process `NamedCollectionFactory` mutex (`src/Common/NamedCollections/NamedCollectionsFactory.cpp:333`) serializes ALTERs within one server, but two servers hold two independent mutexes, so their reads race and the later `set` overwrites the earlier one: ``` A: read {base} B: read {base} A: write {base, keyA} B: write {base, keyB} <- keyA is gone; both ALTERs acked ``` This is a metadata durability loss. Because `S3`, `IcebergS3`, and `DeltaLakeS3` tables re-resolve the collection at query/attach time (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageConfiguration.cpp:98-130`) rather than inlining its values, a concurrently-lost credential or endpoint rotation is then used with no indication that it was dropped. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes. Reproduced on `26.8.1.1` (master). The code path is present in current master. ### How to reproduce Two servers sharing one Keeper, both configured with a Keeper-backed named-collection store: ```xml <!-- both servers --> <named_collections_storage> <type>zookeeper</type> <path>/named_collections</path> </named_collections_storage> <zookeeper> <node><host>127.0.0.1</host><port>KEEPER_PORT</port></node> </zookeeper> ``` ```sql -- on server A CREATE NAMED COLLECTION coll AS base = 'b'; -- (wait a moment for it to appear on server B) ``` Then fire one ALTER on each server concurrently, e.g.: ```bash clickhouse client --port PORT_A -q "ALTER NAMED COLLECTION coll SET keyA = '1'" & clickhouse client --port PORT_B -q "ALTER NAMED COLLECTION coll SET keyB = '1'" & wait ``` Both commands succeed. Inspect the durable collection (after both replicas converge): ```sql SELECT arraySort(mapKeys(collection)) FROM system.named_collections WHERE name = 'coll'; ``` Observed: only one of `keyA` / `keyB` is present (e.g. `['base','keyB']`). Repeating the concurrent pair loses one key on essentially every iteration. Controls that show it is specifically the cross-node, un-versioned write: - Running the two ALTERs **sequentially** (A, then B after it propagates) keeps both keys. - Running the two ALTERs **concurrently against the same server** keeps both keys (the factory mutex serializes them). ### Expected behavior Two concurrent `ALTER NAMED COLLECTION` statements that both report success must both be reflected in the durable state — or one must fail loudly (e.g. a ret/version conflict) rather than being silently discarded. The keeper-backed store should use an optimistic-concurrency check (`set` with the observed version, retrying the read-modify-write on `ZBADVERSION`) instead of an unconditional `createOrUpdate`. ### Error message and/or stacktrace None. Both ALTERs return success; the loss is silent. ### Related issues and pull requests - #107593 — `ALTER NAMED COLLECTION` changes not picked up by Kafka engine tables (a same-node engine cache; different root cause — there the durable collection is correct). - #113455 — `ENGINE = Backup` storage-policy cache key ignores the resolved destination after `ALTER NAMED COLLECTION` (also a same-node cache). ### Additional context Only the Keeper-backed store (`type = zookeeper`/`keeper`) is affected; the `local` store is single-node and serialized by the in-memory factory mutex. The scenario is a normal multi-replica deployment where two operators or two automated jobs rotate different keys of the same collection at about the same time.

signal.title: DeltaLake CDF: the table-function-only guard is constructor-only — SELECT over an existing engine table serves the change stream without meta columns
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** DeltaLake CDF is documented (by its own guard) as table-function-only: constructing a `DeltaLake*` storage while `delta_lake_snapshot_start_version` / `delta_lake_snapshot_end_version` are set throws `Code: 36 Delta lake CDF is allowed only for deltaLake table function`. But the guard lives in the `StorageObjectStorage` constructor, so it fires only when the storage object happens to be built with CDF settings in the query context (e.g. `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = DeltaLakeLocal(...)` inside a query that carries the settings). A plain `SELECT` with CDF settings over an *already-created* engine table bypasses it: the read path (`StorageObjectStorage::read`) happily branches into `ReadFromDeltaLakeTableChangesStep` for any data-lake configuration. The bypassed read is a third, incoherent behavior: it returns the change-stream *row multiset* — for a 1000-row table with 100 deleted rows, `count()` returns 1100, a number that corresponds to no state of the table at any version — but *without* the `_change_type` / `_commit_version` / `_commit_timestamp` meta columns (the engine's schema was fixed at CREATE), so the stream cannot even be filtered into its insert/delete parts. Referencing `_change_type` throws `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1448, 20/20 runs. **How to reproduce** Write a small CDF-enabled table with delta-rs (`pip install deltalake pyarrow`): ```python import pyarrow as pa from deltalake import DeltaTable, write_deltalake def rows(a, b): return pa.table({"k": pa.array(range(a, b), pa.int64()), "v": pa.array([7 * x for x in range(a, b)], pa.int64())}) write_deltalake("/tmp/cdf_table", rows(0, 500), mode="append", configuration={"delta.enableChangeDataFeed": "true"}) write_deltalake("/tmp/cdf_table", rows(500, 1000), mode="append") DeltaTable("/tmp/cdf_table").delete("k < 100") ``` Then, on a server: ```sql CREATE TABLE cdf_eng ENGINE = DeltaLakeLocal('/tmp/cdf_table'); -- the guard fires only if the CDF setting is in context at storage construction: CREATE TABLE cdf_eng2 ENGINE = DeltaLakeLocal('/tmp/cdf_table') SETTINGS delta_lake_snapshot_start_version = 0; -- Code: 36. DB::Exception: Delta lake CDF is allowed only for deltaLake table function. SELECT count() FROM cdf_eng; -- 900, correct SELECT count() FROM cdf_eng SETTINGS delta_lake_snapshot_start_version = 0; -- 1100 (!) — the change-stream row count, no error SELECT count(), countIf(_change_type = 'insert') FROM cdf_eng SETTINGS delta_lake_snapshot_start_version = 0; -- Code: 47 UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER `_change_type` — the meta columns don't exist on the engine's schema -- for contrast, the table function returns the actual usable stream: SELECT _change_type, count() FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/cdf_table') GROUP BY _change_type ORDER BY 1 SETTINGS delta_lake_snapshot_start_version = 0; -- delete 100 -- insert 1000 ``` **Expected behavior** One of the two coherent contracts, consistently: either the engine-table SELECT with CDF settings throws the same `Code: 36` the CREATE-time guard produces (move/duplicate the check into the read path), or engine tables genuinely support CDF, including the meta columns. **Actual behavior** The guard is decorative for existing tables: the SELECT succeeds and returns change-stream row counts that match no table version, with the meta columns unreachable. **Mechanism** `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorage.cpp`: the `is_delta_lake_cdf && !is_table_function` check runs in the constructor only; `StorageObjectStorage::read` branches into the table-changes step for any `isDataLakeConfiguration()` storage with `delta_lake_snapshot_start_version` set, with no table-function check at that point. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/100449 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104667 --- Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signal.title: DeltaLake: the legacy (non-kernel) reader silently loses rows on a deletion-vector table instead of erroring
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** With `allow_experimental_delta_kernel_rs = 0` (the legacy non-kernel DeltaLake reader, still a supported switch of a BETA-tier default), reading a Delta table that contains a deletion vector silently returns a tiny fraction of the table: 10 rows out of 310 written / 260 alive. No error, no warning — for the exact same table the kernel reader (`= 1`, the default) returns the correct 260 rows. This is worse than the reader merely not supporting deletion vectors: a DV-ignorant reader would return 310 (deleted rows resurrected). Instead, whole untouched files vanish. The table declares `minReaderVersion: 3` + `readerFeatures: ["deletionVectors"]`, which per the Delta protocol a reader without deletion-vector support must refuse to read — the legacy reader ignores the protocol action entirely and returns garbage instead of erroring. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1448, 20/20 runs. **How to reproduce** Write a table with a deletion vector using Spark (`pip install pyspark==3.5.3 delta-spark==3.2.1`, needs a JRE) — the same table as in #114933: ```python from delta import configure_spark_with_delta_pip from pyspark.sql import SparkSession b = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[1]") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension") .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")) spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(b).getOrCreate() spark.sql("CREATE TABLE t (k BIGINT, v BIGINT) USING delta LOCATION '/tmp/dv_table' TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableDeletionVectors = true)") spark.sql("INSERT INTO t SELECT id, id*10 FROM range(300)") spark.sql("DELETE FROM t WHERE k < 50") # persisted as a deletion vector, cardinality 50 spark.sql("INSERT INTO t SELECT id, id*10 FROM range(300, 310)") ``` The table holds 260 alive rows. Then: ```bash clickhouse local -q "SELECT count(), sum(k), min(k), max(k) FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table') SETTINGS optimize_trivial_count_query = 0, allow_experimental_delta_kernel_rs = 1" # 260 46670 50 309 <- kernel reader, correct clickhouse local -q "SELECT count(), sum(k), min(k), max(k) FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table') SETTINGS optimize_trivial_count_query = 0, allow_experimental_delta_kernel_rs = 0" # 10 3045 300 309 <- legacy reader: only the last append's file survives, 250 alive rows silently gone ``` **Expected behavior** Either the correct 260 rows, or — since the legacy reader does not implement deletion vectors — a hard error refusing the table: it declares `minReaderVersion: 3` with `readerFeatures: ["deletionVectors"]`, and the Delta protocol requires readers to reject tables whose reader features they do not support. **Actual behavior** 10 rows, silently. **Mechanism** `DeltaLakeMetadata::processMetadataFile` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/DeltaLakeMetadata.cpp`) folds the log into a `std::set<String>` of file paths: `add` inserts, `remove` erases. A deletion-vector `DELETE` commit re-adds the *same* data file path with a `deletionVector` field and also emits a `remove` for that path (Spark writes the `add` line before the `remove` line), so processing the commit in line order first re-inserts the path and then erases it — the 300-row file is dropped from the result entirely, leaving only the later append. Two layered problems: (1) the fold is order-sensitive within a commit and cancels a same-commit re-add, which is what loses the file; (2) even if the file survived, the reader has no deletion-vector handling and no `protocol`-action check, so it would resurrect the 50 DV-deleted rows (310) rather than error. A minimal fail-close fix is to parse the `protocol` action and refuse `minReaderVersion >= 3` / unsupported `readerFeatures`; that would turn every DV table into a clean error on the legacy path. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114933 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/100502 --- Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signal.title: Paimon: pypaimon-written MAP columns make the whole table unreadable (Unsupported Paimon type: MAP<STRING, BIGINT>)
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** A Paimon table with a `MAP` column written by pypaimon 2.0 (the official Apache Paimon Python SDK, `pip install pypaimon`) is completely unreadable by ClickHouse: both `DESCRIBE` and `SELECT` over `paimonLocal` / `paimon` fail with `Code: 36. DB::Exception: Unsupported Paimon type: MAP<STRING, BIGINT>`. The cause is a spelling mismatch in the composite-type kind. For a composite field, Java Paimon serializes the inner `type` as the bare kind (`"MAP"` / `"MAP NOT NULL"`), and ClickHouse's parser requires exactly that: `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/Types.h` strips ` NOT NULL` and then compares `real_type == "MAP"` (and `== "ARRAY"`) for equality. pypaimon 2.0 instead writes the full generic signature into that field, e.g. `"MAP<STRING NOT NULL, BIGINT>"`, so after the ` NOT NULL` strip ClickHouse is left with `MAP<STRING, BIGINT>`, the exact-match fails, and the whole table throws. The `key`/`value` element types are carried in their own JSON fields either way, so the generic arguments in the kind string are redundant — a kind-prefix match would read both spellings. `schema/schema-0` as written by pypaimon 2.0: ```json {"id": 1, "name": "m", "type": {"type": "MAP<STRING NOT NULL, BIGINT>", "key": "STRING NOT NULL", "value": "BIGINT", "nullable": true}} ``` The same table written by Java Paimon carries `"type": "MAP NOT NULL"` in that position and reads fine. `ARRAY` columns are unaffected because pypaimon spells their kind as bare `ARRAY`. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1448, 20/20 runs. **How to reproduce** Write a MAP-bearing table with pypaimon 2.0 (`pip install pypaimon pyarrow`): ```python import pyarrow as pa from pypaimon import CatalogFactory, Schema cat = CatalogFactory.create({"warehouse": "/tmp/pmap_wh"}) cat.create_database("db", ignore_if_exists=True) schema = pa.schema([("k", pa.int64()), ("m", pa.map_(pa.string(), pa.int64()))]) cat.create_table("db.t", Schema.from_pyarrow_schema(schema), ignore_if_exists=True) t = cat.get_table("db.t") wb = t.new_batch_write_builder() bw, cw = wb.new_write(), wb.new_commit() bw.write_arrow(pa.table({"k": pa.array([1, 2], pa.int64()), "m": pa.array([[("a", 1)], [("b", 2)]], pa.map_(pa.string(), pa.int64()))}, schema=schema)) cw.commit(bw.prepare_commit()) ``` Then: ```bash clickhouse local -q "DESCRIBE paimonLocal('/tmp/pmap_wh/db.db/t')" # Code: 36. DB::Exception: Unsupported Paimon type: MAP<STRING, BIGINT>. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) clickhouse local -q "SELECT * FROM paimonLocal('/tmp/pmap_wh/db.db/t')" # same error — the table is entirely unreadable, including columns other than the MAP ``` pypaimon itself reads its own table back fine, so the files are internally consistent from the Python SDK's point of view. **Expected behavior** The table reads (`m` maps to `Map(String, Int64)` with the appropriate nullability), or at minimum the non-MAP columns stay readable. **Actual behavior** `Code: 36 Unsupported Paimon type: MAP<STRING, BIGINT>` on any access to the table, `DESCRIBE` included. **Mechanism / fix direction** In `Types.h`'s composite branch, `real_type` is compared for exact equality with `"ARRAY"` / `"MAP"`. Matching the kind as a prefix (`real_type == "MAP" || real_type.starts_with("MAP<")`, same for `ARRAY`) accepts both the Java and the pypaimon spelling; the element types should keep coming from the dedicated `key` / `value` / `element` fields as today. (Arguably pypaimon's spelling is also worth an upstream report to apache/paimon-python — but tables in that format exist in the wild either way.) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113337 --- Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signal.title: Fix hang in `--queries-file` / `-q` when stdin is a pipe with no data
signal.text: `ClientBase` eagerly called `isStdinNotEmptyAndValid` to check for trailing stdin data on every `INSERT`. That helper calls `!std_in.eof()`, which performs a blocking `read(0, ...)`. When stdin is a pipe that is open but has no data and no `EOF` (common in CI, Docker, stress tests, and `--queries-file` invocations), the read blocks indefinitely and the client hangs until it is killed by timeout. Concretely, this caused an exception (signal 11 after timeout) in the stress test `03538_analyzer_scalar_correlated_subquery_fix`: the process hung on `read(0, ...)` and was killed. The fix replaces the eager blocking probe with a non-blocking one: `poll(timeout=0)` first asks "does stdin appear to have data right now?", and only when it does we fall through to `isStdinNotEmptyAndValid` to confirm and consume it. This: - avoids the hang on open empty pipes — `poll` returns 0 immediately; - preserves deterministic rejection of `inlined data + stdin` mixed input — when stdin actually contains data (the case asserted by `04064_inline_insert_data`), `poll` returns `POLLIN` and we still throw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`; - is best-effort by design: a slow producer pipe (e.g. `(sleep 1; echo) | clickhouse-client ...`) may not have written by the time `poll` runs, in which case the trailing stdin payload is ignored. This is preferable to the alternative of a hard hang, and is documented in the helper. Covered cases (`is_async_insert_with_inlined_data`, `is_inline_insert_data`, and the appending-stdin path in `sendData`) all go through the same probe so the hang is closed for `--queries-file`, `-q`, and `--inline-insert-data` modes. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=b9e68f4b9b0b33c7db43b00afb3eff4ff2050694&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_debug%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a hang in `clickhouse-client` for `INSERT` queries in `--queries-file`/`-q`/`--inline-insert-data` mode when stdin is an open pipe with no data and no `EOF` (common in CI, Docker, and stress tests). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)
