signal.title: Avoid copying data for the NONE compression codec when writing
signal.text: Avoid copying data for the `NONE` compression codec when writing. For `CODEC(NONE)` the compressed block on disk is byte-identical to the input, so the payload does not need to be copied between the compressor's working buffer and the output buffer. When a `CompressedWriteBuffer` exclusively owns its output buffer, the working buffer is now pointed directly into the output buffer (reserving room for the checksum and header in front of the data), so the caller writes the uncompressed data straight to where it will be flushed; `nextImpl` only fills in the header and checksum in place, with no payload copy. The header is written by a new `ICompressionCodec::writeHeader` helper factored out of `compress`. When the output buffer is too small, the writer falls back to the previous owned-buffer copy path. This is the same zero-copy buffer-aliasing technique that `HashingWriteBuffer` already uses. The zero-copy path (`out_buffer_is_exclusive`) is enabled only where the compressor is the sole, sequential writer of its output buffer: the wide-part column data streams, the primary-index stream, and the temporary-data buffer. It is intentionally left off where the output buffer is shared and written interleaved — the per-column streams of compact parts (which share one `plain_hashing`) and the network protocol buffer (interleaved with raw packet framing) — because there the reserved window could be overwritten by another writer. It is also left off for the marks streams of wide and compact parts: their `marks_file` has a small fixed-size buffer (4096 bytes), so the direct path would clamp `NONE`-coded mark blocks to it instead of the configured `marks_compress_block_size`; the regression test `04539_marks_compression_codec_none_block_size` covers this. Note: for `NONE`, compressed block sizes become bounded by the output buffer size, so the on-disk byte layout can differ slightly from before (an occasional shorter block at buffer boundaries). This is deterministic and does not affect reads. The read side already decompresses `NONE` data directly into the destination column via `readBig`, so no change is needed there. ### Performance evidence Measured with two `clickhouse` binaries built from the same base commit, differing only by this PR (cherry-picked onto the same parent), so the comparison isolates exactly this change. Isolated write-path microbenchmark — 4 GiB through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with the `NONE` codec into a discarding sink (no disk), 1 MiB blocks and output buffer, toggling only `out_buffer_is_exclusive`: | `out_buffer_is_exclusive` | throughput | |---|---| | `false` (old copy path) | ~8.5–9.2 GB/s | | `true` (zero-copy path) | ~13.6–14.0 GB/s | | **speedup** | **~1.5–1.6x** | End-to-end `INSERT` of 8 wide `String CODEC(NONE)` columns (3M rows, single insert thread, no dedup/squashing/sparse, merges stopped; baseline = exact parent commit; median of interleaved reps): **2.96s → 2.62s (~1.13x, ~13% faster)**. The end-to-end gain is below the disk-free microbenchmark because disk I/O and data generation (equal in both binaries) dominate the rest of the insert. A focused performance test, `tests/performance/codec_none_read.xml`, is added. It scans `CODEC(NONE)` columns, so in the PR-vs-master comparison the table is filled by each side's own write path (old vs new block layout) and then read by the identical read code. This guards against a read regression from the slightly changed `NONE` block layout, and tracks `NONE` read throughput in general (relevant for incompressible data such as vector embeddings). Measured read time is unchanged before/after (~0.62s vs ~0.61s for 100M rows, single thread), confirming the write-path change is read-neutral. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid an extra data copy when writing columns and temporary data compressed with the `NONE` codec by writing the data directly into the output buffer. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Push down volume-reducing functions in query plan
signal.text: Adds a query plan optimization that pushes volume-reducing functions (`length`, `lengthUTF8`, `empty`, `notEmpty`) below the `Sorting` and `Filter` steps, so those steps carry the fixed-size result instead of the original `String` / `FixedString` argument. The rewrite is done with `ActionsDAG::split`: the function nodes form the first part, which becomes a new step below the child, and the second part becomes the parent step's `ActionsDAG` and reads the results as inputs. It only fires when the wide argument column really stops flowing through the child step — the column is removed from the child's output, and unless the child reads it itself it is not even produced below the child. `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` and `trySplitFilter` keep the pushed functions where they are, so the optimizations do not move the same nodes in opposite directions. For the shape from the issue below, `SELECT avg(length(s)) FROM test WHERE notEmpty(s)`, the filter still needs `s` to evaluate its condition, but `length(s)` is now computed before the filter, so the wide column is not copied for the surviving rows. Enabled by default; can be turned off with `query_plan_push_down_volume_reducing_functions = 0`. An earlier attempt at the same optimization was https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86139 by @talmawash, credited as a co-author. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/82378 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86139 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a query plan optimization that pushes volume-reducing functions (`length`, `lengthUTF8`, `empty`, `notEmpty`) below the `Sorting` and `Filter` steps, replacing the wide `String` / `FixedString` argument with the fixed-size result, so it is neither buffered by a sort nor copied by a filter. Controlled by the new setting `query_plan_push_down_volume_reducing_functions`, enabled by default. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Disable the sampling query profiler under Memory Sanitizer
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100242 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106591 Every `MemorySanitizer` report produced in CI since 2026-05-28 is truncated to a single line: ``` ==117==WARNING: MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value MemorySanitizer: nested bug in the same thread, aborting. ``` No stack trace, no `SUMMARY`, no origin — so no MSan failure can be located. In the CI database, `msan` checks recorded 1009 reports with a usable stack in 2026-04 and 0 in 2026-07, while `asan`, `tsan` and `ubsan` reports are unaffected and still carry full stacks. The regression window matches #100242 (merged 2026-05-28), which enabled the sampling query profiler for sanitizer builds. Printing an MSan report takes the sanitizer runtime seconds, because it symbolizes every frame through an `llvm-symbolizer` subprocess, and it holds `ScopedErrorReportLock` for the whole time. A profiler signal delivered to that thread meanwhile runs instrumented code in the handler and trips a second MSan check; compiler-rt treats a same-thread re-entry into the report lock as unrecoverable, writes `nested bug in the same thread, aborting.` with `CatastrophicErrorWrite` and calls `internal__exit`, so the report that was already being written to `MSAN_OPTIONS=log_path` stops after its header line. Reproduced with the `arm_msan` binary built from master `3885f7b7bbf1`, running the same query against the same server three times and forcing a sanitizer report with `max_allocation_size_mb=32 allocator_may_return_null=0`: | configuration | result | | --- | --- | | profiler on (default `global_profiler_real_time_period_ns`) | `nested bug in the same thread, aborting.`, 1-line report | | `<trace_log remove="1"/>` (no profiler at all) | full 31-line report with stack | | `trace_log` on, `global_profiler_*_period_ns = 0`, per-query profiler off | full 31-line report with stack | So it is the profiler timer signals, not the trace collector. This turns `QUERY_PROFILER_SUPPORTED` off under MSan, next to the existing TSan-on-macOS exclusion. The trace collector stays enabled: the memory profiler, `trace_profile_events` and `SYSTEM INSTRUMENT` all feed it from ordinary code rather than from a signal handler. Other sanitizers keep the profiler, because their checks fire only on genuinely invalid accesses, which the handler does not perform. `00974_query_profiler` and `01569_query_profiler_big_query_id` assert that samples reach `system.trace_log`, so they get `no-msan` back. The other profiler and `trace_log` tests either already carry `no-msan`, exercise the memory profiler / `trace_profile_events` / `SYSTEM INSTRUMENT` (unaffected), or make no assertion on sample counts. This does not fix the uninitialized read that the `BuzzHouse (amd_msan)` run below hit — that one is unidentifiable as reported. It makes the next occurrence diagnosable. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=3885f7b7bbf1b8791021e1c97ca2e4eea132de04&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_msan%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signal.title: Preserve unchanged TOAST values in MaterializedPostgreSQL
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83517 Preserve PostgreSQL columns encoded as unchanged TOAST references in `MaterializedPostgreSQL` replication instead of replacing them with default values. The consumer resolves the previous value from an earlier row in the same replication buffer when possible. Otherwise, it reads the current row from the nested `ReplacingMergeTree` by replica identity, batching key lookups to avoid a query per value. The old replica identity tuple is used when an update changes the key. An unchanged TOAST value in a replica identity column is rejected because the replication message does not contain a value that could identify the row. The integration test covers a regular update, multiple updates of the same row in one PostgreSQL transaction, and a replica identity change. The user-facing documentation is updated for both `MaterializedPostgreSQL` engines. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `MaterializedPostgreSQL` now preserves unchanged PostgreSQL `TOAST` values during updates instead of replacing them with default values.

signal.title: Parallelize read-in-order from a single part with PrefetchingConcatProcessor
signal.text: When a single MergeTree part is split into multiple streams for read-in-order, use the new `PrefetchingConcatProcessor` instead of relying on the downstream `MergingSortedTransform`. The key difference: - `MergingSortedTransform` marks all inputs as needed but only consumes from one stream at a time (for non-overlapping ranges), and each port can only buffer 1 block — so after initial prefetch, reading becomes sequential. - `PrefetchingConcatProcessor` marks all inputs as needed AND pulls data from non-current inputs into internal buffers, keeping upstream sources busy. It outputs data in strict input order (concatenation), which is correct because ranges from a single part are non-overlapping and pre-sorted. This avoids both the merge comparison overhead and the sort overhead, while enabling true parallel IO and filtering across range groups. Benchmark on 100M rows (4 threads, single part, poor PK selectivity): - Single-thread read-in-order: 1.57s - Parallel + sort (no read-in-order): 1.27s - PrefetchingConcat: 0.61s (2.6x faster) ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve the performance of queries that are reading in the order of the primary key. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes read-in-order execution and introduces a new buffering processor in the query pipeline; incorrect gating or backpressure/buffering behavior could impact result ordering or memory usage in some MergeTree reads. > > **Overview** > **Adds `PrefetchingConcatProcessor`**: a new concat-like processor that keeps *all* inputs marked needed and buffers per-input chunks (bounded by `max_buffered_chunks`) to prefetch non-current streams while still outputting streams strictly in order. > > **Wires it into MergeTree read-in-order**: `ReadFromMergeTree` now conditionally replaces `MergingSortedTransform` with `PrefetchingConcatProcessor` when reading in ascending order from a *single part* split into multiple streams and only when there is filtering work (`PREWHERE` or row-level filter); it also adds `prefer_multiple_streams`/`setPreferMultipleStreams()` so aggregation-/distinct-in-order paths can opt out to avoid collapsing parallel streams. > > **Tests/bench coverage updated**: adds a new stateless test asserting `PrefetchingConcat` appears only for single-part reads and preserves sort order, adjusts an existing buffering test to force multi-part behavior, and adds a performance scenario guarding against regressions for filter-less `ORDER BY` reads. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit c0ba40d2f630976681024d2ac941261c4abdbe57. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: Fix reading a tuple element through a positional Tuple structure hint
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114991 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114991 Reading a tuple element through a positional structure hint returned default values instead of the file's data. Over a Parquet file written as `t Tuple(x UInt64, y String)`: ```sql SELECT tupleElement(t, 1) FROM file('p.parquet', Parquet, 't Tuple(UInt64, String)'); -- returned 0, 0, 0 instead of 0, 1, 2 ``` `WHERE tupleElement(t, 1) = 1` matched no rows, and with `input_format_parquet_allow_missing_columns = 0` the query failed with `THERE_IS_NO_COLUMN`. Silent wrong results, on default settings. Root cause: an unnamed tuple names its elements `1`, `2`, ..., so `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` rewrote `tupleElement(t, 1)` to the subcolumn `t.1`. The existing guards there consult the storage snapshot, which is built from the structure argument and does contain `t.1`. The Parquet reader then resolves a flattened element name by string against the file's real field names `t.x`, `t.y`, found no match, and substituted a missing column filled with defaults. The fix suppresses the rewrite when the element name is a bare ordinal and the source resolves subcolumn names against a file schema. Named hints keep their pushdown, and storages serving subcolumns from their own metadata (MergeTree and friends) are unaffected. This regressed in #113383 and is master-only: that merge is an ancestor of no release branch and is in no release tag, hence `Not for changelog`. That category also skips `Bugfix validation`, so the reddening check below is the evidence. Validated on a Debug build, with a regression arm added to `04706_tuple_subcolumn_pushdown_parquet`: - Reddening: removing only the new guard term makes the new arm fail while the pre-existing arms stay green. - Preservation: `t.x` pushdown survives for a named hint by name and by ordinal, and `t.1` still pushes down for MergeTree's unnamed tuple. - `04706`, `04707`, `04708`, `04873` pass; a `subcolumn`/`tuple_element`/`functions_to_subcolumns` sweep has no failure absent from an unmodified-master control; 50 randomized runs pass.

signal.title: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend
signal.text: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106136 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes silently missing rows when a query filters on `intDiv(constant, key)` or `divide(constant, key)`. Primary-key and partition analysis reports the wrong direction of monotonicity for a constant divided by a key column, so matching granules are pruned away and the query returns fewer rows with no error. Also fixes `intDiv` with an unsigned constant dividend whose high bit is set, stops claiming monotonicity when a `Decimal` operand makes the division compute in the decimal's native width, and stops key analysis from raising `Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long` for a valid query that divides an `IPv4`/`IPv6` constant by a key column. ### Description `FunctionBinaryArithmetic::getMonotonicityForRange` reports the direction of `c / x` incorrectly in its `const / variable` branch, so `KeyCondition::applyMonotonicFunctionsChainToRange` inverts the transformed range exactly when it must not, the range matches no granule, and matching rows are dropped with no error and exit code 0. Reproduced at completely default settings (no `SETTINGS` clause), 20000-row `Int32`-keyed MergeTree: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t WHERE intDiv(toInt32(-1000000), a) >= 11; -- keyed MergeTree: 0 ENGINE = Memory oracle: 10909 ``` #### Root cause For `f(x) = c / x` on an interval excluding 0, `d/dx (c/x) = -c/x²`, whose sign is `-sign(c)` for every `x != 0` — the `x²` denominator is positive on both sides of 0. So the direction is governed by `sign(c)` alone and is the *same* on the negative and the positive branch; only the values differ. The code instead treated the two arms as needing opposite polarity, which is the intuition that `1/x` "flips" across the branches. It does not: it is monotone on each branch separately, which is exactly why the strict range-sign guards are there. The two arms are now one return with a single `!is_constant_positive`, and the strict guards are kept verbatim. Fixing only that is not sufficient, and on its own would be *worse* than the current code for one shape. Three further defects live in the same branch: * **Unsigned constant dividend.** `intDiv` casts the dividend through `make_signed_t` whenever either operand is a signed integer (`DivisionUtils.h`), so an unsigned constant whose high bit is set divides as negative — `intDiv(toUInt8(200), x)` is `intDiv(toInt8(-56), x)` — while the raw `Field` still compares as positive. The boundary is `2^(8 * width - 1)` of the dividend's own width (verified for 8/16/32/64/128/256-bit dividends; the divisor width is irrelevant). This is reachable with no cast at all, because the literal `200` is `UInt8`. On a *negative* range the un-negated arm is accidentally correct for this shape, so adding the missing `!` alone would turn a correct answer into a wrong one. A new `intDivConstDividendReinterpretsNegative` helper corrects the effective sign; it deliberately does not reuse the existing `intDivConstReinterpretsNegative`, whose width early-out has the opposite polarity here. * **`Decimal` operand.** With a `Decimal` on either operand and no `Float` operand, the division computes in the decimal's native width (`DecimalBinaryOperation` casts both operands to `NativeResultType` and substitutes the integral operation even for `divide`). The divisor is then truncated, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), x)` is periodic in `x` with period `2^32` and not even monotonic. Nothing is claimed for that combination, mirroring the rejection the sibling `variable / constant` branch already performs. A `Decimal`/`Float` pair is exempt: it is converted to `Float64` before the operation, never truncates, and is itself a carrier of the direction defect, so those shapes are fixed rather than rejected. The rejection is deliberately keyed on the operand types and not on the constant's value, so it also covers a *zero* dividend and therefore runs ahead of the `constant == 0` fast path. That ordering is load-bearing: the truncation moves where the quotient is defined, so a range that strictly excludes 0 can still contain a point where the function is undefined, which is exactly what the zero-constant guard assumes away. With `Decimal32` the divisor truncates to `Int32`, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), key)` over an `Int64` key range around `2^32` raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`; letting the zero guard win would claim monotonicity, prune the raising row away, and return a silent answer instead. Pinned by `c5iv`. * **Non-numeric operand (pre-existing exception on a valid query).** `IPv4`/`IPv6` are substituted with `UInt32`/`UInt128`, so their declared width does not describe the arithmetic, and their raw `Field` cannot be compared with a numeric zero. Two existing comparisons against zero therefore raise `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD "Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long"` during key analysis today: one in the single-value fast path (reached when a granule's min equals its max) and one in the zero-constant guard (reached otherwise). Both roles are affected — `intDiv(toIPv4('192.168.0.1'), numeric_key)` and `intDiv(1, ipv4_key)` — and one of them fires even when the key range spans 0. A numeric gate hoisted above the fast path removes both; after it each query returns the correct rows with no pruning. Placing the gate inside the `const / variable` block would cover only the second site, which the new test pins at two granularities. Scope note: "both roles" here means the IP value as the dividend constant and as the key column, both with the constant on the left. The mirror shape, an IP constant as the *divisor* (`intDiv(numeric_key, toIPv4(...))`), still raises the same exception, as do `plus`/`minus`/`multiply` with an `IPv4`/`IPv6` operand. Both are pre-existing (measured byte-identical on `origin/master`) and are tracked separately rather than widened into this PR, since a correct fix for them also has to touch the `multiply` arm and the shared fast path. #### Behaviour changes to be aware of * **Two pre-existing key-analysis exceptions disappear.** As above, a non-numeric operand now reports non-monotonic instead of raising, so the query succeeds unpruned. This is a scope extension beyond "fix the direction", included because those same comparisons against zero are the mechanism being corrected and an exception on a valid query is a bug either way. * **Pruning is lost for `Decimal` shapes with no `Float` operand.** Measured with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`: | shape | before | after | |---|---|---| | `Decimal32(0)` key, `intDiv(toInt32(-1000), a) = -25`, positive range | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 4/4` | | `UInt64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), a) = 250` | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 3/4` | | `Int64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), a) = 5`, range around `2^32` | `Granules: 0/2` | `Granules: 2/2` | The first two queries return the same rows before and after — the index simply stops filtering. The third is the zero-dividend case: it must stop pruning, because the pruned plan silently returned `0` for a query that correctly raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`. This mirrors the decision already shipped for the `variable / constant` branch, where the same truncation applies. `Decimal`/`Float` pairs keep pruning and are additionally fixed. No committed reference in the repository changes. * **Everything else keeps pruning.** Strictly-positive ranges with a signed constant, both-unsigned operands, `Float` divisors, and unsigned key ranges crossing the divisor's own `2^(8W-1)` are all unaffected. That last group is worth naming: the *values* jump across the wrap while the *order* is preserved, which satisfies the non-strict definition of `Monotonicity`, so rejecting them would delete pruning that is correct today. The new test pins them, with plan-level assertions. #### Testing `04651_intdiv_const_variable_monotonicity` compares a keyed MergeTree against an identical `ENGINE = Memory` table on the same data, so each of its 84 count rows prints `1` when index-based pruning agrees with the full-scan ground truth. It covers both range signs for both functions and both constant signs, unsigned dividends at several widths, `Decimal` in either role plus the `Decimal`/`Float` exemption, `Float64`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable` keys, ranges that span zero or have zero as an endpoint, the unsigned wrap shapes, and the `IPv4`/`IPv6` cases at two granularities. Ten further rows assert with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` that the surviving shapes still prune (so the fix cannot silently degrade into "no pruning at all") and that the zero-dividend `Decimal` shape stops pruning — 94 asserted rows in total. On a master-HEAD binary the test fails: 28 rows print `0` and it then aborts with `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD`. On this branch it passes, including 50/50 runs with randomized settings. Each of the four edits was mutation-tested individually — reverting the negation, the sign correction, the `Decimal` rejection, the `Float` exemption, the numeric gate, the gate's hoisted position and its role restriction each make specific named rows fail. `index_granularity` decides whether the range handed to `getMonotonicityForRange` is strictly negative, strictly positive or spans zero, so it is pinned per DDL and the test carries `no-random-merge-tree-settings` with that reason stated inline.

signal.title: Use Gaussian centroids for truncated QBit codes
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109405 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110911 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve reduced-precision `L2DistanceTransposedQuantized`, `cosineDistanceTransposedQuantized`, and `dotProductTransposedQuantized` by reconstructing `p < 8` `QBit(Int8)` codes with Gaussian conditional-mean prefix centroids. Full precision (`p = 8`) remains bit-exact; reduced-precision approximate distances may change, and recall/latency gains are workload-dependent. ### Motivation The existing reduced-precision path selects one middle fine Lloyd-Max reconstruction level for every truncated prefix. That value is not the conditional mean of the complete Gaussian interval represented by the prefix. This change uses the conditional mean `(phi(lo) - phi(hi)) / (Phi(hi) - Phi(lo))` which minimizes scalar MSE for that prefix under the standard-normal source model of the existing Lloyd-Max codec. The 127 positive values are evaluated from the existing `Float32` boundaries at high precision, rounded once to `Float32`, stored as hexadecimal literals, and mirrored exactly for negative prefixes. This keeps the hot distance loop as one LUT lookup and avoids platform-dependent libm work during LUT initialization. ### Validation - A new stateless regression fails on the exact official `26.7.1.1315` binary for all 20 reduced-precision centroid/sign checks and passes its `p = 8` control. The candidate passes all 20 checks and the control. - An independent all-raw probe covers every raw byte and every `p = 1..8`: expected level counts, finiteness, symmetry, prefix-block invariance, index-order monotonicity, independent Gaussian means (maximum 0 ULP), and bit-exact legacy `p = 8` reconstruction. - An engine probe covers all raw bytes and precisions, non-strided and `QBit(Int8, 16, 8)`, `used_dims` 8/16, dot/L2/cosine, and `optimize_qbit_distance_function_reads` 0/1. Partial-read modes match bitwise; bounded SimSIMD tolerances are used for L2/cosine. - Debug `programs/clickhouse` build passes. Updated `04504_transposed_distance_quantized` and new `04628_qbit_lloyd_max_prefix_centroid` match their references with empty stderr in clean `clickhouse local` paths. On 103,000 source-disjoint Nomic embedding vectors (768 dimensions, 200 queries, four randomized-Hadamard seeds), scalar coordinate MSE decreases at every changed precision. The transformed-space retrieval proxy is deliberately reported separately because it is not a production ClickHouse latency benchmark: | `p` | scalar MSE delta | recall@10 delta (pp) | hit@1 delta (pp) | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | -3.83% | 0.000 | 0.000 | | 2 | -3.49% | -0.250 | -0.375 | | 3 | -0.89% | +0.538 | +0.750 | | 4 | -15.17% | +1.738 | +1.625 | | 5 | -17.70% | +1.300 | +1.875 | | 6 | -24.08% | +0.800 | +0.125 | | 7 | -44.32% | +0.588 | +0.250 | | 8 | unchanged | 0.000 | 0.000 | There is no universal retrieval improvement claim: `p = 2` regresses slightly in this proxy. There is also no latency claim until a matched Release-build p50/p95 benchmark is available. The intentional compatibility boundary is numerical output at `p < 8`; function signatures, storage, and `p = 8` results are unchanged. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1507` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.4.48` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Build Debian packages for the release builds only
signal.text: The `Stress test` was the only job installing the Debian packages of the debug, sanitizer and CFI builds, and it can take the plain `clickhouse` binary instead — that binary is built and uploaded for every build type anyway. Every other consumer of the packages (`Install packages`, `Compatibility check`, `Upgrade check`, the server Docker images and the release jobs) runs on a release build. So the release builds keep their packages, and nine of the eleven packaging steps go away, together with the `DESTDIR` install that copies the whole binary, and the upload and download of the resulting packages. The stress test now sets up the paths the packages own from the binary: `install_binary` in `stress_tests.lib` symlinks `/usr/bin/clickhouse*` at it, installs the default `config.xml` and `users.xml`, and unpacks the self-extracting archive up front — decompressing a sanitizer build under `clickhouse start` would eat into its wait for the pid file and race any concurrent `clickhouse local`. `install_packages` stays for the upgrade check, which installs an actual release. Symbolization is unaffected: `clickhouse_split_debug_symbols` leaves `programs/clickhouse` untouched and strips only the copy it installs, so the binary artifact carries its debug info even for a release build. For the sanitizer builds `clickhouse-common-static-dbg` was empty to begin with, since they do not set `SPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1500` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Retry the SQLStorm repo clones so one transient timeout cannot abort the check
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `SQLStorm test` failed on step `Clone OLAPBench repo` after a single attempt: ``` fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/SQL-Storm/OLAPBench.git/': Failed to connect to github.com port 443 after 135221 ms: Connection timed out ERROR: command failed after 1/1 attempt(s), exit code: 128 ``` `Shell.check` forwards `retries` to `Shell.run` and both default to `retries=1` (`ci/praktika/utils.py:231`, `:323`), and neither clone in `ci/jobs/sqlstorm_test.py` opted in. Because every later step is gated on `results[-1].is_ok()`, one transient egress timeout to a third-party host aborted a check whose budget is 3 hours. This passes `retries=3` to both `git clone` calls, matching the existing git-clone retry at `ci/jobs/docker_server.py:439-444`. The sibling SQLStorm clone has identical exposure, so both are fixed. Measured, driving the real closures with the upstream command strings and a git shim that reproduces the observed failure (rc=128, and git removes its own partial target, so a retry starts clean): | attempts that fail | before | after | |---|---|---| | 1 (the observed failure) | fails, `1/1` | succeeds on attempt 2 | | 2 | fails, `1/1` | succeeds on attempt 3 | | all | fails, `1/1` | fails, `3/3` | A genuine outage still fails the check, with the full stderr, and each argument is independently load-bearing. Worst case on a permanent outage is about 6.8 min, 3.8% of the 10,800 s job budget; a fast permanent error costs 6.0 s. The `fetch` branches, taken when the repo directory already exists, now carry the same `retries=3` and measure the same way. That branch is unreachable in CI, since every job block scheduling this check runs an unconditional `rm -rf ./ci/tmp` before the run step, but it is reachable on a local rerun, where no workflow step runs and praktika never removes its temp dir. Both `git checkout` calls are local only. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1505` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Replace the AggregatingInOrderTransform cancellation test with a failpoint integration test
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110104 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107941 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110104 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107941 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `04512_aggregation_in_order_cancellation.sh` guards the per-key-interval cancellation check from #110104, but asserts on aggregation CPU as a multiple of scan CPU after a shell-issued `KILL`. It prints `not cancelled in time` on master again: 6 such failures on 2026-08-13 (2 on master, 4 on unrelated PRs), 5 on `amd_asan_ubsan, distributed plan, parallel`. Eighth rewrite of the assertion. The oracle prices the window between "rows are read" and "the `KILL` flips `is_cancelled`", and two `clickhouse-client` startups sit on that path; `04410_primes_source_cancellation.sh:48-49` records ~8 s for one invocation on a loaded sanitizer build. On all five failures that printed the CPU diagnostics the checkpoint was firing, stopping at 48-75 % of the loop, not 100 %: only the window grew, and the shell cannot close it, since read progress is published only after the source's `work()` returns (`ExecutionThreadContext.cpp:57-75`). So this adopts the mechanism `LimitByTransform` already uses (`e20a67394329867` and follow-ups): a `PAUSEABLE_ONCE` failpoint on interval 6, after the cancellation check and inside the loop, a `LOG_TEST` marker in the existing cancellation branch, and an integration test that pauses there, kills, resumes and asserts the marker appears exactly once. No timing, no threshold, no free constant. Exactly once, not merely present: `is_cancelled` latches, so dropping only the `return` prints the marker once per remaining interval (94 here) while every other assertion still passes. Mid-loop matters for the same reason: a pre-loop pause resumes straight into the first `isCancelled()`, staying green with that check hoisted out of the loop, which is what #110104 fixed. All three mutations (checkpoint deleted, check hoisted, `return` deleted) redden the new test, the failpoint still pausing in each so no arm is vacuous. Removing `SYSTEM ENABLE FAILPOINT` fails loudly; `test_limit_by_transform_kill_query` stays green. Hot-path cost is not measurable, and dropping the 40 M-row fixture removes its `max_estimated_execution_time` exposure. `04409_skip_index_build_cancellation.sh` has a weaker form of the same pattern (bounded `KILL ... SYNC` at `timeout 10`); left unchanged.

signal.title: Revert "Revert "Use a lock-free queue for asynchronous logging""
signal.text: Reintroduces #107363, reverted in #112793, together with the fix for the shutdown race it exposed. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107363 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112793 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112753 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110816 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Asynchronous logging now uses a bounded lock-free queue: threads writing log messages never block on a mutex or wake up the logging threads. ### Description Replace the mutex + `condition_variable` + deque based `AsyncLogMessageQueue` with the lock-free Vyukov queue from `NonblockingBoundedQueue.h`, and remove the wrapper class entirely: threads writing log messages just `tryPush` (dropping on overflow), and the consumer threads poll their queues, sleeping for 10 ms when there is nothing to dequeue, so producers never block on a mutex or pay for a futex wake. The warning about messages dropped on overflow is now generated by the consumer after it has drained the queue, so it coalesces per overflow episode and cannot displace real messages. ### What is different from the reverted version The second commit folds in the fix originally submitted as #112753, which must land together with this change rather than after it. `clickhouse-local` never stopped the asynchronous logging threads (one `AsyncLogger` per log channel plus `AsyncTextLog`) started by `Loggers::buildLoggers`. Unlike the server, where `~BaseDaemon` calls `stopLogging`, `LocalServer` had no such call, so `OwnAsyncSplitChannel::close` never ran and the threads were still consuming the log queues while `exit` ran static destructors. That was a pre-existing defect, but the previous consumers blocked in `condition_variable::wait` forever, so at process exit ThreadSanitizer saw them as still running and ignored them. The polling consumers introduced here reach the finished state instead, and ThreadSanitizer reports finished but unjoined threads as leaks: ``` WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: thread leak (pid=460390) Thread T3 'AsyncLogger' (tid=460394, finished) created by main thread at: #3 DB::OwnAsyncSplitChannel::open() src/Loggers/OwnSplitChannel.cpp:276:25 #4 Loggers::buildLoggers(...) src/Loggers/Loggers.cpp:297:12 #5 DB::LocalServer::processConfig() programs/local/LocalServer.cpp:1321:9 ``` Since sanitizers run with `abort_on_error=1`, the report aborts `clickhouse-local`. The `Scraping system tables` CI step dumps every `system.*_log` table with a separate `clickhouse-local` invocation, so an affected run reports those dumps as failed. The `amd_msan` `use-of-uninitialized-value` in `OwnPatternFormatter::formatExtended` is the same shutdown race caught in the act: the `AsyncLogger` thread was still formatting a message using Poco's static priority-name strings after `exit` had destroyed them. The fix mirrors `BaseDaemon`: `~LocalServer` stops and joins the asynchronous logging threads (`OwnAsyncSplitChannel::close` flushes the queues before joining), so they never overlap with static destruction. Exit codes are unchanged on both the success and the error path. The folded diff is byte-identical to #112753, which was green on a base that already contained #107363, so the combination in this pull request is the one that was tested there. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Fix LOGICAL_ERROR in normal projection optimization with correlated subqueries
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/103695 (same `Invalid number of columns in chunk pushed to OutputPort` error family) ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a `LOGICAL_ERROR` raised when a normal projection was used to read the input of a correlated subquery (decorrelated into a join) and all parts were served from the projection. Depending on the settings it was reported as `Invalid number of columns in chunk pushed to OutputPort` or as `Block structure mismatch in joined block stream`. It is an exception in release builds and aborts the server in debug and sanitizer builds. ### Description Found by the AST fuzzer, reproduces on current master and is unrelated to the pull requests it was seen on: [amd_msan on #100332](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100332&sha=766a499fbbfcfb5b1cbd865a4f435f75c7b5ee28&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_msan%29) (STID 2270-3452), [amd_tsan on #92472](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=92472&sha=0d58afae81ce01111323d3f73a59d6d032d199f7&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29) (STID 0993-3a3c), and `Stress test (arm_debug)` on #108289. Root cause: `optimizeUseNormalProjections` reads the projection over `required_columns = reading->getAllColumnNames()`. Columns of that set which the rebuilt `query.dag` does not consume survive as pass-throughs, because `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` appends every un-consumed input, and they widen the rewritten read's output header. The all-parts-from-projection branch spliced that widened node into the plan without the `blocksHaveEqualStructure` check the Union branch already had, so a downstream step received more columns than its declared header. The default `query_plan_remove_unused_columns = 1` masks both asserts by re-narrowing the stream, so CI hits this only under `compatibility = '25.3'`. Change: hoist the materialize-constants and equal-structure guard so it protects both replacement branches, and on a mismatch skip the projection and keep the regular read. `filterPartsByProjection` mutates the parent analysis result in place, so it now runs only after the check passes and a skipped projection no longer drops parts from the regular read. `has_parent_parts` therefore moves ahead of the filter, computed non-destructively as "does any remaining part belong to `best_candidate->parent_parts`" (equivalent, because the filter keeps exactly those parts). The skipped candidate's stat description is rewritten so `EXPLAIN projections = 1` reports the rejection. Validation: both carriers and both asserts abort before the change and run cleanly after, and projection-on results equal projection-off results. Removing only the hoisted check from the fixed build makes all of them abort again with the original messages. Regression tests for both carriers are in `04410_normal_projection_correlated_subquery_part_offset`. The guard only skips the optimization for queries that were previously failing. <details><summary>Both carriers: error signatures</summary> Carrier 1, virtual columns (`_part_offset` in the projection), output port assert: ``` Invalid number of columns in chunk pushed to OutputPort. Expected 2, found 4 src/Processors/Port.h:425 src/Processors/Transforms/JoiningTransform.cpp:101 DB::JoiningTransform::prepare() ``` Carrier 2, real columns. The inner decorrelation join's right side carries exactly one column by design, so the leaked columns trip its structure check instead of the output port one: ``` Block structure mismatch in joined block stream: different number of columns: __table3.timestamp UInt64 UInt64(size = 0) __table3.timestamp UInt64 UInt64(size = 2), payload String String(size = 2), id UUID Sparse(size = 2, UUID(size = 1), UInt64(size = 0)) src/Core/Block.cpp:863 DB::assertBlocksHaveEqualStructureAllowReplicated src/Interpreters/ConstantJoin.cpp:230 DB::ConstantJoin::addBlockToJoin src/Processors/Transforms/JoiningTransform.cpp:373 DB::FillingRightJoinSideTransform::work() ``` `correlated_subqueries_use_in_memory_buffer = 0` selects the `ConstantJoin` assert; adding `correlated_subqueries_default_join_kind = 'left'` selects the output port one. Runnable reproducers for both are the statements in the new test file. </details>

signal.title: Precompute hashes and prefetch for fixed-size-keys aggregation methods
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104475 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): For the `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256` family of aggregation methods (several fixed-size keys packed into one integer), precompute the per-row canonical hashes in one pass over the batch-packed keys and reuse them to software-prefetch the target bucket and to skip rehashing the key in `emplace`. Previously the look-ahead prefetch computed every key and its hash twice per row. --- This extends the precomputed-hash + prefetch mechanism that #104475 introduced for the `prealloc_serialized` family to `HashMethodKeysFixed` (multi-key `GROUP BY` over numeric columns, e.g. ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q32). When the whole block of keys is batch-packed upfront (`prepared_keys`), the per-row canonical hashes are computed in one pass on the first `emplace`/`find` call and reused both for the look-ahead prefetch and for the insert itself, replacing the generic look-ahead in `Aggregator::executeImplBatch` that builds every key holder and hashes it a second time per row. Details: - The runtime gates mirror `prealloc_serialized`: batch-packed keys available, `enable_software_prefetch_in_aggregation`, and the `min_bytes_for_prefetch` hash-table size threshold (checked lazily on the first call, when `Data` is known). Nullable and low-cardinality variants never use `prepared_keys` and are excluded at compile time. - A new concept `HasPrefetchByHashMemberFunc` compiles the path out for tables without hash-addressed buckets (`FixedHashTable` behind `keys16`). Set, JOIN and `arrayUniq`-style callers of `HashMethodKeysFixed` pass no settings context, so nothing changes for them. - `HashMethodSerializedContext` carried only the settings and is now the shared `HashMethodSettingsContext`, also used by `HashMethodKeysFixed::createContext`. - `HashTable::isEmptyCell` (the `findKey` short-circuit for precomputed hashes, used in the `no_more_keys` mode) is made zero-key-aware: the zero key is stored outside the buffer, so an empty cell at the key's place proves nothing when the zero key is present. The existing user (`prealloc_serialized`) never produces empty keys, so this was latent; an all-zeros fixed key is common (the ClickBench `hits` table has a `SearchEngineID = 0, ClientIP = 0` group). Correctness was verified against an unpatched build of the same commit on the full ClickBench `hits` dataset (identical single part, 99,997,497 rows): full-result checksums for `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256`, nullable keys and `prealloc_serialized`; the all-zero key group; the `no_more_keys` path (`max_rows_to_group_by` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`); and external aggregation (spill + merge). All results are identical. An honest note on measured impact, from the investigation written up in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638#issuecomment-5285053418: in a local interleaved A/B on a (noisy, shared) 96-core aarch64 box, this change measures neutral on ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q35 — the generic look-ahead prefetch already covered these methods, so the remaining saving is one packed-key load plus one CRC per row. The issue's local reproduction numbers for these queries turned out to be dominated by an unrelated effect (the memory-based `max_threads` cap from #100383, which the pre-#100383 baseline build does not have — details in the issue). The perf tests that exercise these exact shapes (`tests/performance/clickbench.xml` Q30/Q31/Q32, `group_by_fixed_keys.xml`, `hash_table_sizes_stats.xml`) should be the arbiter on dedicated hardware.

signal.title: Keep a table function argument marked unresolved when the node is analyzed twice
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83442 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108645 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a logical error `IDENTIFIER is not a table expression` when a remote-family table function with a `view(...)` argument is used on the left side of a `JOIN ... USING` whose key is a `SELECT` list alias, with `analyzer_compatibility_join_using_top_level_identifier = 1`. ### Description Related: #83442 A `TableFunctionNode` analyzed twice lost the record of which arguments are unresolved, so query tree passes walked into a subtree that is deliberately left unresolved. With `analyzer_compatibility_join_using_top_level_identifier = 1`, resolving a `USING` key that matches a `SELECT` list alias reuses the left table expression without cloning and resolves it a second time. On the first pass a `view(...)` argument is force-skipped, because its subquery may reference tables that only exist on the remote server, storing its index in `unresolved_arguments_indexes`. On the second pass the argument is already a `TableFunctionNode`, so it takes the passthrough at `QueryAnalyzer.cpp:4612` and its index is never re-recorded; `TableFunctionNode::resolve` then overwrites the index set with the shorter one. With the index gone, `traverseQueryTree` descends into the `view` argument and its unresolved subquery reaches `RemoveUnusedProjectionColumnsPass`, where `getJoinTreeNodeTyped` asserts on an `IdentifierNode` join tree. The fix carries the index forward there, only when the node already had it, so an argument can retain a skip but never gain one. `TableFunctionNode::resolve` is left alone: making membership monotonic there would re-create an overly broad skip that a later commit had to narrow. The producer defect predates #108645, which made it visible by removing the `extractTableExpressions` IDENTIFIER tolerance that discarded the leaked node. I ran the repro against the current `builds.clickhouse.com` branch binary for all five active release branches. 26.7, 26.6 and 26.5 carry that tolerance and return the correct result. **26.3 reproduces the same defect** (`Code: 49 ... Actual IDENTIFIER`, 5 of 5 runs, server reported 26.3.17.108), throwing from `extractTableExpressions` where master reaches `assertTableExpression`. The source hunk applies cleanly there, so a `v26.3-must-backport` label is the route. 25.8 predates the passthrough and fails earlier with a different logical error this fix does not address. Found by the AST fuzzer on master (STID 3981-42df), check `AST fuzzer (amd_tsan)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=bffd1f1bc64a0d8c11066ca1852b534b043a99a6&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1506` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Automatic LowCardinality serialization based on uniq statistics
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/85145 --> This PR adds automatic `LowCardinality` serialization for `MergeTree`, analogous to the existing automatic `Sparse` serialization. A `String` or `FixedString` column whose declared type is **not** `LowCardinality` can now be stored on disk in dictionary-encoded form when it has a `uniq` statistic with a low cardinality estimate. The encoding is transparent: the column keeps its declared data type, flows through the query pipeline as a (non-native) `ColumnLowCardinality`, and is materialized to a full column at the boundaries that require it. **Motivation:** save disk space and read I/O for low-cardinality string columns without requiring users to declare the column type as `LowCardinality(...)`. **How it works** - A new per-part serialization kind `LOW_CARDINALITY` (shown as `LowCardinality` in `system.parts_columns.serialization_kind`). - The decision is made at write time from the **existing** `uniq` statistic — there are **no changes to statistics serialization**. In `MergeTreeDataWriter`, a `String`/`FixedString` column whose `uniq` estimate does not exceed the new `MergeTree` setting `max_uniq_number_for_low_cardinality` (default `0` = disabled), and which was not already chosen for `Sparse`, is stored with `SerializationLowCardinality`. The column must therefore declare `STATISTICS(uniq)` and have `materialize_statistics_on_insert` enabled. - A new `is_native` flag on `ColumnLowCardinality` makes `getDataType` report the nested type, so the "column class matches data type" invariant holds while such a column flows through the pipeline. It is materialized to a full column in `removeSpecialRepresentations` (aggregation, joins, squashing, blocks), in the merge-input step of `IMergingAlgorithm`, in the sorting and sparse-removing transforms, and in `IFunction`. The `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` pass skips columns stored as non-native `LowCardinality`, since the dictionary encoding does not expose the data type's regular subcolumns. - The kind is independent of sparse serialization: `SerializationInfo` entries for eligible columns are created in the writer, in merges, in mutations and in the per-table serialization hints even when `ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization = 1` disables `Sparse` entirely. **Notes** - Opt-in: disabled by default and requires an explicit `uniq` statistic, so existing tables are unaffected. Requires `allow_experimental_statistics`. - Reading a subcolumn of an encoded column (for example `s.size`) is not supported and reports `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`: the subcolumn's streams do not exist in a dictionary-encoded part. Making it read the full column and extract the subcolumn in memory needs a dedicated serialization and is left for a separate change. - Extracts and reimplements the automatic `LowCardinality` part of the draft #85145 against current `master`, without the statistics-serialization refactoring. That refactoring is still unmerged (#85145 and #109128 are open drafts). Validated locally with a server built from this branch: kind selection for `Wide` and `Compact` parts, `String` and `FixedString`, query correctness, functions, `GROUP BY`/`ORDER BY`/`DISTINCT`/`LIMIT BY`/window functions, joins, `IN` subqueries, `INSERT SELECT`, `UNION ALL`, `OPTIMIZE FINAL` (LowCardinality preserved through merges), mutations, `ALTER RENAME`/`MODIFY COLUMN`, `DETACH`/`ATTACH`, `PREWHERE`, input/output formats with and without `allow_special_serialization_kinds_in_output_formats`, and tables with mixed `Default` and `LowCardinality` active parts. The three tests also pass with `ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization` forced to `0.0` and `1.0`, with `enable_block_offset_column`/`enable_block_number_column`, with compact parts, and over repeated fully randomized runs. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added automatic `LowCardinality` serialization: a `String`/`FixedString` column that has a `uniq` statistic and low cardinality can be stored in dictionary-encoded form on disk while keeping its declared data type. Controlled by the new `MergeTree` setting `max_uniq_number_for_low_cardinality` (disabled by default). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: Enable reading in reverse order with FINAL for ReplacingMergeTree
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58035 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/58361 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111609 When a query with `FINAL` sorts in reverse order of the sorting key, for example `ORDER BY key DESC LIMIT n`, the read-in-order optimization was disabled and the query read the whole table. It now applies for `ReplacingMergeTree`. `ReplacingSortedAlgorithm` learns a `read_in_reverse` mode. A row with a strictly higher version always replaces the selected one; among rows with equal (or absent) versions, the previously selected row is kept unless the current row comes from a newer data part. That mirrors the "last written row wins" rule of the direct reading order, because in the reverse reading order rows within one part arrive backwards while the parts still arrive from the oldest to the newest one. This is what makes the reverse read select the same row of a duplicate key group as a direct read, which is the correctness concern that stopped https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/58361. The other engines keep the previous behavior, since their merging algorithms depend on the direct order of rows: the sequence of sign rows in `CollapsingMergeTree`, the order of rows fed to order-dependent aggregate functions in `AggregatingMergeTree`, and so on. On a 110 million row `ReplacingMergeTree` table with two overlapping parts, `SELECT x FROM t FINAL ORDER BY x DESC LIMIT 1` (measured on a `RelWithDebInfo` build): | | before | after | |---|---|---| | Rows read | 110.1 million | 1.71 million | | Elapsed | 4.5 s | 0.22 s | | Peak memory | 41 MB | 23 MB | Trade-off: as with the already existing direct-order in-order reads with `FINAL`, an in-order plan disables vertical `FINAL` and the splitting of parts ranges into intersecting and non-intersecting ones. A query that reads the full result with `ORDER BY key DESC` and no small `LIMIT` may therefore become slower on a wide or mostly merged table. The new setting `optimize_read_in_reverse_order_final` (default enabled) turns the optimization off, and `compatibility` with an earlier version restores the previous plans. Out of scope, to keep this change reviewable: `Merge` tables over `ReplacingMergeTree`, and the interaction with `topKThroughJoin`, which keeps its own optimization for `... FINAL LEFT JOIN ... ORDER BY key DESC LIMIT n`. Both can follow separately. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Enable the read-in-order optimization for queries with the `FINAL` modifier that sort in reverse order of the sorting key on `ReplacingMergeTree` tables, so that queries such as `SELECT ... FROM t FINAL ORDER BY key DESC LIMIT n` read only the relevant tail of the data instead of the whole table. Can be disabled with the new setting `optimize_read_in_reverse_order_final`.

signal.title: Add `borrow_from_cache` object storage and `memory` metadata types
signal.text: Add a new object storage type `borrow_from_cache` that allocates space in a named filesystem cache using ephemeral `FileSegment`s. Each stored object is backed by a cache segment held alive via `FileSegmentsHolder`; when released, the cache reclaims the space. Add a new metadata type `memory` that keeps all file-to-blob mappings and directory structure entirely in memory with no persistence. On server restart all data is lost, which is acceptable for the intended use case of temporary tables. Configuration example: ``` disk(type=object_storage, object_storage_type='borrow_from_cache', metadata_type='memory', cache_name='some_cache') ``` ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A new object storage type and metadata type suitable for temporary tables. Add a new object storage type `borrow_from_cache` that allocates space in a named filesystem cache and holds it from eviction. Add a new metadata storage type `memory` that keeps the mapping in memory. For example, this could allow creating temporary tables with custom engines in the Cloud without using S3. Closes #75551.

signal.title: Add the `logsql` dialect: LogsQL, the query language of VictoriaLogs
signal.text: <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental `logsql` dialect: LogsQL, the log query language of VictoriaLogs, can now be used to query ClickHouse tables with logs. Enable it with `SET allow_experimental_logsql_dialect = 1, logsql_table = '<table>', dialect = 'logsql'` (plus `logsql_database`, `logsql_time_column`, and `logsql_message_column` as needed). LogsQL queries are translated at parse time into ordinary `SELECT` queries, so text filters expect `String`-backed log columns, while the `math` pipe applies raw arithmetic and needs numeric operand columns (`String` field values are not coerced to numbers). Documentation entry for user-facing changes. - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Implementation notes: - Nearly the whole language is supported: the filters (words, phrases, prefixes, `field:value`, `:=`, `~`, comparisons, `range`, `in` with subqueries, `contains_any`/`contains_all` with subqueries, `seq`, `len_range`, `string_range`, `ipv4_range`, `ipv6_range`, `pattern_match*`, `contains_common_case`/`equals_common_case`, `json_array_contains_any`, `i()`, full `_time:` filters with `day_range`/`week_range`, `_stream:{...}` selectors), and the pipes `fields`, `delete`, `copy`, `rename`, `limit`, `offset`, `sort`/`first`/`last` (including `rank` and `partition by`), `stats` (with `by`-buckets, per-function `if`, `switch`, `rate`), `where`, `uniq`, `top`, `math`, `extract`, `extract_regexp`, `format`, `unpack_json`, `unpack_logfmt`, `join`, `union`, `unroll`, `running_stats`, `total_stats`, `len`, `hash`, `coalesce`, `decolorize`, `split`, `unpack_words`, `time_add`, `sample`, `generate_sequence`, `field_values`, `json_array_len`, `json_array_concat`, `replace`, `replace_regexp`, `pack_json`, `pack_logfmt`. On typed (non-`String`) columns, filters that emit string functions fail with a type error instead of applying VictoriaLogs' schemaless per-value matching. The numeric stats functions (`sum`, `avg`, `median`, `quantile`, `stddev`, `rate_sum`) parse the numeric value out of every field value and skip the values that are not numbers, like VictoriaLogs, which computes its stats in `float64`; a numeric column is therefore aggregated with `Float64` precision and not exactly. - The dialect is modeled on the existing `kusto`/`prql`/`promql`/`polyglot` dialects: a parser under `src/Parsers/LogsQL/` builds a ClickHouse `ASTSelectQuery` directly, so all downstream machinery (analyzer, distributed queries, query log) works as usual. Relational pipes map to real SQL constructs: `join` to `LEFT`/`INNER JOIN ... USING`, `union` to `UNION ALL`, `running_stats`/`total_stats` and the `rank`/`partition by` clauses to window functions. - The lexer and the grammar mirror the reference implementation in VictoriaLogs (`lib/logstorage` of `VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaLogs`, Apache 2.0), including Go-style string literals, compound tokens (`foo-bar.com:123/x`), comments with `#`, and the exact filter/pipe syntax. The test queries are reused from the VictoriaLogs parser tests: 675 of its 878 valid parser-test queries run end-to-end against a ClickHouse table, and 605 of its 612 invalid queries are rejected. - The implicit table is configured by the `logsql_database`/`logsql_table` settings (like `promql_database`/`promql_table`). The special fields `_time` and `_msg` are mapped to columns via `logsql_time_column`/`logsql_message_column`, so real tables (e.g. `system.text_log` with `event_time`/`message`) can be queried after setting those. - Word and phrase filters translate to `hasToken`/`match` with token boundaries, so tables with `tokenbf_v1` indexes on the message column benefit from index analysis. - Documented deviations from VictoriaLogs: word boundaries follow ClickHouse tokenization (ASCII alphanumerics; VictoriaLogs also treats `_` and non-ASCII letters as word characters); numeric comparison filters parse `String` field values per row (rows with non-numeric values do not match) and compare typed numeric columns exactly, but the per-row parsing of field values understands plain numeric text only (decimal integers, floats, scientific notation, `inf`/`nan`) - LogsQL-only spellings such as `10KiB`, `1h`, `0x10`, or `1_000` are supported in query literals but are treated as non-numeric when stored in a field value, whereas VictoriaLogs parses them there too; equality with a non-numeric value compares with the native column type instead of VictoriaLogs' string semantics; `count(field)` counts non-NULL values instead of non-empty strings; `pattern_match*` placeholders are approximated with regular expressions (VictoriaLogs uses a greedy matcher with extra boundary rules); `seq()` matches substrings in order without word-boundary checks. - The only constructs that remain `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` (with clear errors naming the construct) are the ones with no ClickHouse meaning: VictoriaLogs storage introspection (`block_stats`, `blocks_count`, `query_stats`, `value_type`, `histogram` buckets, `set_stream_fields`, `stream_context`), features that require the dynamic set of fields of a schemaless store (`facets`, `field_names`, wildcard field selectors like `foo*:filter`, stats over all fields like `sum(*)`, `unpack_json` without a `fields` list), `unpack_syslog` (a stateful wall-clock-dependent parser), and `collapse_nums` (its number-boundary rules require lookaround which RE2 lacks).

signal.title: Replace ExpressionAnalyzer with Analyzer for standalone expression compilation
signal.text: Replace legacy `ExpressionAnalyzer` with the modern Analyzer framework for standalone expression compilation across storage metadata, MergeTree operations, and query planning. This also rejects invalid `CHECK` constraints containing forbidden subqueries or table names, including `x IN other_table`; direct `x IN (SELECT ...)` remains supported. Key and skip-index expressions reject wildcards and column matchers at DDL time. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Replace legacy `ExpressionAnalyzer` with the modern Analyzer framework for standalone expression compilation. `CHECK` constraints with forbidden subqueries or table names, and key expressions with wildcards or column matchers, now fail with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` at DDL time.

signal.title: Fix an infinite uncancellable loop in `hop` and `windowID` on an interval whose span wraps modulo 2^32
signal.text: <!-- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an infinite, uncancellable loop in functions `hop` and `windowID` when the span of an interval argument in seconds is a multiple of 2^32 (for example, `toIntervalDay(2147483648)`): the wrapped subtraction dodged the time-overflow check, and with constant arguments the loop ran at analysis time, where the query could not even be killed. The same interval could also spin a background thread of a `WINDOW VIEW` forever; such a window view is now rejected at creation. An interval like `toIntervalDay(2147483648)` spans `2^31 * 86400 = 43200 * 2^32` seconds, so subtracting it in the wrapping `UInt32` arithmetic of `AddTime` is a no-op: `wstart == wend`, which dodges the `wstart > wend` time-overflow guard added by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/61523. The window-searching loop of `executeHop` then decrements `wend` by one hop at a time past zero, where it wraps back to ~2^32 while staying congruent to its starting point modulo `gcd(86400, 2^32) = 128`, never hits a value `<= time`, and spins forever. With constant arguments the loop runs during constant folding in `QueryAnalyzer::resolveFunction`, at analysis time, where nothing checks the cancellation. The same loop shape exists in `executeHopSlice` (`windowID`). The fix makes the guard `wstart >= wend` - subtracting a whole positive interval must change the time, and equality only happens on a wrap - and adds a wrap check to the loop itself (the new `wend` coming out greater than the old one throws the same `Time overflow` error), which terminates every wrapping loop regardless of how the pre-loop values were corrupted. The new test `04891_time_window_functions_wrapped_interval_overflow` covers both functions with the fuzzed arguments (both hung before the fix) and checks that a sane `hop`/`windowID` is unaffected. The same "a positive interval must move the time" invariant is relied upon by the loops which advance the window bounds of a `WINDOW VIEW`: the two watermark loops of `updateMaxWatermark`, the window splitting of `getNewBlocks`, and the fire loop of `threadFuncFireProc`. A processing time window view such as `GROUP BY tumble(now(), toIntervalDay(2147483648))` spun in the fire loop forever - `slide_interval` is `0`, so `next_fire_signal` never advances - in a background thread, while holding `fire_signal_mutex`. All these loops now advance through `addTimeStrictly`, which requires the time to move and throws `Time overflow in the window view` otherwise. Since such a window is not representable at all, `innerQueryParser` also rejects the window, slide and slice intervals which cannot move the time, so the window view fails at creation. This is covered by the new test `04892_window_view_wrapped_interval_overflow`. Found by the AST fuzzer in the stress test of a CI run of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112930 (hung check): [Stress test (arm_debug) report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112930&sha=1c5bf0b613146bd6666b6d2bd2be55f539f6c0d8&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_debug%29). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114605 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/61521 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/61523

signal.title: Mongo queries (wire protocol + dialect)
signal.text: Adds two ways to run MongoDB queries against ClickHouse: - a **wire protocol endpoint** (`mongo_port`), so MongoDB drivers and tools such as `pymongo` and `mongosh` can connect to ClickHouse as if it were a MongoDB server; - a **query dialect** (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`), so MongoDB shell syntax can be sent over the usual ClickHouse interfaces. A Mongo database maps onto a ClickHouse database, a collection onto a table, a document onto a row, and a nested field onto an `a.b` column. A collection created by the first `insert` gets one column per field of the first inserted document. The supported commands are `insert`, `find`, `count`, `update`, `delete`, `create`, `drop`, `createIndexes`, `listDatabases`, `listCollections`, `isMaster` and `saslStart`; only the `PLAIN` authentication mechanism is supported, because it is the only one that provides the cleartext password ClickHouse needs. Both are experimental and cover a subset of MongoDB. They are meant for pointing an existing MongoDB application at ClickHouse without rewriting its queries, not as a MongoDB replacement. The limitations are listed in `docs/en/interfaces/mongo.md`. Task: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58394 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol endpoint (the `mongo_port` server setting) and a MongoDB query dialect (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`) for basic collection operations.

signal.title: Stop SeaweedFS deleting live object folders in stateless CI
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113828 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Since 2026-08-12, `s3 storage` stateless jobs intermittently fail an ordinary INSERT with `Code: 499 ... Immediately after upload: Object ... suddenly disappeared (S3_ERROR)`. The object really was destroyed: SeaweedFS's asynchronous empty-folder cleaner deletes a folder it has just observed to be empty, and the delete lists the folder's children and then bulk deletes them (`filer_delete_entry.go:83` to `:134`). A PUT committing inside that window has its row removed by the bulk delete, after S3 answered 200. From a failing master run's own artifacts: ``` 16:18:17.675651 EmptyFolderCleaner: deleting empty folder /buckets/test/test/jys 16:18:17.676290 PUT of the object SUCCEEDS, 282 bytes 16:18:17.678805 verifying HEAD -> 404 16:18:17.681060 WriteBufferFromS3: Nothing to abort (so ClickHouse did not remove it) ``` This started with #113828, which replaced MinIO with SeaweedFS. ClickHouse keys objects as `<prefix>/<3 chars>/<random>`, so the bucket holds thousands of shallow folders that empty and refill continuously, and that churn arms the race: in one job 34,819 of 45,578 cleaner log lines were deletions, peaking at 3,238 per minute. CIDB has 0 hits in the preceding 180 days, then hits on 2026-08-12 only. I set the filer's empty-folder cleanup delay past any job's lifetime, so no folder becomes eligible for deletion while the suite runs. The cleaner keeps running and keeps queueing; only its eligibility window moves, and the folders persist in an instance destroyed at job end. No `src/` change: `s3_check_objects_after_upload` caught a genuinely destroyed write. Retrying or relaxing it would have hidden a real lost object. Validated against the shipped script, arms differing only by these lines: without the change the cleaner deletes 13 folders and 0 of 12 survive; with it, 0 deletions and 12 of 12 survive while the queue still holds its 12 items past 3m03s, where the baseline drained at 2m03s. The race is upstream's, which already carves `.uploads` out of this same cleaner for the identical reason (`empty_folder_cleaner.go:247`); this only keeps CI out of its way. Reported upstream as https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/10779. Example: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=e9f46105394805fb1a160303c4f40b52ad053522&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20parallel%2C%202%2F3%29&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20parallel%2C%202%2F3%29
