signal.title: Positional Tuple hint over Parquet: tupleElement rewrite yields default values
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **`SELECT tupleElement(t, 1) FROM file('x.parquet', Parquet, 't Tuple(UInt64, String)')` returns zeros/empty strings instead of the file's values once the tuple-element rewrite is enabled for `StorageFile`. `WHERE tupleElement(t, 1) = 1` matches 0 rows instead of 1. With `input_format_parquet_allow_missing_columns = 0` the same query throws `THERE_IS_NO_COLUMN: Column t.1 was not found in parquet schema`.** - **Root cause:** For an unnamed `DataTypeTuple` the element name produced by `getSubcolumnForElement` is the ordinal (`"1"`, `"2"`), so `optimizeTupleOrVariantElement` builds the subcolumn name `t.1`. Its guards check the DECLARED structure only (`canOptimizeToSubcolumn` queries the storage snapshot built from the structure argument), which of course contains `t.1`. Nothing checks whether the format resolves that element by name or by position — and Parquet resolves the tuple type positionally (`SchemaConverter.cpp:723-731`) but the flattened subcolumn name by string. The PR's opt-in comment 'a tuple element is a real leaf in the file, so the format can serve `t.x` on its own' is false for a positional tuple hint. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `getTypedNodesForOptimization` (FunctionToSubcolumnsPass.cpp:858) now admits `StorageFile` via `storageAllowsTransformer` -> `supportsOptimizationToTupleElementSubcolumns` (StorageFile.h:132) -> `optimizeTupleOrVariantElement` (FunctionToSubcolumnsPass.cpp:428) replaces the function with a `ColumnNode` named `t.1` -> the Parquet reader resolves that flattened name by string lookup (`SchemaConverter.cpp:232`, `sample_block->findPositionByName(node.name, ...)`) against the file's real field names `t.x`/`t.y` -> no match -> synthetic missing column filled with defaults. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Analyzer/Passes/FunctionToSubcolumnsPass.cpp:428`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/5c9f28ed5a2c5/src/Analyzer/Passes/FunctionToSubcolumnsPass.cpp#L428) — builds `t.<element>` subcolumn name; new guards do not check `hasExplicitNames` - [`src/Storages/StorageFile.h:132`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/5c9f28ed5a2c5/src/Storages/StorageFile.h#L132) — `supportsOptimizationToTupleElementSubcolumns` returns true unconditionally - [`src/Storages/StorageURL.h:374`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/5c9f28ed5a2c5/src/Storages/StorageURL.h#L374) — same opt-in for `url()` - [`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorage.h:106`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/5c9f28ed5a2c5/src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorage.h#L106) — same opt-in for `s3()`/`azure()` - [`src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/SchemaConverter.cpp:232`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/5c9f28ed5a2c5/src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/SchemaConverter.cpp#L232) — flattened subcolumn name resolved by string lookup, never positionally **Impact:** Silent wrong results for any `file()`/`s3()`/`url()` Parquet read that declares a positional (unnamed) `Tuple` in the structure argument — a documented, supported way to read a struct written by an external writer (Spark, pandas, Arrow) without repeating its field names. Affects both the v3 and the legacy Parquet reader. With `input_format_parquet_allow_missing_columns = 0` the query is rejected instead. ORC is not affected. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `5c9f28ed5a2c5`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/43170dc7-eed8-4aac-9ac4-ab16ab01d90b) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- Test that a positional (unnamed) Tuple structure hint still returns the file's values. SET enable_analyzer = 1; SET optimize_functions_to_subcolumns = 1; INSERT INTO FUNCTION file(currentDatabase() || '_04907.parquet', Parquet, 't Tuple(x UInt64, y String)') SELECT tuple(number, toString(number)) FROM numbers(3) SETTINGS engine_file_truncate_on_insert = 1; SELECT tupleElement(t, 1), tupleElement(t, 2) FROM file(currentDatabase() || '_04907.parquet', Parquet, 't Tuple(UInt64, String)') ORDER BY 1; SELECT count() FROM file(currentDatabase() || '_04907.parquet', Parquet, 't Tuple(UInt64, String)') WHERE tupleElement(t, 1) = 1; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` 0 0 1 1 2 2 1 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0 0 0 0 ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> In `optimizeTupleOrVariantElement`, refuse the rewrite when `!data_type_concrete.hasExplicitNames()` and the storage only opted in through `supportsOptimizationToTupleElementSubcolumns` (the element name is an ordinal that no file schema carries). Alternatively make `SchemaConverter` resolve an ordinal-named subcolumn positionally when the parent tuple hint is unnamed, matching what it already does for the whole tuple. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - The same declared-vs-physical name mismatch may exist for other formats reached through `StorageFile`/`StorageObjectStorage` that resolve subcolumns by name; only Parquet, ORC, CSV and JSONEachRow were probed here (CSV and JSONEachRow behave identically with and without the rewrite). Found during automated review of [PR #113383](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113383). Severity P1 · Finding `h_pr113383_001` </details> cc @groeneai @alexey-milovidov (from #113383)

signal.title: DeltaLake: trivial `SELECT count()` over a table with deletion vectors counts the deleted rows (`numRecords` summed, DV cardinality ignored)
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** A Delta table where a `DELETE` was persisted as a deletion vector (the default for Spark/Databricks-written tables with `delta.enableDeletionVectors = true`) returns a wrong `SELECT count()`: the trivial-count path answers from file-level `numRecords` statistics and never subtracts the deletion vector's `cardinality`, so every DV-deleted row is still counted. Any query that actually scans the data (`sum`, `min`/`max`, a selective predicate) returns the correct result — the deletion-vector *scan* path works — which makes the wrong `count()` inconsistent with every other answer the same table gives. Version-pinned reads via `delta_lake_snapshot_version` have the same wrong count. `optimize_trivial_count_query = 0` is a workaround. `optimize_count_from_files = 0` does **not** help — the shortcut is the storage's `totalRows`, not the files-count path. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1448 (also checked master snapshots back to 26.8.1.820). **How to reproduce** Write a table with a deletion vector using Spark (`pip install pyspark==3.5.3 delta-spark==3.2.1`, needs a JRE): ```python from delta import configure_spark_with_delta_pip from pyspark.sql import SparkSession b = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[1]") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension") .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")) spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(b).getOrCreate() spark.sql("CREATE TABLE t (k BIGINT, v BIGINT) USING delta LOCATION '/tmp/dv_table' TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableDeletionVectors = true)") spark.sql("INSERT INTO t SELECT id, id*10 FROM range(300)") spark.sql("DELETE FROM t WHERE k < 50") # persisted as a deletion vector, cardinality 50 spark.sql("INSERT INTO t SELECT id, id*10 FROM range(300, 310)") ``` The table now holds 260 rows (Spark: `SELECT count(*)` → 260, `VERSION AS OF 2` → 250). Then: ```bash clickhouse local -q "SELECT count() FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table')" # 310 <- wrong, counts the 50 DV-deleted rows clickhouse local -q "SELECT count(), sum(k), min(k) FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table')" # 260 46670 50 <- scan path, correct clickhouse local -q "SELECT count() FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table') SETTINGS optimize_trivial_count_query = 0" # 260 <- workaround clickhouse local -q "SELECT count() FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table') SETTINGS delta_lake_snapshot_version = 2" # 300 <- wrong; Spark's VERSION AS OF 2 says 250 (a scanning query with the same pin correctly returns 250) ``` An `strace` of the wrong read shows neither the data files nor the `deletion_vector_*.bin` file is ever opened — only the `_delta_log` JSON files. **Expected behavior** `SELECT count()` returns 260 (and 250 at `delta_lake_snapshot_version = 2`), matching what the same queries return when they scan. **Actual behavior** 310 and 300: the count is answered from metadata as the plain sum of `numRecords` across add actions, ignoring each file's `deletionVector.cardinality`. **Mechanism** `DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel::totalRows` serves the trivial-count from `TableSnapshot::getTotalRows`. Both row-accumulation sites in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/DeltaLake/TableSnapshot.cpp` (the scan callback that fills `data_files`, and the `StatsVisitor` stats-only path) receive the file's `dv_info` handle from delta-kernel, yet unconditionally do `total_rows.value() += stats->num_records`. Fail-close would be setting `total_rows = std::nullopt` whenever `dv_info` is present (forcing the scan path); the precise fix is subtracting the deletion vector's cardinality. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/93852 --- Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: S3Queue: swallowed `after_processing='delete'` failure silently re-ingests files as duplicates
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse QA (durability testing) ### Describe what's wrong An `S3Queue`/`AzureQueue` table with `after_processing = 'delete'` can **silently re-ingest already-consumed files, producing duplicate rows in the destination**, when the post-processing delete fails and the failure is swallowed. After a batch is successfully inserted into the destination (through the materialized view), the engine applies the `after_processing` action, retries it `after_processing_retries` times (default 10), and then — on exhaustion — **swallows the exception with a bare `LOG_WARNING` and marks the file `Processed` in Keeper anyway**: ```cpp // src/Storages/ObjectStorageQueue/ObjectStorageQueuePostProcessor.cpp:66-87 (DELETE) if (after_processing_action == ObjectStorageQueueAction::DELETE) { LOG_TRACE(log, "Removing {} objects", objects.size()); try { doWithRetries([&]{ object_storage->removeObjectsIfExist(objects); }); } catch (...) { LOG_WARNING(log, "Failed to tag all {} objects with exception: {}", objects.size(), getExceptionMessage(std::current_exception(), false)); } ProfileEvents::increment(ProfileEvents::ObjectStorageQueueRemovedObjects, objects.size()); } ``` There is no durable record of the un-done delete anywhere — not in Keeper, not in `system.s3queue_log`, not in a retry queue — so it is never re-attempted. The object **stays in the bucket while its file is marked `Processed`**, i.e. `after_processing = 'delete'` has silently degraded to `after_processing = 'keep'`. That degradation is invisible until the tracked-files set is bounded. In **`mode = 'unordered'`** (the engine default), the processed node is later cleaned by `tracked_files_limit` (default 1000) or `tracked_file_ttl_sec`, both documented as "the file will be processed again" / "re-imported". After ageout, the surviving object is re-listed as new and **re-ingested — duplicate rows in the destination table**, with no crash and no operator-visible signal. An operator chooses `after_processing = 'delete'` precisely so that ageout can never re-encounter a file. The swallow defeats exactly that guarantee. The trigger is not only a permanent misconfiguration: **any transient delete failure that exceeds `after_processing_retries` (default 10)** — S3 throttling, a temporary IAM/credential problem, a network partition to the object store — reaches the same swallow and produces the same silent duplicates. There is also a minor observability defect in OSS (fixed in the internal tree): `ProfileEvents::ObjectStorageQueueRemovedObjects` is incremented **outside** the `try` (line 87), so the "removed objects" counter reports success even when every delete failed; and the DELETE branch's warning text reads "Failed to **tag** all …" (copy-paste from the TAG branch). ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced on 26.8.1.1. The swallow is present on current `master` for both S3 and Azure (`ObjectStorageQueuePostProcessor.cpp`, DELETE / TAG / MOVE branches). ### How to reproduce A durability rig reproduces it 5/5 with two controls that isolate the mechanism. The realistic deterministic trigger is a **least-privilege consumer credential**: a MinIO user whose policy allows `s3:GetObject` + `s3:ListBucket` but denies `s3:DeleteObject` (the classic read-only-consumer setup). The queue lists and reads fine, ingests and acks through the MV, and the delete fails `AccessDenied` — exactly the "delete fails 10× then is swallowed" path. 1. MinIO with a bucket of N small CSV files (N distinct ids), and a consumer user with the policy above. 2. Create the destination `MergeTree`, an `S3Queue` table pointed at the bucket with the consumer credential, `mode = 'unordered'`, `after_processing = 'delete'`, and a small `tracked_files_limit` (e.g. 3) so the ageout is observable in test time, and a materialized view from the queue to the destination. 3. Observe: the destination reaches N distinct rows (all files consumed and acked), all N objects remain in the bucket (deletes denied), and after the processed nodes age out the destination count grows beyond N with `count() > uniqExact(id)` — duplicates of already-acked rows. Controls that pin the mechanism: - **`after_processing = 'keep'`, same `tracked_files_limit`:** the documented re-import is observed (count grows past N) — proves the ageout lever fires. - **`after_processing = 'delete'` with full credentials:** the bucket drains and the count HOLDS at N through the same window — proves delete-mode is normally harmless even at a tiny `tracked_files_limit`, so the duplicates in the failing arm are the swallowed delete's doing. ### Expected behavior A swallowed `after_processing` action should not be reported as full success. At minimum, when the post-processing action fails after all retries, the file should **not** be marked `Processed` as if the action had completed (so it is not silently re-ingested later), or the failure should be surfaced durably (a `Failed` state / a retryable record) rather than a single log line. `after_processing = 'delete'` should not silently degrade to `'keep'` and thereby to at-least-once with duplicate rows in the destination. Note the honest caveat: post-processing is documented as best-effort, and re-processing after `tracked_files_limit`/`tracked_file_ttl_sec` ageout is documented. What this report is about is the **combination**: a swallowed delete failure marks the file `Processed`, and the documented ageout then turns that into silent **duplicate acked rows** in the destination, which the operator cannot detect (`system.s3queue_log` shows the file as `Processed`, and the `ObjectStorageQueueRemovedObjects` counter reports it as removed). ### Error message and/or stacktrace No error is surfaced — that is the defect. The only trace is a rate-limited server log line: ``` <Warning> ObjectStorageQueuePostProcessor: Failed to tag all N objects with exception: ... Access Denied. ``` ### Additional context Related but distinct: #112341 (S3Queue marks files `Processed` while **discarding** their rows when the MV is detached mid-batch — opposite polarity, rows lost not duplicated), #111537 (loss on power loss — at-most-once, not duplicate-on-swallow), #112041 (`DatabaseReplicated` recovery destroys the processed-files registry and re-ingests the whole bucket — a different mechanism). Found by an internal durability-testing harness (crash/fault campaign over ClickHouse commit protocols); the finding was surfaced by an audit lens for "a deferred/background apply step that converts an error into silent success".
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: BACKUP to S3: a crash after the .lock PUT permanently wedges the destination (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS 'is being written already'), no in-server recovery
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong If a `BACKUP ... TO S3(...)` is interrupted (server crash / power loss / OOM kill) after it has created its `.lock` object but before it finalizes, the destination is left **permanently unusable**: every subsequent `BACKUP` to the same destination fails with `Code: 598. DB::Exception: Backup S3('...') is being written already. (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS)`, and nothing in the server ever reclaims the leftover `.lock`. The only recovery is to manually delete the `.lock` object from the bucket. `BackupImpl::createLockFile` (`src/Backups/BackupImpl.cpp`) does an unconditional PUT of `<dest>/.lock` near the start of the backup, before the bulk of the entries and long before `.backup` is finalized. The only places that remove `.lock` are in-process: `removeLockFile` in the normal finalize, and `tryRemoveAllFiles` on an in-process failure. A crash runs neither, and there is no TTL, age, or liveness check on the lock anywhere in `src/Backups/` — so a `.lock` orphaned by a crash survives forever. `BackupImpl::checkBackupDoesntExist` then rejects the next backup to that destination on the mere *existence* of the lock: ```cpp if (writer->fileExists(file_name_to_check_existence)) // ".backup" — absent after a crash, so this passes throw Exception(ErrorCodes::BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS, "Backup {} already exists", ...); if (!params.is_internal_backup) { if (writer->fileExists(lock_file_name)) // ".lock" — the stale one from the crash throw Exception(ErrorCodes::BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS, "Backup {} is being written already", ...); } ``` Because `.backup` was never written, the first guard passes and the second throws on the stale `.lock`. The destination name is bricked until an operator cleans it up out of band. This is distinct from #112407: that issue is about two *concurrent live* backups racing the check-then-create claim. This one is a *single* backup that crashes and never recovers its own destination — a crash-recovery gap, not a concurrency one. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced on `26.8.1.1`; the code path above is present on current `master`. ### How to reproduce `26.8.1.1`, single node, BACKUP to S3/MinIO. Kill the server after the `.lock` PUT reaches the object store and before `.backup` is finalized (e.g. an S3 proxy that forwards the `.lock` PUT and then holds while the server is `SIGKILL`ed): ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, v String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(2000); BACKUP TABLE t TO S3('http://.../bucket/dest/', 'key', 'secret'); -- SIGKILL the server while this is in flight, after <dest>/.lock has been PUT -- (before <dest>/.backup exists). -- restart the server, then retry the same destination: BACKUP TABLE t TO S3('http://.../bucket/dest/', 'key', 'secret'); -- Code: 598. DB::Exception: Backup S3('.../bucket/dest/') is being written already. (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS) -- ... and so is every retry thereafter, until <dest>/.lock is deleted by hand. ``` The bucket after the crash holds `<dest>/.lock` (durable) and no `<dest>/.backup`. Deterministic rig (fault proxy forwards the `.lock` PUT, then `SIGKILL`s the server; a clean BACKUP+RESTORE control and a pre-`.lock` crash control that succeeds on retry, isolating the stale lock as the cause): `5/5` wedge, controls green. ### Expected behavior After a crash mid-backup, the destination remains usable: a subsequent `BACKUP` to the same destination either reclaims/overwrites the stale `.lock` left by the dead writer (there is no `.backup`, so no committed backup is at risk) or reports a clearly recoverable error rather than an indefinite `BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS`. A crashed backup should not permanently claim its destination with no in-server way to recover. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 598. DB::Exception: Backup S3('.../') is being written already. (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS) ``` ### Additional context `backups.allow_concurrent_backups` defaults to `true`, so no non-default setting is involved. Related but distinct: #112407 (concurrent live racers on the same `.lock` claim-check). The lock's UUID-content comparison in `checkLockFile` is a *later* guard used while writing; the initial `checkBackupDoesntExist` gate rejects on existence alone, so a stale lock from any prior (dead) UUID blocks every future backup to that destination.
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: BACKUP to S3: concurrent backups to the same destination can both be acked BACKUP_CREATED, one unrestorable (.lock claimed by check-then-create, no conditional write)
signal.text:
### Company or project name ClickHouse QA — durability testing (ClickFawkes crash/commit-protocol campaign) ### Describe what's wrong `BACKUP ... TO S3(...)` protects a destination against concurrent writers with an existence-check-then-create sequence on the `.lock` object, not with a conditional write. When one backup's `.lock` `PUT` is slower than a competing backup's entire runtime, **both backups are acked `BACKUP_CREATED`** against the same destination prefix. Only one `.backup` metadata object survives, so the loser's data objects are physically present but unreferenced, and restoring it fails with `BACKUP_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND`. The user-visible defect is the ack: a `BACKUP` that returns `BACKUP_CREATED` is unrestorable. An operator who backs up on a schedule and checks the query result has no signal that the backup does not exist. Verified empirically, 5/5, with a control (details below). Default configuration — `backups.allow_concurrent_backups` defaults to `true` (`BackupsWorker.cpp:337`).
Code walk (upstream/master @ 1e31a058a12) `BackupImpl::checkBackupDoesntExist` — the claim is a plain existence check: ```cpp /// Check that no other backup (excluding internal backups) is writing to the same destination. if (!params.is_internal_backup) { chassert(!lock_file_name.empty()); if (writer->fileExists(lock_file_name)) throw Exception(ErrorCodes::BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS, "Backup {} is being written already", backup_name_for_logging); } ``` `BackupImpl::createLockFile` — the create is an unconditional overwrite: ```cpp void BackupImpl::createLockFile() { /// Internal backup must not create the lock file (it should be created by the initiator). chassert(!params.is_internal_backup); chassert(uuid); auto out = writer->writeFile(lock_file_name); writeUUIDText(*uuid, *out); out->finalize(); } ``` Between the check and the create there is no atomicity. `checkLockFile` (called at `:257`, `:433`, `:1233`) re-reads the object and compares contents to the backup's own UUID, which closes the *fast* race — the last writer wins and the earlier writer notices at its next check. It does not close the case where the losing racer's `PUT` lands late: by then the other backup has already read back its own UUID, finished, and returned `BACKUP_CREATED`. A conditional write would close it outright, and the mechanism already exists in the codebase but is not wired to the backup writer: - `WriteBufferFromS3.cpp:643-644` sets `SetIfNoneMatch` from `write_settings.object_storage_write_if_none_match`. - `git grep -c -E "if_none_match|SetIfNoneMatch" -- src/Backups/` → **0**. - The only writer of `object_storage_write_if_none_match` anywhere is Iceberg (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/Utils.cpp`); `getWriteSettingsForBackup` (`BackupsWorker.cpp`) never sets it. So the `.lock` `PUT` on the BACKUP path is always unconditional, last-writer-wins.
### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Server 26.8.1.270 (also confirmed on 26.8.1.119), default config plus a `backups` allowed path; MinIO as the S3 endpoint. Two tables so the two backups are distinguishable: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; CREATE TABLE t2 (a UInt64, s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(10000000); INSERT INTO t2 SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(1000); ``` Run two backups to the **same** destination prefix, where the first one's `.lock` `PUT` is stalled longer than the second one's whole runtime. I did this with a byte-transparent TCP relay in front of MinIO that sleeps before forwarding the first `PUT .../.lock` (a raw byte relay, so the SigV4 `Host` header the client signed passes through and MinIO accepts the signature). Backup A goes through the relay, backup B straight at MinIO; both URIs resolve to the same bucket and prefix: ```sql -- A (through the relay on :29923, .lock PUT stalled 3 s) BACKUP TABLE t TO S3('http://127.0.0.1:29923/bkt1/dest', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); -- B (direct to MinIO on :29910, started ~150 ms later) BACKUP TABLE t2 TO S3('http://127.0.0.1:29910/bkt1/dest', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); ``` Both return `BACKUP_CREATED`. Then: ```sql RESTORE TABLE t FROM S3('http://127.0.0.1:29910/bkt1/dest', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); -- RESTORED, 10000000 rows RESTORE TABLE t2 FROM S3('http://127.0.0.1:29910/bkt1/dest', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); -- fails, see below ``` A stall is the mechanism I used to make the window deterministic; in a real deployment the same window opens whenever the `.lock` `PUT` is slow relative to a competing backup — one S3 `SlowDown` retry on that `PUT`, or a small/fast backup racing a slow one. The requirement is only *stall > other backup's runtime + start skew*. **Results, 5/5 with a control.** Both backups acked `BACKUP_CREATED` in all 5 attempts (A `dt ≈ 3.15 s`, B `dt ≈ 0.25 s`), 144 objects under the shared prefix, exactly **one** `.backup` (A's). `RESTORE t` → `RESTORED`, `rows = 10000000`. `RESTORE t2` → `BACKUP_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND`. The negative control is the identical two-endpoint topology and the identical 150 ms stagger with the stall set to **0.0 s**: 5/5 `ONE_CREATED`, with B correctly rejected — `Code: 598 ... A concurrent backup writing to the same destination ... (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS)`. So the topology is not the confound; the stall is causal. Threshold sweep (stall duration → outcome): 0.05 / 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 s → one created; **0.5 / 1.0 / 3.0 s → both created**. ### Expected behavior At most one of two concurrent `BACKUP`s to the same destination is acked `BACKUP_CREATED`; the other fails with `BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS`. A `BACKUP` acked `BACKUP_CREATED` is restorable. ### Error message and/or stacktrace The second backup is acked, and its restore then fails: ``` Code: 605. DB::Exception: Table default.t2 not found in backup. (BACKUP_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND) (version 26.8.1.270 (official build)) ``` The control arm (no stall), where the behaviour is correct: ``` Code: 598. DB::Exception: A concurrent backup writing to the same destination S3(...) detected. (BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS) ``` ### Additional context **Suggested fix (not verified — this is a prediction):** claim `.lock` with a conditional write by setting `write_settings.object_storage_write_if_none_match = "*"` for the `createLockFile` write, so the create fails when the object already exists instead of overwriting it. The plumbing is already there (`WriteBufferFromS3.cpp:643-644`, and the Azure buffers have the equivalent), it is simply never set on the backup path. Backends that cannot express a conditional write would need to keep the current best-effort behaviour, which is the `cas_downgrade` shape. Even when the loser *is* correctly rejected, both racers pass the existence check and write data objects into the shared prefix before one is caught at finalize (`system.backups` showed the loser reaching `num_files: 281` before failing). Its `tryRemoveAllFiles` then correctly bails at the `checkLockFile(false)` guard, so it destroys nothing — but it leaves up to ~92 orphan objects in the winner's prefix. That is a leak, not data loss, and is secondary to the ack defect above. **Test coverage gap:** the only test referencing `BACKUP_ALREADY_EXISTS` is `tests/integration/test_backup_restore_on_cluster/test_disallow_concurrency.py`, which runs with `configs/disallow_concurrency.xml`. The **default-config** same-destination race is untested. **One-step falsification:** run the two backups above with the stall at 0.0 s. If the second is still acked `BACKUP_CREATED`, my control was invalid and the topology (not the stall) is the cause. It was rejected with `Code: 598` in 5/5 control attempts.

signal.title: A failed BACKUP finalize deletes a backup that already completed, making any incremental chained onto it unrestorable
signal.text:
### Company or project name ClickHouse (ClickFawkes crash-durability testing) ### Describe what's wrong `BackupImpl::finalizeWriting` publishes the backup and only *then* arms the guard that protects it, so an error in the four lines in between deletes a backup that is already complete and externally usable — and takes any incremental chained onto it down with it.
The window (src/Backups/BackupImpl.cpp:1300-1315) ```cpp writeBackupMetadata(); // :1307 `.backup` lands. The backup is complete // and is now a valid `base_backup` target. closeArchive(/*finalize=*/ true); // :1308 setCompressedSize(); // :1309 removeLockFile(); // :1310 a live object-store DELETE LOG_TRACE(log, "Finalized backup {}", backup_name_for_logging); ... writing_finalized = true; // :1314 the guard arms HERE ``` The guard is `setIsCorrupted`, which refuses to mark a finalized backup corrupt and says why in its own log line (`:1339-1343`): ```cpp if (writing_finalized) { LOG_WARNING(log, "An error happened after the backup was completed successfully, the backup must be correct!"); return false; } ``` That is exactly the right intent. It is just armed one step too late to cover the interval in which the backup is already published. `removeLockFile` (`:851-855`) is `checkLockFile(false)` followed by `writer->removeFile(lock_file_name)` — a single object-store DELETE. When it fails: 1. `BackupStarter::onException` (`src/Backups/BackupsWorker.cpp:524`) calls `setIsCorrupted()`, which **succeeds** because `writing_finalized` is still false; 2. `should_remove_files_in_backup` is true — `remove_backup_files_after_failure` defaults to **true** (`BackupsWorker.cpp:340`); 3. `tryRemoveAllFiles` (`BackupImpl.cpp:1363`) builds `files_to_remove` with `".backup"` **first** (`:1385`) plus every data file, and its one bail-out — `if (!checkLockFile(false)) return false;` (`:1395`) — does not fire, because the lock file is still present precisely because deleting it is what failed.
The client is told the `BACKUP` failed, which is why this is easy to miss: it looks like ordinary cleanup of a failed backup. It is not. The backup had already completed, and between `writeBackupMetadata` and the deletion any concurrent `BACKUP ... SETTINGS base_backup = ` succeeds and is acked `BACKUP_CREATED`. An incremental holds none of its base's bytes — only a locator, a UUID and per-file `(base_size, base_checksum)` pairs (`BackupImpl.cpp:485-486`, `:522-530`). Nothing validates the base until a `RESTORE` reaches a file with `base_size != 0` (`BackupImpl.cpp:1037`), by which point the restore has already created databases and tables. So the incremental reports success, is unrestorable from the moment the base is deleted, and only says so partway through a recovery. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce ClickHouse 26.8.1 (`clickhouse-master-now`), single node, MinIO, default settings other than the retry bound noted below. Put a proxy between ClickHouse and the object store that fails `DELETE ///.lock` persistently (a one-shot failure is not enough — the AWS SDK retries it into a success), then: ```sql CREATE TABLE bfs_src (id UInt64, v UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO bfs_src SELECT number, number * 7 FROM numbers(200); -- The `.lock` DELETE for this destination is failed by the proxy. BACKUP TABLE bfs_src TO S3('http://.../bug_bk/', 'minio', 'minioadmin') SETTINGS backup_restore_s3_retry_attempts = 2; -- -> reports failure; `.backup` was written, then deleted along with every data file ``` For the chain, start the base backup, wait until its `.backup` object exists, and only then take the incremental: ```sql BACKUP TABLE bfs_src TO S3('http://.../chain_inc/', 'minio', 'minioadmin') SETTINGS base_backup = S3('http://.../chain_base/', 'minio', 'minioadmin'), backup_restore_s3_retry_attempts = 2; -- -> Backup ... was created successfully RESTORE TABLE bfs_src AS bfs_chain_restored FROM S3('http://.../chain_inc/', 'minio', 'minioadmin'); -- -> Code: 599. DB::Exception: Backup ... not found ``` `backup_restore_s3_retry_attempts` is lowered only to bound the reproduction: it defaults to 1000, so a brief transient blip will be retried away and will not reach this window. The reachable case is an outage that outlasts the retries — expired credentials, a bucket-policy change, or a partition lasting minutes. The retry count changes how long the endpoint has to stay broken, not what happens once the retries are exhausted. Reproduced 3/3 with an automated rig (`tests/clickfawkes`, `--mode backup-finalize-selfdestruct`) that is positive-control gated: | arm | fault | `.backup` published | `.backup` survives | |---|---|---|---| | `control_clean` | none | yes | yes — base + incremental + restore of 200 rows all succeed | | `control_early` | a data-file `PUT` fails, i.e. before `.backup` is written | no | no — cleanup here is correct, and proves the injector really can destroy a backup | | `bug` | the `.lock` `DELETE` fails, i.e. after `.backup` is written | **yes** | **no** | | `chain_victim` | same, with an incremental taken inside the window | yes | no — the incremental is acked `BACKUP_CREATED`, then `RESTORE` fails with `Code: 599` | The `control_early` arm is what makes the `bug` arm meaningful: the same injector, one step earlier in the same sequence, produces the intended behaviour. ### Expected behavior Once `.backup` has been written the backup is complete, and a later error must not delete it — the same rule `setIsCorrupted` already enforces for errors after `writing_finalized`. A failure in `closeArchive`/`setCompressedSize`/`removeLockFile` should leave the backup in place (a leftover `.lock` object is a much smaller problem than a destroyed backup) and, ideally, still report the failure to the client. Setting `writing_finalized = true` immediately after `writeBackupMetadata()`, or having `tryRemoveAllFiles` refuse once `.backup` exists, would both close it. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 599. DB::Exception: Received from 127.0.0.1:19141. DB::Exception: Backup S3('http://127.0.0.1:19113/clickfawkes/chain_inc/', 'minio', '[HIDDEN]') not found ``` raised from the `RESTORE` of an incremental that had reported `BACKUP_CREATED`. ### Additional context Found by ClickFawkes' commit-protocol audit (the `backup_to_s3_finalize` protocol, `ambiguous_cleanup` lens). Distinct from #46211, which is a leaked coordination znode after a failed backup rather than destruction of a completed one.

signal.title: Fix: max_execution_timeout_leaf with parallel replicas
signal.text: `max_execution_time_leaf` and `timeout_overflow_mode_leaf` settings are now effective for queries with parallel replicas. Previously these settings were silently ignored for task-based parallel replicas when the local replica pipeline was used (the leaf timeout was substituted into `max_execution_time` only for remote replicas, while the local replica shares the initiator's `QueryStatus` and was therefore unbounded). This is fixed for both `SELECT` and `INSERT SELECT` (with `parallel_distributed_insert_select = 2`) by skipping the local pipeline when the leaf timeout is set, so all leaf reading happens on remote replicas where the leaf timeout is honored. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `max_execution_time_leaf` and `timeout_overflow_mode_leaf` being ignored for queries executed with parallel replicas (including `INSERT SELECT` with `parallel_distributed_insert_select = 2`). signal.title: Make column data write during INSERT respond to query cancellation
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108212 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108351 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108353 --> ## Problem A cancelled or `KILL`ed `INSERT` can keep writing a data part for a long time while serializing column data — for example a large block of wide / `Dynamic` / `Variant` columns. The query stays in `system.processes` with `is_cancelled = 1` and does not stop until the whole block is written. This is the dominant uninterruptible location behind the chronic `Stress test` "Hung check failed, possible deadlock found" (issue #107941): the server-side AST fuzzer feeds boundary-sized blocks and the hung query sits in `MergeTreeDataPartWriterWide::writeSingleGranule` → serialization. ## Root cause `MergeTreeDataPartWriterWide::writeColumn` and `MergeTreeDataPartWriterCompact::writeDataBlock` write a block granule by granule with no cancellation point. The INSERT pipeline only enforces query limits *between* blocks, so once execution is inside `MergeTreeDataWriter::writeTempPart` → writer → column serialization, neither cancellation nor `max_execution_time` is observed until the whole block's columns are written. ## Fix Add `MergeTreeDataPartWriterOnDisk::checkWriteCancellation` (shared base of both writers) and call it per granule in both column-write loops. Because this is the hottest, most universal writer path (every column of every INSERT and merge), it is kept cheap: - The query status is fetched once and cached. It is null outside a query (e.g. background merges), so the check is a no-op there. - `checkTimeLimit` is called only every 65536 rows, so the check frequency is decoupled from `index_granularity` and never degenerates to a per-row check at small granularity. `checkTimeLimit` honors both cancellation and `max_execution_time` (throw mode). A single pathologically large granule of a slow-serializing column is still not interruptible mid-granule, but the multi-minute hangs are many-granule, so per-granule is sufficient. Performance is unchanged within noise — `INSERT INTO t SELECT number FROM numbers(100000000)`, 3 runs: before 1.802 / 1.908 / 2.046 s, after 1.747 / 1.872 / 1.943 s. Regression test `04411_column_write_cancellation.sh`: a single large block of high-entropy strings with `CODEC(ZSTD(22))` (so column serialization is the active multi-second phase, on a forced `Wide` part with no skip index) is cancelled mid-write; the test requires `KILL QUERY ... SYNC` to return within a `timeout` bound *and* the background `INSERT` to fail with `QUERY_WAS_CANCELLED`. ## Relationship to the hung-check umbrella @groeneai — this is complementary to your #108212. Your fuzzer-executor cancel callback enables cancellation *between* tasks but (as your analysis notes) cannot interrupt a single in-flight `generate`/part-write; this PR makes the column-write part of that in-flight work interruptible at granule granularity, which also helps real (non-fuzzer) large `INSERT`s respond to `KILL` / timeout. Siblings: #108351 (skip-index build) and #108353 (the `primes` source, which was the actual hung query in #108212's own arm_tsan run). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a cancelled or `KILL`ed `INSERT` continuing to write a data part for a long time while serializing column data (for example a large block of wide or `Dynamic` columns). The write now stops promptly when the query is cancelled or its `max_execution_time` is exceeded.

signal.title: WIP Add parallel gz deflating buffer
signal.text: Add the `max_generic_compression_threads` setting that makes `gzip` output compression run in parallel while keeping the result a standard, fully-compatible `gzip` stream. When the setting is greater than 1, `gzip`-compressed output (for `INTO OUTFILE`, file/URL/object-storage sinks and the HTTP/gRPC output paths) is produced by `ParallelGzipDeflatingWriteBuffer`, which deflates independent blocks in parallel on the shared IO thread pool (the `pigz` scheme) and writes them as one ordinary `gzip` member. The output decompresses identically to the single-threaded buffer and can be read by any `gzip` decompressor; only the writing side is parallelized. The setting defaults to 1 (single-threaded), so the behavior is unchanged unless it is explicitly enabled. The work originates from the coursework in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/29601. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Add the `max_generic_compression_threads` setting to optionally compress `gzip` output streams in parallel while keeping standard `gzip` output. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Fix TopK filtering dropping NULL and NaN rows from the answer
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113406 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107074 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` silently omitting rows that belong in the answer when TopK filtering is active. A `Float32`/`Float64`/`BFloat16` column holding `NaN` was affected at default settings; nested-`NULL` types such as `Array(Nullable(T))` and `Map(K, Nullable(V))` were affected under `ASC NULLS FIRST` and `DESC NULLS LAST` with `use_top_k_dynamic_filtering_for_variable_length_types` enabled. A sort column containing `JSON`, `Variant` or `Dynamic` at any depth was affected in either direction, and additionally raised a `LOGICAL_ERROR` for `Tuple(Dynamic)` and `Tuple(Variant(...))`. ### Description TopK filtering must order values the way the sorter does. Three mechanisms broke that. `__topKFilter`'s fast path compares through `lessOrEquals`/`greaterOrEquals`. For a composite type those resolve to `GenericComparisonImpl`, which hardcodes the nan/nulls-direction hint to "NULLs and NaNs are greatest", contradicting `ORDER BY` whenever `nulls_direction` is -1. For a float, IEEE comparison leaves `NaN` unordered against everything including itself, so a `NaN` row fails both comparators in every direction. `use_skip_indexes_for_top_k` loses the same rows independently, via `MinMaxGranuleItem::operator<`. Third, a runtime-typed sort column. The threshold reaches `TopKThresholdTracker` as a bare `Field` (`IColumn::get`), which keeps a `Variant`/`Dynamic` payload without its discriminator, while `ColumnVariant::compareAt` ranks by discriminator first. Measured on one constant value per part: `Tuple(Dynamic)` returned `(0)` for `ORDER BY v DESC LIMIT 2` where the answer is `(1000)`, and `Tuple(Variant(UInt64, UInt8))` returned `(3)` for `ASC` where it is `(900)`. Both hold a single runtime type, so mixed alternatives are not required. Floats and nested `NULL`s are routed to the existing general path, which honours `nulls_direction`, and floats are added to the two skip-index gates. Runtime-typed columns instead install no filter, since no comparison here can recover the discriminator. Both predicates recurse over the type rather than listing wrappers, and test the sort column's own type, so sorting on a static subcolumn such as `v.f` of `JSON(f Float64)` keeps the filter. Cost: no pruning for float or runtime-typed sort columns. On a NaN-free `Float64`, 10M rows, `ORDER BY f ASC LIMIT 10` goes from 7 ms to 15 ms and reads 10M rows instead of 81,920; integers are unaffected. The two `TODO`s in the code note what would recover it. The test runs 42 carriers on and off and requires each pair to agree, 12 of them controls. Each guard term is mutation-checked: reverting it reddens only the arm it exists for.

signal.title: Allow overriding the HTTP method for SELECT through the url table function and URL engine
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/62352 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `http_method='POST'` — as a key-value argument of the `url` table function and the `URL` table engine, or through the `http_method`/`method` named collection keys — now applies to `SELECT` queries: reads use `POST` instead of the default `GET`, for servers that accept only `POST`. Schema inference follows the configured method. `PUT` keeps its write-only meaning: a `SELECT` through a configuration with `http_method='PUT'` still uses `GET`. ### Implementation notes - `IStorageURLBase::getReadMethod()` now returns `POST` when the configured `http_method` is `POST`. `PUT` still applies to writes only (pre-signed upload URLs, #44326), and `INSERT` behavior is unchanged: `POST` by default, `PUT` when configured. - The write path no longer mutates the shared `http_method` member when defaulting to `POST` — the storage instance is shared between queries, so persisting the write default would have flipped subsequent reads of the same table from `GET` to `POST` (and raced concurrent reads). - Schema inference (`getTableStructureAndFormatFromData` and the URL read-buffer iterator) uses the same effective read method instead of hardcoded `GET`, for both `url()`/`URL` and `urlCluster`. - The `http_method = '...'` (or `method = '...'`) key-value argument is parsed by `StorageURL::evalArgsAndCollectHeaders` alongside `headers(...)`, kept in the `CREATE` AST (so it survives `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and DETACH/ATTACH), validated to be `POST`/`PUT`, and rejected when the URL scheme dispatches to another backend (`file://`, `s3://`, ...), mirroring `headers(...)`. - In the analyzer, the argument's left-hand identifier is excluded from column resolution (`skipAnalysisForArguments`), like `headers(...)`. - Documentation for the `url` table function and the `URL` engine is updated. The new stateless test `04869_url_select_http_method` asserts the method actually used on the wire via `system.query_log.http_method`: default `GET`, `POST` override for both the data and the schema-inference requests, `PUT`-configured `SELECT` staying on `GET`, the `URL` engine path, rejection of unsupported methods, and persistence of the argument in the table DDL. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: optimize_aggregation_in_order over a mixed-direction sorting key (a, b DESC) collapses GROUP BY groups — silent wrong result
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** With a mixed-direction sorting key `ORDER BY (a, b DESC)` and `optimize_aggregation_in_order = 1`, a plain `GROUP BY a, b` silently returns one row per `a` instead of one row per distinct `(a, b)` — groups are collapsed and the query succeeds with a wrong result. The same query is correct with the optimization off, and correct on an all-ascending key `ORDER BY (a, b)`. `optimize_read_in_order` over the same table is correct, so this is specific to the aggregation-in-order path. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on masters 26.7.1.1169, 26.7.1.1188 and 26.8.1.102 (`eb577ff401a3`), single part and multi-part alike, with the analyzer on or off. **How to reproduce** ```sql CREATE TABLE md (a UInt32, b UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (a, b DESC); INSERT INTO md SELECT number % 4, number FROM numbers(20); INSERT INTO md SELECT number % 4, number + 7 FROM numbers(20); SELECT count() FROM (SELECT a, b FROM md GROUP BY a, b); -- 40 (correct: 40 distinct (a, b) pairs) SELECT count() FROM (SELECT a, b FROM md GROUP BY a, b) SETTINGS optimize_aggregation_in_order = 1; -- 4 after OPTIMIZE TABLE md FINAL (one row per `a`), 8 on the unmerged two-part layout ``` The surviving rows keep only one `b` per `a`: ```sql SELECT a, b FROM md GROUP BY a, b ORDER BY a, b SETTINGS optimize_aggregation_in_order = 1; -- 0 23 -- 1 24 -- 2 25 -- 3 26 ``` **Expected behavior** `optimize_aggregation_in_order` must either produce the same 40 groups or not apply to a stream whose sort direction does not match the aggregation key order. The `b DESC` key column makes the stream descending in `b` within each `a`, but the in-order aggregation appears to consume it as if it were ascending, so every `(a, b)` group after the first within an `a` run is merged away. Control: with `ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (a, b)` (no `DESC`) the same query returns 40 groups with the optimization on. Found by the optimizer-correctness tester (`opt_toggle`/`truthy`/`forced_plan`/`physical_design` oracles all diverged on the same query over the mixed-direction fixture; reduced by hand — `optimize_aggregation_in_order = 1` is the single culprit setting at otherwise-default settings).

signal.title: JSONEachRow schema inference fails for valid integer literals above UInt64
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour `JSONEachRow` schema inference fails when an input contains a syntactically valid JSON integer literal larger than `UInt64`. The same value can be parsed successfully when an explicit `Int128`, `UInt128`, `Decimal`, or `String` schema is provided. The failure occurs only when ClickHouse must infer the schema. `input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1` works when ClickHouse has a known `String` destination column: it preserves the unquoted JSON number as its original textual representation. However, it does not prevent the failure during schema inference, where no destination type exists yet. This setting also works as intended with `INSERT`, rather than `DESCRIBE`, since the destination table has a known schema. This prevents applications from discovering the schema of NDJSON containing arbitrary-precision integers before choosing an appropriate target type. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Tested with 26.6.1.1193 ### How to reproduce Schema inference fails: ```sql DESCRIBE TABLE format( 'JSONEachRow', '{"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"}' ); ``` Result: ```text Code: 636. DB::Exception: The table structure cannot be extracted from a JSONEachRow format file. Error: Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected ',' before: '251392,"name":"Matt"}'. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) ``` The setting intended to allow JSON numbers to be read as strings does not change the schema-inference result: ```sql DESCRIBE TABLE format( 'JSONEachRow', '{"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"}' ) SETTINGS input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1; ``` However, parsing succeeds when the structure is known: ```sql DESCRIBE TABLE format( 'JSONEachRow', 'num Int128, name String', '{"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"}' ); ``` It also succeeds for a known `String` target with `input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1` when used during an `INSERT`: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_json_numbers ( num String, name String ) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO test_json_numbers SETTINGS input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1 FORMAT JSONEachRow {"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"} SELECT * FROM test_json_numbers; ``` Result: ```text ┌─num──────────────────────┬─name─┐ │ 2942420318599003496251392 │ Matt │ └──────────────────────────┴──────┘ ``` ### Expected behavior Schema inference should not reject a valid JSON numeric literal solely because it exceeds `UInt64`. Because the same JSON token is accepted for a known `String` destination with `input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1`, schema inference should honor that setting too—for example, infer `String` for this field rather than fail. Alternatively, ClickHouse could infer a wider supported numeric type or document a deliberate inference limit and provide a setting to select a safe fallback type. Example: ``` DESCRIBE TABLE format( 'JSONEachRow', '{"num":2942420318599003496251392,"name":"Matt"}' ) SETTINGS input_format_json_read_numbers_as_strings = 1; ``` returns both columns as String ### Error message and/or stacktrace Code: 636. DB::Exception: The table structure cannot be extracted from a JSONEachRow format file. Error: Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected ',' before: '251392,"name":"Matt"}'. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context JSON permits arbitrary-length number literals. Quoting such values is a workaround, but is not always possible for third-party NDJSON sources.

signal.title: Do not analyze the shared row policy AST in place in `Merge`
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/68569 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68321 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467 Fixes a `ThreadSanitizer` data race found by the stress test: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=66467&sha=b48cf3b340cdcc0e2275b3c1a5a4ba34034deb4d&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29 The report is unrelated to that pull request (it is about the `Chimp` codec); the race is on `master`. There is no open issue for it. I could not find an existing fix - the closest one, https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68321, fixed the same class of bug for the sampling key AST and closed https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/68569, where the same `const_cast` in `ActionsVisitor` was already questioned. `RowPolicyFilter::expression` is the parsed policy condition owned by `RowPolicyCache`. It is parsed once, in `RowPolicyCache::PolicyInfo::setPolicy`, and then handed out as is: every query of every user reading the table gets the same AST nodes, and a policy defined on a whole database is shared by all of its tables. `FiltersMixer` combines the parsed conditions without copying them, so the pointer a query receives points straight into the cache. `ReadFromMerge::RowPolicyData` passed that AST to `TreeRewriter` and `ExpressionAnalyzer`, both of which rewrite the AST they are given in place - they normalize identifiers, substitute the results of scalar subqueries for the subqueries themselves, and record `ASTLiteral::unique_column_name`. So reading a `Merge` table mutated the shared cache. This has two consequences. **A scalar subquery inside a policy is evaluated once and then frozen.** This is deterministic and does not need any concurrency: ```sql CREATE TABLE src (x UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO src SELECT number FROM numbers(10); CREATE TABLE limits (v UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY v; INSERT INTO limits VALUES (3); CREATE ROW POLICY p ON src USING x <= (SELECT max(v) FROM limits) TO ALL; CREATE TABLE m (x UInt64) ENGINE = Merge(currentDatabase(), '^src$'); SELECT count() FROM m; -- 4, correct INSERT INTO limits VALUES (7); SELECT count() FROM m; -- 4, expected 8 SELECT count() FROM src; -- 4, expected 8 - the direct read is affected too ``` The one `SELECT` through `m` replaced the subquery with the literal `3` in the cached policy AST, so the policy keeps that value for the rest of the server's lifetime, for every user and for direct reads of the table as well. Because the frozen value can be either more or less permissive than the current one, a policy can end up showing rows it is supposed to hide. **Concurrent queries race on the shared AST.** `ThreadSanitizer` reported the write to `ASTLiteral::unique_column_name` from `ActionsMatcher::visit`, reached through `ReadFromMerge::RowPolicyData`, against a concurrent `ASTLiteral::clone` performed by `buildQueryTree` for another table protected by the same policy. The fix is to analyze a clone. `generateFilterActions` in `InterpreterSelectQuery` already clones the policy expression for the same reason, as does `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor::getSampling` for the sampling key, and `ASTLiteral::clone` resets `unique_column_name` precisely because it is per-analysis scratch state. `ReadFromMerge::RowPolicyData` was the last consumer of a row policy filter that rewrote the cached AST: the other ones either clone (the analyzer, through `buildQueryTree`), only visit it with a const visitor (`StorageMergeTreeTextIndex`), or only test `isAlwaysTrue`. After this change nothing writes to the shared AST - the only remaining mutable member of `IAST` is the atomic reference counter. The new test `04812_merge_row_policy_shared_ast` reproduces the frozen subquery: it prints `4 4 4 4` before the change and `4 4 8 8` after. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a row policy containing a scalar subquery being evaluated only once and then reused forever after the table had been read through a `Merge` table. The parsed policy condition is cached and shared by all queries, and reading it through `Merge` rewrote the cached expression in place, which also caused a data race between concurrent queries using the same policy. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Backported to: `26.7.4.22`, `26.6.3.43`, `26.5.7.39`, `26.3.18.20`, `25.8.30.17` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix undefined behavior in DateTime64 reservoir quantiles
signal.text: The reservoir-sampling implementation of `quantile` and `quantiles` interpolates values in `Float64`. `DateTime64` ticks close to the upper `Int64` boundary can round to 2^63 exactly, making the conversion back to the native representation undefined. signal.title: Hudi Merge-on-Read: uncompacted log files are silently ignored, returning stale rows
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse QA (data-lake durability testing) ### Describe what's wrong Reading an Apache Hudi **Merge-on-Read** (MoR) table that has uncompacted log files returns **stale rows silently** — no error, no warning. ClickHouse's Hudi reader parses only the base Parquet files per file group and never reads the Avro `.log.*` delta files that a MoR upsert writes, so any row updated after the last compaction is served at its **superseded** value. `HudiMetadata.cpp` states this directly: ```cpp /* There can be two types of data files * 1. base files (columnar file formats like Apache Parquet/Orc) * 2. log files * Currently we support reading only `base files`. ``` The problem is not the limitation itself but that it is **silent**: the row count is correct and the query succeeds, so a user cannot tell that the values are out of date. Every other Hudi reader (Spark, Presto/Trino, Hive) merges the log files and returns the current values, so ClickHouse and every reference engine disagree on the same table with no indication that ClickHouse is wrong. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — the code path (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/HudiMetadata.cpp`, `getDataFilesImpl`) is unchanged on current master. Verified on 26.8.1.1. ### How to reproduce 1. With Apache Spark + `hudi-spark3.5-bundle`, write a Merge-on-Read table to S3, then upsert a few existing keys **without compaction** (so the updates land in `.log` files, not a new base file): ```python opts = { "hoodie.table.name": "h_mor", "hoodie.datasource.write.table.type": "MERGE_ON_READ", "hoodie.datasource.write.recordkey.field": "id", "hoodie.datasource.write.precombine.field": "ts", "hoodie.datasource.write.operation": "upsert", "hoodie.compact.inline": "false", "hoodie.compact.inline.max.delta.commits": "999", } # base: id 0..29, v = id*7 spark.createDataFrame([(i, i*7, 1) for i in range(30)], ["id","v","ts"]) \ .write.format("hudi").options(**opts).mode("overwrite").save(path) # uncompacted update: ids 0..4 get a new value 999000..999004 spark.createDataFrame([(i, 999000+i, 2) for i in range(5)], ["id","v","ts"]) \ .write.format("hudi").options(**opts).mode("append").save(path) ``` 2. Spark (the reference reader) returns the **updated** values: ``` spark.read.format("hudi").load(path) # ids 0..4 -> v = 999000..999004 ``` 3. ClickHouse returns the **old base** values for the same keys, with the same row count and no error: ```sql SELECT id, v FROM hudi('http://<endpoint>/<bucket>/h_mor', '<key>', '<secret>') WHERE id < 5 ORDER BY id; -- 0 0 -- 1 7 -- 2 14 -- 3 21 -- 4 28 -- stale; the committed values 999000..999004 are ignored SELECT count() FROM hudi(...); -- 30 (correct count, wrong values) ``` Running Hudi compaction (so the updates are merged into a new base file) makes ClickHouse return the correct values — confirming the divergence is specifically the ignored log files, not a general read failure. ### Expected behavior Reading a Merge-on-Read table should return the current merged values (base + log files), matching every other Hudi reader. If merging log files is genuinely unsupported, ClickHouse should **fail loudly** (throw) when a queried MoR table has uncompacted log files, rather than silently returning stale rows. ### Error message and/or stacktrace None — the query succeeds and returns a correct row count with stale values. That silence is the core of the report. ### Additional context Copy-on-Write Hudi tables are unaffected (every update rewrites the base file). The issue is specific to Merge-on-Read tables with uncompacted deltas, which is the default write path for streaming/upsert Hudi ingestion.

signal.title: Preserve non-clonable sources for deferred set builds
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619#issuecomment-5230196558 The speculative ordered-set build used for index analysis consumed non-clonable source plans before it knew whether the set was complete. If a `ReadFromRemote` pipeline stopped on an unavailable shard before `Set::finishInsert`, the deferred build had no source left and `FunctionIn` received a not-ready set. Preserve non-clonable local sources by skipping the speculative index optimization and letting `DelayedCreatingSetsStep` perform the authoritative build. The regression test uses the deterministic five-part `test_unavailable_shard` reproducer from the linked issue comment and verifies that `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED` propagates normally. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix queries with an `IN` subquery over unavailable remote shards potentially raising the `Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument` logical exception instead of the underlying connection exception.

signal.title: Absent-column refusal disables a freshly materialized skip index with no ALTER MODIFY
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **On a wide part, `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN c ... DEFAULT ...` is metadata-only, so the part's `columns.txt` never lists `c`. A subsequent `ADD INDEX idx c` + `MATERIALIZE INDEX idx` writes correct granules into that part, but the new gate refuses the index at read time forever after. Pruning drops from 1/16 granules to 16/16 - the index is built, occupies disk, and never skips anything. Results stay correct.** - **Root cause:** `MergeTreeIndices.cpp:299` - the `return false` for a required column the part does not carry treats 'no part-side type to compare' as 'incompatible'. The granule was in fact built from the metadata type in force at `MATERIALIZE INDEX` time, so it is compatible whenever no `MODIFY COLUMN` happened in between; the code has no way to tell the two apart and fails closed on both. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor.cpp:2533` (and every other read path) -> `IMergeTreeIndex::getDeserializedFormat` (`MergeTreeIndices.cpp:365`) -> `IMergeTreeIndex::isPartTypeCompatible` (`MergeTreeIndices.cpp:292`) -> `part.tryGetColumn("c")` is nullopt because the wide part holds no `c`, `isSerializationDefinedSubcolumn` is false (`c` is a plain physical column), so the loop returns false and the format is reported as `{0, {}}` = not materialized. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndices.cpp:292`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/5c9f28ed5a2c5/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndices.cpp#L292) — `if (!part_column)` branch in `isPartTypeCompatible` refusing a column absent from the part - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndices.cpp:365`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/5c9f28ed5a2c5/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndices.cpp#L365) — `getDeserializedFormat` returns `{0, {}}` when `isPartTypeCompatible` is false **Impact:** Any skip index backfilled with `MATERIALIZE INDEX` over a column added by a metadata-only `ALTER ADD COLUMN` is silently inert on every wide part that predates the ADD COLUMN. Measured: `Granules: 1/16` before the PR vs `Granules: 16/16` after, i.e. the whole part is scanned instead of one granule (16x granule read amplification on this fixture; in general the index stops pruning entirely). The part recovers only when it is merged, which for parts above `max_bytes_to_merge_at_max_space_in_pool` may never happen. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `5c9f28ed5a2c5`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/d2f78ba3-4ea6-4ddc-8996-4faf9f33f308) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- Test: a skip index materialized over a column that a wide part does not physically hold must still prune. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_absent; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_present; SET use_skip_indexes = 1; SELECT '-- column absent from the part (ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT is metadata-only for wide parts)'; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_absent; CREATE TABLE t_absent (k UInt64, other String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 4, index_granularity_bytes = 0, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, min_rows_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO t_absent SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(64); ALTER TABLE t_absent ADD COLUMN c UInt64 DEFAULT k * 3 SETTINGS mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2; ALTER TABLE t_absent ADD INDEX idx c TYPE set(100) GRANULARITY 1 SETTINGS alter_sync = 2; ALTER TABLE t_absent MATERIALIZE INDEX idx SETTINGS mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2; SELECT count() = 0 FROM system.parts_columns WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND table = 't_absent' AND active AND column = 'c'; SELECT sum(secondary_indices_uncompressed_bytes) > 0 FROM system.parts WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND table = 't_absent' AND active; SELECT count() > 0 FROM (EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT count() FROM t_absent WHERE c = 150) WHERE explain ILIKE '%Granules: 1/16%'; SELECT count() FROM t_absent WHERE c = 150; SELECT '-- control: same index, column present in the part'; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_present; CREATE TABLE t_present (k UInt64, other String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 4, index_granularity_bytes = 0, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, min_rows_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO t_present SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(64); ALTER TABLE t_present ADD COLUMN c UInt64 DEFAULT k * 3 SETTINGS mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2; ALTER TABLE t_present MATERIALIZE COLUMN c SETTINGS mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2; ALTER TABLE t_present ADD INDEX idx c TYPE set(100) GRANULARITY 1 SETTINGS alter_sync = 2; ALTER TABLE t_present MATERIALIZE INDEX idx SETTINGS mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2; SELECT count() > 0 FROM (EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT count() FROM t_present WHERE c = 150) WHERE explain ILIKE '%Granules: 1/16%'; SELECT count() FROM t_present WHERE c = 150; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_absent; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_present; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` -- column absent from the part (ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT is metadata-only for wide parts) 1 1 1 1 -- control: same index, column present in the part 1 1 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` -- column absent from the part (ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT is metadata-only for wide parts) 1 1 0 1 -- control: same index, column present in the part 1 1 ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Do not treat 'required column absent from the part' as incompatible on its own. Options, in increasing cost: (a) restore the pre-PR verdict for this branch and rely on the type comparison only for columns the part actually records - the granule of an absent column was built from the metadata type at MATERIALIZE time, so it is only stale if a later `MODIFY COLUMN` touched that column, which the existing `canUseIndex` pending-mutation check already covers for the un-killed case; (b) record the index's build-time column types in the part (checksums or a small sidecar) so the question can be answered instead of guessed. Trade-off for (a): the killed-mutation sequence in the PR's case 11 would again prune with a stale granule, so it trades this pruning regression back for that narrower correctness hole. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - The same refusal applies to text indexes, where `MergeTask::addBuildTextIndexesStep` (`MergeTask.cpp:3076`) then rebuilds the index on every merge instead of carrying the existing segments forward - extra merge CPU on top of the lost pruning. Not measured. Found during automated review of [PR #112484](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112484). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr112484_001` </details> cc @groeneai @alexey-milovidov @shankar-iyer (from #112484)

signal.title: New 1 GiB JSON guard measures the whole column chars buffer, not one value
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **Valid JSON input is rejected with `Code: 131. DB::Exception: JSON string is too large, maximum size is 1073741824 bytes` even though no individual string comes close to 1 GiB. Whether the same file is accepted or rejected depends on `max_block_size`.** - **Root cause:** [`src/IO/ReadHelpers.cpp:1298`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/da67f74224255/src/IO/ReadHelpers.cpp#L1298) uses `s.size()` as a proxy for the current value's length. `s` is an append-target that callers pre-populate; the correct quantity is `s.size()` minus the size recorded at function entry. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `JSONEachRowRowInputFormat::readRow` -> `SerializationString::deserializeTextJSON` ([`src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationString.cpp:536`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/da67f74224255/src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationString.cpp#L536)) passes `ColumnString::Chars & data` — the destination column's whole chars buffer, which already holds every previous row of the current block — as the `Vector & s` argument of `readJSONStringInto`. The new check at [`src/IO/ReadHelpers.cpp:1298`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/da67f74224255/src/IO/ReadHelpers.cpp#L1298) tests `s.size()`, i.e. the accumulated column size, not the size of the value being read. **Affected locations:** - [`src/IO/ReadHelpers.cpp:1298`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/da67f74224255/src/IO/ReadHelpers.cpp#L1298) — readJSONStringInto: check on cumulative destination vector size - [`src/IO/ReadHelpers.cpp:1356`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/da67f74224255/src/IO/ReadHelpers.cpp#L1356) — readJSONObjectOrArrayPossiblyInvalid: identical cumulative check - [`src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationString.cpp:536`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/da67f74224255/src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationString.cpp#L536) — passes ColumnString::Chars (whole block) as the append target - [`src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationString.cpp:502`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/da67f74224255/src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationString.cpp#L502) — same for readJSONObjectPossiblyInvalid under input_format_json_read_objects_as_strings - [`src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationFixedString.cpp:292`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/da67f74224255/src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationFixedString.cpp#L292) — passes ColumnFixedString::Chars as the append target **Impact:** Any `JSONEachRow` ingest whose String/FixedString column accumulates more than 1 GiB within a single block now fails with `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` on perfectly valid data. `input_format_max_block_size_bytes` defaults to 0, so blocks are row-bounded only (`max_insert_block_size` ~ 1048449 rows for INSERT), i.e. ~1 KB average string length is enough. The limit is hardcoded and cannot be raised or disabled by any setting. The same check also fires inside the `ReturnType = bool` instantiations (`tryReadJSONStringInto`, `readJSONObjectPossiblyInvalid<..., bool>`), throwing where the try-contract requires returning `false`, so `Variant`/`Dynamic` fallbacks turn into query errors. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `da67f74224255`). ### How to reproduce _See root cause description and affected locations above._ ### Expected behavior ``` 3 1258291200 in both arms - no individual JSON string exceeds 1 GiB, so neither arm should be rejected, and the outcome must not depend on max_block_size. ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Arm A (default max_block_size): Code: 131. DB::Exception: JSON string is too large, maximum size is 1073741824 bytes: (while reading the value of key a): (at row 3) : (in file/uri (fd = 0)): While executing JSONEachRowRowInputFormat: While executing File. (TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE) Arm B (max_block_size=2, identical data): 3 1258291200 Object variant (input_format_json_read_objects_as_strings=1), d ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Record `const size_t initial_size = s.size();` at function entry and compare `s.size() - initial_size` against the limit in both `readJSONStringInto` and `readJSONObjectOrArrayPossiblyInvalid`. Also route the `ReturnType = bool` instantiations through the existing `error()` lambda instead of an unconditional `throw`, and consider making the cap configurable rather than hardcoded. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `NullOutput::size()` was added returning 0, so the skip path is exempt — intentional, but it means the same input is bounded or unbounded depending on whether the column is materialized. Found during automated review of [PR #107669](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107669). Severity P1 · Finding `h_pr107669_001` </details> cc @Avogar @Manerone (from #107669)
